But there is nothing alleged for this opinion from antiquity, except the one passage of Cicero concerning Aristotle: who seems to have meant no more than this, that there was no such poet as Orpheus, anterior to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> that the verses vulgarly called Orphical, were not written by Orpheus. However, if it should be granted that Aristotle had denied the existence of such a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, there seems to be no reason why his single testimony should preponderate against the universal consent of all antiquity: which agrees, that Orpheus was the son of Oeager, by birth a Thracian, the father or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> founder of the mythological and allegorical <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> amongst the Greeks, and of all their most sacred religious rites and mysteries; who is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> supposed to have lived before the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, that is, in the time of the Israelitish judges, or at least to have been senior both to Heliad and Homer; and to have died a violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, most affirming that he was torn in pieces by women. For which reason, in the vision of Herus Pamphylius, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, Orpheus's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> passing into another body, is said to have chosen that of a swan, a reputed musical animal, on account of the great hatred he had conceived for all women, from the death which they had inflicted on him. And the historic truth of Orpheus was not only acknowledged by Plato, but also by Iococrates, who lived before Aristotle, in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> in praise of Bufris; and confirmed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> historian Diodorus Siculus, who says, that Orpheus diligently applied himself to literature, and when he had learned ἀπὸ μυθολογίας, or the mythological <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of theology, he travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, where he soon became the greatest proficient among the Greeks in the mysteries of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, theology, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. Neither was his history of Orpheus contradicted by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, when so justly provoked by Celsus, who had preferred him to our Saviour; and, according to Suidas, Orpheus the Thracian was the first inventor of the religious mysteries of the Greeks, and that religion was thence called Θρησκεία, as it was a Thracian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>. On account of the great antiquity of Orpheus, there have been numberless fables intermingled with his history, yet there appears no reason that we should disbelieve the existence of such a man." The bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a> speaks no more doubtfully of the existence of Orpheus, than of Homer and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>, with whom he ranks him, not only as a poet, but also as a theologian, and founder of religion. The family of Orpheus is traced by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton for several generations: "Sefac passing over the Hellespont, conquers Thrace; kills <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and gives his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> and one of his singing-women to Oeagrus, the son of Tharops, and father of Orpheus; hence Orpheus is said to have had the muse Calliope for his mother." He is allowed by most ancient authors to have excelled in poetry and music, particularly the latter; and to have early cultivated the lyre, in preference to every other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>: so that all those who came after him were contented to be his imitators; whereas he adopted no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, says Plutarch; for before his time no other music was known, except a few <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>. Music was so closely connected in ancient times with the most sublime sciences, that Orpheus united it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> of not only with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, but with theology. He abstained from eating animal food; and held eggs in abhorrence as aliment, being persuaded that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a> subsisted before the chicken, and was the principle of all existence: both his knowledge and prejudices, it is probable, were acquired in Egypt, as well as those of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a> many ages after. With respect to his abstaining from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of oxen, Gellner supposes it may have proceeded from the veneration shewn to that animal so useful in tillage, in the Eleusinian mysteries, instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. He might have added that, as these mysteries were instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of those established in Egypt in honour of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a> and Isis, this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> from animal food was of the origin, and a particular compliment to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APIS">Apis</a>. But likeabé Fraguier, in an ingenious dissertation upon the Orphic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>, gives still more importance to the prohibition; for as Orpheus was the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> and humanizer of the wild and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> Thracians, who were cannibals, a total abolition of eating <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> flesh could only be established by obliging his countrymen to abstain from every thing that had life. With respect to theology, Diodorus Siculus tells us, that his father Oeagrus gave him his first instructions in religion, imparting to him the mysteries of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, as they were then practised in Thrace. He became afterwards a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of the Idaei Dachyli in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, and there acquired new <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> concerning religious ceremonies. But nothing contributed so much to his skill in theological matters, as his journey into Egypt; where being initiated into the mysteries of Isis and Osiris, or of Ceres and Bacchus, he acquired a knowledge concerning initiations, expiations, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNERAL_RITES">funeral rites</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of religious worship, far superior to any one of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and country. And being much much connected with the descendants of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a>, the founder of Thebes in Bœotia, he resolved, in order to honour their origin, to transport into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of Osiris, and apply it to the family of Cadmus. The credulous people easily received this tale, and were much flattered by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of the ceremonies in honour of Osiris. Thus Orpheus, who was held in great veneration at the Grecian Thebes, of which he was become a citizen, admirably adapted this fable, and render it respectable, not only by his beautiful verses, and manner of singing them, but by the reputation he had acquired of being profoundly skilled in all religious concerns. At his return into Greece, according to Pausanias, he was held in the highest veneration by the people, as they imagined he had discovered the secret of expiating crimes, purifying criminals, curing diseases, and appeasing the angry gods. He formed and promulgated an idea of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, from the funeral ceremonies of the Egyptians, which was received throughout all Greece. He instituted the mysteries and worship of Hecate among the Eginetæ, and that of Ceres at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-JUSTIN_MARTYR">Justin <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr</a> says, that he introduced among the Greeks near 360 gods; Hesiod and Homer pursued his labours, and followed the same clue, agreeing in the like doctrines, having all drank at the same Egyptian fountain. Profane authors look upon Orpheus as the inventor of that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> called evocation of the manes, or raising ghosts; and indeed the hymns which are attributed to him are mostly pieces of incantation, and real conjuration. Upon the death of his wife Eurydice, he retired to a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in Thespia, called Aornas, where an ancient oracle gave answers to such as evoked the dead. He there fancied he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> his dear Eurydice, and at his departure flattered himself that she followed him; but upon looking behind him, and not seeing her, he was so afflicted, that he soon died of grief. There were persons among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> who made public profession of conjuring up ghosts, and there were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> where the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of conjuration was to be performed. Pausanias speaks of that which was in Thespia, where Orpheus went to call up the ghost of his wife Eurydice. It is this very journey, and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> which put him upon it, that made it believed he went <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into hell. But it is not only the poets who speak of conjuring up spirits; examples of it are to be found both in sacred and profane history. Periander, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of Corinth, visited the Thespianians, to consult his wife about something left with her in trust; and we are told by the historians, that the Lacedæmonians having starved Pausanias their general to death, in the temple of Pallas, and not being able to appease his manes, which tormented them without intermission, sent for the magicians from Thessaly, who, when they had called up the ghosts of his enemies, so effectually put to flight the ghost of Pausanias, that it never more chose to shew its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>. The poets have embellished this story, and given to the lyre of Orpheus, not only the power of silencing Cerberus, and of suspending the torments of Tartarus, but also of charming even the infernal deities themselves, whom he rendered so far propitious to his intreates as to restore to him Eurydice, upon condition that he would not look at her till he had quitted their dominions; a blessing which he soon forfeited by a too eager and fatal curiosity. All dangers past, at length the lovely <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> In safety goes, with her melodious guide; Longing the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> again to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, And draw the vital breath of upper <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>: He flies, and she behind him follow'd she; For such was Proserpine's severe <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>. When strong desires, th' impatient youth invade, By little caution, and much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> betray'd: A fault which easy <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> might receive, Were lovers judges, or could hell forgive. For near the confines of celestial light, And longing for the glimmering of a sight, Th' unwary lover <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> a look behind, Forgetful of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, nor <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of his mind. Straight all his hopes exhale in empty <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>; And his long toils were forfeit for a look. Dryden's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>. Tzetzes explains the fable of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> his wife Eurydice from hell, by his great skill in medicine, with which he prolonged her life, or, in other words, snatched her from the grave. Æsculapius, and other physicians, have been said to have raised from the dead, those whom they had recovered from dangerous diseases. The bishop of Gloucester, in his learned, ample, and admirable account of the Eleusinian mysteries, says, "While these mysteries were confined to Egypt their native country, and while the Grecian lawgivers went thither to be initiated, as a kind of delegation to their office, the ceremony would be naturally described in terms highly allegorical. This way of speaking was used by Orpheus, Bacchus, and others; and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> even after the mysteries were introduced into Greece, as appears by the fables of Hercules, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> into hell; but the allegory was so circumstanced, as to discover the truth concealed under it. So Orpheus is said to get to hell by the power of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>: Thracia fretus citbard, fidibusque canoris, Virg. Æn. VI. ver. 119. That is, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of lawgiver; the harp being the known symbol of his laws, by which he humanized a rude and barbarous people.—Had an old poem, under the name of Orpheus, entitled, A descent into Hell, been now extant, it would perhaps have shewn us, that no more was meant than Orpheus's initiation." Many ancient writers, in speaking of his death, relate, that the Thracian women, enraged at being abandoned by their husbands, who were disciples of Orpheus, concealed themselves in the woods, in order to satiate their vengeance; and, notwithstanding they postponed the perpetration of their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> some time thro' fear, at length, by drinking, to a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of intoxication, they so far fortified their courage as to put him to death. And Plutarch assures us, that the Thracians stigmatized their women, even in his time, for the barbarity of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. Our venerable bard is defended by the author of the Divine Legation, from some insinuations to his disadvantage in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laertius. "It is true (says he) if uncertain report was to be believed, the mysteries were were corrupted very early; for Orpheus himself is said to have abused them. But this was an art the debauched mystae of later times employed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> their enormities; as the detestable pederasts of after-ages, scandalized the blameless <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>. Besides, the story is so ill laid, that it is detected by the surest records of antiquity: for in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of what they fabled of Orpheus in the mysteries, they pretended he was torn in pieces by the women; whereas it appeared from the inscription on his monument at Dium in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, that he was struck dead with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, the envied death of the reputed favourites of the gods." This monument at Dium, consisting of a marble urn on a pillar, was still to be seen in the time of Pausanias. It is said, however, that his sepulchre was removed from Libethra, upon mount Olympus, where Orpheus was born, and from whence it was transferred to Dium by the Macedonians, after the ruin of Libethra by a sudden inundation which a dreadful storm had occasioned. This event is very minutely related by Pausanias. Virgil bestows the first place in his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELYSIUM">Elysium</a> upon the legislators, and those who brought mankind from a state of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>: Magnanimi heroës, nati melioribus annis. At the head of these is Orpheus, the most renowned of the European law-givers, but better known under the character of poet: for the first laws being written in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, to allure men to learn them, and, when learnt, to retain them, the sable would have it, that by the force of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> Orpheus softened the savage inhabitants of Thrace: —Thricius longa cum uceste sacerdes Obloquitur numeris sibuum disfimina vocum: Jamque eadem digitis, jam petine pulleat eburne. Æn. lib. vi. ver. 645. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> strings given by the poet in this passage to the lyre of Orpheus, is a circumstance somewhat historical. The first Mercurean lyre had, at most, but four strings. Others were afterwards added to it by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, or Amphion: but according to several traditions preserved by Greek historians, it was Orpheus who completed the second tetrachord, which extended the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> to a heptachord, or seven sounds, implied by the septem disfimina vocum. For the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of many writers, that Orpheus added two new strings to the lyre, which before had seven, clashes with the claims of Pythagoras to the invention of the octachord, or addition of the sound proflambaro-vocum to the heptachord, of which almost all antiquity allows him to have been the inventor. And it is not easy to suppose, that the lyre should have been represented in ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> with four or five strings only, if it had had <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> so early as the time of Orpheus, who flourished long before sculpture was known in Greece. See the article Lyre. With respect to the writings of Orpheus, he is mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a> as author of the Argonautics, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> speaks of his Orphics. His hymns, says Pausanias, were very short, and but few in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>: the Lycomides, an Athenian family, knew them by heart, and had an exclusive privilege of singing them, and those of their old poets, Musæus, Onomacritus, Pamphus, and Olen, at the celebration of the Eleusinian mysteries; that is, the priesthood was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> in this family. Jamblicus tells us, that the poems under the name of Orpheus were written in the Doric dialect, but have since been transdialected, or modernized. It was the common opinion in antiquity that they were genuine; but even those who doubted of it, gave them to the earliest Pythagoreans, and some of them to Pythagoras himself, who has frequently been called the follower of Orpheus, and been supposed to have adopted many of his opinions. Of the poems that are still subsisting under the name of Orpheus, which were collected and published at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> 1702, by Andr. Christ. Eschenbach, and which have since been reprinted at Leipzig 1764, under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Ὀρφεῖος ἀπίστα, several have been attributed to Onomacritus, an Athenian, who flourished under the Pythiadæ, about 500 years before Christ. Their titles are, 1. The Argonautics, an epic poem. 2. Eighty-six hymns; which are so full of incantations and magical evocation, that Daniel Heinsius has called them veram Satanae liturgiam, "the true liturgy of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>." Pausanias, who made no doubt that the hymns subsisting in his time were composed by Orpheus, tells us, that tho' less elegant, they had been preferred for religious purposes to those of Homer. 3. De lapidibus, a poem on precious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. 4. Fragments, collected by Henry Stevens. Orpheus has been called the inventor, or at least the propagator, of many arts and doctrines among the Greeks. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of letters, or the art of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. 2. Music, the lyre, or cithara, of seven strings, adding three to that of Mercury. 3. Hexameter <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. 4. Mysteries and theology. 5. Medicine. 6. Magic and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>. 7. Astrology. Servius upon the fifth Æneid, p. 450, says Orpheus first instituted the harmony of the spheres. 8. He is said likewise to have been the first who imagined a plurality of worlds, or that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> were inhabited.

ORPIMENT

Pages 262-262

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a fossile substance usually found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, composed of thin flakes like the tales; these easily split, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, not <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>, soluble in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, fusible in a moderate fire, and yield in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> an offensive smell like garlic.

ORRERY

Pages 262-263

a curious machine for representing the motions <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> phases of the heavenly bodies. See ASTRO-NOMY, p. 317. It would be too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> an undertaking here to give an account of the mechanism of the larger sort of orreries, which represent the movements of all the heavenly bodies; nor indeed can it be done either by diagram or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, to render it intelligible to the most discerning reader: but, instead of that, we shall exhibit an idea of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> and structure of an useful, concise, and portable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANETARIUM">planetarium</a>, which any <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> may have made for a small expense, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> exhibit, very justly, the motions of all the primary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> about the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, by wheel-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>; and those that have secondaries, or moons, may have them placed about their primaries moveable by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, so that the whole shall be a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> representation of the solar system, or true state of the heavens, for any given <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the year. In order to this we must compare, and find out the proportion, which the periodical times, or revolutions of the primary planets, bear to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>: And they are such as are expressed in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a> below, where the first <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> is the time of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> in days and decimal parts; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, that of the planets; the third and fourth are numbers in the same proportion to each other: as, \[ \begin{align*} 36525 : 88 & \quad \text{for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>.} \\ 36525 : 2247 & \quad \text{for Venus.} \\ 36525 : 6869 & \quad \text{for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>.} \\ 36525 : 433245 & \quad \text{for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>.} \\ 36525 : 107593 & \quad \text{for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>.} \end{align*} \] <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we now suppose a spindle or arbour with six <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> fixed upon it in an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> position, having the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> in each, corresponding to the numbers in the third column, viz. the wheel AM of 83 teeth, BL of 52, CK of 50 (for the earth), DI of 40, EH of 7, and FG of 5; and another set of wheels moving freely about an arbor, having the number of teeth in the fourth column, viz. AN of 20, BO of 32, CP of 50 (for the earth), DQ of 75, ER of 83, and FS of 148; then, if those two arbors of fixed and moveable wheels are made of the size, and fixed at the distance from each other, as here represented in the scheme, the teeth of the former will take those of the latter, and turn them very freely when the machine is in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. These arbors, with their wheel, are to be placed in a box, of an adequate size, in a perpendicular position: the arbor of fixed wheels to move in pivots at the top and bottom of the box; and the arbor of moveable wheels to go thro' the top of the box, to a proper height, on the top of which is to be placed a round <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, gilt with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> to represent the sun. On each of the moveable wheels is to be fixed a socket, or tube, ascending above the top of the box, and having on the top a wire fixed, and bent at a proper distance into a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> upwards, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> on the top a small round ball, representing its proper planets. If then on the lower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the arbor of fixed wheels be placed a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PINION">pinion</a> of screw-teeth, a winch <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> a spindle with an endless screw, playing in the teeth of the arbor, will turn it with all its wheels; and these wheels will move the others about, with their planets, in their proper and respective periods of time, very exactly. For while the fixed wheel CK moves its equal CP once round, the wheel AM will move AN a little more than four times round, and so will nicely exhibit the motion of Mercury; and the wheel FG will turn the wheel FS about \(\frac{1}{29.5}\) round, and so will truly represent the motion of Saturn: and the same is to be observed of all the rest. **Orrery (<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">Earl</a>'s of).** See Boyle. **Orrice.** See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRIS">Iris</a>. **Orsato (Sertorio),** a celebrated antiquarian, historian, and poet, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, in 1617, and early discovered a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for literature and the sciences. He applied himself to searching out antiquities and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>; for which purpose he travelled through all the different parts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> was his amusement. When advanced in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he taught <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> in the university of Padua. He was also a member of the academy of the Ricovrati. Having presented to the doge and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Padua, which he had dedicated to them, he made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> speech, during which he struggled with a natural want, and died of suppression of urine, on the 3rd of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1678. He wrote a great number of books which are esteemed, some in Latin, and others in Italian. He ought not to be confounded with John Baptist Orsato, an able physician and antiquary, who was born at Padua, in 1673, and wrote, 1. *Dissertatio epistolaris de Lucernis antiquis.* 2. A dissertation De paterna antiquorum. 3. A small treatise De ferrinis veterum; and some other works. **ORSI (John <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>),** an ingenious philologer and poet, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a> in the year 1652; and studied polite literature, philosophy, the civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was a kind of academy, where many persons of literature regularly assembled. He wrote many ingenious sonnets, pastorals, and other works in Italian, and died in 1733. **Ortegal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">cape</a>,** the most northern promontory of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, where there is also a castle of the same name. W. Long. 8. 20. N. Lat. 44. 0. **Ortelius' (<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>),** a celebrated geographer, born at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, in 1527, was well skilled in the languages and the mathematics; and acquired such reputation by his skill in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, that he was named the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> of his time. Julius Lipfus, and most of the great men of the 16th century, were Ortelius's friends. He resided at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, in the reign of Edward VI. and came a second time into England, in 1577. His *Theatrum Orbis* was the completest work of the kind that had ever been published, and gained him a reputation equal to his immense labour in compiling it. He also wrote several other excellent geographical works; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are his *Thesaurus,* and his *Synoima Geographica.* The world is likewise obliged to him for the *Britannia,* which he persuaded Camden to undertake. He died at Antwerp, in 1598. **Orthodox,** in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-history, an appellation given to those who are found in all the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. **Orthographic projection of the Sphere,** that wherein the eye is supposed to be at an infinite distance; so called, because the perpendiculars from any point of the sphere will all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> intersection of the sphere with the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the projection. See Geography, no 13. 41. and Projection. **Orthography,** that part of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> which teaches the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and affections of letters, and the just method of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPELLING">spelling</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> words, with all the proper and necessary letters; making one of the four greatest divisions or branches of grammar. See Grammar. **Orthography,** in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, the art of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> or delineating the fore-right <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of any object, and of expressing the heights or elevations of each part. It is called Orthography, for its determining things by perpendicular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> falling on the geometrical plane. **Orthography,** in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, the elevation of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. **Orthography,** in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, is the fore-right side of any plane, i.e. the side or plane that lies <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to a straight line, that may be imagined to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through

ORTHOPNOEA

Pages 263-264

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of asthma, where there is such a difficulty of respiration, that the patient is obliged to sit or stand upright, in order to be able to breathe. See Medicine, n° 396.

ORTIVE

Pages 264-264

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, the same with equtern. The ortive <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> eastern amplitude, is an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of the horizon intercepted between where a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a> rises, and the east point of the horizon, or point where the horizon and equator intersect.

ORTNAU

Pages 264-264

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Germany, in the circle of Swabia, lying along the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and separating it from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALSACE">Alsace</a>. It is bounded on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the margravate of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BADEN">Baden</a>, and on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Würtemberg. It contains three imperial <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; namely, Ollenburg, Gegenbach, and Zell. It belongs partly to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, partly to the bishopric of Spire, and partly to the county of Hannau.

ORVIETO

Pages 264-264

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the patrimony of St <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, with a bishop's see and a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> there is a deep well, into which mules descend by one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of stairs to fetch up <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and ascend by another. It is seated on a craggy rock, near the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Pagli and Chiana. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 10. N. Lat. 42. 42.

ORYZA

Pages 264-264
rice; a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the hexandra class of plants. There is but one species, namely the sativa or common rice. This plant is greatly cultivated in most of the eastern countries, where it is the chief support of the inhabitants; and great quantities of it are brought into England and other European countries every year, where it is much esteemed for puddings, &c. it being too tender to be produced in these northern countries without the affluence of artificial heat; but from some seeds which were formerly sent to Carolina, there have been great quantities produced, and it is found to succeed as well there as in the eastern countries. This plant grows upon moist soils, where the ground can be flooded over with water after it is come up. So that whoever would cultivate it in this country should sow the seeds upon a hot-bed; and when the plants are come up, they should be removed into pots filled with light rich earth, and placed in pans of water, which should be plunged into a hot-bed; and, as the water wastes, it must from time to time be renewed again. In July these plants may be set abroad in a warm situation, still preserving the water in the pans, otherwise they will not thrive; and, toward the latter end of August, they will produce their grain, which will ripen tolerably well, provided the autumn proves favourable.—The leaves of rice are long, like the reed, and fleshy; the flowers blow on the top, like barley; but the seed which follows is disposed in clutters, each of which is inclosed in a yellow husk, ending in a spiral thread. The seed is oblong, or rather oval and white. Rice is the chief commodity and riches of Damietta in Egypt. Dr Hafslquist gives the following description of the manner in which they dress and separate it from the husks. "It is pounded by hollow iron pestles of a cylindrical form, lifted up by a wheel worked by oxen. A person sitting between the two pestles, pushes forward the rice when the pestles are rising; another sits, winnows, and lays it under the pestles. In this manner they continue working it until it is entirely free from chaff and husks. When clean, they add a 30th part of salt, and pound them together; by which the rice, formerly grey, becomes white. After this purification, it is passed through a fine sieve to part the salt from the rice; and then it is ready for sale." Damietta sells every year 60,800 sacks of rice, the greatest part of which goes to Turkey, some to Leghorn, Marseille, and Venice. Rice, according to Dr Cullen, is preferable to all other kinds of grain, both for largeness of produce, quantity of nourishment, and goodness. This, he says, is plain from macerating the different grains in water; for, as the rice swells to the largest size, so its parts are more intimately divided. Rice is said to affect the eyes; but this it purely prejudice. Thus it is alleged a particular people of Asia, who live on this grain, are blind-eyed: but if the soil be sandy, and not much covered with herbage, and as these people are much employed in the field, this affection of their eyes may be owing to the strong reflection of the rays of light from this sandy soil; and our author is the more inclined to this opinion, because no such effect is observed in Carolina, where rice is very commonly used. Dr Percival informs us, that as a wholesome nourishment, rice is much inferior to sago. He digested several alimentary mixtures prepared of mutton and water, beat up with bread, tea-biscuit, sago, rice flour, sugar powder, potato, old cheese, &c. in a heat equal to that of the human body. In 48 hours they had all acquired a vinous smell, and were in brisk fermentation, except the mixture with rice, which did not emit many air-bubbles, and was but little changed. The third day several of the mixtures were sweet, and continued to ferment; others had lost their intestine motion, and were sour; but the one which contained the rice was become putrid. From this experiment it appears that rice, as an aliment, is slow of fermentation, and a very weak corrector of putrefaction. It is therefore an improper diet for hospital patients; but more particularly for sailors, in long voyages, because it is incapable of preventing, and will not contribute much to check the progress of that fatal disease, the sea-sickness. Under certain circumstances, rice seems disposed of itself, without mixture, to become putrid. For by long keeping, it sometimes acquires an offensive flavor. Nor, according to our author, can it be considered as a very nutritive kind of food, on account of its difficult solubility in the stomach. Experience confirms the truth of this conclusion; for it is observed by the planters in the West-Indies, that the negroes grow thin, and are less able to work, whilst they subsist upon rice.

OSBORN

Pages 264-264

an eminent English writer in the 17th century. He was educated in a private manner; and at ripe years frequented the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> to William <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>. Upon the breaking out of the civil wars, he adhered to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> party, and had several public employments conferred upon him. In the latter <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he lived at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, in order to print several books, and to look after his son, for whom, by the favour of the parliament, he procured a fellowship in All Souls...

OSIRIS

Pages 264-265

the son of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Niobe, reigned over the Argives; but afterwards delivered his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Ægialeus, and took a voyage into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, of which he made himself <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and married Io <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Isis. He established good laws there, and they were both after their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> worshipped as gods.

OSNABURG

Pages 265-265

a bishopric of Germany, situated in the centre of the circle of Westphalia between the Weser and the Ems, having <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINDEN">Minden</a> on the east, Münster on the west, Diepholtz on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAVENSBURG">Ravensburg</a> on the south-west. It is about 45 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 25 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, producing some rye, several sorts of turf, coals, marble, and good pasturage. The inhabitants, who are a mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> and Roman-catholics, breed a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cattle, especially hogs, of which they make excellent <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACON">bacon</a> and hams; but a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> consists of heaths. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> concluded here in 1648, the bishopric was to be an alternative between the Roman-catholics and Lutherans; and the Lutheran bishop was to be a younger <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>-Lüneburg, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, on failure thereof, of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this settlement, his Britannic majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son is now bishop of Osnaburg. The bishop is able to raise 2500 men, his revenue being between 20,000 and 30,000 l. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of the country are a coarse kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth and yarn, which are said to bring into it annually above 1,000,000 of rix-dollars. There are also some woollen manufactures in Osnaburg and Bramsche. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>-estates of the bishopric are the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, the knights, and the four <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. The diets are held at Osnaburg, when called together by the bishop. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">Bar</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> seneschal or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of knights. The bishop is a prince of the empire; and, in the matricula, is rated at 6 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and 36 foot, or 216 florins monthly in lieu of them. To the chamber of the empire he contributes, each <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>, 81 rix-dollars, 14 kruiters and a half. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of this bishopric is Osnaburg, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OSNABRUCK">Osnabruck</a>. It was formerly an imperial <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANSE">Hanse</a>-towns; but is now subject to the bishop, though it still enjoys many privileges, and a revenue of about 8000 or 9000 rix-dollars. It has its name from a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river Hase, or Ose, which divides it into the Old and New Town, and stands 67 miles west of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, and 30 north-east of Münster, being surrounded with walls and ditches, but commanded by a mountain within cannon-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>. The magistracy of this city, which is reelected yearly on the second of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, is Lutheran; and the churches belong, some to the Lutherans, and some to the Papists. Both parties have the full and free <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, whether the bishop is Protestant or Papist. The bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> was built by bishop Ernest-Augustus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> George I. It is well fortified, and separated from the town by a bridge. In one of the apartments of it died king George I. in the arms of his brother, on the 11th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1722. This was the first town in Westphalia which received the Lutheran doctrine. Osnaburg <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the South <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> discovered by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> Wallis in 1767. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, round island, not above a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> in circuit; in some parts covered with trees, in others a naked rock. S. Lat. 22. 48. W. Long. 141. 34.

OSSAT

Pages 265-265

born in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Auch in 1536, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> parentage, was taken notice of by a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> in the diocese, who made him <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> with his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARD">ward</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> of Caillenau de Magnac. He studied the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> at Dijon under Cujace, and applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. He was secretary at Rome to M. de Foix, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a>; to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-ESTE">Este</a>; and afterwards to cardinal de Joyeuse, by the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s express command. After rising to the highest dignities both in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and state, in 1599 he was created a cardinal by pope Clement VIII. He died in 1604. An eminent French writer gives him the following character. "He was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of prodigious penetration; applied himself so closely to affairs, and especially so judiciously in forming his resolutions, that it is almost impossible to find out one false step in the many negotiations in which he was concerned." His works, and especially his letters, have been much esteemed in the learned world.

OSSIAN

Pages 265-269

the son of Fingal *, a celebrated Celtic poet, who flourished about the end of the third and beginning of the fourth century. Several incidents in his poems point out this as his era: particularly the engagement of Fingal with Caracul, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARACALLA">Caracalla</a>, the son of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Severus, styled by Ossian, The Son of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a> of the World; and another expedition under the conduct of Oscar, against the usurper Carausius, the Caros of Ossian, who assumed the purple in the year 287. This corresponds pretty nearly with the account given by the Irish histories, which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Fingal in the year 283, and the death of Oscar (who died many years before his father Ossian) in the year 296. At such a distance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it cannot be expected we should be able to give a particular account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Ossian. The first expedition on which his father sent him was, to raise a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> on the banks of Crona, to perpetuate the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of a victory which the king of Morven had obtained at that place. The Highlanders talk of this as being emblematical of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> which heroes were to receive from his future compositions. In this expedition he was accompanied by Toscar, father to the beautiful Malvina, the amiable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of his grief, after the death of her beloved Oscar, his son. It appears from his poems, that, in one of his early expeditions to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, he had fallen fallen in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with and married Evirallin, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to Branno, petty king of Lego. "I went in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of the maid of Lego's sable lurge; twelve of my people were there, the sons of dreary Morven. We came to Branno, friend of strangers; Branno of the sounding mail.—'From whence,' he said, 'are the arms of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>? Not easy to win is the maid that has denied the blue-eyed sons of Erin. But blest be thou, O son of Fingal! happy is the maid that waits thee.' Though twelve daughters were mine, thine were the choice, thou son of fame."—Then he opened the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of the maid; the dark-haired Evirallin. This Evirallin was the mother of his son Oscar, whose exploits he celebrates in many of his poems, and whose death he laments in the first book of Temora. Evirallin died some time before Olcar, (Fingal B. iv.), who seems to have been her only child; and Ossian did not marry afterwards; so that his posterity ended in the death of Olcar; who seems to have died as he was about to be married to Malvina, the daughter of Tofcar. Several of her lamentations for her lover are recorded by Ossian, which paint her grief in the strongest and most beautiful colours.—"It is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of my love! few are his visits to my <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>.—But thou dwellest in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of Malvina, son of mighty Ossian. My sighs arise with the beams of the east; my tears descend with the drops of night. I was a lovely tree in thy presence, Oscar, with all my branches round me: but thy death came like a blast from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, and laid my green head low; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> returned with its showers, but no green <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of mine arose." Poem of Cromla. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> residence of Ossian was in the vale of Cona, now Glencoe, in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ARGYLESHIRE">Argyleshire</a>. See Fingal, in APPENDIX. His poems relate many of his expeditions to Ireland, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCANDINAVIA">Scandinavia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, and Tweed or Teutha. His exploits on these occasions, after making a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> allowance for poetical exaggeration, shew him to have been no less a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> than a poet. See Ossian's Works, in the poems Calibon and Colmal, Lathmon, Berration, &c. By these expeditions, which were always undertaken for the relief of the distressed, the mind of Ossian seems to have been cultivated and enlarged beyond what is usually to be met with in so rude a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> as that in which he lived. His poems breathe throughout, such a spirit of generosity and tenderness, especially towards the fair <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, as is seldom or never to be met with in the compositions of other poets who lived in a more advanced state of civilization. He lived to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; having survived all his family and friends, many of whom perished by a fatal accident, recorded in one of his poems called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">Fall</a> of Tara*. Malvina, alone, the love of his son Oscar, remained with him till within a few years of his death, and paid him every <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> that could be expected from the tender relation in which she stood to him. To her he addresses many of his poems, which seem to have been composed for the most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> in his old age. Her death is pathetically lamented by him in the poem of Berdration: towards the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of which, he gives the preludes of his own departure; an event which he often wishes for, under the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLINDNESS">blindness</a> and other calamities of his declining years. "Roll on, ye dark-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> years, for ye bring no joy on your course. Let the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> open to Ossian, for his strength has failed. The sons of the song are gone to reit: my voice remains, like a blast, that roars lonely, on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-surrounded rock, after the winds are laid. The dark moss whistles there, and the distant mariner sees the waving trees†." But Ossian is a tree that is withered. Its branches are blasted and bare; no green leaf covers its boughs. From its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> no young shoot is seen to spring. The breeze whistles in its grey mists: the blast shakes its head of age.—The storm <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> soon overturn it, and flay all its dry branches with thee, O Dermid! and with all the rest of the mighty dead, in the green winding vale of Cona*." It is not certain at what age Ossian died; but from his poem of having been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> with years, and from the many contrasts, between his present and past situations, in poems composed, as it would appear, at a considerable distance of time from each other, it is most likely he lived to an extreme old age. The current <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> is, that he died in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of a Culdee, called the Son of Alpin, with whom he is said to have held several conferences about the doctrines of Christianity. One of these dialogues is still preserved, and bears the genuine marks of a very remote antiquity; (Dissertation prefixed to Ossian's Works.) Several of Ossian's poems are addressed to this son of Alpin, who was probably one of those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> whom the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> under Diocletian had driven beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> of the Roman empire. The poems of Ossian, tho' always held in the highest esteem by those who knew them, were allowed to remain in the obscurity of their original Galic, till Mr Macpherson, about 20 years ago, translated a collection of them into English, which immediately attracted the attention of every person who had a true <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. Dr Blair, in particular, introduced these poems into the world with those critical remarks, which do no less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to himself than to the poet. According to that eminent critic, the two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> characteristics of Ossian's poetry are tenderness and sublimity. Ossian is, perhaps, the only poet who never relaxes, or lets himself <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and amusing strain. He moves perpetually in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> region of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and pathetic. The events which he records are all serious and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>; the scenery wild and romantic. We find not in him an imagination that sports itself and drestles out gay trifles to please the fancy. His poetry, more perhaps than that of any other, deserves to be styled the poetry of the heart. It is a heart penetrated with noble sentiments, with sublime and tender passions; a heart that glows and kindles the fancy; a heart that is full, and pours itself forth. Of all the great poets, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> is the one whose manner and whose times come the nearest to Ossian's. Homer's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> were more enlarged, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> more diversified. Ossian's ideas fewer, but of the kind fittest for poetry; the bravery and generosity of heroes, the tenderness of lovers, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> of friends. Homer is diffuse; Ossian abrupt and concise. His images are a blaze of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, which flash and vanish. Homer has more of impetuosity and fire; Ossian of a solemn and awful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. In the pathetic, Homer has great power; but Ossian exerts that power much oftener, and has the character of tenderness more deeply imprinted. printed on his works. No poet knew better how to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> and melt the heart. With regard to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of sentiment, we must be surprised to find that the pre-eminence must clearly be given to the Celtic bard. This appears nowhere more remarkable than in the sentiments which he expresses towards his enemies. "U- "thai fell beneath my <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and the sons of Berra- "thon fled.—It was then I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him in his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, "and the tear hung in my eye. Thou art fallen, young "tree, I said, with all thy beauty round thee. Thou "art fallen on thy plains, and the field is bare. The "winds come from the desert, and there is no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> "in thy leaves! Lovely art thou in death, son of car- "borne Larthmore *!" His supposition, that all the little feuds and differences of this life should be forgot in a future state, and that those who had once been foes would "stretch their arms to the same shell in "Loda," gives us the highest idea of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> as well as of the poet. "Daughter of beauty, thou art low! "A strange shore receives thy corse. But the ghosts "of Morven will open their halls, when they see thee "coming. Heroes around the feast of dim shells, in "the midst of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, shall admire thee; and virgins "shall touch the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MIST">mist</a> f."—"The feuds of "other years by the mighty dead are forgotten. The "warriors now meet in peace, and ride together on "the tempest's wing. No clang of the shield, no noise "of the spear, is heard in their peaceful dwellings. "Side by side they sit, who once mixed in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> their "steel. There, Lochlin and Morven meet at the mu- "tual feast, and listen together to the song of their "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARDS">bards</a> f." But the sublimity of moral sentiments, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they wanted the softening of the tender, would be in hazard of giving a stiff <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> to poetry. It is not enough that we admire. Admiration is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> feeling in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of that deep <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> the heart takes in tender and pathetic scenes. With scenes of this kind Ossian abounds; and his high merit in these is incontrovertible. He may be blamed for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> tears too often from our eyes; but that he has the power of commanding them, no man who has the least <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> can question. His poems awake the tenderest sympathies, and inspire the most generous emotions. No reader can rise from him without being warmed with the sentiments of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, virtue, and honour. But the excellency of these poems occasioned in many persons a doubt of their authenticity. Their genuineness, however, has been very ably defended by Dr Blair and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kames, and warmly supported by the author of the Galic Antiquities, who has given the public some more remains of Ossian's poetry. As the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of our <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> will not allow us to treat this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> at full length, we shall only give a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> view of the arguments offered in support of the authenticity of these poems, referring our readers to the authors <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> now mentioned for fuller satisfaction. These compositions, say they, have all the internal marks of antiquity so strongly impressed upon them, that no reader of taste and judgment can deny their claim to it. They exhibit a lively <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of customs which have disappeared for ages, as could be drawn only from nature and real life. The features are so distinct, that few portraits of the life continually passing before us are found to be drawn with so much likeness. The manners uniformly relate to a very early stage of society; and no hint, no allusion to the arts, customs, or manners, of a more advanced period, appears throughout the poems. To that distinction of ranks, which is always found in adult <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, the poet appears to have been a perfect stranger. The first heroes prepare their own repasts, and indiscriminately condescend to the most menial services. Their quarrels arise from causes generally slight, but in such a period extremely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>. A rivalry in love, an omission at a feast, or an affront at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOURNAMENT">tournament</a>, are often the foundation of a quarrel among single heroes. And the wars in which whole tribes are engaged, are carried on with a view, not to enlarge their territory, but to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> perhaps the killing of a few deer on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, or the taking forcibly away one of their women. Their occupation was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> and hunting, and their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ambition was to have their fame in the songs of the bards. The notions of a future state, exhibited in these poems, are likewise strongly marked with the characters of antiquity. A creed so uncommon that the imagination of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> could not be supposed to grasp so strong an idea of it from <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> fancy, is uniformly supported throughout. This creed is extremely simple, but admirably suited to the times. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> too, and the structure, of these poems, bear the most striking characters of antiquity. The language is bold, animated, and metaphorical, such as it is found to be in all infant-states; where the words, as well as the ideas and objects, must be few; and where the language, like the imagination, is strong and undisciplined. No <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a>, and few general terms appear in the poems of Ossian. If objects are but introduced in a simile, they are always particularized. It is "the young pine of Inithuna;" it is "the bow of the flowery <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENA">Lena</a>." This character, so conspicuous in the poems of Ossian, is a striking feature in the language of all early states; whose objects and ideas are few and particular, and whose ordinary conversation is of course highly figurative and poetical. A picture, therefore, marked with such striking features, could not be drawn without an original. The whole texture of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is also, like the language, bold, nervous, and concise; yet always plain and artless; without any thing of that modern refinement, or elaborate <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a>, which attend the advancement of literature. No foreign ornaments are hunted after. The wild and grand nature which lay within the poet's view, is the only source from which he draws his ornaments. Beyond this circle, his imagination, though quick and rapid, seldom made any excursion. We perceive his language always to be that of a person who saw and felt what he describes; who bore a part in the expeditions which he celebrates, and who fought in the battles which he sings. In giving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> and more positive proofs of the authenticity of Ossian's poems, it is observed,—That there have been in the Highlands of Scotland, for some ages back, a vast many poems ascribed to Ossian: That these poems have been held in the highest veneration, repeated by almost all persons, and on all occasions. These are facts so well known, that nobody as yet has been hardy enough to deny them: There is not an old man in the Highlands, who will not declare, that he heard such poems repeated by his father and grandfather, as pieces of the most remote antiquity. There is not a district in the Highlands where there are not many places, waters, hills, caves, and mountains, which, from time immemorial, are called after the names of Ossian's heroes.—There is not a lover of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> tale or poetry, however illiterate, who is not well acquainted with almost every single name, character, and incident, mentioned in those translations of Ossian's poems, which he may have never heard of.—Bards, who are themselves several centuries old, quote those poems, imitate them, and refer to them.—The ordinary conversation and comparisons of the Highlanders frequently allude to the customs and characters mentioned in them;—and many of their most <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> proverbs, established by the most ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> borrowed from the poems of Ossian. * See examples under each of these heads in the Gallic Antiquities, p. 93, 94, 95. † Ibid. p. 194, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. ‡ Kames's Sketches, B. I. § Gallic Antiquities, p. 93, 118. || See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of names, Appendix to Dr Blair's Disertation, Ossian's Works, 2d edit. cultivated with most success in the earliest stages of society; that in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINUS">Linus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>, and Homer, wrote their admirable poems some ages before anything had been written in prose in the Greek language; that the book of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOB">Job</a>, written in a very early period of society, is highly poetical; that among the tribes of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, there have been found, in the earliest state, some excellent pieces of poetry. That the Caledonians in particular, had some peculiar institutions, which tended to improve their poetry: their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a> were among the most learned philosophers which perhaps any age or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> produced; their bards or poets were the disciples of those druids, and were always a standing order, to which none but the most promising geniuses were admitted. This standing <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of poets was furnished, not only with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of their own long <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and observation, but also with as much as merited to be preserved of the compositions of their predecessors in office, since the "light of the song" first dawned. They had the advantage of one another's conversation; which would excite their emulation, and make them aspire to eminence: They were always present, and generally engaged, in every grand operation that was transacted; which could not fail to inspire their muse with the truest poetic fire. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of Ossian was particularly favourable. He lived in an age when manners came to a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of refinement under the care of the Bards and Druids. Poetry in his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> was considerably advanced; and the language, though strong and figurative, had undergone some degree of cultivation, and learned to flow in regular numbers, adapted to the harp, the favourite <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of the times. As a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and a warrior, his mind must have been expanded and much enlarged by his excursions to other countries. At home he had Ullin, Alpin, Carril, and Ryno, to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with; all of them poets of eminence, who would have advantaged him greatly by their example and conversation. All these advantages, meeting with a native fire and enthusiasm of genius, as in the case of Ossian, may well be supposed to have produced poems that might challenge the veneration of ages. But it is not to their merit alone that we owe the preservation of these poems so long by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORAL">oral</a> tradition. Other circumstances concurred; of which, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of the Bards deserves particular notice. In a country, the only one perhaps in the world in which there was always, from the earliest period almost to the present age, a standing order of poets, we cannot reasonably be surprized, either at finding excellent poems composed, or, after being composed, carefully preserved from oblivion. A great part of the business of this order was to watch over the poems of Ossian. In every family of distinction there was always one principal bard, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of disciples, who vied with each other in having these poems in the greatest perfection. Should the institution of the bards last for ever, the poems of Ossian could never perish. Nor were they only the bards of great families who took an interest in these poems: the vassal, equally fond of the song with his superior, entertained himself in the same manner. This, with a life free from care, a spirit unbroken by labour, and a space of time unoccupied by any other employment or diversion, contributed to render the Highlanders a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of fingers. OSS From such a people, the superior merit of Ossian's poems would naturally procure every encouragement, which they always retained as long as the manners of the people remained unchanged. Many other reasons conspired to preserve the poems of Ossian.
