The martial and intrepid spirit which they breathed, made it the interest of the chieftains to preserve them: the strain of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, generosity, and humanity, which runs through them, recommended them to the superintendents of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, who well knew how much the morals of a people must be tinctured with those songs which they are continually repeating, and which have all the advantages of poetry and of music. In superstitious ages, the people revered these poems from their being addressed generally to some "son of the rock," supposed to be the tutelar saint of the place, or the great Irish <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> St Patrick. Besides, every hill and dale which the natives of the Highlands walked over, was classic ground. Every mountain, rock, and river, was immortalized in the song. This song would naturally be suggested by the sight of these objects, and every body would hum it as he walked along. All the proverbs and customs to which these poems gave rise, would operate in the same manner. The son would ask what they meant, and the father would repeat the song from which they were taken. The distinct and unshaken state in which the Highlanders remained for so long a course of ages, every clan, one <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> after another, inhabiting the same valley, till towards the present century, contributed much to preserve their traditions and their poems; and the constant and general <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of repeating these in the winter-nights, kept them always alive in their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a>. To these causes and customs the preservation of Ossian's poems, for so many ages, has been ascribed. But these causes and customs have ceased to exist; and the poems of Ossian, of course, have ceased to be repeated.—Within a century back, the Highlands of Scotland have undergone a greater revolution than it had done for ten before that period. With a quicker pace the feudal system vanished; <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> fluctuated; new laws and new customs swept in, and supplanted the old: and all this, with such sudden and such violent convulsions, as may well account for the shaking of a fabric which had stood so many ages, that it seemed to have bidden defiance to all the injuries of time. Even since Mr Macpherson gathered the poems in his collection, the amusements, employments, and taste of the Highlanders are much altered. A greater attention to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, and pasturage, has quite engrossed that partial attention which was paid, even then, to the song of the bard. In twenty years hence, if manners continue to change so fast as they do at present, the faintest traces will scarce be found of these tales and poems. "Ossian himself is the last of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a>; and he too shall soon be no more, for his grey branches are already strewn on all the winds." Among the causes which make these poems vanish so rapidly, poverty and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> rod should come in for a large share. From the baneful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a> of the muse, the light of the song must fast retire. No other reason needs be given why the present Highlanders neglect so much the songs of their fathers.—Once, the humble, but happy vassal, sat at his ease, at the foot of his grey rock or green tree. Few were his wants, and fewer still his cares; for he beheld his herds sporting around him, on his then unmeasured mountain. He hummed the careless song, and tuned his harp with joy; while his soul in silence blessed his children.—Now, we were going to draw the comparison: fed Cythinas aurem Vellit et admodum. It is more agreeable to remark, as another cause for the neglect of ancient poems and traditions, the growth of industry, which fills up all the blanks of time to more advantage, and especially the increase of more useful knowledge.—But above all, the extinction of the order of the bards hastened the catastrophe of Ossian's poems. By a happy concidence Macpherson overtook the very last that remained of this order, (Macvurch, bard to Clanronald), and got his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>. This fact (with the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> book furnished by Mr Macdonald of Croidart, and some other MSS.) accounts for Mr Macpherson's having found these poems in greater number and perfection than they could ever since be met with. The fragments, however, which have since been gathered, give a credibility to everything that has been said of the original grandeur of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. After giving this abstract of the arguments urged for the authenticity of Ossian's poems, and of the answers to objections started against them, we shall conclude with referring those who wish to see the subject discussed on a different footing, namely, by an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to facts, to two pamphlets recently published, Shaw's Inquiry, and Clark's Answer: From the former of which, the authenticity of Ossian's poems seemed to sustain a very formidable attack; till the latter appeared, exposed the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPOTENCE">impotence</a> of the attempt, and shewed the unhaken basis on which the object of it rested. So that now we seem authorised to conclude, without the imputation of partiality, that the controversy is at last come to an end; and that the genuineness of the poems will be as universally established in other nations, as the originals have been admired for ages in the Highlands.

the formation of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a>; but more particularly the conversion of parts naturally soft to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> and consistence of bones.

the west <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. OSSORY (<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALE">Bale</a> bishop of). See BALE.

OSSUNA

Pages 270-270

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; with an university, an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. N. Lat. 37. 8. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 18.

OSTADE

Pages 269-270

an eminent Dutch painter born at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LUBEC">Lubec</a> in 1610. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Francis Hals, in whose school Brouwer was <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with him, where they contracted an intimate friendship. The subjects of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> were always of a low kind, he having nearly the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENIERS">Teniers</a>; diverting himself with clowns and drunkards in stables, alehouses, and kitchens. His pictures are so transparent and highly finished, that they have the polish and lustre of enamel: they have frequently a force superior to Teniers; yet it were to be wished that he had not designed his figures so short. He is perhaps one of the Dutch masters who best understood the chiaro obscuro; and he was often employed to paint figures for the best landscape painters of his countrymen. He died in 1685. OST Offuna 1685. His works, especially those of his best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> and manner, are very scarce; so that when they are to be purchased, no price is thought too much for them. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> etched by himself, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and small, consist of 54 pieces.

OSTALRIC

Pages 270-270

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in Catalonia. It had a strong castle, but was taken by the French and demolished in 1695. It is seated on the river Tordera, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 45. N. Lat. 24. 44.

OSTEND

Pages 270-270

a very strong <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, with a good harbour, and a magnificent town-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. It is not very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, but is very well fortified. This <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was taken by the Dutch in 1706, but restored to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> in 1723; when an East <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> was established here, but entirely suppressed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> in 1731. It was taken by the French in August 1745, after ten days siege; but rendered back by the treaty of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a> la Chapelle. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 48. N. Lat. 51. 17.

OSTEOCOLLA

Pages 270-270

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, though supposed by many to be an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, is truly a crustaceous kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAR">spar</a> defaced by earth, and therefore not transparent. It is usually found coating over vegetables, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other bodies, in form of incrustations; so that the true osteocolla is a tubular crustaceous spar of a very fine and coarse texture; and carries with it much more the appearance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a> than of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of spar. The masses of osteocolla, though regularly of the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, are very different in size; some of them not being thicker than a crow quill, while others are five and six inches in diameter; it is always, however, of a tubular figure, and a wrinkled rough surface. Osteocolla is frequent in Germany; where it is found buried near the surface of the earth, sometimes in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of sand, but more frequently among marls; it should be chosen, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, the purest that can be had, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and of a tolerably firm and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> texture.—It has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been famous for bringing on a calus in fractured <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a>; its name, osteocolla, signifies "bone-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>," or the "bone-binder." It is also recommended as a diuretic, and as good in the fluor albus; but the present practice has rejected it.

OSTEOLOGY

Pages 270-270

that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of anatomy which treats of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. See ANATOMY, Part I.

OSTERVALD

Pages 270-270

a famous Protestant divine, was born at Neufchatel in 1663; and made such rapid progress in his studies, that he became <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAUMUR">Saumur</a> before he was 16 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He afterwards studied at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a> and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. At his return to Neufchatel in 1699, he became pastor of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> there; and contracted a strict friendship with the celebrated John Alphonse Turretin of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, and the illustrious Samuel Wezenfels of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>. The union of these three divines, which was called the Triumvirate of the divines of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, lasted till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Mr. Ostervald acquired the highest reputation by his virtues, his zeal in instructing his disciples, and restoring <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>. He wrote many books in French; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. A Treatise concerning the Sources of Corruption; which is a good moral piece. 2. A Catechism, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Instruction in the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>; which has been translated into German, Dutch, and English; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">Abridgment</a> of the Sacred <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, which he prefixed to it, was translated and printed in Arabic, in order to be sent to the East Indies, by the care of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> for the propagation of the Gospel; and that Society, established in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, honoured him, by admitting him an honorary member. 3. A Treatise against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPURITY">Impurity</a>. 4. An edition of the French <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> of Geneva, with Arguments and Reflections, in folio. 5. Ethica Christiana. 6. Theologia Compendium, &c. He died in 1747, regretted by all who knew him.

OSTIA

Pages 270-270

a town formerly of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, on the left <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> fourth side and at the mouth of the Tiber, whence its name; the first Roman colony led by Ancus Martius, called Colonia Ostiensis. At this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> it lies in ruins, only retaining its name. There were <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-works there, called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALINA">Salina</a> Ostiensis, as early as the times of Ancus Martius, (Livy); from which the Via Salaria, which led to the Sabines, took its name, (Varro) It gave name to one of the gates of Rome, which was called Ostiensis, (Amian).

OSTIACKS

Pages 270-270

a people of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, who inhabit the banks of the river Obi. See SIBERIA.

OSTRACION

Pages 270-270

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMPHIBIA">amphibia</a> nautae claus. It has ten <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> cylindrical obtuse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> in each jaw; the aperture is linear; the body is covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONY">bony</a> substance, and it has no belly-fins. There are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; principally distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of their bodies, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fins near their tail.

OSTRACISM

Pages 270-271

in Grecian antiquity, denotes the banishment of such persons whose merit and influence gave umbrage to the people of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, lest they should attempt any thing against the public <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> was called ostracism, from the Greek word ostrakon, which properly signifies a "shell;" but when applied to this object, it is used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILLET">billet</a> on which the Athenians wrote the names of the citizens whom they intended to banish. The learned are divided with regard to the substance of which this billet was formed; some insist that it was a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a piece of brick; some, that it was a piece of bark; and others assert, that it was a shell. The word admits most of these interpretations. But what determines its true <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is the epithet given it by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors, of ceramic majestis; which words signify, "The punishment of potter's clay:" and this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> seems to us a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, that the word ostrakon, when applied on this occasion, signifies a "piece of baked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, in the form of a shell;" and undoubtedly the Latin authors had this idea of the word here, for they translated it by testula. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> are likewise divided with regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> when ostracism was instituted. But they all agree, that the person who moved the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, was its first victim. But as to the name of its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, and the time of its establishment, they differ extremely. Many are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that ostracism owes its origin to very remote times. However that be, the punishment of ostracism was inflicted by the Athenians when their liberty was in danger. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a>, for instance, jealousy or ambition had sowed <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> among the chiefs of the republic; and if different parties were formed, which threatened some revolution... Ostracism revolution in the state; the people assembled to propose <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> proper to be taken in order to prevent the consequences of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> which in the end might be fatal to freedom. Ostracism was the remedy to which they usually had recourse on these occasions; and the consultations of the people generally terminated with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>, in which a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> was fixed for a particular <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, when they were to proceed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of ostracism. Then they who were threatened with banishment, omitted no affluence or art which might <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> them the favour of the people. They made harangues to evince their innocence, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> injustice that would be done them if they were banished. They solicited, in person, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of every citizen; all their party exerted themselves in their behalf; they procured informers to vilify the chiefs of the opposite <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACTION">faction</a>. Some time before the meeting of the assembly, a wooden inclosure was raised in the forum, with ten doors, i.e., with as many as there were tribes in the republic; and when the appointed day was come, the citizens of each tribe entered at their respective door, and threw into the middle of the inclosure the small brick on which the citizen's name was written whose banishment they voted. The archons and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> presided at this assembly, and counted the ballots. He who was condemned by 6000 of his fellow-citizens, was obliged to quit the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> within ten days; for 6000 voices, at least, were requisite to banish an Athenian by ostracism. The Athenians, without doubt, foresaw the inconveniences to which this law was subject; but they chose rather, as Cornelius Nepos hath remarked, sometimes to expose the innocent to an unjust censure, than to live in continual alarms. Yet as they were sensible that the injustice of confounding virtue and vice would have been too flagrant, they softened, as much as they could, the rigour of ostracism. It was not aggravated with the circumstances which were most dishonourable and shocking in the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of exile. They did not confiscate the goods of those who were banished by ostracism. They enjoyed the produce of their effects in the places into which they were banished; and they were banished only for a certain time. But in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> banishment, the goods of the exiles were always confiscated, and no hopes were given them of ever returning to Athens. The scholast of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a> informs us of a third <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> betwixt ostracism and the common banishment. He says, that a particular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of retirement was assigned to those who were banished by ostracism, which was not appointed to the other exiles. We suspect, however, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this observation; for Themistocles was certainly not limited in his banishment. That great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, as we are told by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a>, tho' his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> residence was at Argi, travelled over all the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>. This punishment, far from conveying the idea of infamy, became, at Athens, a proof of merit, by the objects on which it was inflicted; as Arditides the sophist justly observes, in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECLAMATION">declamation</a> against the Gorgias of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, where he says, that ostracism was not an effect of the vindictive spirit of the people against those whom it condemned; that the law, whether good or bad (for he enters not into an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the question), was only meant to prune the luxuriant growth of transcendent merit; that it condemned on an exile of ten years, only those illustrious men who were accused of being exalted far above other citizens by their conspicuous virtue; and that none of that public indignation was shewn to the exiles by ostracism, which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> breaks out against criminals. Such were the mitigations with which this law was introduced among the Athenians: and by them we see that they were sensible of all the inconveniences to which it was subject. They were indeed too enlightened a people, not to foresee the many instances of injustice which it might produce; that if in some respects it would be favourable to liberty, in others it would be its enemy, by condemning citizens without allowing them a previous <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, and by making a capricious and envious people arbiters of the fate of great men; that it might even become pernicious to the state, by depriving it of its best subjects, and by rendering the administration of public affairs an odious employment to men of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> talents and virtue. However great the inconveniences of Ostracism were, it would not have been impossible to avoid them; and we may add, that this law would have been of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the state, if the people by whom it was instituted had always had discernment enough only to give it force on such occasions as endangered liberty. But its fate was like that of almost all other laws which the wisest legislators have planned for the good of communities. Deceived by their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> to maintain order, to repress injustice, and to protect innocence, men have found ways to pervert their application, and have made them instruments to gratify their private passions. Thus ostracism was established to prevent the dangerous enterprises of the great, and to preserve the vigour of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEMOCRACY">democracy</a>; but the people of Athens, naturally jealous and envious, exerted that law, to remove men of eminent merit from the state, by whose presence they were reproved and intimidated. The fear of tyranny was commonly but a specious <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> with which they veiled their malignity. The repeated victories which they had gained over the Persians, had rendered them, says Plutarch, proud and insolent. Intoxicated with their prosperity, they arrogated all its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> to themselves; they were jealous of those citizens, whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> talents were the subjects of public eulogium. They thought the glory acquired by great men diminished their own reputation. An Athenian no sooner distinguished himself by a splendid <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, than he was marked out as a victim by public envy. His reputation was a sufficient reason for his banishment.

OSTRACITES

Pages 271-271

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name which authors have given the fossil oyster-shell. Ostracites has the same medical virtues with other absorbent and calcareous earths.

OSTREA

Pages 271-272

the oyster, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of vermes tellacea. The shell has two unequal valves; the cardo has no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, but a small hollowed it with transverse lateral streaks. There are 31 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, principally distinguished by peculiarities in their shells. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> oyster is reckoned an excellent food; and is eaten both raw, and variously prepared. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> has been noted for oysters from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Juvenal, who, satyrizing an epicure, says, *Circaeis nota forent, an* *Lucrinum <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> Saxum, Rutopinovae edia fundo,* *Ostrea, calcebat primo depredare meru.* *He, whether Circe's rock his oysters bore,* *<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">Or</a> Lucrine lake, or distant Richborough's shore* *Knew at first <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>.* The luxurious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were very fond of this fish, and had their layers or stews for oysters as we have at present. Sergius Orata was the first inventor, as early as the time of L. Crassus the orator. He did not make them for the sake of indulging his appetite, but thro' avarice, and made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> profits from them. Orata got great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> for his Lucrine oysters; for, says Pliny, the Britith were not then known. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> eat them raw, and sometimes roasted. They had also a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of stewing them with mallows and docks, or with fish, and esteemed them very nourishing. Britain still keeps its superiority in oysters over other countries. Most of our coasts produce them naturally; and in such places they are taken by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DREDGING">dredging</a>, and are become an article of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, both raw and pickled. The very shells, calcined, become an useful medicine as an absorbent. In common with other shells, they prove an excellent manure. Stews or layers of oysters are formed in places which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> never allotted as habitations for them. Those near <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a> have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> famous; at present there are others that at least rival the former, near the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>. The oysters, or their spat, are brought to convenient places, where they improve in taste and size. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> to suppose, that the fine green observed in oysters taken from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> beds, is owing to copperas; it being notorious how destructive the substance or the solution of it is to all fish. We cannot give a better account of the cause, or of the whole treatment of oysters, than what is preserved in the learned bishop Sprat's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, from p. 307, to 309. "In the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of May, the oysters <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> their spawn, (which the dredgers call their spat;) it is like to a drop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, and about the bigness of a half-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>. "The spat cleaves to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, old oyster-shells, pieces of wood, and such like things, at the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which they call cultch. "It is probably conjectured, that the spat in 24 hours begins to have a shell. "In the month of May, the dredgers (by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>) have <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to catch all manner of oysters, of what size forever. "When they have taken them, with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> they gently raise the small brood from the cultch, and then they throw the cultch in again, to preserve the ground for the future, unless they be so newly spat, that they cannot be safely severed from the cultch; in that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> they are permitted to take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or shell, &c. that the spat is upon, one shell having many times 20 spats. "After the month of May, it is felony to carry away the cultch, and punishable to take any other oysters, unless it be those of size, (that is to say,) about the bigness of an half-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> piece, or when, the two shells being shut, a fair <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> rattle between them. "The places where these oysters are chiefly caught, are called the Pent-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNHAM">Burnham</a>, Malden, and Colne-waters; the latter taking its name from the river of Colne, which passeth by Colne-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, gives the name to that town, and runs into a creek of the sea, at a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-HYTHE">Hythe</a>, being the suburbs of the town. "This brood and other oysters, they carry to the creeks of the sea, at Bricket-Sea, Merly, Langno, Fingrego, Wivenho, Tollesbury, and Saltcoate, and there throw them into the channel, which they call their beds or layers, where they grow and fatten, and in two or three years the smallest brood will be oysters of the size aforesaid. "Those oysters which they would have green, they put into pits about three feet deep in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-marshes, which are overflowed only at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>, to which they have sluices, and let out the salt-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> until it is about a foot and half deep. "These pits, from some <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> co-operating with the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, will become green, and communicate their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to the oysters that are put into them in four or five days, tho' they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> let them continue there six weeks or two months, in which time they will be of a dark green. "To prove that the sun operates in the greening, Tollesbury pits will green only in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>; but that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> hath the greater power, Bricket-Sea pits green both winter and summer: and for a further <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, a pit within a foot of a greening-pit will not green; and those that did green very well, will in time lose their quality. "The oysters, when the tide comes in, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> with their hollow shell downwards; and when it goes out, they turn on the other side: they remove not from their place, unless in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, to cover themselves in the oufe. "The reason of the scarcity of oysters, and consequently of their dearth, is, because they are of late years bought up by the Dutch. "There are great penalties by the admiralty court, laid upon those that fish out of those grounds which the court appoints, or that destroy the cultch, or that take any oysters that are not of size, or that do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a> under their feet, or throw upon the shore, a fish which they call a five-finger, resembling a spur-rowel, because that fish gets into the oysters when they gape, and sucks them out. "The reason that such a penalty is set upon any that shall destroy the cultch, is, because they find that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> that be taken away, the oufe will increase, and the muscles and cockles will breed there, and destroy the oysters, they having not wherein to stick their spat. "The oysters are sick after they have spat; but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> they begin to mend, and in August they are perfectly well: the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> oyster is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-fick, having a black substance in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIN">fin</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>-fick (as they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> it), having a milky substance in the fin. They are salt in the pits, salter in the layers, but falteft at sea."

OSTUNI

Pages 272-273

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the Terra di <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OTRANTO">Otranto</a>, with a bishop's see. Its territory is well cultivated, and abounds with olives and almonds. It is seated on a mountain near the gulph of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 49'. N. Lat. 49° 59'.

OSWEGO

Pages 273-273

a fort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, seated on the south side of the lake <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ONTARIO">Ontario</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 70° 35'. N. Lat. 45° 15'.

OSWEIZEN

Pages 273-273

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a> of Cracovia, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. It carries on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VISTULA">Vistula</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19° 47'. N. Lat. 50° 1'.

OTACOUSTIC INSTRUMENT

Pages 273-273
or Auricular Tube, an instrument to facilitate the hearing. See Acoustics, p. 26.

OTAHEITEE

Pages 273-284

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the South <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 149° 13'. S. Lat. 17° 46'. It was discovered by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Wallis in 1767; afterwards Mr Bougainville touched there, and it was visited by Captain Cook in 1773 and 1774. The island consists of two distinct kingdoms, which are united by a narrow neck of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>; the larger being called by the natives Tiaraabou, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> O-Tabeitee-Nue; the smaller one, Opoureouou, or O-Tabeitee-Ete. The circumference of both <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> is about 40 leagues; the larger <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> being divided into 43 districts. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> has a delightful romantic appearance. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> viewed from the sea, presents a most beautiful prospect, being elevated like an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>. The island is skirted with a reef of rocks, and towards the sea is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, being covered with fruit-trees of various kinds, particularly the cocoa-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>. At the distance of about three miles from the shore, the country rises into lofty hills that are covered with wood, and terminate in peaks, from which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are precipitated into the sea. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> everywhere appear to have been burnt, not one being found which did not give manifest signs of fire; so that there is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reason for supposing, that this and the neighbouring islands are either the shattered remains of a continent, or were torn from rocks, which from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of the world have been the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the sea, and thrown up in heaps to a height which the waters never reach. What is further extraordinary, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> does not gradually grow shallow as we approach the shore, but is of immense depth <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by the land; and the islands in this neighbourhood are almost everywhere surrounded by reefs, which appear to be rude and broken in the manner that some violent concussion would naturally leave the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> substance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and Mr Forster <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a rock with projecting longitudinal <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> basaltes. The exterior ranges of hills are sometimes entirely barren, and contain a great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of yellowish clay, mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> ochre; but others are covered with mould and wood like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in the internal parts of the country. Pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-QUARTZ">quartz</a> are sometimes met with here; but no indications of precious minerals or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> of any kind have been observed, iron only excepted. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is extremely healthy and pleasant; the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is not troublesome; and fresh meat <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> keep very well for two days, and fish one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The winds do not blow constantly from the east, but generally a little breeze from east to south-south east. The tide rises very little; and, being governed by the winds, is very uncertain. "The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>," says Mr Bougainville, "is so healthy, that notwithstanding the hard labour of the ships companies while on shore, though the men were continually in the water, and exposed to the meridian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, though they slept upon the bare foil, and in the open air, none of them fell sick; those who were afflicted with the scurvy, and were sent on shore, regained their strength; although they were obliged to assist in the erecting of a fort, and had scarce one uninterrupted night, yet they were so far recovered in the short space of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> they <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> there, that they were afterwards perfectly cured on board." Notwithstanding the great height of the inland mountains of Otaheitee, none of their rocks have the appearance of barrenness, every one of them being covered with woods. "We hardly believed our eyes," says M. de Bougainville, "when we saw a peak covered with woods up to its highest summit, which rises above the level of the mountains in the anterior parts of the southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of this island. Its apparent size seemed to be more than 30 toises in diameter, and grew less in breadth as it rose higher. At a distance it might have been taken for a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> of immense height, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of an able sculptor had adorned with garlands and foliage." One of the mates of the dolphin, with a party of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARINES">marines</a> and seamen, penetrated into the interior parts of the island; and having ascended, with great difficulty, a mountain which they supposed to be a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, they discovered mountains before them so much higher, that with respect to them they seemed to be in a valley; towards the sea the view was enchanting, the sides of the hills were beautifully clothed with wood, villages were everywhere interperfed, and the valleys between them afforded a still richer prospect; the houses stood thicker, and the verdure was more luxuriant; and Mr Forster, with other gentlemen, ascended to the summit of one of the highest mountains in the island, from whence they had a prospect of the island of Huahine, and some others lying at the distance of 40 leagues; from which we may form some judgment of the prodigious height of that mountain. The view of the fertile plain below them, and of a river making innumerable meanders, was delightful in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. The vegetation on the upper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the mountains was luxuriant, and the woods consisted of many unknown sorts of trees and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of this island is a rich fat earth, of a black-soil and ash <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. It produces spontaneously, or with the slightest culture imaginable, a great variety of the most excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; such as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-fruit, cocoa nuts, bananas of 13 sorts, plantains, potatoes, yams, a fruit known here by the name of jambu, and reckoned most delicious; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canoe, which the inhabitants eat raw; ginger; turmeric; a root of the salsep kind, called by the inhabitants <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>; a plant called thee, of which the root only is eaten; a fruit that grows in a pod like that of a large kidney-bean, by the natives called ache; a tree called wharra, which produces fruit something like the pine-apple, and which is known in the East Indies by the name of pandanus; a shrub called nono; the morinda, which also produces fruit; a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fern; a plant called theve; and the Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>-mulberry, of the bark of which they make their cloth; Otaheitee, an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a> which the inhabitants eat raw; its flavour somewhat resembling that of the West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> spinach called callotom, but its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> very different; a plant which the natives call <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AVA">ava</a> or avaa, from the root of which they express a liquor, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> drank to excess, intoxicates like wine or distilled spirits. Here are a sort of shady trees covered with a dark-green foliage, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a>-coloured apples, which, in juiciness and flavour, resemble the ananas or pine-apple. One of the most beautiful trees in the world received here the name of Barringtonia; it had a great abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> larger than lilies, and perfectly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, excepting the tips of their numerous chives, which were of a deep crimson. Such a quantity of these flowers were seen dropped off, that the ground underneath the tree was entirely covered with them. The natives called the tree buddees; and said, that the fruit, which is a large nut, when bruised and mixed up with some shell-fish, and thrown into the sea, intoxicates the fish for some time, so that they come to the surface of the water, and suffer themselves to be taken with people's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Several other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> plants in tropical climates are found to have the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Mr Dalrymple describes the method of catching fish with these plants as follows: The plant is thrust under the coral rocks or hollows where the fish haunt; the effect is most sensible in still water, though it is effectual in the open sea; for the same <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> says, he has seen fish soon after float on the surface of the water half dead, and some totally without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and where the effect is less violent, the fish will be seen under the water to have lost their poise, without coming up to the surface. Fish caught in this manner are not in the least noxious or ill tasted. In this island they have <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> exactly resembling those of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>: besides which there are wild ducks; also beautiful green turtle-doves; large pigeons of a deep blue plumage and excellent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; a small sort of paroquets, very singular on account of the various mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> and blue in their feathers; also another sort of a greenish colour, with a few red spots; the latter are frequently tamed, and are valued on account of their red feathers. Here is a kingfisher of a dark green, with a collar of the same hue round his white throat; a large cuckoo, and a blue heron. Small birds of various kinds dwell in the shady trees; and, contrary to the generally received <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that birds in warm climates are not remarkable for their song, have a very agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. There were no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> but dogs, hogs, and rats; and for these last the natives were said to have a scrupulous regard, inasmuch that they would by no means kill them; however, Capt. Cook, in 1773, turned about 14 cats on the island, which have probably reduced the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of these <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a>. No frogs, toads, scorpions, centipedes, or any kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>, have been found here; the ants, however, are troublesome, but not very numerous. When the Endeavour first arrived here in 1679, the flies were found excessively troublesome; but musquito nets and fly-flaps in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> removed the inconvenience. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SYDNEY">Sydney</a> Parkinson, in his journal, says, that notwithstanding these flies are so great a nuisance, the natives, from a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> principle, will not kill them. But there is a strange disagreement in the accounts of different voyagers concerning this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. For Mr Bougainville says, "this Otaheitee island is not infested by those myriads of troublesome insects that are the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> of other tropical countries." And Mr Forster says, "not a gnat or musquito hummed unpleasantly about us, or made us apprehensive of its bite." This inconvenience must therefore be felt at certain seasons of the year, and in certain districts of the country, more sensibly than at other times and places. There is great variety of excellent fish; and, according to Aitourou, a native who embarked with M. de Bougainville, there are sea-snakes on the shore of Otaheitee, whose bite is mortal. The inhabitants of Otaheitee are stout, well-made, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, and comely people. The stature of the men, of the inhabitants, &c., in general, is from five feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> to five feet ten inches; the tallest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> seen by Captain Wallis measured six feet three inches and an half; and Captain Cook, in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> voyage, describes O'Too, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Otaheitee, to be of that height. "In order to paint 'an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> or a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>," says M. de Bougainville, "one could nowhere find such beautiful models." They are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>; in general their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> is black, and finely frizzled; they have black eyes, flat noses, large mouths, and fine white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; the men wear their beards in many fashions, all of them plucking out a great part, and have prominent bellies. Most of them smell strong of the cocoa-nut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. The women, in general, are much smaller, especially those of the lower <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> or tawtows, which is attributed to their early and promiscuous intercourse with the men; whilst the better sort, who do not gratify their passions in the same unbridled manner, are above the middle stature of Europeans. Their skin is most delicately smooth and soft; they have no colour in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>; their nose is generally somewhat flat, but their eyes are full of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, and their teeth beautifully even and white. "The women," says M. de Bougainville, "have features not less agreeable than the generality of Europeans, and a symmetry of body and beautiful proportion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> which might vie with any of them." The complexion of the men is tawny; but those who go upon the water are much more red than those who live on shore. Some have their hair brown, red, or flaxen, in which they are exceptions to all the natives of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, who have their hair black universally; here, in the children of both sexes, it is generally flaxen. The strongest expression is painted in the countenances of these people; their walk is graceful, and all their motions are performed with great vigour and ease. "I never beheld stouter men," says Sydney Parkinson. "The men of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> on the island wear the nails of their fingers long, which they consider as a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> badge of distinction, since only such people as have no occasion to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> can suffer them to grow to that length. This <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> they have in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with the Chinese; but the nail of the middle finger on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>-hand is always kept short, the meaning for which peculiarity could not be learned. Only one single cripple was met with among them, and he appeared to have been maimed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. The women always cut their hair short round their heads. Both sexes have a custom of staining their bodies, which they call <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TATTOOING">tattooing</a>; both men and women have the hinder part of their thighs and loins marked very thick with black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. Otahitee lines in various forms; these marks are made by striking the teeth of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> somewhat like a comb <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> through the skin, and rubbing into the punctures a kind of paste made of root and oil, which leaves an indelible stain. The boys and girls under twelve years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> are not marked; a few of the men, whose legs were marked in chequers by the same method, appeared to be persons of superior rank and authority. Mr Banks saw the operation of tattooing performed upon the backside of a girl about thirteen years old. The instrument used upon this occasion had thirty teeth; and every stroke, of which at least a hundred were made in a minute, drew an ichor or serum a little tinged with blood. The girl bore it with most stoical <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> for about a quarter of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>; but the pain of so many hundred punctures as she had received in that time, then became intolerable. She first complained in murmurs, then wept, and at last burst into loud lamentations, earnestly imploring the operator to desist. He was, however, inexorable; and when she began to struggle, she was held <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by two women, who sometimes soothed and sometimes chid her; and now and then when she was most unruly, gave her a smart blow. Mr Banks laid in a neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> an hour, and the operation was not over when he went away; yet it was performed but upon one side, the other having been done some time before; and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> upon the loins, in which they most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> themselves, and which give more pain than all the rest, were still to be done. Both men and women are not only decently but gracefully clothed, in a kind of white cloth that is made of the bark of a shrub, and very much resembles coarse <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a> paper. Their dress consists of two pieces of this cloth; one of them, having a hole made in the middle to put the head through, hangs down from the shoulders to the mid-leg before and behind; another piece, which is between four and five yards long, and about one yard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, they wrap round the body in a very easy manner: This cloth is not woven; but is made like paper, of the macerated fibres of the inner bark spread out and beaten together. Their ornaments are feathers, flowers, pieces of shell, and pearls; the pearls are worn chiefly by the women. In wet <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> they wear matting of different kinds, as their cloth will not bear wetting. The dress of the better sort of women consists of three or four pieces: one piece, about two yards wide and eleven long, they wrap several times round their waist, so as to hang down like a petticoat as low as the middle of the leg; and this they call pa-ron. This simple drapery affords the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a> an opportunity of displaying an elegant <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> to the greatest advantage, according to the talents and taste of the wearer: no general fashions force them to disfigure instead of adorning themselves, but an innate gracefulness is the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of simplicity. To this cloth they give a very strong <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> which they make of their houses is to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> in them; for unless it rains, they eat in the open air under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of a tree. These houses are no other than sheds, all built in the wood between the sea and the mountains: they are erected on an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; their width is nearly half of their length; they are nothing more than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, not quite four feet from the ground, raised on three rows of pillars, one row on each side, and one in the middle. The roof resembles our thatched houses in England, and consists of two flat sides inclining to each other. Their thatch consists of palm-leaves. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of their dwelling is covered with hay, over which they spread mats. Some of these erections are furnished with a stool, which is appropriated solely to the use of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the family: they consist of no other furniture except a few blocks of wood, which being square, one side is hollowed into a curve; and these they use as pillows, and with their apparel they cover themselves. In these open dwellings the whole family repose themselves at night. The size of the house is proportioned to the number that constitutes the family. The established order in these dormitories is, for the master and his wife to sleep in the middle; round them the married people; in the next circle the unmarried women; and in the next, at the same distance, the unmarried men; and the servants at the extremity of the shed; but in fair weather, the latter sleep in the open air. Some few dwellings, however, constructed for greater privacy, are entirely inclosed with walls of reeds, connected together with transverse pieces of wood, so as to appear somewhat like large <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>-cages closely lined; in these houses there is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> a hole left for the entrance, which can be closed up with a board. Their candles are made of the kernels of a kind of oily nut, which they stick one above another on a skewer that is thrust through the middle of them; the upper one being lighted burns to the second, at the same time consuming that part of the skewer that goes through it; the second taking fire burns in the same manner down to the third, and so to the last; they burn a considerable time, and afford a pretty good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. The natives generally retire to rest about an hour after it is dark. The food of the common people entirely consists of Food, vegetables. There are, the bread-fruit, with bananas, the of plantains, yams, apples, and a four fruit, which, though cookery, not pleasant by itself, gives an agreeable relish to roasted bread-fruit, with which it is frequently beaten up. See the article Bread-Tree. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, which is reserved for the tables of the great, is either poultry, hogs, or dogs; the flesh of their fowls is not well tasted, but that of dogs is esteemed by the natives beyond pork. The smaller fish are generally eaten raw, as we eat oysters: every thing that can be procured from the sea is made an article of their food; for they will eat not only sea-insects, but what the seamen call blubber, though some of them are so tough that they are obliged to fester them to become putrid before they can be chewed. A very large shark being caught by the Dolphin's people was given to the natives; who soon cut it to pieces, and carried it away with great satisfaction. They kill the animals they intend for food by suffocating them, which is done by stopping the mouth and nose with their hands; they then lunge off the hair, by holding the animal over a fire, and scraping him with a shell; with this instrument they cut him up, and take out the entrails; which are washed, and put into cocoa-nut shells, together with the blood. Dogs are eaten that are fed wholly upon bread-fruits, cocoanuts, yams, and other vegetables, and are never suffered to taste any animal food; and those who have tasted the flesh of a dog thus fed, have declared it to be little inferior to English lamb. In order to dress their food, they kindle a fire, by rubbing the end of one piece of dry wood upon the side of another, in the manner as a carpenter with us whets a chisel. They then dig a pit about half a foot deep, and two or three yards in circumference; they pave the bottom with large pebble stones, which they lay down very smooth and even, and then kindle a fire in it with dry wood, leaves, and the husks of cocoa-nuts. When the stones are sufficiently heated, they take out the embers, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a> up the ashes on every side; they then cover the stones with a layer of green cocoa-nut leaves, and wrap up the animal that is to be dressed in the leaves of the plantain. If it is a small <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>, they wrap it up whole; if a large one, they split it. When it is placed in the pit, they cover it with the hot embers, and lay upon them bread-fruit and yams, which are also wrapped up in the leaves of plantain. Over these they spread the remainder of the embers, mixing among them some of the hot stones, with more cocoa-nut-tree leaves upon them, and then close up all with earth, so that the heat is kept in; the oven is kept thus closed a longer or shorter time, according to the size of the meat that is dressed. The meat, when taken out, is said to be better dressed than any other way. They use shells for knives; and carve very dexterously with them, always <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> from themselves. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> attendants on Oberea, attempting the use of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> and fork, could not feed himself therewith; but, by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> force of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, his hand came to his mouth, and the victuals at the end of his fork went way to his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. They are quite unacquainted with the method of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water, as they have no vessels among them that will bear the fire. Whilst the noble Oberea was one morning at breakfast with captain Wallis on board the Dolphin, the surgeon filled the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEA">tea</a>-pot by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the cock of a vase that stood upon the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. One of the lady's attendants observed this practice very attentively, and soon after turning the cock himself, received the water upon his hand; he no sooner felt himself scalded, than he roared and danced about in an extravagant manner. The other Indians, unperturbed of the cause of these emotions, stood gazing at him in amazement, and not without some mixture of terror: but the gentlemen in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, who soon perceived the cause of the outcry, dispelled the apprehensions of their visitants; and some ointment being applied to the scald, good-humour and confidence were again restored. The gunner of the ship, who was appointed comptroller of the market which was established on shore with the natives, used to dine on the spot; the astonishment of these people was very great to see him dress his pork and poultry in a pot; at length an old man, who was extremely serviceable in bringing down <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> to be exchanged, was put into possession of an iron pot, and from that time he and his friends ate boiled meat every day. Several iron pots were likewise given to Oberea and some of the chiefs; which were in constant use, and drew everybody to see them; but although the particulars of two successive voyages of captain Cook to this island are circumstantially related, we hear no more of this improvement in the culinary art, or of the further assistance which has been rendered those people in supplying them with pots for boiling; but however de- fious the natives might be to eat boil'd meat, it was not advisable to have such an article of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARTER">barter</a> as iron kettles, when a few spike nails, or a common <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HATCHET">hatchet</a>, would procure one of their largest hogs. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">Salt</a> water is the usual sauce to their food; those who live near the sea have it furnished as it is wanted, others at a distance keep it in large bamboos. The kernels of the cocoa-nuts furnish them with another sauce; these, made into a paste something of the consistence of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, are <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> up with salt water, which has a very strong flavour; but though at first it seemed very nauseous, yet when the taste became familiar, it was much relished. Their general drink is water, or the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> of the cocoa-nut. They shewed in general an aversion to strong liquors; and whenever any one of them happened to drink to freely with any of the ship's company as to be intoxicated, he resolutely refused to taste anything that was likely to produce the same effect again; but they have a plant which they call ava ava, from the root of which they procure a liquor which has an inebriating quality. Their manner of preparing this strong drink is as simple as it is disgusting to an European. Several of the people take some of the root, and chew it till it is soft and pulpy; they then spit it out into a platter or other vessel, every one into the same: into this general receptacle water is poured according to the quantity prepared. The juice thus diluted, is strained through some <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> stuff like fine shavings, after which it is fit for drinking, and it is always prepared for present use: it has a peppery taste; drinks flat, and rather insipid; and though it intoxicates, yet captain Cook saw but one instance where it had that effect, as the natives generally drink it with great moderation, and but little at a time. Sometimes they chew this root as Europeans do <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and sometimes they will eat it wholly. They eat alone, or at least only in company with a guest that happens to call in; and the men and women never sit down together to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>: the shade of a spreading tree serves them for a parlour; broad leaves spread in great abundance serve for a table-cloth; and if a person of rank, he is attended by a number of servants who seat themselves round him; before he begins his meal, he washes his mouth and hands very clean, and repeats this several times whilst he is eating. The quantity of food which these people eat at a meal is prodigious. Captain Cook says, he has seen one man devour two or three fishes as big as a perch; three bread-fruits, each bigger than two fists; 14 or 15 plantains, or bananas, each six or seven inches long and four or five round, and near a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUART">quart</a> of the pounded bread-fruit. Men of rank are constantly fed by their women; and one of the chiefs who dined on board the ships in 1769, shewed such reluctance to feed himself, that one of the servants was obliged to feed him to prevent his returning without his meal. In one of the excursions which the gentlemen of the ships made into the country in 1773, they arrived at a neat house, where a very fat man, who seemed to be a chief of the district, was lolling on his wooden pillow; before him two servants were preparing his dinner, by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> up with water some bread-fruit and bananas in a large wooden bowl, and mixing with it a quantity of ferment- ted four paste called mahie. While this was doing, a woman who sat down near him, crammed down his throat by handfuls the remains of a large baked fish, and several bread-fruits, which he swallowed with a voracious appetite; his countenance was the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of phlegmatic insensibility, and seemed to testify that all his thoughts centered in the gratification of his appetite. He scarce deigned to look at the strangers; and a few monosyllables which he uttered, were extorted from him to remind his feeders of their duty; when by gazing at them they grew less attentive to him. That these people, who are remarkably fond of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and particularly that of their women, should exclude its pleasures from the table, where, among all other nations, whether civil or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>, they have been principally enjoyed, is truly inexplicable. How a meal, which every where else brings families and friends together, comes to separate them here, was a singularity much inquired about, but never accounted for. "They ate alone," they said, "because it was right;" but why it was right to eat alone, they never attempted to explain. Such, however, was the force of habit in this instance, as it is in every other, that they expressed the strongest dislike, and even disgust, at their visitants eating in society, especially with women, and of the same victuals. "At first (says captain Cook) we thought this strange singularity arose from some superstitious opinion; but they constantly affirmed the contrary. We observed also some caprices in the custom, for which we could as little account as the custom itself. We could never prevail with any of the women to partake of the victuals at our table, when we were dining in company; yet they would go five or six together into the servants apartments, and there eat very heartily of whatever they could find; nor were they in the least disconcerted if we came in while they were doing it. When any of us have been alone with a woman, she has sometimes eaten in our company; but then she has expressed the greatest unwillingness that it should be known, and always extorted the strongest promises of secrecy. Among themselves, even two brothers and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> have each their separate baskets of provisions, and the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of their meal. When they first visited us at our tents, each brought his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> with him; and when we sat down to table, they would go out, sit down upon the ground, at two or three yards distance from each other, and turning their faces different ways take their repast without exchanging a single word. The women not only abstain from eating with the men, and of the same victuals, but even have their victuals separately prepared by boys kept for that purpose, who deposit it in a separate shed, and attend them with it at their meals. But though they would not eat with us, or with each other, they have often asked us to eat with them, when we have visited those with whom we were particularly acquainted at their houses; and we have often upon such occasions eaten out of the same basket, and drank out of the same cup. The elder women, however, always appeared offended at this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; and if we happened to touch their victuals, or even the basket that contained it, they would throw it away." After meals, and in the heat of the day, the middle-aged people of the better sort generally sleep. They are indeed extremely indolent; and sleeping and eating are almost all that they do. Those that are older are less drowsy, and the boys and girls are kept awake by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and sprightliness of their age. These islanders, who inhabit huts exposed to all the diseases, winds, and hardly cover the earth, which serves them for a bed, with a layer of leaves, are remarkably healthy and vigorous, and live to an old age without enduring any of its infirmities; their senses are acute, and they retain their beautiful teeth to the last. M. de Bougainville describes an old man, whom they saw on their landing, who had no other character of old age, than that respectable one which is imprinted on a fine figure.
