Afterwards it was mounted with marble, and beautified with walks and galleries, as also with a tribunal, or seat of justice. Within this precinct or inclosure, the people were called to give their suffrages for the election of magistrates. The ascent into the ovilia was not by stairs, but by pontes, or narrow boards, laid there for the occasion; on which account de ponte dejici, signified "to be deprived of the privilege of voting;" and persons thus dealt with were called deportanti.

OVIPAROUS

Pages 287-287

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to such animals as bring forth their young from eggs; as birds, insects, &c.

OVIS

Pages 287-288

the Sheep, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a> class, and of the order of pecora; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are these: The horns are concave, turned backwards, and full of wrinkles; there are eight fore-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> in the under-jaw, and no dog-teeth. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. Aries, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> ram and ewe, the horns of which are shaped like a half-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, and compressed. The sheep, unquestionably a mild and gentle creature, is also represented by Buffon as the most stupid, defenceless, and timid of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>; insomuch that, without the assistance of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, it could never, he thinks, have subsisted or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> its species in a wild state. "The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> is absolutely devoid of every art and of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. The arms of the ram are feeble and awkward. His courage is only a kind of petulance, which is useless to himself, inconvenient to his neighbours, and is totally destroyed by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASTRATION">castration</a>. The wedder is still more timid than the sheep. It is fear alone that makes sheep so frequently assemble in troops: upon the smallest unusual noise, they run <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together; and these alarms are always accompanied with the greatest stupidity. They know not how to fly from danger, and seem not even to be conscious of the hazard and inconvenience of their situation. Wherever they are, there they remain obstinately fixed; and neither <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> nor snow can make them quit their station. To force them to move or to change their route, they must be provided with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, who is learned to begin the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a>: the motions of this chief are followed, step by step, by the rest of the flock. But the chief himself would also continue immoveable, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he were not pushed off by the shepherd, or by his dog, an animal which perpetually watches over their safety, which defends, directs, separates, assembles, and, in a word, communicates to them every movement necessary to their preservation. "Of all quadrupeds, therefore, sheep are the most stupid, and derive the smallest resources from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a>. The goat, who so greatly resembles the sheep in other respects, is endowed with much more sagacity. He knows how to conduct himself on every emergency: he avoids danger with dexterity, and is easily reconciled to new objects. But the sheep knows neither how to fly nor to attack: however imminent her danger, she comes not to man for assistance so willingly as the goat; and, to complete the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of timidity and want of sentiment, she allows her lamb to be carried off, without attempting to defend it, or showing any marks of resentment. Her grief is not even expressed by any cry different from that of ordinary bleating." But the annotator upon this article, in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> translation of Buffon, denies the above to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> character of the animal. "All tame animals," he observes, "lose a portion of that sagacity, dexterity, and courage, which they are obliged to employ against their enemies in a wild state; because they have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> accustomed to rely upon the protection of man. Sheep, when enslaved by men, tremble at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of the shepherd or his dog. But, on those extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> where they are allowed to range without control, and where they seldom depend on the aid of the shepherd, they assume a very different <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of behaviour. In this situation, a ram or a wedder boldly attacks a single dog, and often comes off victorious. But when the danger is of a more alarming <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, like man, they trust not to the prowess of individuals, but have recourse to the collected strength of the whole flock. On such occasions, they draw up into one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> body; they <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the young and the females in the centre; and the strongest males take the foremost ranks, keeping close by each other's sides. Thus an armed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> is presented on all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, and cannot be attacked without the greatest hazard of destruction. In this manner they wait, with firmness and intrepidity, the approach of the enemy. Nor does their courage fail them in the moment of attack. For, if the aggressor advances within a few yards of the line, the ram darts upon him with such impetuosity, as lays him dead at their feet, unless he saves himself by flight. Against the attacks of single dogs, or foxes, they are, when in this situation, perfectly secure. Besides, a ram, regardless of danger, often engages a bull, and never fails to conquer him; for the bull, by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOWERING">lowering</a> his head, without being sensible of his defenceless condition, receives between his horns the stroke of the ram, which usually brings him to the ground. "In the selection of food, few animals discover greater sagacity than the sheep; nor does any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animal show more dexterity and cunning in its attempts to elude the vigilance of the shepherd, and to steal such delicacies as are agreeable to its palate. When perfectly tamed, and rendered domestic, the sportive gambols and troublesome tricks of the animal, are too well known to require any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>." As to the accusations contained in the latter <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the character above quoted; every person, it is observed, who has attended to those animals, at least in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, must know that they are not altogether <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a>. Individuals in a state of subjection, seem to have no idea of resisting the attacks of an enemy. But they soon learn that their protection lies in the shepherd or his dog; for, when it becomes necessary, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, to watch the flocks, in order to prevent assaults from foxes or dogs, upon the first alarm the whole flock run with violence to the place where the watchmen are stationed; so that, when they chance to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, they are often hurt by the sheep trampling upon them. On other occasions, they never choose to make a very close approach either to men or dogs; but the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of immediate danger makes them forget their usual timidity, and their sagacity teaches them where their safety lies. When the female is robbed of her lamb, she bleats in a manner that strongly marks the anguish she feels. In the eagerness of her search, her eye-balls seem to start from their sockets; and her <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> and distracted motions, joined to the violence and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> of her bleatings, are evident indications of the most pungent grief. But whatever may be its manners or its mental qualities, this animal is of the most extensive utility to man. We are clothed by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEECE">fleece</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is a delicate and wholesome food. The skin, dressed, forms different parts of our apparel; and is used for covers of books. The entrails, properly prepared and twisted, serve for strings for various musical instruments. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> calcined (like other bones in general), form materials for tests for the refiner. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> is thicker than that of cows, and consequently yields a greater <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> and cheese; and in some places is so rich, that it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not produce the cheese without a mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> to make it part from the whey. The dung is a remarkably rich manure; infomuch that the feeding of sheep is become too useful a branch of husbandry for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> to neglect. Nature, in short, has given this animal nothing that does not redound to our benefit. The ram is capable of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 18 months; and the ewe can be impregnated when a year old. One ram is sufficient for 40 or 40 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EWES">ewes</a>. He ought to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and well proportioned; his head should be thick and strong, his front wide, his eyes <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, his nose flat, his neck thick, his body long and tall, his testicles mussy, and his tail long. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a> is the best <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> for a ram. The ewes whose <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> is most plentiful, bushy, long, soft, and white, are most proper for breeders, especially when at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> they are of a large size, have a thick neck, and move nimbly. In this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> ewes fed in good pastures admit the ram in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> or August; but September or October are the months when the greatest part of our ewes, if left to nature, take the ram. They go with young about five months, and generally bring forth but one at a time, though frequently two: in warm climates, they may bring forth twice in a year; but in Britain, France, and most parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, only once. They give milk plentifully for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight months. They live from 10 to 12 years: they are capable of bringing forth as long as they live, when properly managed; but are generally old and useless at the age of seven or eight years. The ram, who lives 12 or 14 years, becomes unfit for propagating when eight years old. When the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a> are not intended to be kept for propagation, but fattened for food, they ought to be castrated at the age of five or six months. This operation is performed two ways: in the one, an incision is made, and the testicles taken out; in the other, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGATURE">ligature</a> is tied tight round the scrotum, above the testicles, which soon destroys the vessels which nourish them. After castration they are called wethers. The ram, ewe, and wether, when one year old, lose the two foreteeth of the under jaw; six months afterwards, they lose the two foreteeth next to these; and at the age of three years, the teeth are all replaced. The age of a ram may likewise be discovered by their horns, which always appear the first year, and frequently as soon as they are brought forth. These horns uniformly acquire an additional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> every year, as long as the creature lives. The ewes <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> have no horns, but a kind of long protuberances in place of them: however, some of them have two, and some four horns. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and the southern parts of Europe, the flocks are kept in shades or stables during the night; but in Britain, where there is now no danger from wolves, they are allowed to remain without, both night and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>; which makes the animals more healthy, and their flesh a more wholesome food. Dry and mountainous grounds, where thyme and sheep's fescue grass abound, are the best for the pasturing sheep. The sheep is subject to many diseases: some arise from insects which deposit their eggs in different parts of the animal; others are caused by their being kept in wet pastures; for as the sheep requires but little drink, it is naturally fond of a dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a>, vertigo, (the pendro of the Welsh), the phthisis, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JAUNDICE">jaundice</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>, annually make <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> havoc among our flocks: for the first <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, the shepherd finds a remedy by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the infected into fields of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>; which plant has been also found to be very efficacious in the same disorder among the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> species.—The sheep is also infected by different sorts of insects: like the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, it has its peculiar cestus or gadfly, which deposits its eggs above the nose in the frontal sinuses; when these turn into maggots, they become excessive painful, and cause those violent agitations that we so often see the animal in. The French shepherds make a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> practice of easing the sheep, by trepanning and taking out the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGGOT">maggot</a>; this practice is sometimes used by the English shepherds, but not always with the same success. Besides these insects, the sheep is troubled with a kind of tick and louse, which magpies and starlings contribute to ease it of, by lighting on its back, and picking the insects off. 2. The guineafowl, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> sheep, has pendulous ears, lax hairy <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEW">dew</a> lips, and a prominence on the hind part of the head. The wool is short, like that of a goat. It is a native of Guinea. 3. The strepiferos, or Cretan sheep, has straight crinated horns, twisted in a spiral manner. It is a native of Mount Iola.

OWEN

Pages 289-290

a judge of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-pleas, was the son of Richard Owen, Esq.; of Conderow in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; whether in Christchurch <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Broadgate <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, is not determined. Having taken a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> in arts, he left the university, and entered himself of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s inn in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he became an eminent counsellor. In 1583 he was elected <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>-reader to that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. In 1590 he was made serjeant at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s serjeant soon after. He arrived at length at the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of judge of the common-pleas; which office he is said to have executed, during five years, with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abilities and integrity. He died in 1598; and was buried on the south side of the choir in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, where a monument was erected to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. He had the reputation of a learned <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of literature. He was the author of "Reports in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS">common pleas</a>, wherein are many choice <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, most of them thoroughly argued by the learned serjeants, and after argued and resolved by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> judges of those times, with many cases wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of the year-books are reconciled and explained." Lond. 1656, fol. Owen (Dr John), an eminent and learned dissenting minister, was born in 1616, at Hadham, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>, of which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> his father was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>. He made such surprising proficiency in learning, that at twelve years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> he was admitted into Queen's College, Oxford, and in 1635 was made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts: but soon after, disapproving the new regulations made by archbishop Laud their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, with which he refused to comply, he was obliged, in 1637, to leave the college; when taking orders, he became chaplain to Sir Robert Dormer of Alcote in Oxfordshire, and was at the same time <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to his eldest son. He was afterwards chaplain to John <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Lovelace of Hurley, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>; when the civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> breaking out, he openly avowed the cause of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; which was so resented by an uncle, who had intended to leave him his estate, that he discarded him, and left it to another. Yet though Lord Lovelace sided with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, he treated his chaplain with great civility: but on his going to join the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, Mr Owen went to London, and soon after joined the non-conformists. In 1642 he published his book, intitled, A display of Arminianism, which laid the foundation of his future advancement: for the committee for purging the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of scandalous ministers were so pleased with it, that Mr <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a> their chairman sent him a presentation of the living of Fordham in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>: but when he had been there about a year and a half, the patron hearing that the sequestered incumbent was dead, presented another to the living; upon which the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a> gave Mr Owen the living of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COGGESHALL">Coggeshall</a>. He had not, however, been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> at that town before he left the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>; and, joining the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">independents</a>, formed a church there. He was now sent for several times to preach before the parliament; and among the rest on the 28th of February 1648-9, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUMILIATION">humiliation</a> for the intended expedition to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. Cromwell, who was present at this last discourse, and had never heard him before, was extremely pleased with it, and desired his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> into Ireland, and that he would reside in the college of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. This he did; but returned in about half a year. Soon after Cromwell sent him into Scotland; but he also returned from thence after about half a year's stay at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. He was then promoted to the deanery of Christ-church, Oxford; whither he went in 1651; and Cromwell, being now chancellor of the university, nominated him his vice-chancellor. The next year he was created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> by diploma. Dr Owen enjoyed the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a> of vice-chancellor five years; during which he behaved with the greatest moderation: for, though often solicited, he never molested the meeting of the royalists at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Dr Willis the physician, where divine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> was performed according to the liturgy of the church of England; and though he was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> for ejecting scandalous ministers, he frequently overruled his brethren in favour of those royalists who were distinguished by their merit. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Cromwell, he was removed from the vice-chancellorship; and at the Restoration was ejected from his deanery of Christ-church. But he had provided himself a comfortable retreat at an estate he had purchased at Hadham. He now employed himself in preaching as often as he had an opportunity, and in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> books; one of which, intitled Fiat Lux, falling in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Lord Clarendon, he was so pleased with it, or (as is said) from policy pretended to be so, that he sent for Dr Owen, and, acknowledging the service he had done by it to the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, offered to prefer him in the church, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he would conform; but he desired to be excused.—His moderation drew him respect from persons of opposite principles; and in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his friends were Dr Wilkins bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, and Dr Barlow bishop of London. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EALING">Ealing</a> in 1689. His works are printed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> volumes, folio.

OWLING

Pages 290-290

so called from its being usually carried on in the night, is the offence of transporting <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> sheep out of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, to the detriment of its staple manufacture. This was forbidden, at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and more particularly by statute 11 Edw. III. c. 1., when the importance of our woollen manufacture was first attended to; and there are now many later statutes relating to this offence, the most useful and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are those enacted in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, and since. The statute 8 Eliz. c. 3., makes the transportation of live sheep, or embarking them on board any ship, for the first offence forfeiture of goods, and imprisonment for a year, and that at the end of the year the left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> shall be cut off in some public market, and shall be there nailed up in the openest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> offence is felony. The statutes 12 Car. II. c. 32. and 7 & 8 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">Will</a>. III. c. 28., make the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of wool, sheep, or fuller's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, liable to pecuniary penalties, and the forfeiture of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the ship and cargo by the owners, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> privy; and confiscation of goods, and three years imprisonment to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and all the mariners. And the statute 4 Geo. I. c. 11. (amended and farther enforced by 12 Geo. II. c. 21. and 19 Geo. II. c. 34.), makes it transportation for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years, if the penalties be not paid.

OXALIS

Pages 290-290

wood <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SORREL">sorrel</a>; a genus of the pentagynia order, belonging to the decandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the only remarkable is the acetofella, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> wood-sorrel. This grows naturally in moist shady woods, and at the sides of hedges in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, so is but seldom admitted into gardens. The roots are composed of many scaly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, which propagate in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty. The leaves arise immediately from the roots upon finger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> footstalks, and are composed of three heart-shaped lobes. They are gratefully acid, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in the scurvy and other putrid disorders.

OXFORD

Pages 290-291

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name in England, celebrated for its university, and pleasantly situated in a plain, with a fine fruitful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> all around. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of the name is obvious. In the British times it seems to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; but in the Saxon era, it was noted only for a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> dedicated to St Frideswide, till Alfred built three colleges, one for grammarians, another for philosophers, and a third for divines. Learning <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to flourish till the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> was sacked and burnt by the Danes in the reign of Etheldred; and after that, Harold, surnamed Harefoot, treated it with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> severity upon some provocation he had received. It seems to have been besieged and taken by William the Conqueror, and to have been deserted by the learned from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> till about the year 1129, when one Robert Pulein began to read lectures in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>: and such was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of students to it, that in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a> John there were not fewer than three thousand. Robert d'Oilly, a Norman, to whom William the Conqueror had given the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, built a castle on the west side in 1071; and he is also supposed to have surrounded it with walls. In a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> built by Henry I. was born Richard I. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Cœur de Lion. About the tenth of King John, there happened a quarrel between the citizens and students; in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which many of the latter quitted it, but returned again a few years afterwards. Here Henry III. held a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the differences betwixt him and his barons; when he confirmed the privileges granted to the university by his predecessors, and added others of his own. In this reign the students are said to have been 30,000; who were all excommunicated by the pope for some rudeness to his legate. In Edward III.'s time, they were split into two factions, called the northern and southern men; a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> which was attended with many disorders and much violence, but in a short time concord and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> again prevailed. III. | | <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a> | Richard Fleming, bishop of Lincoln | Henry VI. | | All Souls | Hugh Chicheley, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> | Henry VI. | | Magdalen | William Waynflete, bishop of Winchester, lord chancellor | Henry VI. | | Brasenose | William Smith, bishop of Lincoln, and Richard Sutton, Esq. | Hen. VIII. | | Corpus-Chrisit | Richard Fox, bishop of Winchester, and lord privy-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> | Hen. VIII. | | Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> | Henry VIII. | Hen. VIII. | | Trinity | Sir Thomas Pope | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>. | | St John Baptist | Sir Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a>, merchant of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> | Mary. | | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> | Queen <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> | Elizabeth. | | Wadham | Nicholas and Dorothy Wadham | James I. | | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a> | Thomas Tidale, Esq. and Dr Richard Whitwick | James I. | | <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a> | Sir Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>, and made collegiate. Hartford was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HART">Hart</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> till 1740, that it was erected into a college. | | All these are richly endowed, and have fine gardens, <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>, chapels, &c. The halls in which the students maintain themselves, except a few that have exhibitions, are these: St Edmund's, belonging to Queen's college; Magdalen, to Magdalen college; St Alban's. ban's, to Merton; St Mary's, to Oriel; New-Inn, to New-College. Several persons have been great benefactors to particular colleges, as Dr Ratcliffe to University-college; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a> Codrington and Dr Clarke, to All-souls; queen Caroline, to Queen's; the before-mentioned Dr Clarke and Mrs Eaton, to Worcester; Dr Wake, archbishop of Canterbury, to Christ-church. The most considerable of these colleges are Magdalen's and Christ-Church, which are as noble foundations as any in the world. The church of the latter is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, and has a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, eight canons, eight chaplains, eight singing men, eight choiristers, a teacher of music, and an organist. Each of the colleges has its visitor appointed by its statutes, except Christ-Church, which is subject to the visitation of the Sovereign alone. The other remarkable buildings belonging to the university are, first, the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>; secondly, the Bodleian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> public library; thirdly, Ratcliffe's library, a most elegant structure, for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and furnishing which, Dr Ratcliffe left £40,000; fourthly, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, built by Sheldon, archbishop of Canterbury; fifthly, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>, in which is an elaboratory and a repository for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> rarities and antiquities; sixthly, the Clarendon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>-house, so called, because it was built partly with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> arising to the university by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of Lord Clarendon's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. To the south of Magdalen college lies the physic garden, instituted by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Danby, and much improved by Dr Sherrard. It contains five acres, in which is a complete <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> as grow naturally, disposed in their respective classes; together with two neat and convenient green-houses, stocked with a valuable collection of exotics, and a hot-house, where various plants brought from the warmer climates are raised. The whole body of the university, including professors, fellows, and students of all sorts, exceeds 3000. Each college has its particular statutes and rules for its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. There are four terms in the year for public exercises, &c., and particular days and hours for public lectures by the several professors. The university is governed by a chancellor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, vice-chancellor, two proctors, a public orator, a keeper of the archives, a registrar, three squire-beadles, and three yeomen-beadles. As to the city, it has had the same privileges granted to it as London, particularly an exemption from toll all over England. It is governed by a mayor, high-steward, recorder, four aldermen, eight assistants, two bailiffs, a town-clerk, two chamberlains, all that have borne the office of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> and chamberlain, and twenty-four <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-councilmen; but these are subject to the chancellor or vice-chancellor of the university in all affairs of moment; and not only the mayor, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> citizens, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of the county, take an oath to maintain the privileges of the university. The city, including the colleges, is one of the largest in England, having thirteen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-churches, besides the cathedral, well built, clean, and regular. At the entrance of the town from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOODSTOCK">Woodstock</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANBURY">Banbury</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, a neat <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> hath been lately erected by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> of Dr Ratcliffe's benefaction, out of the surplus money remaining after defraying the expense of his library. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> line of the family of Vere, to whom the city had given the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl for 500 years, failing in Aubrey de Vere, who was twentieth earl, queen <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> conferred the title upon Robert Harley, a descendant of the Veres, in whose family it still continues. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> trade of the city is in malt, conveyed in barges to London. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>, a county of England, bounded on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>; on the south, where it is broadest, the river Isis divides it from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>; on the east, it is bounded by Buckinghamshire; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, where it terminates in a narrow point, it has on the one side <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>, and on the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>. It extends from Cleydon to Caverham 42 miles in length, and from Cleydon to Faringdon 26 in breadth, making about 130 in circumference; within which are contained one city, 15 market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 280 parishes, 14 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, 534,000 acres, and about 120,000 souls. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is sweet and pleasant, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> rich and fertile. The lower parts consist of meadows and corn-fields, and the higher were covered with woods till the civil wars; in which they were so entirely destroyed, that wood is now extremely scarce and dear, except in what is called the chiltern, and so is coal; of consequence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> bears an exorbitant price. The county is extremely well watered; for besides the Isis, Tame, Cherwell, Evenlode, and Windrush, there is a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of lesser <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and brooks. One of the four great Roman ways passes quite through it, entering at the parish of Chinner, and going out at that of Gorring. There is another lesser one, that extends between Colnbrook and Wallinford, called Gremeflake. The county sends <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> members to parliament, viz. two for the shire, two for the city, two for the university, two for new Woodstock, and one for Banbury.

OXGANG

Pages 291-291
or OXGATE, is generally taken, in our old law-books, for 15 acres, or as much ground as a single ox can plough in a year. OXUCLÆ, in href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural history, the name of a genus of fossils of the class of felsite, but of the columnar, not the rhomboidal kind. Of this genus there are only two known species: 1. A fine kind with thin flakes and transverse filaments, found in the clayey banks of the river Nen, near Peterborough in Northamptonshire; and, 2. A dull kind with thick plates and longitudinal filaments. This is not uncommon in Yorkshire, and lies sometimes in a yellow, and sometimes in a blue clay.

OXYCRATE

Pages 291-291

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, a mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, proper to affluage, cool, and refresh. The usual proportion is one spoonful of vinegar to five <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> six spoonfuls of water.

OXYGLYCU

Pages 291-291

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of drink prepared of the sweetest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>-combs macerated and boiled. The combs, from which all the honey has been expressed, are put into a pot with pure <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and boiled till they seem to have deposited all their contained honey in the water. This liquor is to be kept; and, when diluted with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water, is to be drank in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, in order to remove thirst.

OXYMEL

Pages 291-291

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. See PHARMACY.

OYSTER

Pages 292-292

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, see Ostrea. The oyster affords the curious in microscopic observations a very pleasing entertainment. In the clear liquor many little round living animalcules have been found, whose bodies being conjoined, form spherical figures, with tails not changing their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> otherwise than by sinking to the bottom, as being heavier than the fluid; these have been seen frequently separating, and then coming together again. In other oysters, animalcules of the same kind were found, not conjoined, but <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> by one another, whence they seemed in a more perfect state, and were judged by Mr Lieuwenhoek to be the animalcules in the roe <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> semen of the oyster. A <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> oyster being opened, incredible multitudes of small embryo oysters were seen, covered with little shells, perfectly transparent, and swimming along slowly in the liquor; and in another female, the young ones were found of a browner <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and without any appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. Monsieur Joblot also kept the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> running from oysters three days, and it appeared full of young oysters swimming about nimbly in it; these increased in size daily; but a mixture of wine, or the vapour of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, killed them. In the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of August oysters are supposed to breed, because young ones are then found in them. Mr Lieuwenhoek, on the 4th of August, opened an oyster, and took out of it a prodigious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of minute oysters, all alive, and swimming nimbly about in the liquor, by means of certain exceeding small organs, extending a little way beyond their shells; and these he calls their beards. In these little oysters, he could discover the joinings of the shells; and perceived that there were some dead ones, with their shells gaping. These, tho' so extremely minute, are seen to be as like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> oysters in form as one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a> is to another. As to the size of them, he computes, that 120 of them in a row would extend an inch; and consequently, that a globular body, whose diameter is an inch, would, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were also round, be equal to 1,728,000 of them. He reckons 3000 or 4000 are in one oyster, and found many of the embryo oysters among the bairds; some fastened thereto by slender filaments, and others lying loose; he likewise found animalcules in the liquor 500 times less than the embryo oysters. It is not very uncommon to see on oyster-shells, when in a dark place, a shining <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> or bluish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of brimstone, which sticks to the fingers when touched, and continues shining and giving light for a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, though without any sensible <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. This shining matter being examined with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, was found to consist of three sorts of animalcules; the first whitish, and having 24 or 25 legs on a side, forked, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> speck on one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the head, the back like an eel with the skin stripped off. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> sort, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, resembling the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> glow-worm, with folds on its back, but legs like the former; a nose like a dog's, and one eye in the head. The third sort, speckled, with a head like a foal, with many tufts of whitish hairs on the sides of it. Some much larger and greyish might be seen, having <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> heads, two horns like a snail's, and six or eight whitish feet; but these did not seem to shine. OYSTER-CATCHER. See Hematopus. OYSTER-SHELLS. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, no 345. OZÆNA, a foul and malignant ulcer of the nose, distinguished by its odor, and often accompanied with a caries of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the nose.

OZANAM

Pages 292-293

an eminent French mathematician, born at Bolignieux in Bresse, in 1640, of a wealthy family. His father gave him a good <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and designed him for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but some mathematical books falling into his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, inspired him with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> for that science; and though he had no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to instruct him, he made such progress in it, that, at 15 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he wrote a piece in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, which he thought proper to insert in the works he afterwards published. He at length taught that science at Lyons; and his mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> brought him in a considerable revenue, till the year 1701: at which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> breaking out on the succession to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, he lost almost all his scholars, and was reduced to a very melancholy situation; and his wife dying the same year, he was so afflicted, that he never perfectly recovered it. In 1702, he was admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy of Sciences; and died of an apoplexy, in 1717.—He was of a mild and serene temper, of singular generosity, and of a cheerful disposition.—He would not allow himself to know more of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> than the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people. He used to say, that "it was the business of the doctors of Sorbonne to dispute, of the Pope to decide, and of a mathematician to go to heaven in a perpendicular line." His works are very numerous, and have met with the approbation of the learned. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> are, 1. Practical <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, 12mo. 2. A mathematical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>. 3. A course of mathematics, 5 vols, 8vo. 4. Mathematical and philosophical recreations, the most complete edition of which is that of 1724, in 4 vols 8vo. 5. An easy method of surveying. 6. New elements of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> much commended by Mons. Leibnitz. 7. Theoretical and practical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, &c. P, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> p, the 15th <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> and 11th consonant of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of which is formed by expressing the breath somewhat more suddenly than in forming the sound of b; in other respects these two sounds are pretty much alike, and are often confounded one with another. When p stands before t or s, its sound is lost; as in the words psalmi, psychology, ptolemaic, ptifan, &c. When placed before h, they both together have the sound of f; as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, physic, &c. As an abbreviation, P. stands for Publicus, Pondo, &c. P.A.DIG. for Patricia Dignitas; P.C. for Patres Conscripti; P.F. for Publii Filius; P.D. for Propositum, or Propositum publice; P.R. for Populus Romanus; P.R.S. for Pratoris sententia, P.R. S.P. for Praefi <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. In the Italian music, P. stands for piano, or "softly;" and P.P.P. for pianissimo, or "very softly." Among astronomers, P.M. is used to denote <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a> meridiem, or afternoon. Among physicians, P. stands for pupil, or the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of an handful, P.Æ. partes aquae, or equal parts of the ingredients; P.P. signifies pulvis patrum, or Jesuit's bark in powder; and ppr. preparatus, or prepared. As a numeral, P signifies the same with G, viz. 400; and with a dash over it thus, Ġ, 400,000.

OZELL

Pages 292-292

a well known translator, was educated in Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>, was possessed of a competent fortune, and always enjoyed good places; being auditor-general of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> accounts, of St Paul's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, and of St Thomas's hospital. Notwithstanding his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to business, he still retained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> for polite literature; and though he did not appear as an original author, yet having made himself <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of most of the living languages, he favoured the world with many translations from these, as well as from the Latin and Greek; which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are not the most elegant, are generally faithful and true to the originals. He died in the year 1743.

PACE

Pages 293-293

a learned Englishman, born about the year 1482. He was educated at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of Thomas Langton bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, whom he served as an amanuensis, and afterwards entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> Bainbridge. His accomplishments rendered him so acceptable to Henry VIII. that he made him secretary of state; and, entering into orders, he was admitted prebendary in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a>, archdeacon of Dorset, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of St Paul's, &c. which preferments were conferred on him during his absence on foreign embassies. In 1524, he was sent to Rome on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of pope Leo X., to solicit the papal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> for cardinal Wolsey; but a new Pope was elected before his arrival, a circumstance that proved the epocha of his troubles. He fell under the displeasure of the disappointed cardinal; and being soon after employed as <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, he was so neglected and hardly used, that he was seized with a phrenzy: upon which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> ordered him home; and being carefully attended by the physicians at the king's command, he was in a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> restored to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his reason, and then applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> tongue. Being now introduced to his Majesty, he remonstrated against the Cardinal's cruelty: who being ordered to clear himself, summoned Pace before him, sitting in judgment with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> and others; who condemned Pace, and sent him to the Tower; where he remained two years, till he was discharged by the king's command.—When he was enlarged, he resigned his deaneries, and died in retirement at <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol20.html#article-STEPNEY">Stepney</a> in 1532; after having wrote several works, and enjoyed the esteem of the learned among his contemporaries; especially of Sir Thomas More, and Erasmus.

PACHAMAC

Pages 293-293

a valley of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, in South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, ten miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIMA">Lima</a>; celebrated for its pleasantness and fertility, but more on account of a magnificent temple built by the Incas of Peru, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of their god. When the Spaniards conquered Peru, they found immense <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> therein.

PACHODECARHOMBIS

Pages 293-293

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name of a genus of fossils, of the class of salamanders, expressing a thick rhomboidal body composed of ten planes.

PACHSU

Pages 293-293

a small <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, near the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Epirus, and in European <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>. It lies south of Corfu, and is subject to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol13.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">PACIFIC ocean</a>, that vast ocean which separates <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. It is called Pacific, from the moderate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> the first mariners who sailed in it met with between the tropics: and it was called South Sea, because the Spaniards crossed the isthmus of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, when they first discovered it; tho' it is properly the Western ocean, with regard to America.

PACKAGE

Pages 293-293

is a small duty of one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a>,

PACKET

Pages 293-293
or PACKET-BOAT, a vessel appointed by the government to carry the mail of letters, packets, and expresses, from one kingdom to another by sea, in the most expeditious manner. Thus, the packet-boats, under the direction of the post-master-general of Great Britain, carry the mails from Dover to Calais, from Falmouth to Lisbon, from Harwich to Helvoetfluyt, and from Parkgate to Dublin.

PACTOLUS

Pages 293-293

a river of Lydia, called Chrysaorhoas, from its rolling <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> sand, according to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, Plutarch, Pliny, and Strabo; rising in mount Tmolus, (Strabo). From this river Croesus is thought to have had all his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>. In Strabo's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> it ceased to roll down any. It ran thro' Sardes; after which it fell into the Hermus, and both together into the Ægean <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> at Phocæa in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>. A river celebrated by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Ovid, Lucan, Lycophron, Horace, Apollonius.

PACUVIUS

Pages 294-294

of Brundusium in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, a tragic poet in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation about the year of Rome 600. He was nephew of Ennius; published several theatrical pieces, though we have only some fragments of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> remaining; and died at Tarentum at above 90 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

PADANARAM

Pages 294-294

literally the plains of Aram, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>; translated by the Seventy, simply Mesopotamia, or Mofopotamia, of Syria; by the Vulgate, Syria; the Syrians on this and on the other side of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, not differing remarkably from each other in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> and manners, as Josephus allows.

PADDERBORN

Pages 294-294

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the above bishopric. It stands 40 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Cassel, 50 south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, and 60 south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>; being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, well built, and well fortified <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Its name is compounded of pader, a rivulet, which rises <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> altar of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, i.e. a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. It was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANSE">Hanse</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; and, till 1604, an imperial city. The cathedral is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> fabric, inferior to few in the empire. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRUCIFIX">crucifix</a> in it of 60 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, presented by Otho II. The university, of which the Jesuits have the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, was founded in 1592, and the walls were built in the beginning of the 11th century. In 1530, an attempt was made to introduce Lutheranism; but 16 of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> citizens who had embraced it were executed, and the rest obliged to abjure it. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> Christian of Brunswic carried off from hence, in 1692, the silver images of the 12 apostles, and the silver <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a> of St Lotharius; and had them coined into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, with this inscription, God's Friend, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">Priest</a>'s Enemy. The trade of this town, though formerly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, is now inconsiderable; and the inhabitants subsist mostly by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, and breeding of cattle. Though the bishop has a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> in the city, he resides (when he vouchsafes to visit this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which is seldom, having other and more valuable benefices) at Neuhaus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles off, where he has a magnificent castle. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, and other emperors, sometimes resided here, and held diets of the empire.

PADDOC

Pages 294-294
or PADDOC COURSE, a piece of ground encompassed with pales or a wall, and taken out of a park for exhibiting races with greyhounds, for plates, wagers, or the like. A paddoc is generally a mile long, and a quarter of a mile broad: at the one end is a little house where the dogs are to be entered, and whence they are flipped; near which are pens to inclose two or three deer for the sport. Along the course are several posts, viz. the low post, which is 160 yards from the dog-house and pens; the quarter of a mile post, half-mile post, and pinching post; besides the ditch, which is a place made to receive the deer, and preserve them from farther pursuit. And near this place are seats for the judges chosen to decide the wager. The keepers, in order to flip the dogs fairly, put a sliding collar upon each, flipped round a ring; and the deer being turned loose, and put forward by a teaser, as soon as he is arrived at the low-post, the dog-house door is thrown open, and the dogs flipped. If now the deer swerve so much, as that his head is judged nearer the dog-house than the ditch before he arrive at the pinching-post, it is no match, and must be run over again three days after: but if the deer runs straight beyond the pinching-post, then that dog which is nearest when he swerves, or is blanched by any accident, wins the match; but if no such swerve happens, then the match is won by the dog who first leaps the ditch.

PADERBORN

Pages 294-294

a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Germany in the circle of Westphalia, has the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIPPE">Lippe</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and west; <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>-Cassel and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALDECK">Waldeck</a>, on the south; and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, with the duchy of Westphalia, on the west. Its greatest length from east to west is about 40 miles, and its breadth where widest 30. Some parts of it yield good pasture, and breed abundance of cattle; but it is not very fruitful in corn. There is a heath called the Senne <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Sende, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, but very barren and desolate. There are, however, good <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, plenty of deer and other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a>; and it is watered with several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> abounding with fish, as the Weser, the Dimer, the Bever, the Nette, the great Emmer, the Lippe, the Alme, and the Pader. It contains 54 parishes, in which are 25 market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 16 monasteries. The Roman Catholic is the predominant <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the country, yet there are also many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> in it. The bishopric was erected by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the eighth century; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> was consecrated by pope Leo in person, anno 796. The bishop is sovereign of the Paderborn country, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the empire, and suffragan of the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>. His revenue is about 30,000 pounds a year, and he is able to raise 3000 men. In the matricula, his assessment is 18 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and 34 foot, or 352 florins monthly in lieu of them. Towards the charges of the sovereign courts of the empire, he pays for each <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>, 162 rix-dollars and 29 krutners. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> consists of 24 capitular canons, who must prove their noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> by four decents. The arms of the bishopric are a crois or, in a field <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GULES">gules</a>. For the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of it, and the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, there are several councils and colleges under the bishop. Here are also a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> marshal, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEWER">sewer</a>, cup-bearer, chamberlain, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, and purveyor. It was in this bishopric that Quintilius Varus, with the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> under his command, was routed by the Germans under Arminius.

PADUA

Pages 294-295

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, with an university and a bishop's see. It is also <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Paduano; but is much less considerable than it was formerly; for it now contains no more than 30,000 inhabitants, whereas it formerly had 100,000, and many of the houses are gone to ruin; however, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> where <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> is administered, is a superb structure. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of the university, are in that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> called the Old Town; and there are piazzas under all the houses, where persons may walk without being exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. The garden of the university is curious, on account of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. Here a student may take his degrees, let him be of what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Christianity he <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>; nay, though he should be a Jew <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a Turk. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of this city is St Anthony, who lies in the cathedral; they have such a veneration for him, that the beggars beggars do not ask <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> in the name of God, but for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of St Anthony. The Jews live in a distinct part of the city; and the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> produce excellent wine and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, with delicious fruit. It was taken by the Venetians in 1706. It is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Brentac and Bachiiglione, in a fine plain; and is about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles in circumference. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 55. N. Lat. 45. 24.

PADUAN

Pages 295-295

among the medalists, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> medal struck in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the antique, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a new medal struck with all the marks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of antiquity. This name is properly applicable to those medals only that were struck, in the seventh century, by an Italian painter, born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>; who succeeded so well in the imposture, that the best judges are at a loss to distinguish his medals from the genuine ones. Tho' it is frequently used in general for all medals of this kind.

PADUANO

Pages 295-295

a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, bounded on the east by the Dogado, on the south by the Polidino di <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROVIGO">Rovigo</a>, on the west by the Veronese, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Vicentino. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is well watered; and is one of the most fertile in Italy. The province is about 40 miles in length, and 35 in breadth. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

PADUS

Pages 295-295

anciently called Eridanus, especially by the Greeks; a river famous for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of Phaeton, (Ovid). It rises in mount <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>, in the Alpes Cottiae, from three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, dividing the Cisalpine <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> into the Transpadana and Cispadana, (Strabo); and, swelled by other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> falling into it on each side from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> and Appennines, it discharges itself with a course from west to east, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> mouths, into the Adriatic, (Mela). The lake thro' which it discharges itself into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, is called by the natives the Seven Seas. Now the Po.

PAEAN

Pages 295-295

in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a foot consisting of four syllables; of which there are four kinds, the paean primus, secundus, &c. The paean primus consists of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> and three short ones, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a trocheus and pyrrhichius, as temporibus; the paean secundus consists of a short syllable, a long, and two short, or an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IAMBUS">iambus</a> and a pyrrhichius, as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POTENTIA">potentia</a>; the paean tertius consists of two short syllables, a long and a short one, or a pyrrhichius and a trocheus, as animatus; the paean quartus consists of three short syllables and a long one, or a pyrrhichius and iambus, as celebritas. PAEDOBAPTISM; infant-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, or that conferred on children.

PAGAN

Pages 295-295

a heathen, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENTILE">gentile</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> idolater; one who adores false gods. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">MYTHOLOGY</a>.

PAGANALIA

Pages 295-295

certain festivals observed by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>. They were instituted by Servius Tullius, who appointed a certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of villages (pagi), in each of which an altar was to be raised for annual sacrifices to their tutelar gods; at which all the inhabitants were to assist, and give presents in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, according to their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, by which means the number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-people was known. The servants upon this occasion offered cakes to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> and Tellus, to obtain plentiful harvests.

PAGANISM

Pages 295-295

the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of pagans; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of idols and false gods. See IDOLATRY and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">MYTHOLOGY</a>.

PAGEANT

Pages 295-295

a triumphal car, chariot, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other like pompous <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a>, variously adorned with colours, flags, &c. carried about in public shows, processions, &c.

PAGI

Pages 295-295

a very famous Cordelier, and one of the ablest critics of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born at Rogne in Provence in 1624. He took the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> in the convent at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARLES">Arles</a> in 1641, and was at length four times <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> of his order; but his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> duties did not prevent his vigorous application to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, in which he excelled. His most considerable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> is, "A Critique upon the Annals of Baronius;" where, following the learned <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> year by year, he has rectified an infinite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of mistakes, both in chronology and in the representation of facts.
