He published the first volume in 1689, dedicated to the clergy of France, who allowed him a pension: the whole was printed after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in 4 vols. folio, at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, in 1705, by the care of his nephew Francis Pagii, of the same order. He wrote some other things before his death, which happened in 1699; and had the character of an able historian as well as of a learned and candid critic. His nephew, Francis, above mentioned, wrote "A Chronological <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">Abridgment</a> of the history of the Popes," in Latin, 3 vols. 4to. Francis had also a nephew, Anthony Pagii, who added three more volumes to the History of the Popes; of which two more were intended, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not executed.

PAGNINUS

Pages 295-296

a Dominican, illustrious for his skill in the Oriental languages, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a> in 1466. He applied himself to examine the vulgar translation of the Scriptures; and believing it to be either not of Jerom, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> greatly corrupted, he undertook a new one from the present <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> text. It appears by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from Pious Mirandula to him, that he spent 25 years on this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which is the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> translation from the Hebrew; and the Jews who read read it, affirmed it to be more exact than the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> translations; this, however, was his fault; for his scrupulous servile adherence to the letter of the original text, has, according to father Simon, made his translation obscure, barbarous, and full of solecisms. He afterward translated the New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> from the Greek, as he had done the Old from the Hebrew, laying the Vulgar all the while before him; and dedicated it to pope Clement VII. He was also the author of a Hebrew <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a> and Lexicon, which Buxtorf made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in compiling his; and died in 1536.

PAGOD

Pages 296-296
or Pagoda, is also the name of a gold and silver coin, current in several parts of the East Indies. PAIN. See Metaphysics, n° 23, 71. As the brain is the seat of sensation, so it is of pain. Boerhaave, and most other authors on this subject, assign a stretching of the nerves as the only immediate cause of pain; but as the nerves do not appear to consist of fibres, this cause of pain does not seem to be well-founded; nor indeed will it be easy to treat this subject clearly, but in proportion as the means of sensation are understood. Many kinds of pain are met with in authors: such as, A gravitative pain; in which there is a sense of weight on the part affected, which is always some fleshy one, as the liver, &c. A pultative pain; which, Galen says, always succeeds some remarkable inflammation in the containing parts, and is observed in abscesses while suppurating. A tenitive pain, which is also called a distending pain; it is excited by the diffusion of some nervous, muscular, or membranous part, either from some humour, or from flatulence. An acute pain is, when great pain is attended with quick and lively sensations: A dull pain is, when a kind of numbness is as much complained of as the pain is. The mediate and more remote causes of pain are generally obvious; and when so, the cure will consist for the most part in removing them: for though in many instances the chief complaint is very distant from the seat of these causes, yet their removal is the proper method of relief. See Medicine, passim. Perhaps all pains may be included, with irritation, in those that have spasm or inflammation for their source. When pain is owing to inflammation, the pulse is quicker than in a natural state; it is also generally full, hard, and tense; the pain is equal, throbbing, and unremitting. If a spasm is the cause, the pulse is rarely affected; at intervals the pain abates, and then returns with some degree of aggravation; gentle motion sometimes abates, or even cures, in some instances: but in inflammatory cases no such effects are ever experienced. See Dr. Lobb's Treatise on Painful Distempers. The pain so frequently attendant on child-bed women, called after-pains (from their happening only after being delivered of a child), are often occasioned by scooping to fetch away coagulated blood, which is a needless endeavour. When no improper treatment in delivering the fecundines can be suspected, the irritability of the uterus alone is to be considered as the cause. Care should be taken not to confound these after-pains with, or mistake the pains attending puerperal fevers for, the colic. After-pains come by fits, and soon go off; but return at different intervals, which are longer each day, and after two or three days are usually at an end, though sometimes they continue seven or eight: notwithstanding these pains, the lochia flow properly, and generally more abundantly after the cessation of each fit; this does not happen in colicky complaints, nor is the belly so free from tumefaction when the puerperal fever is attendant. As these pains are of the spasmodic kind, anodynes and gentle opiates, with frequent draughts of warm caudle, camomile tea, &c. are all that are required in order to their relief. Among the various causes of pain, a singular one is related in the third vol. of the Lond. Med. Obs. and Inq. p. 241, &c. Some persons who had taken cold during their being salivated, were afflicted with pains which resisted all the usual methods of relief: at length the author of the narrative referred to, suggested the cause; and by exciting a fresh salivation, the pains abated; the spitting was kept up a little while, and permitted to abate with some caution; and thus the cures were completed.

PAINTING

Pages 323-328

Landscape. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">Study</a> those objects at least, which they shall have most frequent occasion to represent. Painters usually comprise, under the word study, anything whatever, which they either <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> paint separately, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; whether figures, heads, feet, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, draperies, animals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, trees, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, or whatever may confirm them in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of these things is what they call study; whether they be for instruction in design, or only to assure them of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and to perfect their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. In fact, this word study is the more properly used by painters, as in the diversity of nature they are daily making new discoveries, and confirming themselves in what they already know. As the landscape-painter need only study such objects as are to be met with in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, we would recommend to him some order, that his drawings may be always at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> when he wants them. For instance, he should copy after nature, on separate papers, the different effects of trees in general, and the different effects of each kind in particular, with their trunks, foliage, and colours. He should also take the same method with some sorts of plants; because their variety is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ornament to terraces on fore-grounds. He ought likewise to study the effects of the sky in the several times of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and seasons of the year, in the various dispositions of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, both in serene, thundering, and stormy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; and in the off-shoot, the several sorts of rocks, waters, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> objects. These drawings, which may be made at times, should be collected together; and all that relate to one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> be put into a book, to which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> may have recourse at any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> for what he wants. Now, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the fine effects of nature, whether in shape or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, whether for an entire <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> or a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of one, be the artist's study; and if the difficulty lies in choosing those effects well, he must for this purpose be born with good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and a fine genius; and this genius must be cultivated by the observations which ought to be made on the works of the best masters, how they choose nature, and how, while they corrected her, according to their art, they preserved her character. With these advantages, derived from nature, and perfected by art, the painter cannot fail to make a good choice; and, by distinguishing between the good and the bad, must needs find great instruction, even from the most <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> things. To improve themselves in this kind of studies, painters have taken several methods. There are some artists who have designed after nature, and in the open fields; and have there quite finished those parts which they had chosen, but without adding any colour to them. Others have drawn, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>-colours, in a middle-tint, on strong <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>; and found this method convenient, because, the colours sinking, they could put colour on colour, though different from each other. For this purpose they took with them a flat box, which commodiously held their pallet, pencils, oil, and colours. This method, which indeed requires several implements, is doubtless the best for drawing nature more particularly, and with greater exactness, especially if, after the work be dry and varnished, the artist return to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where he drew, and retouch the principal Landscape, things after nature. Others have only drawn the out-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of objects, and slightly washed them in colours near the life, for the ease of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. Others have attentively observed such parts as they had a mind to retain, and contented themselves with committing them to their memory, which upon occasion gave them a faithful account of them. Others have made drawings in pastil and wash together. Others, with more curiosity and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, have gone several times to the places which were to their taste: the first time they only made choice of the parts, and drew them correctly; and the other times were spent in observing the variety of colouring, and its alterations through change of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. Now these several methods are very good, and each may be practised as best suits the student and his temper: but they require the necessaries of painting, as colours, pencils, pastils, and leisure. Nature, however, at certain times, presents extraordinary, but transient beauties, and such as can be of no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the artist who has not, as much time as is necessary to imitate what he admires. The best way, perhaps, to make advantage of such momentary occasions, is this: The painter being provided with a quire of paper, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK_LEAD"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, let him quickly, but slightly, design what he sees extraordinary; and, to remember the colouring, let him mark the principal parts with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, which he may explain at the bottom of the paper, as far as is necessary for himself to understand them: a cloud, for instance, may be marked A, another cloud B, a light C, a mountain D, a terrace E, and so on. And having repeated these letters at the bottom of the paper, let him write against each, that it is of such or such a colour; or for greater brevity, only blue, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, violet, grey, &c. or any other shorter abbreviation. After this, he must go to painting as soon as possible; otherwise most of what he has observed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>, in a little time, slip out of his memory. This method is the more useful, as it not only prevents our losing an infinity of sudden and transitory beauties, but also helps, by means of the aforesaid marks and characters, to perfect the other methods we have mentioned. If it be asked, Which is the properest time for these studies? the answer is, That nature should be studied at all times, because she is to be represented at all seasons; but autumn yields the most plentiful <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> for her fine effects: the mildness of that season, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the sky, the richness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and the variety of objects, are powerful inducements with the painter to make the proper inquiries for improving his genius and perfecting his art. But as we cannot see or observe every thing, it is very commendable to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of other men's studies, and to look upon them as if they were our own. Raphael sent some young men into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> to design such things as he thought would be of service to him, and accordingly made use of them as to good purpose as if he himself had designed them on the spot: for this, Raphael is so far from deserving censure, that he ought, on the contrary, to be commended; as an example, that painters ought to leave no way untried for improving in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>. The landscape painter may, may, accordingly, make use of the works of all those who have excelled in any kind, in order to acquire a good manner; like the bees, which gather their variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> from different flowers. 38. General remarks on Landscapes. As the general rules of painting are the basis of all the several kinds of it, we must refer the landscape painter to them, or rather suppose him to be well acquainted with them. We shall here only make some general remarks on this kind of painting. I. Landscape supposes the knowledge and practice of the principal rules in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, in order to maintain <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>. II. The higher the leaves of trees are to the earth, the larger they are, and the greener; as being aptest to receive, in abundance, the sap which nourishes them; and the upper branches begin first to take the redness or yellowness which colours them in autumn. But it is otherwise in plants; for their stocks renew all the year round, and their leaves succeed one another, at a considerable distance of time, insomuch that nature, employed in producing new leaves to adorn the stock as it rises, does by degrees <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> the under ones; which, having first performed their office, are the first that die: but this effect is more visible in some than in others. III. The under parts of all leaves are of a brighter green than the upper, and almost always incline to the silverish; and those which are <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>-thrashed are known from others by that colour: but if we view them from beneath, when penetrated by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s rays, they discover such a fine and lively green as is far beyond all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>. IV. There are five principal things which give spirit to landscape, viz. figures, animals, waters, wind-shaken trees, and thinness of pencilling; to which add <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, when there is occasion to introduce it. V. When one colour predominates throughout a landscape, as one green in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, or one red in autumn, the piece will look either as of one colour, or else as unfinished. We have seen many of Bourdon's landscapes, which, by handling the corn one way throughout, have lost much of their beauty, though the situations and waters were very pleasant. The ingenious painter must endeavour to correct, and, as they say, redeem the harsh unsightly colouring of winter and spring by means of figures, waters, and buildings; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> and autumn subjects are of themselves capable of great variety. VI. Titian and Carrache are the best models for inspiring good taste, and leading the painter into a good track, with regard to forms and colours. He must use all his efforts to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a just idea of the principles which those great men have left us in their works; and to have his imagination filled with them, if he would advance by degrees towards that perfection which the artist should always have in view. VII. The landscapes of these two masters teach us a great many things, of which discourse can give us no exact idea, nor any general principle. Which way, for example, can the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of trees in general be determined, as we determine those of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body? The tree has no settled proportions; most of its beauty lies in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> of its branches, an unequal distribution of boughs, and, in short, a kind of whimsical variety, which nature delights in, and of which the painter becomes a judge when he has thoroughly relished the works of the two masters aforesaid. But we must say, in Titian's praise, that the path he struck out is the surest; because he has exactly imitated nature in its variety with an exquisite taste, and fine colouring: whereas Carrache, though an able artist, has not, more than others, been free from manner in his landscapes. VIII. One of the greatest perfections of landscape, in the variety it represents, is a faithful imitation of each particular character: as its greatest fault is, a licentious practice, which brings us to do things by rote. IX. Among those things which are painted practically, we ought to intermix some done after nature, to induce the spectator to believe that all are so. X. As there are styles of thought, so there are also styles of execution. We have handled the two relating to thought, viz. the heroic and pastoral; and find that there are two also with regard to execution, viz. the firm style, and the polished; these two concern the pencil, and the more or less ingenious way of conducting it. The firm style gives life to work, and excuse for bad choice: and the polished finishes and brightens every thing; it leaves no employment for the spectator's imagination, which pleases itself in discovering and finishing things which it ascribes to the artist, though, in fact, they proceed only from itself. The polished style degenerates into the soft and dull, if not supported by a good opening or situation; but when those two characters meet, the picture is fine. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. III. Of Portraiture. 39. If painting be an imitation of nature, it is doubly so in a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a>; which not only represents a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> in general, but such an one as may be distinguished from all others. And as the greatest perfection of a portrait is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> likeness, so the greatest of its faults is to resemble a person for whom it was not made; since there are not in the world two persons quite like one another. But before we proceed to the particulars which let us into the knowledge of this imitation, it is necessary, for shortening this part of our subject, to attend to some general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>. I. Imitation is the essence of painting: and good choice is to this essence what the virtues are to a man; they raise the value of it. For this reason, it is extremely the painter's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to choose none but good heads, or favourable moments for drawing them, and such positions as may supply the want of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>. II. There are views of the natural, more or less advantageous; all depends upon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> it well, and taking it in the favourable moment. III. There is not a single person in the world who has not a peculiar character, both in body and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>. IV. Simple and genuine nature is more proper for imitation; and is a better choice than nature much formed, and embellished too artificially. V. To adorn nature too much, is doing it a violence; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> which attends it can never be free, when its ornaments are not easy. In short, in proportion as we adorn nature, we make it degenerate from itself, and. VI. Some means are more advantageous than others, to come at the same end. VII. We must not only imitate what we do see in nature, but also what we may possibly see that is advantageous in art. VIII. Things are valuable by comparison; and it is only by this we are enabled to make a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> judgment of them. IX. Painters easily accustom themselves to their own tints, and the manner of their masters: and after this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> is rooted in them, they view nature, not as she really is, but as they are used to paint her. X. It is very difficult to make a picture, the figures of which are as big as the life, to have its effect near, as at a distance. A learned picture pleases the ignorant only when it is at some distance; but judges will admire its artifice near, and its effect at a distance. XI. Knowledge makes work pleasant and easy. The traveller who knows his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, comes to his journey's end with more speed and certainty than he who inquires and gropes it out. XII. It is proper, before we begin a work, to meditate upon it, and to make a nice coloured sketch of it, for our own satisfaction, and an help to the memory. We cannot too much reflect on these propositions; and it is necessary to be well acquainted with them, that they may present themselves to our mind, of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a>, without our being at the trouble to recall them to our memory, when we are at work. There are four things necessary to make a portrait perfect; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, colouring, attitude, and dress. 40. Of Air. The air respects the lines of the face, the head-attire, and the size. The lines of the face depend upon exactness of draught, and agreement of the parts; which all together must represent the physiognomy of the person painted in such a manner, that the picture of his body may seem to be also that of his mind. It is not exactness of design in portraits that gives spirit and true air, so much as the agreement of the parts at the very moment when the disposition and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a> of the sitter are to be <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> off. We see several portraits which, though correctly designed, have a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, languishing, and stupid air; whilst others, less correct in design, strike us however, at first sight, with the sitter's character. Few painters have been careful enough to put the parts well together: Sometimes the mouth is smiling, and the eyes are sad; at other times, the eyes are cheerful, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> lank: by which means their work has a false air, and looks unnatural. We ought therefore to mind, that, when the sitter puts on a smiling air, the eyes <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, the corners of the mouth draw up towards the nostrils, the cheeks swell, and the eyebrows widen: but in a melancholy air, these parts have a contrary effect. The eye-brows, being raised, give a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and noble air; but if arched, an air of astonishment. Of all the parts of the face, that which contributes most to likeness is the nose; it is therefore of great moment to set and draw it well. Though the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of the head seems to be part of the dress, which is capable of various forms, without altering the air of the face; yet the head-attire which one has been most accustomed to creates such a likeness, that we scarce know a familiar acquaintance on his putting on a periwig somewhat different from that which he used to wear. It is necessary therefore, as far as possible, to take the air of the head-ornament, and make it accompany and set off that of the face, if there be no reason to the contrary. As to the stature, it contributes so much to likeness, that we very often know people without seeing their face: It is therefore extremely proper to draw the size after the sitter himself, and in such an attitude as we think fit; which was Vandyke's method. Here let us remark, that, in sitting, the person appears to be of a less free make, through the heaving of his shoulders; wherefore, to adjust his size, it is proper to make him stand for a small time, swaying in the posture we would give him, and then make our observation. But here occurs a difficulty, which we shall endeavour to examine: "Whether it is proper, in portraiture, to correct the defects of nature?" Likeness being the essence of portraiture, it would seem that we ought to imitate defects as well as beauties, since by this means the imitation will be more complete: It would be even hard to prove the contrary to one who would undertake the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of this position. But ladies and gentlemen do not much approve of those painters who entertain such sentiments, and put them in practice. It is certain that some complaisance in this respect is due to them; and there is little doubt but their pictures may be made to resemble, without displeasing them: for the effectual likeness is a just agreement of the parts that are painted with those of nature; so that we may be at no loss to know the air of the face, and the temper of the person, whose picture is before us. All deformities, therefore, when the air and temper may be discovered without them, ought to be either corrected or omitted in women's and young men's portraits. A nose somewhat awry may be helped, or a shrivelled neck, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> shoulders, adapted to good air, without going from one extreme to another. But this must be done with great <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>: for, by endeavouring to correct nature too much, we insensibly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into a method of giving a general air to all our portraits; just as, by confining ourselves too much to the defects and littlenesses of nature, we are in danger of falling into the low and tattleless manner. But in the faces of heroes and men of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, distinguished either by dignities, virtues, or great qualities, we cannot be too exact, whether the parts be beautiful or not: for portraits of such persons are to be standing monuments to posterity; in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, every thing in a picture is precious that is faithful. But after whatever manner the painter acquires himself in this point, let him never forget good air nor <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>; and that there are, in the natural, advantageous moments for hitting them off. 41. Of Colouring.—Colouring, in portraiture, is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of nature, discovering the true temper of persons; and the temper being essential to likeness, it ought to be handled as exactly as the design. This part is the more valuable, as it is rare and difficult to hit. A great many painters have come to a likeness by strokes and outlines; Portraiture: outlines; but certainly they are few who have shewn in colours the tempers of persons. Two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> are necessary in colouring; exactness of tints, and the art of setting them off. The former is acquired by practice, in examining and comparing the colours we see in life with those by which we would imitate it: and the art of those tints consists in knowing what one colour will produce when set by another, and in making good what either distance or time may abate of the glow and freshness of the colours. A painter who does nothing more than what he sees, will never arrive at a perfect imitation; for though his work may seem, on the easel, to be good to him, it may not appear so to others, and perhaps even to himself, at a distance. A tint which, near, appears disjointed, and of one colour, may look of another at a distance, and be confounded in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> it belongs to. If you would have your work, therefore, to produce a good effect in the place where it is to hang, both the colours and lights must be a little loaded; but learnedly, and with discretion. In this point consult Titian, Rubens, Vandyke, and Rembrandt's methods; for indeed their art is wonderful. The tints usually require three times of observation. The first is at the person's first sitting <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, when he has more spirit and colour than ordinary; and this is to be noted in the first <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of his sitting. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is when, being composed, his look is as usual; which is to be observed in the second hour. And the third is when, through tiredomeness by sitting in one posture, his colour alters to what weariness usually creates. On which account, it is best to keep to the sitter's usual tint, a little improved. He may also rise, and take some turns about the room, to gain fresh spirits, and shake off or prevent tiredomeness. In draperies, all sorts of colours do not <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> all sorts of persons. In men's portraits, we need only observe great truth, and great force: but in women's there must also be charms; whatever beauty they have must appear in a fine light, and their blemishes must by some means or other be softened. For this reason, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, lively, and bright tint, ought never to be let off by a fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, which would make it look like <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>; but rather by colours inclining to green, blue, or grey, or such others as, by their opposition, may make the tint appear more flecky than usual in fair women. Vandyke often made a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FILLET">fillet</a>-motif coloured curtain for his ground; but that colour is soft and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. Brown women, on the other hand, who have yellow enough in their tints to support the character of fleshiness, may very well have yellowish draperies, in order to bring down the yellow of their tints, and make them look the fresher; and, near very high-coloured and lively carnations, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> does wonders. In grounds, two things are observable; the tone and the colour. The colour is to be considered in the same manner as those of draperies, with respect to the head. The tone must be always different from the mass it supports, and of which it is the ground, that the objects coming upon it may not seem transparent, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and raised. The colour of the hair of the head usually determines the tone of the ground; and when the former is a bright chestnut, we are often embarrassed, unless helped by means of a curtain, or some accident of the claro obscuro, supposed to be behind, or unless the ground is a sky. We must further observe, that where a ground is neither curtain nor landscape, or such like, but is plain and like a wall, it ought to very much party-coloured, with almost imperceptible patches or stains; for, besides its being so in nature, the picture will look the more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>. 42. Of Attitude, or Posture. Attitudes ought to suit the ages and qualities of persons and their tempers. In old men and women, they should be grave, majestic, and sometimes bold: and generally, in women, they ought to have a noble simplicity, and modest cheerfulness; for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> ought to be the character of women; a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> infinitely beyond coquetry! and indeed coquettes themselves care not to be painted such. Attitudes are of two kinds; one in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, the other at rest. Those at rest may suit every person: but those in motion are proper for young people only, and are hard to be expressed; because a great part of the hair and drapery must be moved by the air; motion, in painting, being never better expressed than by such agitations. The attitudes at rest must not appear so much at rest as to seem to represent an inactive person, and one who sits for no other purpose but to be a copy. And though the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> that is represented be at rest, yet the painter, if he thinks fit, may give it a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> drapery, provided the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> or ground be not a chamber or close place. It is above all things necessary that the figures which are not employed should appear to satisfy the spectator's curiosity; and for this purpose show themselves in such an action as suits their tempers and conditions, as if they would inform him what they really were: and as most people pretend to sincerity, honesty, and greatness of mind, we must avoid, in attitudes, all manner of affectation; every thing there must appear easy and natural, and discover more or less spirit, nobleness, and majesty, in proportion to the person's character and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. In a word, the attitudes are the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of portraits; and the skilful painter ought to give great <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to them. But the best attitudes are such as induce the spectator to think that the sitter took a favourable opportunity of being seen to advantage, and without affectation. There is only one thing to be observed with regard to women's portraits, in whatever attitude they are placed; which is, that they sway in such a manner as to give their face but little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>; and that we carefully examine whether the lady appear most beautiful in a smiling or in a serious air, and conduct ourselves accordingly. Let us now proceed to the next article. 43. Of Practice in Portraiture. According to De Piles, portraiture requires three different fittings and operations; to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, dead-colouring, second-colouring, and retouching or finishing. Before the painter dead-colours, he must attentively consider what aspect will best suit the sitter, by putting him in different positions, if we have not any settled design before us: and when we have determined this, it is of the last <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to put the parts well together, by comparing always one part with another; for not only the portrait acquires a greater likeness when well designed, but it is troublesome to make alterations at the second fitting, when the artist must only think of painting, that Portraiture, that is, of disposing and uniting his colours. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">Experience</a> tells us, that the dead-colouring ought to be clean, because of the slope and transparency of the colours, especially in the shades: and when the parts are well put together, and become clammy, they must be judiciously sweetened and melted into each other; yet without taking away the air of the picture, that the painter may have the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of finishing it, in proportion as he draws. But if fiery geniuses do not like this method of scumbling, let them only mark the parts slightly, and so far as is necessary, for giving an air. In dead-colouring, it is proper to put in rather too little than too much hair about the forehead; that, in finishing, we may be at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to place it where we please, and to paint it with all possible softness and delicacy. If, on the contrary, you sketch upon the forehead a lock which may appear to be of a good taste, and becoming the work, you may be puzzled in finishing it, and not find the life exactly in the same position as you would paint it. But this observation is not meant for men of skill and consummate experience, who have nature in their heads, and make her submit to their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>. The business of the second fitting is, to put the colours well in their places, and to paint them in a manner that is suitable to the fitter and to the effect we propose: But before they are made clammy, we ought to examine afresh whether the parts are rightly placed, and here and there to give some touches towards likeness, that, when we are assured of it, the work may go on with greater satisfaction. If the painter understands what he is about, and the portrait be justly designed, he ought as much as possible to work quick; the fitter will be better pleased, and the work will by this means have the more spirit and life. But this readiness is only the effect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> study and experience; for we may well be allowed a considerable time to find out a road that is easy, and such as we must often travel in. Before we retouch or finish, it is proper to terminate the hair, that, on finishing the carnations, we may be able to judge of the effect of the whole head. If, at the second fitting, we cannot do all we intended, which often happens, the third makes up the loss, and gives both spirit, physiognomy, and character. If we would paint a portrait at once, we must load the colouring; but neither sweeten, nor drive, nor very much oil it: and if we dip the pencil in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> as the work advances, this will readily enable us to put colour on colour, and to mix them without driving. The use and sight of good pictures give greater light into things than words can express: What hits one artist's understanding and temper may be disagreeable to another's; and almost all painters have taken different ways, though their principles were often the same. We are told that a friend of Vandyke's having observed to him how little time he bestowed on his portraits, Vandyke answered, "That at first he worked hard, and took great pains, to acquire a reputation, and also to get a swift hand, against the time he should work for his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>." Vandyke's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> is said to have been this: He appointed both the day and hour for the person's sitting, and worked not above an hour on any portrait, either in rubbing in or finishing; so that as soon as his clock informed him that the hour was out, he rose up, and made a bow to the fitter, to signify, that he had done enough for that day, and then appointed another hour for some other day; whereupon his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> came to clean his pencils, and brought a fresh pallet, whilst he was receiving another fitter, whose day and hour he had before appointed. By this method he worked on several pictures the same day, with extraordinary expedition. After having lightly dead-coloured the face, he put the fitter into some attitude which he had before contrived; and on a grey paper, with white and black crayons, he designed, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an hour, his shape and drapery, which he disposed in a grand manner and an exquisite taste. After this, he gave the drawing to the skilful people he had about him, to paint after the fitter's own cloaths, which, at Vandyke's request, were sent to him for that purpose. When his disciples had done what they could to these draperies, he lightly went over them again; and so, in a little time, by his great knowledge, displayed the art and truth which we at this day admire in them. As for hands, he had in his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> people of both sexes, whom he paid, and who served as models. This conduct of Vandyke, however, is mentioned rather to gratify the reader's curiosity, than to excite his imitation; he may choose as much of it as he pleases and as suits his own genius, and leave the rest. We must observe by the way, that there is nothing so rare as fine hands, either in the design or colouring. It is therefore convenient to cultivate, if we can, a friendship with some women who will take pleasure in serving for a copy: The way to win them is, to praise their beauty exceedingly. But if an opportunity serves of copying hands after Vandyke, it must not be let slip; for he drew them with a surprising delicacy, and an admirable colouring. It is of great service to copy after the manners which come nearest to nature; as are those of Titian and Vandyke. We must, at such times, believe them to be nature itself; and, at some distance, consider them as such, and say to ourselves—What colour and tint shall I use for such a part? And then, coming near the picture, we ought to examine, whether we are right, or not; and to make a fixed rule of what we have discovered, and did not practise before without uncertainty. It is recommended, before we begin colouring, to catch the very first moments, which are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> the most agreeable and most advantageous, and to keep them in our memory for use when we are finishing; for the fitter, growing tired with being long in the same place, loses those spirits, which, at his first sitting down, gave beauty to the parts, and conveyed to the tint more lively blood, and a fresher colour. In short, we must join to truth a probable and advantageous possibility, which, far from abating likeness, serves rather to set it off. For this end, we ought to begin with observing the ground of a tint, as well what it is in lights as in shades; for the shades are only beautiful as they are proportioned to the light. We must observe if the tint be very lively; whether it partake of yellowness, and where that yellowness is placed; Decorations placed; because usually, towards the end of the sitting, fatigue diffuses a general yellowness, which makes us forget what parts were of this colour, and what were not, unless we had taken due notice of it before. For this reason, at the second sitting, the colours must be everywhere readily clapped in, and such as appear at the first sitting down; for these are always the finest. The surest way to judge of colours is by comparison; and to know a tint, nothing is better than to compare it with linen placed next it, or else placed next to the natural object, if there is occasion. We say this only to those who have little practised nature. The portrait being now supposed to be as much finished as you are able, nothing remains, but, at some reasonable distance, to view both the picture and sitter together, in order to determine with certainty, whether there is anything still wanting to perfect the work. Sect. IV. Of Theatric Decorations: the Designs for Furniture, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMBROIDERY">Embroidery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">Carriages</a>, &c. 46. Of Theatrical Decorations. This is a particular art which unites several of the general parts of painting with the knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, perspective, &c. They who apply themselves to it, would do well to design their decorations by day, and to colour them by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>-light, as they will be much better able to judge of the effect of a painting intended to be viewed by that light. It is proper also to caution the young painter to avoid, as much as possible, the uniting the imitations of nature with nature itself; that is, he should not introduce with his decorations living horses, or other animals, real fountains or caledes, trees, or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, &c. For such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> are the effect of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and a bad taste; they are the resource of painters of little ability; they discover a sterility of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, and produce great inconvenience in the representation. Those pieces which they call moving pictures, where the painted landscape remains immovable, and the figures move by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, form a part of these decorations; and there are some of them, as those of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> and Ghent, that have a pleasing effect. 47. The designs for furniture, carriages, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, and other branches of manufacture, form also a very important article of painting in general, and of academy painting in particular. This is a distinct branch of the art; and without doubt not the least useful of its parts, as it concurs so essentially to the success of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and consequently to the prosperity of a state; and it is an art, to which it were much to be wished that youth of ability and invention would apply themselves. See the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JAPANNING">Japanning</a> and Porcelain. Sect. V. Enumeration of the different Methods of Painting, or the different Means and Materials that painters make use of to imitate all visible objects on a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> superficies. 48. Those now in practice are, 1. Painting in oil; which is preferable to all other other methods, as it is more susceptible of all sorts of expressions, of more perfect gradations of colours, and is at the same time more durable. 2. Mosaic painting; an invention truly wonderful; it is composed of a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small pieces of marble of different colours, joined together with stucco. The works of this kind are made principally at Rome, where this art has been carried so far as to resemble the paintings of the greatest masters; and of these are made monuments for the latest posterity. Paintings in fresco; which is by drawing, with colours diluted with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, on a wall newly plastered, and with which they so incorporate, that they perish only with the stucco itself. This is principally used on ceilings. 4. Painting in water-colours; that is, with colours mixed with water and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a>, or paste, &c. 5. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIATURE">Miniature</a> painting; which differs from the preceding only as it represents objects in the least discernible magnitudes; and is consequently vastly more delicate, seeing it is performed by the smallest strokes possible; whereas the others have the full scope of the pencil. 6. Painting in crayons; for which purpose colours, either simple or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, are mixed with gum, and made into a kind of hard paste like chalk, and with which they draw on paper or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>. 7. Painting in enamel; which is done on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, with mineral colours that are dried by fire, and become very durable. The paintings on the porcelain of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, on Delft <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, &c., are so many sorts of enamel. 8. Painting in wax, or encaustic painting: This is a new invention, and in which there are in France performances highly pleasing. It is done with wax-mixed with varnish and colours. 9. Painting on glass; of which there are various kinds. See all the articles here enumerated, explained in the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">PAIR</a>; two of a sort, a couple.

PAIRING

Pages 328-329

the uniting <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> joining in couples. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a> of pairing is bestowed on every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of animals to which it is necessary for rearing their young; and on no other species. All wild birds <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a>; but with a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between such as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> their nests on trees, and such as place them on the ground. The young of the former, being hatched <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>, and without feathers, require the nursing care of both parents till they be able to fly. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> feeds his mate on the nest, and cheers her with a song. As soon as the young are hatched, singing yields to a more necessary occupation, that of providing food for a numerous issue; a task that requires both parents. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAGLES">Eagles</a> and other birds of prey build on trees, or on other inaccessible spots. They not only pair, but continue in pairs all the year round; and the same pair procreates year after year. This at least is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of eagles: the male and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> hunt together, unless during incubation, during which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the female is fed by the male. A greater <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> than a single pair are never seen in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. Gregarious birds pair, in order probably to prevent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> confined to a narrow space. This is the case particularly of pigeons and rooks. The male and female sit on the eggs alternately, and divide the care of feeding their young. Partridges, plovers, pheasants, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-fowl, grouse, and other kinds that place their nests on the ground, have the instinct of pairing; but differ from such as build on trees in the following particular, that after the female is impregnated, she completes her task without needing any help from the male. Retiring from him, she chooses a safe spot for her nest, where she can find plenty of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> and grass-feed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and her young, as soon as hatched, take foot, and seek food for themselves. The only remaining duty incumbent on the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a> is, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them to proper places for food, and to call them together when danger impends. Some males, provoked at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFECTION">defection</a> of their mates, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the eggs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they stumble on them. Eider ducks pair like other birds that place their nests on the ground; and the female finishes her nest with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> plucked from her own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. If the nest be destroyed by the down, which is remarkably warm and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>, she makes another nest as before. If she is robbed a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time, she makes a third nest; but the male furnishes the down. A lady of spirit observed, that the eider duck may give a lesson to many a married woman, who is more disposed to pluck her husband than herself. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a> never pair: in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, the cock on an eminence crows, and claps his wings; and all the females within hearing instantly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to him. Pairing birds, excepting those of prey, flock together in February, in order to choose their mates. They soon disperse; and are not seen afterward but in pairs. Pairing is unknown to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> that feed on grass. To such it would be useless; as the female gives suck to her young while she herself is feeding. If M. Buffon deserves <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, the roe-deer are an exception. They pair, though they feed on grass, and have but one litter in a year. Beasts of prey, such as lions, tygers, wolves, pair not. The female is left to shift for herself and for her young; which is a laborious task, and often so unsuccessful as to shorten the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of many of them. Pairing is essential to birds of prey, because incubation leaves the female no sufficient time to hunt for food. Pairing is not necessary to beasts of prey, because their young can bear a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> fast. Add another reason, that they would multiply too fast by pairing, as to prove troublesome neighbours to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a>. Among animals that pair not, males fight desperately about a female. Such a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> among horned cattle is finely described by Lucretius. Nor is it unusual for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight lions to wage bloody <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> for a single female. The same reason that makes pairing necessary for gregarious birds, obtains with respect to gregarious quadrupeds; those especially who store up food for winter, and during that season live in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. Discord among such would be attended with worse consequences than even among lions and bulls, who are not confined to one place. The beavers, with respect to pairing, resemble birds that place their nests on the ground. As soon as the young are produced, the males abandon their stock of food to their mates, and live at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>; but return frequently to visit them while they are suckling their young. Hedgehogs pair as well as several of the monkey-kind. We are not well acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of these animals; but it would appear that the young require the nursing care of both parents. Seals have a singular economy. Polygamy seems to be a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> among them, as a male associates with several females. The sea-turtle has no occasion to pair, as the female concludes her task by laying her eggs in the sand. The young are hatched by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and immediately crawl to the sea.

PAISLEY

Pages 329-330

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RENFREWSHIRE">Renfrewshire</a>, in Scotland, situated about six miles west of Glasgow, on the river <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CART">Cart</a>, over which there are two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-bridges of two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> each, and one which consists of three arches. The town is very <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>; but was of much less <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> formerly than it is at present. The old <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of it runs from east to west upon the south slope of a ridge of hills, from which there is a fine prospect of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Glasgow and the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but to the southward, the view terminates in a ridge of green hills, about two miles distant. Including the late buildings and suburbs, it is fully a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and nearly as much in breadth. On the east side of the river Cart, stand the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> and new town; which last was lately freed off by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Abercorn, and already consists of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of handsome buildings. The streets are here laid out in a regular manner, but (rather unfortunately for the conveniency and elegance of some of the houses) not in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>. Here the Earl of Abercorn has built, at his own expense, one of the largest, most commodious, and most elegant inns in Scotland. In the vicinity of this his Lordship is likewise to build several convenient and necessary market-places. A little way south of the inn stands the abbey-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the only one which Paisley, before the year 1735, required. This church, when entire, has been a most noble <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and consisted of several distinct and separate places of worship: what now remains of this magnificent Gothic structure is not yet unworthy the notice of the curious in antiquities. The next church, called the Laigh-Church, is built in form of a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, very well laid out, and capable of containing a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number of people. The one called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a>-Church, is a very fine building; and as it stands on the top of a hill, its lofty spire is visible at a great distance. This church is an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of 82 feet by 62 within the walls, built of free-stone well smoothed, having rustic corners and an elegant stone cornice at the top. In the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> (which is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a> covered with slate, having a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> on the top), there is something very curious, and it is admired by every person of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. The Middle <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> New Church is a very neat building, on much the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> with the High Church, but not quite so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. Besides these, there are also two Seceding Meeting-houses and a Church of Relief. The town-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is a very handsome building of cut stone, with a tall spire and a clock. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-market has a genteel <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of cut stone, and is one of the neatest and most commodious of this kind in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Butchers-meat, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, cheese, fish, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and several other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, are sold here by what they call the tron-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, of 22 English ounces and an half. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>-house is a large building, very well laid out; and stands opposite to the quay, in a fine free <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>. It is supported by a small tax laid upon the inhabitants quarterly. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a> by the Abbey-Church is the Earl of Abercorn's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, the greatest curiosity in Paisley. It is a vaulted Gothic chapel, without pulpit, pew, or any other ornament, but has the finest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECHO">echo</a> perhaps in the world. When the end door (the only one it has) is shut, the noise is equal to a loud and not very distant clap of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> you strike a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of music, you hear the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> gradually ascending, with a great number of repetitions, till it dies away as if at an immense distance, and all the while diffusing itself through the circumambient air. If a good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> sings, or a musical <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> is well played upon, the effect is inexpressibly agreeable. The deepest, as well as the most acute tones, are distinctly reverberated, and these in regular intervals of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. When a musical instrument is sounded, it has the effect of a number of instruments of a like size and kind playing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a>. When a number of different instruments in unison sounds the same note, a good <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a> is able to distinguish the variety of sound produced by each. A single instrument sounding a particular note, and then instantly its fifth, or any other concordant note, the two sounds can be heard, as it were, running into and uniting with each other in a manner peculiarly agreeable. But the effect of a variety of instruments playing in concert, is particularly charming, and must excite such emotions in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> as it is impossible to describe. In this chapel is the monument of Marjory Bruce; she was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Robert Bruce, and wife of Walter, great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of Scotland, and mother of Robert II. In this same chapel were interred <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> Muir and Euphemia Ross, both consorts to Robert II. In 1160, a fine <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> was founded by Walter, great steward of Scotland; but of this there are scarce any vestiges now remaining. The vestiges of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> and praetorium, at the west end of the town, are at present almost annihilated. It was supposed to be vaulted underneath. The inhabitants of Paisley, in 1746, were computed at no more than 4000; but from a very accurate survey which has <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> been made, the number of families in Paisley and suburbs is found to be 3723; and allowing 4½ persons to each family, the number of inhabitants <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be 16,753. Paisley is now the first manufacturing town in Scotland, and is greatly celebrated on account of some of its branches. The manufacture of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>, in this respect, first claims our notice. This branch is brought here to the utmost perfection, and is wrought to an amazing variety of patterns. It has been just computed, that there have been no less than 5000 weavers employed in Paisley and in the country adjacent, in this branch, last year (1781); and the number of widowers, warpers, clippers, and others necessary in other parts of the silk-manufacture, has been likewise computed to be no less than 5000. Each loom will produce in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> value 70l. yearly; the whole will then be 350,000 l. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> branch is likewise carried on here to a very considerable amount, particularly the manufacture of lawns; and vast quantities of foreign yarn are annually imported from France, Germany, &c. for this branch, besides what is made of our home-manufactured yarn. It appears from the stamp-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s books, that from 1st November 1780 to 1st November 1781, there were stamped at Paisley no less than 1,248,843 yards, value 105,930l. 19s. 10½. The making of white stitching thread was introduced into this town about 50 or 60 years ago. A <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> in this place lately discovered the method of making what is called glazed white-thread, to as great perfection as that made by Mr Leland and Son, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The value of this branch is computed at about 60,000l. annually. There are also several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of a more local <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. There are three of hard-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> and tallow-candles, and one of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-soap. The candles, especially the moulded ones, are reckoned the best and most elegant that have been made in Scotland; and great quantities is sent into England, to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and to the West Indies. The annual amount of these last branches are estimated at nearly 20,000l. There are also two or three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a>-works, and a porter brewery, in town; and in the neighbourhood there is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COOPER">cooper</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, a calico <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> work, and two works for the cotton <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> manufacture. The river on which Paisley stands runs from south to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; and falls into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, after it has joined the conflux of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Grief and Black-Cart at Inchinnan <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, about three miles below the town. At <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>, vessels of 40 tons burthen come up to the quay. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> is of great importance to the inhabitants; for in this way they are frequently served with fish of different kinds, and can send their goods and manufactures to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORT_GLASGOW">Port-Glasgow</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREENOCK">Greenock</a>, and to Glasgow likewise; and now, when the canal is finished, they have also a communication with the frith of Forth. Paisley was created a burgh of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> in the year 1488; and the affairs of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> are managed by three bailies, of which the eldest is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of the peace, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, a town-clerk, and 17 counsellors, who are annually elected upon the first Monday after Michaelmas. It gives the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of baron to the earls of Abercorn; the first of whom was a younger son of the Duc de <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHATELLERAULT">Chatellerault</a>. The black-book of Paisley, frequently mentioned in Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, was a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> of the public affairs and remarkable events, kept by the monks who resided in the monastery already mentioned. It agreed in every material fact with the Scotti-chronicon of Fordun; and is by many thought to be the same performance.

PAITA

Pages 330-330

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, and in the audience of Quito. The town consists of about 200 houses but one story <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and the walls are made of split <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANE">cane</a> and mud, and the roofs only a covering of leaves. The only <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of Paita is a fort without either ditch <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> out-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>; but it is surrounded by a brick wall of little or no strength, on which are mounted eight pieces of cannon. Commodore Anson got possession of this fort in 1741; and took and burnt the town, because the governor refused to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> it. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 80°. S. Lat. 5°. 5'.

PALACE

Pages 330-331

Palatium, a name generally given to the dwelling-houses of kings, princes, and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> personages; and taking different epithets, according to the the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the inhabitants, as imperial palace, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> palace, pontifical palace, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> palace, ducal palace, episcopal palace, &c. PALACE-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">Court</a>. See MARSHALSEA. PALÆMON, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Melicertes, in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a marine god, was the son of Athamas, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Thebes and Ino. The latter, fearing the rage of the king her husband, took Melicertes in her arms, and leaped with him into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, when they were both changed into marine deities; the mother under the name Leucothea, supposed by some to be the same with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a>; and her son under that of Palemon, or Portunus, a god who presided over sea-ports. Pausanias says, that Melicertes was saved on the back of a dolphin, and his dead body thrown on the isthmus of Corinth, where <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SISYPHUS">Sisyphus</a>, his uncle, who reigned in that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, instituted to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> the Isthmian games. PALÆMON (Q. Rhemminus), a Latin grammarian, born at Vicenza, was the son of slave. He taught at Rome with great applause under Tiberius and Claudius, and Juvenal mentions him with praises. We have only some fragments of his works. PALÆPAPHOS, (Strabo, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Pliny), a town of Cyprus, where stood a temple of Venus; and an adjoining town called New Paphos; where St Paul struck Elymas <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>, and converted the proconsul Sergius Paulus. PALÆSTRA, in Grecian antiquity, a public <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, where the youth exercised themselves in wrestling, running, playing at quoits, &c. PALÆSTROPHYLAX, was the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the palaestra, and the exercises performed there.

PALAMEDIA

Pages 331-331

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of grallæ. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> is conical, the lower mandible being crooked; and the feet have three divided toes. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, both natives of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>.

PALARIA

Pages 331-331

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> performed at a stake by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. The stake being fixed in the ground, and five feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> above it, the young undisciplined soldiers advanced against it, armed with a hurdle and cudgel, instead of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> and shield, and went through all the rules of attack and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> actually engaged with an adversary. Sometimes they stood at a distance, and attacked with missile weapons; at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> using all the requisite motions for defending themselves, and warding off what might be thrown against them.

PALATE

Pages 331-331

in anatomy, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> that composes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the upper and inner <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, of the mouth. The palate has much the same structure with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>; but it has also a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of glands, discovered so early as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Fallopius: these are principally situated in the hinder part near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-UVULA">uvula</a>, where it is pendulous, in the manner of a curtain, which part is called the velum, or claviflora, of the palate.
