The glands situated particularly in this part, secrete a mucous fluid, serving to lubricate the mouth and throat, and to facilitate deglutition: they have a great number of apertures there for the discharge of this humour into the mouth. The great uses of this membrane are to defend the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the palate from corrupting; and for preventing, by its claviflora or velum, the things to be swallowed from getting up into the nostrils.

PALATINATE

Pages 331-332

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> signory, possessed Palatinately by a palatine. PALATINATE of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, a province of Germany, divided into two parts by the Rhine, called the Upper and Lower Palatinate. The former lies in the circle of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, and belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> thereof; but the latter, in the circle we are now treating, belongs to the elector Palatine. The latter <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> is bounded to the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Katzenelnbogen, the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a>, and part of the territory of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEUTONIC">Teutonic</a> order in Franconia; to the west, by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALSACE">Alsace</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Deuxponts, the county of Sponheim, the duchy of Simmern, and certain districts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of Mentz; to the south, by the duchy of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WURTEMBERG">Wurtemberg</a> and the bishopric of Spire; and to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by a part of archbishopric of Mentz and the county of Katzenelnbogen. It contains 41 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, besides several boroughs; and its greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> is about 80 miles. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is healthful, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> fruitful in corn, pasturage, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, particularly walnuts, chestnuts, and almonds. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> also breeds abundance of cattle, and is well watered by the Neckar, the Nahe, and the Rhine. In the last of these, near Germerstein and Selz, is found <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; the exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of searching for which is farmed out by the elector. The state of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> hath varied greatly here since the Reformation, Lutheranism and Calvinism having been uppermost by turns, till the electorate devolved to the Papist branches of the family, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>, with all its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> and mummery, was established anew: so that the Protestant religion is now on a very precarious footing in the Palatinate, though most of the natives are still of that persuasion: but the two sects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, namely, the Lutherans and Calvinists, have greatly contributed to their own ruin, by their mutual jealousy and animosity, being no less rancorous against one another than against their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> adversaries the Papists. The Lutherans reckon themselves 50,000 strong, and are possessed of about 83 churches; but not one half of their preachers and schoolmasters have a competent maintenance. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Calvinists clergy here is estimated at 500, and that of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> at 400. Besides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> and Jesuits colleges in this country, there is one university, namely, that of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEIDELBERG">Heidelberg</a>; but there is very little trade in it except in wine. Authors are divided about the origin of the name Palatines, or Pfalzgraves, as the Germans call them; but it seems most likely to be derived from the palatia, or palaces, which the old Frankish and German kings and Roman emperors were possessed of in different parts of the country, and over which they appointed supreme stewards or judges, who were called Palatines or Pfalzgraves. The countries where these Palatines kept their courts were, from them, called Palatinates; which name came at last to be appropriated, by way of eminence, to this country, as being the most considerable of them. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> electoral line failing in 1685, the electorate devolved to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>-William <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Neuburg; and upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>-Philip, to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Sulzbach. This elector has the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the empire, as well as the elector of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>-Luneburgh, and is the fifth in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> electors. He is also one of the vicars of the empire alternately with the elector of Bavaria, and enjoys many other prerogatives. In his own dominions, he dispenses of all vacant benefices; but allows the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, composed of two clergymen and two laymen, to present two candidates, of which he chooses one. He is also <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a> in his dominions; but he either grants them to the clergy, or salaries in lieu of them, out of the revenues of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. His title is Pfalzgrave of the Rhine; archtreasurer and elector of the holy Roman empire; duke in Bavaria, Juliers, Cleve, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERG">Berg</a>; prince of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MORS">Mors</a>; marquis of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERGEN_OP_ZOOM"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol2.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>-op-Zoom; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Veldeus, Sponheim, the Mark, and Ravenberg; and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Ravenstein. His quota to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the empire is 30 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and 138 foot, or 914 florins monthly. To the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of Wetzlar he contributes, each <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>, 404 rix-dollars, 82 kruitzers. There is an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> in this country, viz. that of St Hubert; the badge of which is a quadrangular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> pendant to a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> ribbon, with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. The whole of the elector's revenue, arising from the Palatinate, the duchies of Berg and Juliers, the feignory of Ravenstein, and the duchies of Neuburg and Sulzbach, hath been estimated at about 300,000 l. per annum. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> establishment consists of several regiments of horse and foot, besides the horse and Swiss <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>-guards. All the different courts and councils, usual in other countries for the different departments of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, are also to be found here.

PALATINE

Pages 332-333
or Count Palatine, a title anciently given to all persons who had any office or employment in the prince's palace; but afterwards conferred on those delegated by princes to hold courts of justice in the provinces; and on such among the Lords as had a palace, that is, a court of justice, in their own houses. Counties-Palatine in England.—Chester, Durham, and Lancaster, are called counties palatine. The two former are such by prescription, or immemorial custom; or, at least as old as the Norman conquest: the latter was created by king Edward III. in favour of Henry Plantagenet, first earl and then duke of Lancaster; whose heiress being married to John of Gaunt the king's son, the franchise was greatly greatly enlarged and confirmed in parliament, to honour John of Gaunt himself, whom, on the death of his father-in-law, the king had also created duke of Lancaster. Counties-palatine are so called à palatium; because the owners thereof, the earl of Chester, the bishop of Durham, and the duke of Lancaster, had in those counties jura regalia, as fully as the king hath in his palace; regalem potestatem in omnibus, as Bracton expresses it. They might pardon treasons, murders, and felonies; they appointed all judges and justices of the peace; all writs and indictments ran in their names, as in other counties in the king's; and all offences were said to be done against their peace, and not, as in other places, contra pacem domini regis. And indeed by the ancient law, in all peculiar jurisdictions, offences were said to be done against his peace in whose court they were tried; in a court-leet, contra pacem domini; in the court of a corporation, contra pacem baliivorum; in the sheriff's court or tourn, contra pacem vicecomitis. These palatine privileges (so similar to the regal independent jurisdictions usurped by the great Palatine barons on the continent during the weak and infant state of the first feudal kingdoms in Europe), were in all probability originally granted to the counties of Chester and Durham, because they bordered upon enemies countries, Wales and Scotland; in order that the owners, being encouraged by so large an authority, might be the more watchful in its defence; and that the inhabitants, having justice administered at home, might not be obliged to go out of the county, and leave it open to the enemy's incursions. And upon this account also there were formerly two other counties palatine, Pembrokehire and Hexhamshire, the latter now united with Northumberland; but these were abolished by parliament, the former in 27 Hen. VIII. the latter in 14 Eliz. And in 27 Hen. VIII. likewise, the powers before mentioned of owners of counties-palatine were abridged; the reason for their continuance in a manner ceasing: though still all writs are witnessed in their names, and all forfeitures for treason by the common law accrue to them. Of these three, the county of Durham is now the only one remaining in the hands of a subject. For the earldom of Chester, as Camden testifies, was united to the crown by Hen. III. and has ever since given title to the king's eldest son. And the county palatine, or duchy, of Lancaster was the property of Henry of Bolingbroke, the son of John of Gaunt, at the time when he wrested the crown from king Richard II. and assumed the title of Hen. IV. But he was too prudent to suffer this to be united to the crown; lest, if he lost one, he should lose the other also. For, as Plowden and Sir Edward Coke observe, "he knew he had the duchy of Lancaster by sure and indefeasible title, but that his title to the crown was not so assured: for that after the decease of Richard II. the right of the crown was in the heir of Lionel duke of Clarence, second son of Edward III.; John of Gaunt, father to this Henry IV. being but the fourth son." And therefore he procured an act of parliament, in the first year of his reign, ordaining that the duchy of Lancaster, and all other his hereditary estates, with all their royalties and franchises, should remain to him and his heirs for ever; and should remain, descend, be administered, and governed, in like manner as if he never had attained the regal dignity: and thus they descended to his son and grandson, Henry V. and Henry VI.; many new territories and privileges being annexed to the duchy by the former. Henry VI. being attainted in 1 Edward IV. this duchy was declared in parliament to have become forfeited to the crown, and at the same time an act was made to incorporate the duchy of Lancaster, to continue the county palatine (which might otherwise have determined by the attainder), and to make the same parcel of the duchy; and, farther, to vest the whole in king Edward IV. and his heirs, kings of England, for ever; but under a separate guiding and governance from the other inheritances of the crown. And in 1 Hen. VII. another act was made, to resume such part of the duchy lands as had been dismembered from it in the reign of Edward IV. and to vest the inheritance of the whole in the king and his heirs for ever, as amply and largely, and in like manner, form, and condition, separate from the crown of Eng- land and possession of the same, as the three Henrys and Edward IV., or any of them, had and held the fame. The Isle of Ely is not a county-palatine, though sometimes erroneously called so, but only a royal franchise: the bishop having, by grant of king Henry the first, jura regalia within the Isle of Ely; whereby he exercises jurisdiction over all causes, as well criminal as civil. Palatine Games, in Roman antiquity, games instituted in honour of Augustus by his wife Livia, after he had been enrolled among the gods. They were celebrated in the palace, and were confirmed by the succeeding emperors. PALATINUS Mons, or Palatium, the first mountain of Rome occupied by Romulus, and where he fixed his residence and kept his court, as did Tullus Hostilius, Augustus, and all the succeeding emperors; and hence it is that the residence of princes is called palatium. The reason of the name is variously assigned. To the east it has the Mons Celius, to the south the Aventine, to the west the Capitoline, and to the north the Forum.—Palatinus, the surname of Apollo from this place; where Augustus built a temple to that god, adorned with porticos and a library, (Horace).

PALATIUM

Pages 333-333

Pallantium (Pausanias), Palantum (Livy); Pallantum (Solinus). This last is the true <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> grandfather of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVANDER">Evander</a>, from whom it took its name, being called Pallas, not Palas: A town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, which concurred to form Megalopolis (Pausanias). From it the Palatium, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Mons Palatinus, takes also its name, according to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> and Pliny. PALATIUM Diocletiani; the villa of Diocletian, near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALONA">Salona</a>, where he died, (Eusebius). Afterwards called Spalatum; which rose to a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> from the ruins of Salona; situate in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a> on the Adriatic. Now Spalato, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPALATRO">Spalatro</a>. PALATIUM Luculli, (Plintarch), or Villa Luculli; a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between Misenum and Baiae in Campania, of wonderful structure. Now in ruins, and called <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PISCINA">Piscina</a> Mirabile. PALATO-SALPINGÆUS, ? See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> PALATO-STAPHYLINUS, of the Muscles.

PALEARIUS

Pages 333-333

was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of the greatest probity, and one of the best writers of the 16th century. He gained the esteem of the men of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and learning of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> by a noble poem on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. He was appointed professor of polite literature at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>; where his tranquillity was disturbed by contests with an envious colleague, and by the malicious aspersions of his enemies; against which, however, his eloquence proved always a sufficient defense. At last he left Sienna, and accepted the invitation of the magistrates of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>, who gave him several marks of their esteem, and settled a considerable stipend upon him. Some years after, he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>; where he was seized by order of Pope Pius V. and carried to Rome. He was convicted of having spoken in favour of the Lutherans, and against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>; and therefore was condemned to be burnt. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> was executed in 1566. He wrote several pieces in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> and prose; of which the one above-mentioned is the most esteemed.

PALENCIA

Pages 333-333

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Leon, with a rich archbishop's see. It had an university, but it was removed to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a>. It is seated in a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> on the river Carion on the frontiers of Castile, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 7'. N. Lat. 42° 10'.

PALERMO

Pages 333-333

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, rich, and handsome <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> in the Val-di-mazara, with an archbishop's see and a harbour. It was the seat of the ancient kings, and is four miles in circumference. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade; the houses are handsome and superb; it is also well fortified, and very populous. The public buildings, squares, churches, and fountains, are extremely fine. The fountain in the great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> is thought to be the finest in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the inhabitants is above 200,000; and the harbour is very large, having a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> 1300 geometrical paces in length; but the vessels that ride therein are not always very safe. There is a magnificent castle built near the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-side, wherein the viceroy resides six months in the year; and his presence draws a great number of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> to this place. This city has suffered greatly by earthquakes, particularly in 1693; and it was greatly damaged by a fire in 1730, when a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> of powder was blown up, containing 400 tons. It stands in a pleasant fruitful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and at the bottom of the gulph of the same name. E. Lon. 33° 40'. N. Lat. 38° 10'.

PALES

Pages 333-333

in Pagan worship, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of the shepherds; to whom they offered <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, in order that the might deliver them and their flocks from wild beasts and infectious diseases. This goddess is represented as an old woman.

PALESTINE

Pages 333-335

a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, situated between 36° and 38° degrees of E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. and between 31° and 34° of N. Lat. It is bounded by Mount Libanus, which divides it from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; by Mount Hermon, which separates it from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Deserta, on the east; by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Seir and the deserts of Arabia Petraea, on the south; and by the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> on the west. This once fertile and happy spot was first called the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Chanaan, from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>'s grandson. In scripture, however, it is frequently distinguished by other names; such as the land of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, the land of God, the land of Israel, &c. It received the name of Palestine from the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>, or Philistines, who possessed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of it; and it had the name of Judea, or Judaea-Palestina, from Judah, the most considerable of the twelve sons of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> have denominated it the Holy Land; partly on account of the many singular blessings it received from the divine Palestine, vine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>, and partly on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> being made the centre of God's worship and his peculiar habitation; but much more for its being the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of our Saviour's birth, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of his preaching, and manifold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>; especially the place in which he accomplished the great <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a>. As to the name of Judaea, it did not begin to receive that till after the return of the Jews from the Babylonish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, though it had been styled long before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Judah, in opposition to that of Israel, which revolted from it under Jeroboam, in the reign of Rehoboam the son of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>. But after the return, the tribe of Judah, the only one that made any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, settling at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, and in the countries adjacent, quickly gave its name to the whole territory. By profane authors it was called by many different names; such as Syria, Palestina Syria, Cælebria, Iduma, I-dumæa, and Phœnicia or Phœnice; but these are supposed only to have been given out of contempt to the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, whom they looked upon as unworthy of any other name than what distinguished the most obscure parts of the neighbouring provinces. That part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which was properly called the Land of Promise, was inclosed on the west by the Mediterranean; on the east by the lake <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASPHALTITES">Asphaltites</a>, the Jordan, and the sea of Tiberias or of Galilee, and the Samachonite lake; to the north it had the mountains of Lebanon, or rather of Antilibanus, or the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Phœnicia; and to the south, that of Edom or Idumea, from which it was likewise parted by another ridge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountains. The boundaries of the other part, which belonged to the two tribes and an half beyond the river Jordan, are not so easily defined, as well as those of the conquests made by the more prosperous kings of the Jews. All that can be said with any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> is, that the river Arnon was the first northern boundary on that side; and with respect to those on this side the Jordan, there is a considerable disagreement between the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> and Samaritan versions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of this country is likewise variously settled by geographers; some giving it no more than 170 or 180 miles from north to south, and 140 in breadth where broadest, though not much above half that breadth where narrowest. But from the latest and most accurate maps, it appears to extend near 200 miles in length, and about 80 in breadth about the middle, and about 10 or 15 more or less, where it widens or shrinks. It reaches from 31° 30' to 33° 30' N. Lat. and from 34° 50' to 37° 15' E. Long., the longest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> being about 14 hours 15 minutes. These limits are so small, considering that the country is likewise intersected by high ridges or mountains, woods, deserts, &c. that many learned men have been induced to question what we read of its fertility and populousness in former times. It must be owned, indeed, that when we compare its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and flourishing state, when it was cultivated with the utmost diligence by persons well skilled in every branch of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, with what it hath been since the total extirpation of the Jews out of it, and more especially since it fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Turks, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> is amazingly great: but when we consider the many evident causes which have contributed to effect this change, and even yet consider the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the country itself, we find not the least reason to doubt the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of what the sacred historians have related. Moses describes the richness of it in the strongest terms, even before the Israelites got possession of it. It even exceeded the land of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, so much celebrated by ancient historians; especially in the vast numbers of cattle which it produced; in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> and excellence of its wine, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. With respect to the oil and fruits, it is plain, that the olives and oil of Canaan exceeded in goodness those of Egypt, since the tribes sent them thither from thence; and as for vines, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> tells us, that the Egyptians had none at all, but supplied the want of them by a liquor brewed from barley. The presents which Jacob sent to his son <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, spices, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, almonds, and other fruits of Palestine, shew that they must have been much better in the land of Judea than in Egypt. The wines of Gaza, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASCALON">Ascalon</a>, and Saræpta, were famous among the most remote nations; though it is allowed, that the wine which was made at and in the neighbourhood of Bethlehem, in great quantities, was equal at least, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not superior, to any of the rest: and that of Libanus, mentioned by the prophet Hosea, was no less celebrated for its excellent flavour. Several circumstances contributed to this wonderful fecundity: such as, the excellent temperature of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, which was never subject to excessive heats or colds; the regularity of its seasons, especially the former and latter <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> fatness and fertility of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, which required neither dunging nor manuring, and could be ploughed with a single yoke of oxen and a small kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>; for the soil was, and is still, so shallow, that to have gone deep into it, would rather endanger, than improve, the crop. With respect to the excellency of its corn, we are told, that the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> of Jerusalem was preferred above all other; and the tribe of Asher produced the best of both, and in greater quantity than any other tribe; and such plenty was there of it, that, besides what sufficed the inhabitants, who made it their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> sustenance, Solomon, we read, could afford to send 20,000 cors, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, of it, and as many of oil, yearly, to Hiram <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>; besides what they exported into other countries. And we find, even so late as king Herod farnamed Agrippa, the countries of Tyre and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIDON">Sidon</a> received most of their sustenance from his treachery. As to their fruits, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a> were delicious, finely flavoured, and very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. The palm tree and its dates were in no less request; and the plain of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERICHO">Jericho</a>, among other places, was famed for the great plenty and excellence of that fruit; insomuch, that the metropolis of that territory was emphatically styled the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of palm-trees. But what both this plain, and other parts of Palestine, were most celebrated for, was, the balsam shrub, whose balm was esteemed so precious a drug among the Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, Egyptians, and other nations, and is still to this day under the name of balm of Gilead. They had likewise the greatest variety of other fruit-trees in the highest perfection; and which might be, in some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, styled perpetual, because they were not only covered with a constant verdure, but because the new buds always appeared on the same boughs before the old fruit was ripe; and of those buds, which were in too great quantities to be allowed to come to maturity, they gathered enough to make very delightful pickles and sweatmeats, especially of their citrons, oranges, and apples of paradise, which last <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> hung by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> in a cluster, and as big as hens eggs, and of an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and flavour. Their vines yielded grapes twice, and sometimes three times a year, great quantities of which were dried up, and preserved for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, as well as their figs, plums, and other fruits. They had plenty of honey; the very trees distilled it; and the rocks yielded it in great quantities: but whether that of the latter kind were there deposited by the industrious bees, or produced some other way, is much disputed by travellers and naturalists. They likewise cultivated <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes in great abundance; and the cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, were mostly of their own growth and manufacture, except some of a finer sort, that were brought to them from Egypt, and worn by those of the higher <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. Their vicinity to Lebanon made the cedars, cypresses, and other flatly fragrant trees, very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in most parts of the land, but more especially in Jerusalem. Cattle, both large and small, they fed in vast quantities; and the hilly countries not only afforded them variety and plenty of pasture, but also of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which descended thence into the valleys and lowlands, and fertilized them to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> we have seen; besides several other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and brooks, some of the most remarkable of which we shall speak of in their proper places. But the most fertile pasture-grounds were those on each side the river Jordan; besides those of Sharon, or Saron, the plains of Lydda, Jannia, and some others then justly famed for their fecundity. As for fish, the rivers above-mentioned, the lake of Tiberias, and the Mediterranean Sea, afforded, as they do to this day, great plenty and variety. Vast quantities were brought to Jerusalem, on which the inhabitants mostly subsisted; and hence one of the gates of that metropolis was, according to St Jerome, called the fish-gate. The lake Asphaltites yielded <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> in abundance, wherewith to season and preserve their fish, which Galen affirms to have been preferable to any other for wholesomeness, digestion, and extenuation. In short, the Scripture is so pregnant with proofs of the extraordinary richness and fecundity of this once happy land, and the vast <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people that lived in it, almost wholly upon its product, to say nothing of the vast exports of its corn, wine, oil, raisins, and other fruits, &c., that a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> must have taken a strange warp to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a>, that can call it in question, merely on account of the melancholy and quite opposite figure it now makes under its present tyrannical <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. But it ought to be considered, that it was then inhabited by an industrious people, who knew how to improve every inch of their land, and had made even the most desart and barren places to yield some kind of productions, by proper care and manure: so that the very rocks, which now appear quite bare and naked, were made to produce corn, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, or pasture; being, by the industry of the old inhabitants, covered with mould, which, through the laziness of the succeeding proprietors, has been since washed off with rains and storms. We may add, that the kings themselves were not above encouraging all kind of agriculture, both by precept and example; and, above all, that they had the divine blessing promised to their honest endeavours and industry: whereas it is now, and hath been long since, inhabited by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, lazy, indolent people, groaning under an intolerable servitude and all manner of discouragements; by which their aversion to labour and agriculture, farther than what barely serves to supply their present wants, is become, in a manner, natural and invincible. We may farther observe, after the judicious Mr Maundrell, that there is no forming an idea of its ancient flourishing state, when under the influence of heaven, from what it is now under a visible curse. And, if we had not several concurring testimonies from profane authors, who have extolled the fecundity of Palestine, that single one of Julian the apostate, a sworn enemy to Jews and Christians, as well as to all the sacred writings, would be more than sufficient to prove it; who frequently makes mention, in his epistles, of the perpetuity, as well as excellence and great abundance, of its fruits and product. The visible effects of God's <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>, which this country has felt, not only under Titus Vespasian (when myriads of inhabitants were either slain, or perished by the most severe famine, pestilence, and other calamities; and the rest sold for slaves, into all lands; and new colonies sent to re-populate it; who found it in such a desolate state, as quite discouraged them from restoring it to its pristine fruitfulness); but much more since that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, in the invasions of the northern barbarians, of the Saracens, and of the more cruel and destructive Christians during the holy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and in the oppression it now feels under the Turkish yoke; may be easily owned to be more than sufficient to have wrought the dismal change we are speaking of, and to have reduced the far greater part into a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. Nevertheless, if we may <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> those who have viewed it in this doleful condition, they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> tell us, there are still such visible signs of its natural richness and fertility, as plainly shew, that the bare want of culture is the main, if not the only cause of its present poverty and barrenness. We shall hint, as a further <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of this, what a learned traveller hath lately written of it from his own observations. "The Holy Land," says Dr Shaw, "were it as well peopled and cultivated as in former times, would still be more fruitful than the very best part of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Syria and Phoenice; for the soil is generally much richer, and, all things considered, yields a more preferable crop. Thus the cotton that is gathered in the plains of Ramah, Edraclon, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZABULON">Zabulon</a>, is in greater esteem than what is cultivated near Sidon and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>. Neither is it possible for pulse, wheat, or any sort of grain, to be more excellent than what is sold at Jerusalem. The barrenness, or scarcity rather, which some authors may, either ignorantly or maliciously, complain of, doth not proceed from the incapacity or natural unfruitfulness of the country, but from the want of inhabitants, and the great aversion there is to labour and industry in those few who possess it. There are, besides, such perpetual discords and depredations among the petty princes who share this fine country, that allowing it was better peopled, yet there would be small encouragement to sow, when it was uncertain who should gather in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>. Otherwise, the land is a good land, and still

PALFIN

Pages 336-336

an eminent surgeon, anatomist, and reader in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a> at Ghent, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his birth; acquired <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation by his learning and works. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of these are, 1. A treatise on Ostecology, in 12mo, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> 1731. 2. Anatomy of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, in 2 vols 8vo, Paris 1734. He died at Ghent at a great <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, in 1730.

PALFREY

Pages 336-336

is one of the better sort of horses used by noblemen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> others for state; and sometimes of old taken for a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> fit for a woman to ride. Camden says, that William Fauconberge held the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of Cokeny, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, in fereignty, by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of shoeing the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s palfrey when the king should come to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a>.

PALICATE

Pages 336-336

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, on this side of the Ganges. It is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Coromandel, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Carnate, 70 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Fort St George. Here the Dutch have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a>, and fort called the Fort of Guelderland. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 80. 1. N. Lat. 13. 34.

PALINDROMUS

Pages 336-336

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> which runs the same when read either backwards or forwards. Such is the verse, Roma tibi subito motibus ibit amor. Some people of leisure have refined upon the Palindromus, and composed verses, each word of which is the same backwards as forwards; for instance, that of Camden: Odo tenet mulum, madidam mappam tenet <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a>. Anna tenet mappam radidam, mulum tenet Odo.

PALINGENESIA

Pages 336-336

among divines, the same with regeneration. Among chemists, it denotes the producing of a body from its principles.

PALINGENIUS

Pages 336-336

well known by a poem divided into 12 books, and intitled Zodiacus Vitæ, which he was several years of composing, and dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> II. of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-ESTE">Este</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>. Some say he was physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; others <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> him among the learned Lutherans to whom the duchess of Ferrara gave a reception in her <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> and honoured with her protection. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZODIAC">Zodiac</a> contains good things, and is a philosophical satire against immorality and false prejudices. Though this poem has borne a multitude of impressions, the author's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is but little known. He died some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> between the years 1537 and 1543.

PALINOZY

Pages 336-336

a discourse contrary to a preceding one; hence the phrase of palinodiam canere was taken for a recantation.

PALINURI PROMONTORIUM

Pages 336-336

(<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Velleius,) with a cognominal port, was situated at the south extremity of the Sinus Pæstanus, on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUCANIA">Lucania</a>; so called from Palinurus, Æneas's steerman, who there perished. (Mela, Dionysius <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>.)

PALISADES

Pages 336-336

in fortification, stakes made of strong split wood, about <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, six <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> inches <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, three feet deep in the ground, in rows about two and an half or three inches asunder, placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COVERT">covert</a> way, at three feet from, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> or side of the glacis, to secure it from surprise. They are also used to fortify the avenues of open forts, gorges, half-moons, the bottoms of ditches, and in general all posts liable to surprise. They are usually fixed perpendicularly, though some make an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> inclining towards the ground next the enemy, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> over them to tear them up may slip off. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">Turning</a> Palisades; an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of Mr Coehorn, in order to preserve the palisades of the covert way from the besiegers <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>. They are so ordered, that as many of them as stand in the length of a rod, or about ten feet, turn up and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> like traps, so as not to be in sight of the enemy till they <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> bring on their attack; and yet are always ready to do the proper <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of palisades.

PALISSE

Pages 336-336

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> like a range of palisades before a fortification, represented on a fesse, rising up a considerable height, and pointed a-top, with the field appearing between them.

PALISTRINA

Pages 336-336

is one of the largest and most populous of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> called the Lagunes, near <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, and where the most considerable of the noblemen have houses of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. It is 15,000 paces in length, and 400 in breadth; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> harbour has also the same name.

PALLADIO

Pages 336-336

a celebrated Italian <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> of the 16th century, was a native of Vicenza in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Trissino. He made exact drawings of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works of antiquity to be met with at Rome, adding commentaries to them, which went through several impressions. But this, though a very useful <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, was greatly exceeded by the Treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a> in four books, which he published in 1570. Inigo Jones wrote some excellent remarks on it; which were included in an edition of Palladio, published by Leoni, in 2 vols folio, 1742.

PALLADIUM

Pages 336-336

in antiquity, a statue of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Pallas, supposed to have dropped <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from heaven, preserved in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, whereon the fate of that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> is said to have depended. It is said that there was anciently a statue of Pallas preserved at Rome, in the temple of Vesta, which some pretended to be the true palladium of Troy, brought into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> by Æneas: it was kept among the sacred things of the temple, and only known to the priests and vestals. It was esteemed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a> of Rome; and there were several others made perfectly like it to secure it from being stolen,

PALLET

Pages 337-337

is also a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> of a watch <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> movement. See the article Watch.

PALLIATION

Pages 337-337
or a Palliative Cure, in medicine, is when, in desperate and incurable diseases, after predicting the fatal event, the physician prescribes some remedies for mitigating the pain or some other urgent symptoms, as in ulcerated cancers, or cancerous fistulas, and the like.

PALLIUM

Pages 337-337

a word often mentioned in our old historians. Durandus tells us, that it is a garment made of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, after the following manner, viz. The nuns of St Agnes, every year, on the feast-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of their saint, offer two white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a> on the altar of their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> they sing Agnus Dei, in a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>; which lambs are afterwards taken by two of the canons of the Lateran church, and by them given to the Pope's subdeacons, who send them to pasture till shearing time, and then they are shorn, and the pall is made of their wool mixed with other white wool. The pall being thus made, is carried to the Lateran church, and there placed on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> altar, by the deacons of that church, on the bodies of St <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and St Paul; and after an usual watching, it is carried away in the night, and delivered to the subdeacons, who lay it up safe. And because it was taken from the body of St Peter, it signifies the plenitude of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> power: and therefore it was the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of popes, who pretend to be the immediate successors of that saint, to invest other prelates with it; which at first was done nowhere but at Rome, tho' afterwards at other places.

PALM-SUNDAY

Pages 337-337

in the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> next before Easter; being so called in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of our Saviour's triumphal entry into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, when the multitude that attended him flrewed branches on his way.

PALMA

Pages 337-337

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic Ocean</a>, and one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANARIES">Canaries</a>, 36 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Gomera, and about 75 in circumference. It abounds in wine and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>; and has a handsome town of the same name, which carries on a trade in wine to the West Indies and other parts. Their best vines grow in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> called the Brenia, where they make 12,000 butts of wine every year, which is well known by the name of palm-wine. There is plenty of cattle, and all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. In 1625 a volcano broke out in this island, with a most violent earthquake; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> was seen for six weeks together, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ashes were thrown as far as Teneriff. It was conquered by the Spaniards in 1460.

PALMATED

Pages 337-337

something resembling the shape of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>: thus we say, palmated leaves, roots, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, &c.

PALMISTRY

Pages 337-337

a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> rather a deceitful art practised by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GYPSIES">gypsies</a>, who pretend to foretell events by looking upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> and marks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>.

PALPABLE

Pages 339-339

PALPABLE, something perceivable by the senses, particularly that of feeling.

PALPITATION

Pages 339-339

PALPITATION of the Heart. See Medicine, n° 266. 395.

PALSY

Pages 339-339

PALSY. Ibid. n° 190. 377—380. & p. 4870.

PALUDAMENTUM

Pages 339-339

PALUDAMENTUM, in Roman antiquity, a habit that differed but little from the chlamys, except that his last belonged chiefly to the lower class of people.

PALUS MEOTIS

Pages 339-339

PALUS MEOTIS, the ancient name of a gulph between Europe and Asia, to the north of the Black Sea, now called the sea of Zabach, or Azoph.

PALY

Pages 339-339

PALY, or PALE, in heraldry, is when the shield is divided into four or more equal parts, by perpendicular lines falling from the top to the bottom.

PALY BENDY

PALY Bendy, is when the escutcheon is divided by perpendicular lines, which is paly; and also by diagonals, which is called bendy. PAMELUNA

Pages 339-339

PAMELUNA, a town of New Granada in South America, famous for its gold mines and numerous flocks of sheep. W. Long. 68. 30. N. Lat. 6. 30. PAMPHYLIA, the ancient name of a country of Natolia in Asia, now called Carimania and Cey-bay, between Lycia and Cilicia, on the south coast, to the north of the Mediterranean sea. PAN, in Pagan worship, the son of Mercury and Penelope (the wife of Ulysses), who was ravished by that god in the form of a white goat, while she was keeping her father's flocks. He was educated on Mount Menelaus, in Arcadia, by Sirene, and the other nymphs, whom he attracted by his music. He afterwards distinguished himself in the war with the giants, when he entangled Typhon in his nets. He attended Bacchus in his Indian expedition; and when the Gauls were about to pillage the temple of Delphos, he struck them with such a sudden consternation by night, that they fled, though... though none pursued them. He had a contest with Cupid; but was conquered by the little god, who punished him, by inspiring him with a passion for the nymph Syrinx, who treated him with disdain; but he closely pursuing her, overtook her by the river Ladon, when, invoking the Naiads, she was changed into a tuft of reeds, which the disappointed lover grasped in his arms; but observing, that as they trembled with the wind, they formed a murmuring sound, he made of them the pipe for which he became so famous. He charmed Luna in the shape of a beautiful ram, and had several other amours. Pan is represented with a smiling ruddy face, a thick beard, with the horns, legs, feet, and tail of a goat; holding a shepherd's crook in one hand, and his pipe of unequal reeds in the other. The abbe Banner remarks, that if ever the Greeks corrupted ancient history, it was in fabricating the fable of Pan. According to them, says Herodotus, Hercules Dionysius, or Bacchus, and Pan, were the last of all the gods; however, in the opinion of the Egyptians, Pan was one of the eight great divinities that formed the first class in their theology, which were the most powerful and the most ancient of all. Diodorus makes him one of the attendants upon Osiris, in his Indian expedition. "Osiris," says this author, "took with him Pan, a person much respected throughout his dominions: for he had not only his statue afterwards placed in all the temples, but a city was built in the Thebaid; which, in honour of Pan, was called Chamae, or Chamun, a word that signifies in the Egyptian language the city of Pan." The same author, however, tells us, that he was the leader of a troop of fauns and satyrs, or wild and rustic men, much addicted to singing, dancing, and feats of activity, who were presented to Osiris in Ethiopia, and with whom that prince was so much pleased, that he retained them in his service. Pan was regarded by the Egyptians, after his apotheosis, as the god who presided over the whole universe, as Ias, omne, implies. He represented nature and fertility; and was god of the woods and fields, wholly taken up with the pleasures of a country life; dancing constantly with the fauns and satyrs; and running after the nymphs, to whom he was such a terror, that it is supposed the word panic is derived from Panici terrores, with which those who were said to have seen him were seized. Apuleius, however, gives an agreeable description of him. "By chance the god Pan happened to be seated on a little eminence near a river; and, always constant in his love to the nymph Syrinx, transformed into a reed, he taught her to produce all kinds of agreeable sounds, while his goats were skipping round him, and feeding on the banks." Lucian describes him as the companion, minister, and counsellor of Bacchus. He was a kind of scrub, a drudge fit for all work, having been occasionally employed in the capacity of shepherd, musician, dancer, huntman, and soldier. In short, he served not only as magistro di capello, in directing the Bacchanals, but was so expert in playing upon flutes, and was such an excellent piper on the fisula, that Bacchus was never happy without him. He was particularly honoured in Arcadia, where the shepherds offered him milk and honey in wooden bowls: when successful in hunting, they gave him a part of the spoils; but if they caught nothing, they showed their resentment by whipping his image. The Romans adopted him amongst their deities under the names of Lupercus and Lyceus. PANACEA, among physicians, denotes an universal medicine, or a remedy for all diseases; a thing impossible to be obtained. PANADA, a diet consisting of bread boiled in water to the consistence of pulp, and sweetened with a little sugar. PANAMA, the capital city of the province of Darien in South America, where the treasures of gold and silver, and the other rich merchandizes of Peru, are lodged in magazines till they are sent to Europe. W. Long. 82° O. N. Lat. 9° O. This town, which had been the gate through which an entrance was gained into Peru, had risen to great prosperity, when, in 1670, it was pillaged and burnt by pirates. It was rebuilt on a more advantageous spot, at the distance of four or five miles from the first. Its harbour, called Perico, is very secure. It is formed by an archipelago, consisting of 48 small islands, and is capable of containing the largest fleets. This place, a little while after it was founded, became the capital of the kingdom of Terra Firma. Some hopes were at first entertained from the three provinces of Panama, Darien, and Veragua, which composed it; but this prosperity vanished instantaneously. The savages of Darien recovered their independence; and the mines of the two other provinces were found to be neither sufficiently abundant, nor of an alloy good enough to make it worth while to work them. Five or six small boroughs, in which are seen some Europeans quite naked, and a very small number of Indians, who have come to reside there, form the whole of this state, which the Spaniards are not ashamed of honouring with the great name of kingdom. It is in general barren and unwholesome, and contributes nothing to trade but pearls. The pearl fishery is carried on in the islands of the gulph. The greatest part of the inhabitants employ such of their negroes in it as are good swimmers. These slaves plunge and plunge in the sea, in search of pearls, till this exercise has exhausted their strength or their spirits. Every negro is obliged to deliver a certain number of oysters. Those in which there are no pearls, or in which the pearl is not entirely formed, are not reckoned. What he is able to find beyond the stipulated obligation, is considered as his indisputable property; he may sell it to whom he pleases; but commonly he cedes it to his master at a moderate price. Sea monsters, which abound more about the islands where pearls are found than on the neighbouring coasts, render this fishing dangerous. Some of these devour the divers in an instant. The manta fish, which derives its name from its figure, surrounds them, rolls them under its body, and suffocates them. In order to defend themselves against such enemies, every diver is armed with a poinard; the moment he perceives any of these voracious fish, he attacks them with precaution, wounds them, and drives them away. Notwithstanding this, there are always some fishermen destroyed, and a great number crippled.

The greatest part of the inhabitants employ such of their negroes in it as are good swimmers. Those in which there are no pearls, or in which the pearl is not entirely formed, are not reckoned.
