Therefore when, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Danby was impeached by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> treason and other misdemeanors, and pleaded the king's pardon in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of the same, the commons alleged, "That there was no precedent that ever any pardon was granted to any person impeached by the commons of high treason, or other high crimes, depending the impeachment;" and thereupon resolved, "That the pardon so pleaded was illegal and void, and ought not to be allowed in bar of the impeachment of the commons of England:" for which <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> they assigned this reason to the house of lords, "That the setting up a pardon to be a bar of an impeachment defeats the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and effect of impeachments: for should this point be admitted, or fland doubted, it would totally discourage the exhibiting any for the future; whereby the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> for the preservation of the government would be destroyed." Soon after the Revolution, the commons renewed the same claim, and voted, "That a pardon is not pleadable in bar of an impeachment." And at length, it was enacted by the act of settlement, 12 & 13 W. III. c. 2. "That no pardon under the great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of England shall be pleadable to an impeachment by the commons in parliament." But, after the impeachment has been solemnly heard and determined, it is not understood that the king's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> grace is farther restrained or abridged: for, after the impeachment and attainder of the six rebel lords in 1715, three of them were from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time reprieved by the crown; and at length received the benefit of the king's most gracious pardon. The effect of such pardon by the king, is to make the offender a new man; to acquit him of all corporal penalties and forfeitures annexed to that offence for which he obtains his pardon; and not so much to restore his former, as to give him a new <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> and capacity. But nothing can restore or purify the blood when once corrupted, if the pardon be not allowed till after attainder, but the high and transcendent power of parliament. Yet if a person attained receives the king's pardon, and afterwards hath a son, that son may be heir to his father; because the father being made a new man, might transmit new inheritable blood; though, had he been born before the pardon, he could never have inherited at all.

PAREIRA FRAYA

Pages 361-361

in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> root brought from the Brazils.—It is certainly a diuretic of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> character, and has done <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in nephritic <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. In pleurifies and quinsies, it has been attended with more success than almost any medicine we know of singly.

PARELCON

Pages 361-361

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> by which a word <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> is added to the end of another.

PAREMBOLIS

Pages 361-361

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> wherein something relating to the subject is inserted in the middle of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. All the differences between the parembolis and parenthesis, according to Vossius, is, that the former relates to the subject in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, whereas the latter is foreign to it.

PARENCHYMA

Pages 361-361

in anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> introduced by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERASISTRATUS">Erasistratus</a>, signifying all that substance which is contained in the interstices betwixt the blood-vessels of the visera, which he imagined to be extravasated and concreted blood. PARENCHYMA OF <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">PLANTS</a>. Grew applies the term parenchyma to the pith <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> pulp, or that inner <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of a fruit or plant through which the juice is supposed to be distributed. See PLANTS.

PARENT

Pages 361-363

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> of relation applicable to those from whom we immediately derive our being. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">MORAL <a class="</a>xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">PHILOSOPHY</a>, No. 122, 132—135. To this article belongs an inquiry into, 1. The legal duties of parents to their legitimate children. 2. Their power over them. I. The duties of parents to legitimate children consist in three particulars; their maintenance, their protection, and their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. 1. The duty of parents to provide for the maintenance of their children, is a principle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>; an obligation, says Puffendorff, laid on them not only by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> herself, but by their own proper <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, in bringing them into the world; for they would be in the highest manner injurious to their issue, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they only gave their children <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, that they might afterwards see them perish. By begetting them, therefore, they have entered into a voluntary obligation, to endeavour, as far as in them lies, that the life which they have bestowed shall be supported and preserved. And thus the children <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> have a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of receiving maintenance from their parents. And the prudent Montefique has a very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> observation upon this head, that the establishment of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, in all civilized states, is built on this natural obligation of the father to provide for his children; for that ascertains and makes known the person who is bound to fulfil this obligation; whereas, in promiscuous and illicit conjunctions, the father is unknown; and the mother finds a thousand obstacles in her way; shame, remorse, the constraint of her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, and the rigour of laws, that stifle her inclinations to perform this duty; and besides, she generally wants ability. The municipal laws of all well-regulated states have taken care to enforce this duty: though <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a> has done it more effectually than any laws, by implanting in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> of every parent that natural affection, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> ineradicable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of affection, which not even the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a> of person or mind, not even the wickedness, ingratitude, and rebellion of children, can totally suppress or extinguish. The civil law obliges the parent to provide maintenance for his child; and if he refuses, judex de ea re cognoscat. Nay, it carries this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> so far, that it will not suffer a parent at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> totally to disinherit his child, without expressly giving his reason for so doing; and there are 14 such reasons reckoned up, which may justify such disinherition. If the parent alleged no reason, or a bad, or a false one, the child might set the will aside, tanguam testamentium inofficiosum, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a> contrary to the natural duty of the parent. And it is remarkable under what <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> the children were to move for relief in such a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>; by suggesting, that the parent had lost the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his reason when he made the inofficious testament. And this, as Puffendorff observes, was not to bring into dispute the testator's power of disinheritting his own offspring; but to examine the motives upon which he did it; and if they they were found defective in reason, then to set them aside. But perhaps this is going rather too far: every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> has, or ought to have, by the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, a power over his own <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>; and, as Grotius very well distinguishes, natural right obliges to give a necessary maintenance to children; but what is more than that they have no right to, than as it is given by the favour of their parents, or the positive constitutions of the municipal law. Let us next see what provision our own laws have made for this natural duty. It is a principle of law, that there is an obligation on every man to provide for those descended from his loins; and the manner in which this obligation shall be performed, is thus pointed out. The father and mother, grandfather and grandmother of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> impotent persons shall maintain them at their own charges, if of sufficient ability, according as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-sessions shall <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>; and, if a parent runs away, and leaves his children, the churchwardens and overseers of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> shall <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> his rents, goods, and chattels, and dispose of them toward their relief. By the interpretations which the courts of law have made upon these statutes, if a mother or grandmother marries again, and was before such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> marriage of sufficient ability to keep the child, the husband shall be <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> to maintain it; for this being a debt of her's, when single, shall, like others, extend to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> the husband. But, at her death, the relation being dissolved, the husband is under no farther obligation. No person is bound to provide a maintenance for his issue, unless where the children are impotent and unable to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, either through infancy, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, or accident; and then is only obliged to find them with necessaries, the penalty on refusal being no more than 20s. a-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. For the policy of our laws, which are ever watchful to promote industry, did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to compel a father to maintain his idle and lazy children in ease and indolence; but thought it unjust to oblige the parent, against his will, to provide them with superfluities, and other indulgences of fortune; imagining they might trust to the impulse of nature, if the children were deserving of such favours. Yet, as nothing is so apt to flatter the calls of nature as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> bigotry, it is enacted, that if any Popish parent shall refuse to allow his Protestant child a fitting maintenance, with a view to compel him to change his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> shall by order of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> constrain him to do what is just and reasonable. But this did not extend to persons of another religion, of no less bitterness and bigotry than the Popish; and therefore, in the very next year, we find an instance of a Jew of immense <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, whose only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> having embraced Christianity, he turned her out of doors; and on her application for relief, it was held she was entitled to none. But this gave occasion to another statute, which ordains, that if Jewish parents refuse to allow their Protestant children a fitting maintenance, suitable to the fortune of the parent, the lord chancellor, on complaint, may make such order therein as he shall see proper. Our law has made no provision to prevent the disinheriting of children by will; leaving every man's property in his own disposal, upon a principle of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> in this as well as every other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; though perhaps it had not been amiss if the parent had been bound to leave them at the least a necessary subsistence. Indeed, among persons of any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> or fortune, a competence is generally provided for younger children, and the bulk of the estate settled upon the eldest by the marriage-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. Heirs also, and children, are favourites of our courts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and cannot be disinherited by any dubious or ambiguous words; there being required the utmost certainty of the testator's intentions to take away the right of an heir. 2. From the duty of maintenance we may easily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> to that of protection; which is also a natural duty, but rather permitted than enjoined by any municipal laws; nature, in this respect, working so strongly as to need rather a check than a spur. A parent may, by our laws, maintain and uphold his children in their law-suits, without being guilty of the legal crime of maintaining quarrels. A parent may also justify an assault and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the persons of his children; nay, where a man's son was beaten by another boy, and the father went near a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> to find him, and there revenged his son's quarrel by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> the other boy, of which beating he afterwards unfortunately died; it was not held to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, but manslaughter merely. Such <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> does the law shew to the frailty of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> nature, and the workings of parental affection. 3. The last duty of parents to their children is that of giving them an education suitable to their station in life: a duty pointed out by reason, and of far the greatest importance of any. For, as Puffendorff very well observes, it is not easy to imagine or allow, that a parent has conferred any considerable benefit upon his child by bringing him into the world, if he afterwards entirely neglects his culture and education, and suffers him to grow up like a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> beast, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a life useless to others, and shameful to himself. Yet the municipal laws of most countries seem to be defective in this point, by not constraining the parent to bestow a proper education upon his children. Perhaps they thought it <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> enough to leave the parent, who neglects the instruction of his family, to labour under those griefs and inconveniences which his family, so un instructed, will be sure to bring upon him. Our laws, though their defects in this particular cannot be denied, have in one instance made a wise provision for breeding up the rising <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>; since the poor and laborious <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, when past the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of nurture, are taken out of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of their parents, by the statutes for apprenticing poor children; and are placed out by the public in such a manner as may render their abilities, in their several stations, of the greatest advantage to the commonwealth. The rich indeed are left at their own option, whether they will breed up their children to be ornaments or disgraces to their family. Yet in one case, that of religion, they are under peculiar restrictions: for it is provided, that if any person sends any child under his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> beyond the seas, either to prevent its good education in England, or in order to enter into, or reside in, any Popish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, or to be instructed, persuaded, or strengthened in the Popish religion; in such case, besides the disabilities incurred by the child so sent, the parent or person sending shall forfeit 100l. which shall go to the sole use and benefit of him that shall discover the offence. And if any parent, or other, shall send or convey any person beyond <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, to enter into, or be resident in, or trained up in, any priory, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, nunnery, Popish university, college, or school, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Jesuits or priests, or in any private Popish family, in order to be instructed, persuaded, or confirmed, in the Popish religion; or shall contribute any thing towards their maintenance when abroad by any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> whatever, the person both sending and sent shall be disabled to sue in law or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, or to be executor or administrator to any person, or to enjoy any legacy or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> of gift, or to bear any office in the realm, and shall forfeit all his goods and chattels, and likewise all his real estate for life. II. The power of parents over their children is derived from the former consideration, their duty: this authority being given them, partly to enable the parent more effectually to perform his duty, and partly as a recompense for his care and trouble in the faithful discharge of it. And upon this score the municipal laws of some nations have given a much larger authority to the parents than others. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman laws gave the father a power of life and death over his children; upon this principle, that he who gave had also the power of taking away. But the rigour of these laws was softened by subsequent constitutions; so that we find a father banished by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a> for killing his son, though he had committed a very heinous crime, upon this maxim, that patria potestas in pietate debet, non in atrocitate, confert. But still they maintained to the last a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> authority: for a son could not acquire any property of his own during the life of his father; but all his acquisitions belonged to the father, or at least the profits of them, for his life. The power of a parent by our English law is much more moderate; but still sufficient to keep the child in order and obedience. He may lawfully correct his child, being under age, in a reasonable manner; for this is for the benefit of his education. The consent or concurrence of the parent to the marriage of his child under age, was also directed by our ancient law to be obtained: but now it is absolutely necessary; for without it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> is void. And this also is another means which the law has put into the parent's hands, in order the better to discharge his duty; first, of protecting his children from the snares of artful and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> persons; and next, of settling them properly in life, by preventing the ill consequences of too early and precipitate marriages. A father has no other power over his son's estate, than as his trustee or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a>; for though he may receive the profits during the child's minority, yet he must account for them when he comes of age. He may indeed have the benefit of his children's labour while they live with him, and are maintained by him; but this is no more than he is entitled to from his apprentices or servants. The legal power of a father, (for a mother, as such, is entitled to no power, but only to reverence and respect), the power of a father, we say, over the persons of his children ceases at the age of 21; for they are then enfranchised by arriving at years of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, or that point which the law has established (as some must necessarily be established) when the empire of the father, or other guardian, gives <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to the empire of reason. Yet, till that age arrives, this empire of the father continues even after his death; for he may by his will appoint a guardian to his children. He may also delegate part of his parental authority, during his life, to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> or schoolmaster of his child; who is then in loco parentis, and has such a portion of the power of the parent committed to his charge, viz. that of restraint and correction, as may be necessary to answer the purposes for which he is employed. See Children.

PARENTALIA

Pages 363-363

in antiquity, funeral obsequies, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the last duties paid by children to their deceased parents.

PARENTHESIS

Pages 363-363

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, certain intercalary words inserted in a discourse, which interrupt the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> thread, but seem necessary for the better understanding of the subject.

PARENZO

Pages 363-363

a small but strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and in Istria, with a bishop's see and a good harbour; situated on the gulph of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13° 46'. N. Lat. 39° 28'. It submitted to the Venetians in 1267.

PARESIS

Pages 363-363

in medicine, a palsy of the bladder, wherein the urine is either suppressed <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> discharged involuntarily.

PARETONIUM

Pages 363-363

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> found on the shores of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>.

PARGET

Pages 363-363

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a name given to several kinds of gypsum, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>.

PARGETING

Pages 363-363

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, is used for the plastering of walls, and sometimes for platter itself.

PARHELION

Pages 363-364
or PARHELUM, in ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural philosophy, a mock-fun or meteor, in form of a very bright light, appearing on one side of the sun. Appearances of this kind have been made mention of both by the ancients and moderns. Aristotle observes, that in general they are seen only when the sun is near the horizon, though he takes notice of two that were seen in Bosphorus from morning to evening; and Pliny has related the times when such phenomena were observed at Rome. Gasendi says, that, in 1635 and 1636, he often saw one mock-fun. Two were observed by M. de la Hire in 1680; and the same number by Caffini in 1693, Mr Grey in 1700, and Dr Halley in 1702: but the most celebrated appearances of this kind were seen at Rome by Scheiner, by Muffchenbroeck at Utrecht, and by Hevelius at Sedan. By the two former, four mock-funs were observed, and by the latter seven. Parhelia are apparently of the same size with the sun, though not always of the same brightness, nor even of the same shape; and when a number appear at once, there is some difference in both respects among them. Externally, they are tinged with colours like the rainbow; and many have a long fiery tail opposite to the sun, but paler towards the extremity. Parhelia are generally accompanied with corona's, some of which are tinged with rainbow-colours, but others are white. They differ in number and size; but all agree in breadth, which is that of the apparent diameter of the sun. A very large white circle, parallel to the horizon, generally passes through all the parhelia; and, if it were entire, it would go through the centre of the sun. Sometimes there are arcs of lesser circles concentric to this, touching those coloured circles which surround Parhelion surround the sun. They are also tinged with colours, and contain other parhelia. There are also said to have been other circles obliquely situated with respect to all those we have mentioned; but of this we have met with no authentic account. The order of the colours in these circles is the same as in the rainbow; but on the inside, with respect to the sun, they are red, as is also observed in many other corona's. Parhelia have been visible for 1, 2, 3, and 4 hours together; and in North America they are said to continue some days, and to be visible from sun-rise to sun-set. When the parhelia disappear, it sometimes rains, or there falls snow in the form of oblong spicules, as Mavaldi, Weidler, Krafft, and others, have observed; and because the air in North America abounds with such frozen spicules, which are even visible to the eye, according to Ellis and Middleton, such particles have been thought to be the cause of all corona's and parhelia. Mr Wales says, that, at Churchill in Hudson's class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay, the rising of the sun is always preceded by two long streams of red light, one on each side of him, and about 20° distant from him. These rise as the sun rises; and as they grow longer begin to bend towards each other, till they meet directly over the sun, just as he rises, forming there a kind of parhelion or mock-fun. These two streams of light, he says, seem to have their source in two other parhelia, which rise with the true sun; and in the winter-season, when the sun never rises above the haze or fog, which he says is constantly found near the horizon, all these accompany him the whole day, and set with him in the same manner as they rise. Once or twice he saw a fourth parhelion directly under the true sun; but this, he says, is not common. These facts being constant, are very valuable, and may throw great light on the theory of these remarkable phenomena. Sometimes parhelia appear in a different manner; as when three suns have been seen in the same vertical circle, well defined, and touching one another. The true sun was in the middle, and the lowest touched the horizon; and they set one after the other. This appearance was seen by M. Malezew in 1722. Other appearances similar to this are recited by M. Mutchtenbroeck. Sometimes the sun has risen or set with a luminous tail projecting from him, of the same breadth with his diameter, and perpendicular to the horizon. Such an appearance was seen by Cassini in 1672 and 1692, by de la Hire in 1702, and by Mr Ellis in Hudson's Bay. As M. Feuille was walking on the banks of the river La Plata, he saw the sun rising over the river with a luminous tail projecting downwards, which continued till he was six degrees high. Parafelence, or mock-moons, have also been seen, accompanied with tails and coloured circles, like those which accompany the parhelia. An account of several, and a particular description of a fine appearance of this kind, may be seen in Mutchtenbroeck. The Roman phenomenon, observed by Scheiner, is famous on account of its having been the first appearance of the kind that engaged the attention of philosophers. It is represented in fig. 4.; in which A is the place of the observer, B his zenith, C the true sun, AB a plane passing through the observer's eye, Parhelion the true sun, and the zenith. About the sun C, there appeared two concentric rings, not complete, but diversified with colours. The lesser of them, DEF, was fuller, and more perfect; and though it was open from D to F, yet those ends were perpetually endeavouring to unite; and sometimes they did so. The outer of these rings was much fainter, so as scarcely to be discernible. It had, however, a variety of colours; but was very inconstant. The third circle, KLMN, was very large, and all over white, passing through the middle of the sun, and everywhere parallel to the horizon. At first this circle was entire; but towards the end of the appearance it was weak and ragged, so as hardly to be perceived from M towards N. In the interjection of this circle, and the outward iris GKI, there broke out two parhelia or mock-funs, N and K, not quite perfect; K being rather weak, but N shone brighter and stronger. The brightness of the middle of them was something like that of the sun; but towards the edges they were tinged with colours like those of the rainbow; and they were uneven and ragged. The parhelion N was a little wavering, and sent out a spiked tail, NP, of a colour somewhat fiery, the length of which was continually changing. The parhelia at L and M in the horizontal ring were not so bright as the former; but were rounder, and white, like the circle in which they were placed. The parhelion N disappeared before K; and while M grew fainter, K grew brighter, and vanished the last of all. It is to be observed farther, that the order of the colours in the circles DEF, GKN, was the same as in the common halos, namely, red next the sun; and the diameter of the inner circle was also about 45 degrees; which is the usual size of a halo. Various hypotheses have been framed by philosophers to account for this phenomenon. None of them are satisfactory; but the reader who chooses to know them may consult Dr Priestley's History of Vision, Light, and Colours, vol. ii. p. 619.

PARIA

Pages 364-364
or NEW ANDALUSIA, a country of Terra Firma in South America; bounded on the north by the north sea; on the east, by Surinam; on the west, by New Granada and the Caraccas; and on the south, by Guiana. It produces colouring drugs, gums, medicinal roots, Brazil-wood, sugar, tobacco, and some valuable timber; the inland parts being woody and mountainous, but interspersed with fine valleys that yield corn and pasturage. Comana is the capital town.

PARIAN MARBLE

Pages 364-365

in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble used then, and to this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, for carving <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, &c. and called by us at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> flinty marble. Too many of the later writers have confounded all the white marbles under the name of the Parian; and among the workmen, this and all the other white marbles have the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name of alabasters; so that it is in general forgotten among them, that there is such a thing as alabaster different from marble; which, however, is truly the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>. Almost all the world also have confounded the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CARRARA">Carrara</a> marble with this, though they are really very different; the Carrara kind being of a finer structure and clearer white than the Parian; but but less bright and splendid, harder to cut, and not capable of so glittering a polish. The true Parian marble has usually somewhat of a faint bluish tinge among the white, and often has blue veins in different parts of it. It is supposed by some to have had its name from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> Paros, one of the Cyclades in the Aegean <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, where it was first found; but others <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it to have been so called from Agoracritus Parius, a famous statuary, who ennobled it by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> a statue of a Venus in it.

PARIETARIA

Pages 365-367

Pellitory of the wall; a genus of the order of monoeica belonging to the polygamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are six <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, of which one named the officinalis, is used in medicine. This has a creeping root. The stalk grows erect, is rough to the touch, and adhesive. The leaves are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a>, elliptical, lanceolate, veined, and a little rough. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> grow out of the axil of the leaves, in sessile, branched, verticillate clusters, of a greenish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> tinged with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>. The anthers have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of tenacity; for, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> irritated with the point of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIN">pin</a>, they fly from the calyx with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> force, and throw out their powder.—The plant has a cooling and diuretic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Three ounces of the juice taken internally, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a fomentation externally applied, have been found serviceable in the strangury.—The plant laid upon heaps of corn infested with weevils, is said to drive away those destructive insects. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">PARIS</a> (Matthew)**, one of our best historians from William the Conqueror, to the latter end of the reign of Henry III. But of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> few particulars have been transmitted to us. Leland, his original biographer, without determining whether he was born in France or England, informs us, that he was a monk of St Alban's, and that he was sent by pope Innocent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the monks of the convent at Holm in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>. Bishop <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALE">Bale</a>, the next in point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, adds to the above relation, that, on account of his extraordinary gifts of body and mind, he was much esteemed, particularly by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Henry III. who commanded him to write the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of his reign. Fuller makes him a native of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>, because there was an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family of his name in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. He also mentions his being sent by the pope to visit the monks in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>. Bishop Tanner, bishop Nicolson, Monsieur du Pin, and the Nouveau Dictionnaire Historique, add not a single fact to those above related. Matthew Paris died in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of St Alban's in the year 1259. He was doubtless a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of extraordinary knowledge for the 13th century; of an excellent moral character, and, as an historian, of strict integrity. His style is unpolished; but that defect is sufficiently atoned for by the honest freedom with which he relates the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, regardless of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> or sanctity of the persons concerned. His works are, 1. Historia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> Adamo <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> Conquestum Anglie, lib. i. manuscript. col. C. C. Cantab. c. ix. Most of this book is transcribed, by Matthew of Westminster, into the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his Florilegium. 2. Historia <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, seu rerum Anglicarum historia à Gul. Conquestoris adventu ad annum 43 Henrici III. &c. several times printed. The first part of this history, viz. to the year 1235, is transcribed almost verbatim from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a> of Roger <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WENDOVER">Wendover</a>; and the Appendix, from the year 1260, is the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of William Rishanger, who was also a monk of St Alban's. 3. Vitæ duorum Offarum, Mercie regum, S. Albani fundatorum. 4. Gefta 22 abbatum S. Albani. 5. Additamenta chronicorum ad hift. majorem; printed. 6. Historia <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>, five epitomes majoris bifloris; manuscript. Besides many other things in manuscript. Paris, the son of Priam king of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, memorable in history for carrying off Helena the wife of Menelaus king of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a> in his absence, which occasioned the famous siege of Troy. Slain there about 1188 B.C. Paris, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of France; is situate on the river <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of France, being one of the largest and finest cities in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It derived its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name from the ancient Parisii; and is supposed by some to have had the Latin name of Lutetia, from Lutum, "mud," the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it now stands having been anciently very marshy and muddy. Ever since the reign of Hugh Capet, that is, for near 800 years, this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> hath been the usual residence of the kings of France: it is of a circular form, and, including the suburbs, about five French leagues, or 15 English miles, in circumference. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of its inhabitants is computed at about 500,000; that of its streets 912; and that of its houses upwards of 20,000, exclusive of the public structures of all sorts. Its greatest defect, according to some, is the want of good drinking-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but others tell us, that very fine water is brought by an aqueduct from the village of Arcueil, not far from Paris, but own the water of the Seine, and the city, is not good. The streets are of a proper breadth, well built, paved, and lighted. There is a great number of tribunals and offices here; most of which are kept in the Palais, situated on an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, to which it gives name. The number of churches, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, market-places, fountains, gates, and bridges, in this city is very great; besides the university, several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>, public <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> palaces and castles, and above 100 hotels, some of them very stately. But to be more particular, that part called la Cité, lies in the centre, and consists of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THREE_ISLANDS">three <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> formed by the Seine, viz. L'île de Palais, L'île de Notre Dame, and L'île <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOUVIERS">Louviers</a>. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of the three parts into which the city is divided, and contains the following remarkable structures: 1. Several bridges; of which some are of wood and others of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and have most of them a row of houses on each side. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of these are the Pont-neuf and Pont-royal: the first consists of 12 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, which, properly speaking, make two bridges, the one leading from the suburbs of St Germain to the city, and the other from thence to that part called la Ville: there is a carriage-way in the middle, 30 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and footwalks on each side, raised two feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and in the centre stands a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> statue of king Henry IV. on horseback. On this <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> is also the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> called La Samaritaine, from a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of figures upon it representing our Saviour and the Samaritan woman, standing near <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>'s well. Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> to raise the water, which through several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> supplies the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the Louvre, and some other parts of the town. The Pont-royal, which leads to the Tuilleries, was built by order of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIV. in the room of a wooden bridge that was carried away by the current in 1684. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of Notre Dame, or our Lady, being dedicated to the Holy Virgin, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flatly Gothic structure, said to have been founded by king Childeric, and built in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. Here, besides other great personages, are interred the cardinals de Retz and Noailles. From the two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> towers belonging to it, is a noble prospect of the city and neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Here is a vast <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver plate, rich <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, and fine paintings; and the number of the canons is no less than 50. Near it stands the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the archbishop, in which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> library: the revenue of the archbishop amounts to about 180,000 livres; and his <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome is 4283 guilders. 3. The priory and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Bartholomew; the last of which is the most beautiful in all this part of the city, and stands near the Palais. 4. The Palais, which gives name to an island, and in which the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, with a great many other courts, are held. It was anciently the residence of the kings; but was given to the officers of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> the Fair, who also settled the parliament here in 1302. The parliament, consisting of several chambers, each of which has its department, is opened the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> after Martinmas with a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, celebrated by a bishop, and continues sitting till the 8th of September, when a vacation-chamber is appointed during the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>, for criminal causes, and others which require dispatch. The jurisdiction of this court is of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. There is a beautiful chapel belonging to the Palais; in which is also the prison, or jail, for the jurisdiction of the parliament, called in French La Conciergerie. 5. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOTEL">Hotel</a> Dieu, the most ancient and largest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> in Paris, in which 8000 sick and infirm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> are taken care of, and attended by the nuns of the order of St Augustine. 6. The hospital of St Catharine, where poor women and maidens are entertained three days, and attended by the abovementioned nuns. 7. The Grande Chatelet, where some of the inferior courts of justice hold their sessions. 8. Fort l'Eveque, in which is the mint and a prison. It stands in or near the street La Ferroniere, in which Henry IV. was stabbed by Ravillac. 9. St Germain l'Auxerrois, which is called the royal palace church; because the palaces of the Louvre and Tuilleries stand in its parish. 10. The Louvre, an ancient royal palace, of which a part was rebuilt by Lewis XIV. Had it been completed on the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, it would have been a most magnificent structure. On one of its gates is the following inscription, *Dum totum impleat orbis:* the meaning of which is, "May it last till the owner of it hath extended his sway over the whole world;" which implies what the French kings have constantly aimed at. Another inscription shews, at the same time, the vanity of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and their abject flattery of their grande monarque. It may be rendered in English thus: Louvre is a palace for great Lewis fit: God him alone exceeds, as heaven does it. This palace is joined to the Tuilleries by a gallery, in which are 180 models of fortresses, some situated in France, and some in other countries, executed with the utmost accuracy. Here is a valuable collection of paintings, the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the mint where the king's medals are struck, together with a prodigious quantity of rich tapestry hangings, and a collection of ancient arms, among which are those worn by Francis I. at the famous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>. Here also the French academy, the academy of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> and belles lettres, the royal academy of sciences, the academy of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, and the royal academy of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, have their meetings. The first of these was founded for the improvement of the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; and as for the others, their names explain the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>. 11. Le Palais Royal, which was built by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> Richlieu, in the year 1636, and belongs to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>. It is said to contain pictures to the value of four millions of livres, which were purchased by the regent of that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, and of which a part belonged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. 12. The palace des Tuilleries, so called from a tile or brick-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KILN">kiln</a> which stood there formerly. This palace, as we observed above, communicates with the Louvre by a gallery. Behind it are exceeding pleasant gardens, adorned with fine walks, planted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">evergreens</a>, and other trees, and with beautiful parterres, where are to be seen, all the year round, every flower according to its season. There are also three fine fountains, the garden, and a canal. Behind the Tuilleries, on the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river, are pleasant walks, composed of four rows of lofty elms, to which vast crowds of people <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> in the fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, as well as to the gardens. In the palace is a spacious and magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, and hard by it are the Elysian fields, where a surprising number of coaches are to be seen in fair weather: not far off is the church of St Roche, where the celebrated poet Corneille is interred. 13. La place de <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> le <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a>, a very beautiful square, in the centre of which is an equestrian statue of that king, which is justly accounted a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>-piece. 14. The Place, or Square des Victoires, which is round, and contains a statue of Lewis XIV. of gilt brass, erected to him by the duke de la Fuillade, with this inscription, *Vivo immortalis.* 15. The Royal Library in the Rue Vivien, which contains 94,000 printed books, 30,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, and a prodigious collection of copperplates and medals. Near by, in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, lies the famous comic poet Moliere. 16. The parish church of St Eustace, which stands in the quarter of the same name, and contains the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of the great minister Colbert. 17. The gate of St Dennis, which was erected as a triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Lewis XIV. 18. The gate of St Martin, erected also in form of a triumphal arch, in honour of the same king. Not far from hence, in the churchyard of St Nicholas des Champs, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Gassendi, and other learned men, are buried. 19. La Greve, an open place, where all public rejoicings are celebrated, and malefactors executed. 20. The Hotel de Ville, which is a large building of Gothic architecture, adorned with columns of the Corinthian order. 21. The arsenal in the quarter of St Paul, consisting of many spacious buildings, among which are a foundry, and a house for making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>. Here is a musquetoon of two barrels, which it is said <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> pierce a thick board at the distance of six miles; and, for discovering an object at that distance, has a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a> fixed to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>. 22. The Bastile, a kind of fortress like the the Tower of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, which is used as a prison for state-criminals, and for such as are taken up by letters de cachet, i.e., by warrants signed by the king, and sealed. 23. Le Temple, a commandery of the knights of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, which gives name to a quarter, wherein being a privileged place, artificers, that are not freemen, may carry on their business without molestation. The temple is the residence of the grand <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> of the French nation. 24. That formerly called La Maison professe des Jésuites, in the quarter of St Anthony, in the church of which the hearts of Lewis XIII. and XIV. are preserved, each in a casket of gold, supported by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> of massy silver, and as big as the life, hovering with expanded wings. In the same quarter is a fine looking-glass manufacture, where above 500 persons are employed in polishing plates <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> at St Gobin; with a convent of Franciscans, the monks of which are called Pique-pucres, or Prick-pleas. In that part of the city called the University, the principal places are, 1. The university which gives name to it, and which was first founded, as it is said, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the Great: all the arts and sciences are taught here, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, physic, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. There are above forty colleges; of which the chief are those of Sorbonne, of Navarre, of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of physic, and of the four nations; but lectures are read only in eleven of them. The head of the university is the rector, who is chosen every three months, but sometimes is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> several years. All the professors have settled salaries; the whole annual income of the university amounting, it is said, to about 50,000 livres. 2. The Gobelins, a house or palace, where a great number of ingenious artists, in various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> and handicrafts, are employed by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. The most curious tapestry of all sorts is made here. 3. The General Hospital, a most noble foundation for the poor of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, near 7000 objects being taken care of and provided for. The sick are carefully tended; and those that are in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> are obliged to work; different wards being allotted for foundlings, for girls who sew or knit, prostitutes, idiots, and poor women; of the last, some are kept gratis, and others pay a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. In the cattle of Bicetre, belonging to this hospital, and consisting of many large buildings, are near 4000 persons of the other sex, among which are persons disordered in their senses, and such as are afflicted with the venereal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. To this hospital are also sent children who abuse their parents, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> dissolute lives. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUND">fund</a> for the maintenance of it, and the hospital de la Piété, where poor children are brought up, together with the Hotel Dieu, amounts to above two millions of livres per annum. 4. The King's Physic Garden, in which are an infinite variety of plants and trees, a certain sum being allotted by the king for keeping the garden in order, and improving it, and for lectures on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>. A curious collection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> curiosities is kept here. 5. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St Victor, in which is a public library, containing some very ancient and scarce books, several curious manuscripts, and a prodigious collection of maps and copperplates. 6. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of Physicians, to which belong five professors. 7. The Little Chatelet, an old fortress, now used for a prison. 8. The Rue St Jacques, chiefly inhabited by bookellers. 9. The Royal College, and that of Lewis the Great; to the former belong twelve professors. 10. The Abbey of St Genevieve, in which is the marble monument of king Clovis, the shrine of St Genevieve, a large library, with a cabinet of antiquities and natural curiosities. 11. The Royal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBSERVATORY">Observatory</a>, a most stately edifice, built on the highest part of the city. Several astronomers are maintained here by the king. 12. The Royal Academy of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, instituted in 1731. 13. The Convent of Franciscans, in the quarter of St Andrew, the richest in France. In the same quarter are some remains of the palace of Julian the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">Apostle</a>, in which Childebert, and some other kings of the Franks, afterwards resided. 14. The Play-house. 15. The Convent of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARTHUSIANS">Carthusians</a>, in the quarter of Luxemburg, containing fine paintings. 16. The Palace of Luxemburg, or Orleans, a magnificent structure, containing also some fine paintings by Rubens, and embellished with a noble garden. In the Hotel des Ambassadeurs, ambassadors extraordinary are entertained for three days, and those of remote countries all the time they stay at Paris. 17. The Abbey of St Germain des Pres, which contains a very valuable library, the manuscripts alone making 8,000 volumes: here also is a cabinet of antiquities. 18. The Hotel royal des Invalides, erected by Lewis XIV. in which lame and superannuated officers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> are maintained. The buildings take up no less than 17 acres. The number of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> soldiers here amount to about 3000, and of officers to about 500. The chapel is very magnificent. Hard by is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> academy, in which 500 young gentlemen are instructed in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Paris, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a> Paris, or truelove; a genus of the trigynia order, belonging to the octandra clas of plants. There are but one species, growing naturally in woods and shady places both in Scotland and England. It hath a fingle naked stem, greenish blossoms, and bluish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> berries.—The leaves and berries are said to partake of the properties of opium; and the juice of the berries is useful in inflammations of the eyes. Linnaeus says, that the root will vomit as well as ipecacuanha, but must be taken in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the quantity. Goats and sheep eat the plant; cows, horses, and swine, refuse it.

PARISH

Pages 367-368

the precinct of a parochial <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a circuit of ground inhabited by people who belong to one church, and are under the particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of its minister. The word comes from the Latin parochia, the Greek παροχία, "habitation;" compounded of παρά, "near," and οχις, "<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>."—Accordingly Du Cange observes, that the name παροχία was anciently given to the whole territory of a bishop, and derives it from neighbourhood; because the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, not daring to assemble openly in cities, were forced to meet secretly in neighbour-houses. In the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> church there was one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> edifice in each <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> for the people to meet in; and this they called parochia, parish. But the signification of the word was afterwards enlarged, and by a parish was meant a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the jurisdiction of a bishop, consisting of several churches; unless we <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> suppose, as some do, that those <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> were only only pastors of single churches. See Diocese and Bishop. Du <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIN">Pin</a> observes, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> parishes had not their origin before the 4th century; but those of cities are more ancient. The city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> is said to have been the first that was divided into parishes.

PARISII

Pages 368-368

(anc. geog.), a people of Gallia Celtica, inhabiting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about the Sequana and Matrona. Now a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of France.—Parisii, (<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>), a people of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, having the Brigantes to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and west, the German <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to the east, and the Coritani to the south, from whom they were separated by the Humber. Now Holderness, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of the East Riding of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. PARISIORM CIVITAS. See LUTETIA.

PARIUM

Pages 368-368

(anc. geog.), a noble <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MYSIA">Mysia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, with a port on the Propontis; called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADRIA">Adria</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, according to Pliny; but Strabo distinguishes them: according to others, the Pasfloros of Homer. Partian, the people, (Strabo). The birthplace of Neoptolemus farnamed Glofographus, (Strabo). Here stood a Cupid equal, in exquisite workmanship, to the Cnidian Venus.

PARK

Pages 368-371

(French parques, i.e. locus inctus), is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ground inclosed and privileged for wild beasts of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>. See Chase and Forest. Manwood defines a chase to be "a privileged <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for beasts of venery, and other wild beasts of the forest and chase, tam Sylvictrices, quam Campefrees?" and differs from a chase or warren, in that it must be inclosed: for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it lies open, it is good cause of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZURE">seizure</a> into the king's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, as a thing forfeited: as a free chase is, if it be inclosed: besides, the owner cannot have an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> against such as hunt in his park, if it lies open. No <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> can erect a park without licence under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>; for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> does not encourage <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, which brings no profit to the commonwealth. But there may be a park in reputation, erected without any lawful warrant; and the owner may bring his action against persons killing his deer. To a park three things are required. 1. A grant thereof. 2. Inclosures by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, wall, or hedge. 3. Beasts of a park; such as the buck, doe, &c. And where all the deer are destroyed, it shall no more be accounted a park; for a park consists of vert, venison, and inclosure; and if it is determined in any of them, it is a total disparking. Parks as well as chases are subject to the common law, and are not to be governed by the forest laws. Park, as connected with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>. See Gardening. A park and a garden are more nearly allied than a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FARM">farm</a> and a garden *, and can therefore be accommodated to each other without any disparagement to either. A farm loses some of its characteristic properties by the connection, and the advantage is on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the garden; but a park thus bordered retains all its own excellencies; they are only enriched, not counteracted, by the intermixture. The most perfect <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of a place that can be imagined, consists of a garden opening into a park, with a short walk through the latter to a farm, and ways along its glades to ridings in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but to the farm and the ridings the park is no more than a passage; and its woods and its buildings are but circumstances in their views; its scenes can be communicated only to the garden. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> of the two subjects is so <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, that it would be difficult to draw the exact line of separation between them. Gardens have lately encroached very much both in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and in style on the character of a park; but still there are scenes in the one which are out of the reach of the other. The small sequestrated spots which are agreeable in a garden would be trivial in a park; and the spacious lawns which are among the noblest features of the latter, would in the former fatigue by their want of variety; even such as, being of a moderate extent, may be admitted into either, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> seem bare and naked, if not broken in the one; and lose much of their greatness, if broken, in the other. The proportion of a part to the whole is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of its dimensions: it often determines the proper size for an object, as well as the space fit to be allotted to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>; and regulates the style which ought to be assigned to either. But whatever distinctions the extent may occasion between a park and a garden, a state of highly cultivated <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is consistent with each of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>; and may in both be of the same kind, though in different degrees. The excellencies both of a park and of a garden are happily blended at Hagley (A), where the scenes are equally elegant and noble. It is situated in the midst of a fertile and lovely country, between the Clent and the Witchberry hills; neither of which are within the pale, but both belong to the place. The latter rise in three beautiful swells. One of them is covered with wood; another is an open sheep-walk, with an obelisk on the summit; on the third, the portico of the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>, exactly on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of that at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, and little less in the dimensions, stands boldly out upon the brow, backed by the dark ground of a fir plantation, and has a most majestic appearance above the steeples which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> before and beside it. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is seen to the greatest advantage from these eminences, and every point of them commands some beautiful prospect. The busy town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STOURBRIDGE">Stourbridge</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> below them; the ruins of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUDLEY">Dudley</a> castle rise in the offskip; the country is full of industry and inhabitants; and a small portion of the moor, where the minerals, manufactured in the neighbourhood, are dug, breaking in upon the horizon, accounts for the richness, without derogating from the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, of the landscape. From the Clent hills the views are still greater; they extend on one side to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ridge which appears, at 60 miles distance, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the unwieldy heap of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALVERN">Malvern</a> hills, and the solitary peak of the Wrekin, each 30 miles off, and as many asunder. The smok of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, the churches in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a>, and the houes in Stourbridge, are distinctly visible. The country is a mixture of hill and dale, and strongly inclosed; except in one part, where a heath, varied by rising grounds, pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and several objects, forms an agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> to the cultivation which surrounds it. From the other extremity of the Clent hills, the prospect is less extensive; but the ground is more rude and broken: it is often overspread with large and beautiful woods; and the view is dignified with numerous seats. The hills also being (A) Near Stourbridge, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WORCESTERSHIRE">Worcestershire</a>, the seat of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Lyttelton. being very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, large advanced promontories frequently interrupt the sight, and vary the scene; in other parts, deep valleys shelving <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> towards the country below, exhibit the objects there in different lights. In one of these hollows is built a neat cottage, under a deep <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, sheltered besides by plantations, and presenting <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of retirement in the midst of so much open exposure; from the heights above it, is seen all that view which before was commanded from the Witchberry hills, but which is seen here over Hagley park; a noble fore-ground, beautiful in itself, and completing the landscape. The house, though low in the park, is yet above the adjacent country, which it overlooks to a very distant horizon. It is surrounded by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a> of fine uneven ground, and diversified with large clumps, little groups, and single trees. It is open in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, but covered on one side by the Witchberry hills; on the other side, and behind, by the eminences in the park, which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and steep, and all overspread with a lofty hanging wood. The lawn pressing to the foot, or creeping up the slopes of these hills, and sometimes winding along glades into the depth of the wood, traces a beautiful outline to a sylvan scene, already rich to luxuriance in masses of foliage and stateliness of growth. But though the wood appears to be entire, it in reality opens frequently into lawns, which occupy much of the space within it. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, the variety, and the beauty of these lawns, in the shades of the separations between them, in their beauties also, and their varieties, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of Hagley consists. No two of the openings are alike in dimensions, in shape, or in character. One is of no more than five or fix acres; another of not less than fifty; and others are of all the intermediate sizes. Some stretch out into lengthened glades; some widen every way: they are again distinguished by buildings, by prospects, and often by the style only of the plantations around them. The boundary of one is described by a few careless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; that of another is composed of many parts, very different and very irregular; and the ground is never flat; but falls sometimes in steep declents, sometimes in gentle declivities waves along easy swells, or is thrown into broken inequalities, with endless variety. An octagon seat, sacred to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Thomson, and erected on his favourite spot, stands on the brow of a steep; a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEAD">mead</a> winds along the valley beneath, till it is lost on either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> behind fome trees. Opposite to the seat, a noble wood crowns the top, and feathers down to the bottom of a large, oval, swelling hill. As it descends on one side, the distant country becomes the offskip. Over the fall, on the other side, the Clent hills appears. A dusky antique tower stands just below them, at the extremity of the wood; and in the midst of it is seen a Doric portico, called Pope's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">Building</a>, with part of the lawn before it. The scene is very simple: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> features are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; they prevail over all the rest, and are intimately connected with each other. The next opening is small, circling about a rotunda on a knole, to the foot of which the ground rises every way. The trees which surround it are large; but their foliage is not very thick; and their stems appearing beneath, their ramifications between the boughs are, in so confined a spot, very distinguished and agreeable circumstances. It is retired; has no prospect; no visible outlet but one, and that is short and narrow, to a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> with a portico upon it, which terminates a piece of water.
