It was covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> trees, (Virgil); and originally called Larndius, from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>'s larname <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> ark, thither conveyed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, (Stephanus, Scholiast on Apollonius); after the flood, Parnassus; from Har Nahas, changing the b into p, the hill of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a> or augury, Peucerus; the oracle of Delphi standing at its foot.

PARNELL

Pages 379-379

a very ingenious divine and poet in the early <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of this century. He was archdeacon of Clogher, and the intimate friend of Mr Pope; who published his works, with an elegant copy of recommendatory verses prefixed. He died in 1718, aged 39.

PARODY

Pages 379-379

is also a poetical pleasantry, consisting in applying the verses written on one subject, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>, to another; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> a serious <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> into a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a>, by afflicting to observe as near as possible the same rhymes, words, and cadences.

PAROLE

Pages 379-379

means also a word given out every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> in orders by the commanding officer, both in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> and garrison, in order to know friends from enemies.

PARONOMASIA

Pages 379-379

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, a pun; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> whereby words nearly alike in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, but of very different meanings, are affectedly or designedly used. See **ORATORY**, n° 76.

PAROS

Pages 379-379

(anc. geog.), an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Aegean <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, one of the Cyclades, with a strong cognominal town, 38 miles distant from Delos, (Pliny, Nepos). Anciently called Patye and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a>, (Pliny); also Demetrias, Zacynthus, Hyria, Hylecissa, and Cabarnis, (Nicanor). The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Archilocheus, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IAMBIC">Iambic</a> poet, (Strabo). An island famous for its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Horace, Ovid), called lychnites, because dug with lamps, (Pliny).

PAROXYSM

Pages 379-379

in medicine, the fever fit of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, under which it grows higher <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> exaggerated; as of the gout, &c.

PARR

Pages 379-382

was the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir Thomas Parr of Kendall. She was first married to John Nevil, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Latymer; after whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> she so captivated her amorous sovereign, that he raised her to the throne. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> nuptials were solemnized at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPTON">Hampton</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">Court</a> on the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1543. Being religiously disposed, she was, in the early <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, a zealous observer of the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> and ceremonies; but, in the dawning of the Reformation, she became as zealous a promoter of the Lutheran doctrine; yet with such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and circumspection as her perilous situation required. Nevertheless, we are told, that she was in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> danger of falling a sacrifice to the Popish <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACTION">faction</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of whom was bishop Gardiner: he drew up <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> against her, and prevailed on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> to sign a warrant to remove her to the Tower. This warrant was, however, accidentally dropped, and immediately conveyed to her majesty. What her apprehensions must have been on this occasion, may be easily imagined. She knew the monarch, and she could not help recollecting the fate of his former queens. A sudden illness was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. The news of her indisposition brought the king to her apartment. He was lavish in expressions of affection, and sent her a physician. His majesty being soon after also somewhat indisposed, she prudently returned the visit; with which the king seemed pleased, and began to talk with her on <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> subjects, proposing certain questions, concerning which he wanted her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. She answered, that such profound speculations were not suited to her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; that it belonged to the husband to choose principles for his wife; the wife's duty was, in all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, to adopt implicitly the sentiments of her husband; and as to herself, it was doubly her duty, being blessed with a husband who was qualified, by his judgment and learning, not only to choose principles for his own family, but for the most wise and knowing of every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. "Not so, by St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>," replied the king; "you are now become a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>, Kate, and better fitted to give than receive instruction." She meekly replied, that she was sensible how little she was entitled to these praises; that though she usually declined not any conversation, however sublime, when proposed by his Majesty, she well knew that her conceptions could serve to no other purpose than to give him a little momentary amusement; that she found the conversation a little apt to languish when not revived by some opposition, and she She had ventured sometimes to feign a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRARIETY">contrariety</a> of sentiments, in order to give him the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of refuting her; and that she also proposed, by this innocent artifice, to engage him into topics whence she had observed by frequent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that she reaped profit and instruction. "And is it so, sweetheart?" replied the king, "and then we are perfect friends again." He embraced her with great affection, and sent her away with assurances of his protection and kindness. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> being now come when she was to be sent to the Tower, the king, walking in the garden, sent for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, and met her with great good humour; when lo the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, with forty of the guards, approached. He fell upon his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, and spoke softly with the king, who called him <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNAVE">knave</a>, arrant knave, beast, fool, and commanded him instantly to depart. Henry then returned to the queen, who ventured to intercede for the chancellor: "Ah <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>!" said the king, "thou little knowest how evil he deserves this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> at thy <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Of my word, sweetheart, he hath been toward thee an arrant knave; and so let him go." The king died in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1547, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> three years and a half after his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Catherine; who in a short time was again espoused to Sir Thomas Seymour lord-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of England; for, in September 1548, she died in childbed. The historians of this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> generally insinuate, that she was poisoned by her husband, to make way for his marriage with the lady <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. That Catharine Parr was beautiful, is beyond a doubt: that she was pious and learned, is evident from her writings: and that her prudence and sagacity were not inferior to her other accomplishments, may be concluded from her holding up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> of a capricious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> as a shield against her enemies; and that at the latter end of his days, when his passions were enfeebled by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and his peevish austerity increased by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. She wrote, 1. Queen Catharine Parr's lamentation of a sinner, bewailing the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of her <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> life; Lond. 8vo, 1548, 1563. 2. Prayers <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> meditations, wherein the mind is stirred patiently to suffer all afflictions here, to set at nought the vain prosperity of this world, and always to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> for the everlasting felicity. Collected out of holy works, by the most virtuous and gracious princess Katharine, queene of Englannde, France, and Irelande. Printed by John Wayland, 1545, 4to.—1561, 12mo. 3. Other Meditations, Prayers, Letters, &c. unpublished. Parr (Thomas), or Old Parr, a remarkable Englishman, who lived in the reigns of ten kings and queens; married a second wife when he was 120, and had a child by her. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONGEVITY">Longevity</a>. Parrels, in a ship, are frames made of trucks, ribs, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, which having both their ends fastened to the yards, are so contrived as to go round about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, that the yards by their means may go up and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon the mast. These also, with the breasting-ropes, fasten the yards to the masts. Parrhesia. See Oratory, no 88. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARRICIDE">Parricide</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of one's parents or children. By the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, it was punished in a much fewer manner than any other kind of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMICIDE">homicide</a>. After being scourged, the delinquents were sewed up in a leathern sack, with a live dog, a cock, a viper, and an ape, and so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Solon, it is true, in his laws, made none against parricide; apprehending it impossible that one should be guilty of so unnatural a barbarity. And the Persians, according to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, entertained the same notion, when they adjudged all persons who killed their reputed parents to be bastards. And upon some such reason as this must we account for the omission of an exemplary <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for this crime in our English laws; which treat it no otherwise than as simple murder, unless the child was also the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>. For though the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of natural relation is unobserved, yet the breach of civil or ecclesiastic connections, when coupled with murder, denominates it a new offence; nor less than a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> called parva proelio, or petit treason: which, however, is nothing else but an aggravated <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of murder; although, on account of the violation of private <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, it is stigmatized as an inferior species of treason. And thus, in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, we find the breach both of natural and civil relations ranked in the same class with crimes against the state and sovereign. Parrot, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PSITTACUS">Psittacus</a>. Parsley, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. See Apium. Parsnip, in botany. See Pastinaca. Parson and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VICAR">Vicar</a>. A parson, persona ecclesiae, is one that hath full possession of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of a parochial <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. He is called parson, persona, because by his person the church, which is an invisible body, is represented; and he is in himself a body corporate, in order to protect and defend the rights of the church (which he personates) by a perpetual succession. He is sometimes called the rector or governor of the church: but the appellation of parson (however it may be depreciated by familiar, clownish, and indiscriminate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>) is the most legal, most beneficial, and most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> that a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> can enjoy; because such a one (Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> observes) and he only, is said vicem seu personam ecclesiae gerere. A parson has, during his life, the freehold in himself of the parsonage-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the glebe, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a>, and other dues. But these are sometimes appropriated; that is to say, the benefice is perpetually annexed to some spiritual corporation, either sole or aggregate, being the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of the living; whom the law esteems equally capable of providing for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the church as any single private clergyman. See article Apportionment. The appropriating corporations, or religious houses, were wont to depute one of their own body to perform divine service, and administer the sacraments, in those parishes of which the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> was thus the parson. This officiating minister was in reality no more than a curate, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, or vicegerent of the appropriator, and therefore called vicarius, or "vicar." His stipend was at the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the appropriator, who was, however, bound of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to find somebody, qui illi de temporalibus, episcopo de spiritualibus, debet respondere. But this was done in so scandalous a manner, and the parishes suffered so much by the neglect of the appropriators, that the legislature was forced to interpose: and accordingly it is enacted, by statute 15 Ric. II. c. 6, that in all appropriations of churches... churches the diocesan bishop shall ordain (in proportion to the value of the church) a competent sum to be distributed among the poor parishioners annually; and that the vicarage shall be sufficiently endowed. It seems the parish were frequently sufferers, not only by the want of divine service, but also by withholding those alms for which, among other purposes, the payment of tithes was originally imposed: and therefore in this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> a pension is directed to be distributed among the poor parishioners, as well as a sufficient stipend to the vicar. But he, being liable to be removed at the pleasure of the appropriator, was not likely to insist too rigidly on the legal sufficiency of the stipend; and therefore, by statute 4 Hen. IV. c. 12, it is ordained, that the vicar shall be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> person, not a member of any religious house; that he shall be vicar perpetual, not removable at the caprice of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>; and that he shall be canonically instituted and inducted, and be sufficiently endowed, at the discretion of the ordinary; for these three express purposes, to do divine service, to inform the people, and to keep hospitality. The endowments, in consequence of these statutes, have usually been by a portion of the glebe or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> belonging to the parsonage, and a particular share of the tithes, which the appropriators found it most troublesome to collect, and which are therefore generally called privy, or small tithes; the greater, or predial tithes, being still reserved to their own use. But one and the same rule was not observed in the endowment of all vicarages. Hence some are more liberally, and some more scantily, endowed; and hence the tithes of many things, as wood in particular, are in some parishes rectorial, and in some vicarial tithes. The distinction therefore of a parson and vicar is this: The parson has for the most part the whole right to all the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> dues in his parish; but a vicar has generally an appropriator over him, entitled to the best part of the profits, to whom he is in effect perpetual curate, with a standing salary. Though in some places the vicarage has been considerably augmented by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> share of the great tithes; which augmentations were greatly assisted by the statute 27 Car. II. c. 8, enacted in favour of poor vicars and curates, which rendered such temporary augmentations (when made by the appropriators) perpetual. The method of becoming a parson or vicar is much the same. To both there are four requisites necessary; holy orders, presentation, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, and induction. The method of conferring the holy orders of deacon and priest, according to the liturgy and canons, is foreign to the present purpose; any farther than as they are necessary requisites to make a complete parson or vicar. By common law, a deacon, of any age, might be instituted and inducted to a parsonage or vicarage; but it was ordained, by statute 13 Eliz. c. 12, that no person under twenty-three years of age, and in deacon's orders, should be presented to any benefice with cure; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he were not ordained priest within one year after his induction, he should be ipso facto deprived: and now, by statute 13 and 14 Car. II. c. 4, no person is capable to be admitted to any benefice, unless he hath been first ordained a priest; and then he is, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the law, a clerk in orders. But if he obtains orders, or a licence to preach, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> or corrupt practices, (which seems to be the true, though not the common, notion of simony), the person giving such orders forfeits 40l. and the person receiving, 10l. and is incapable of any ecclesiastical preferment for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years after. Any clerk may be presented to a parsonage or vicarage; that is, the patron, to whom the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ADVOWSON">advowson</a> of the church belongs, may offer his clerk to the bishop of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> to be instituted. But when he is presented, the bishop may refuse him upon many accounts. As, 1. If the patron is excommunicated, and remains in contempt 40 days; or, 2. If the clerk be unfit: which unfitness is of several kinds. First, with regard to his person; as if he be a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a>, an outlaw, an excommunicate, an alien, under age, or the like. Next, with regard to his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> or morals; as for any particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, or vice that is malum in se; but if the bishop alleges only in general's, as that he is schismaticus incesteratus, or objects a fault that is malum prohibitum merely, as haunting taverns, playing at unlawful games, or the like, it is not good cause of refusal. Or, lastly, the clerk may be unfit to discharge the pastoral office for want of learning. In any of which cases, the bishop may refuse the clerk. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> the refusal is for heresy, schism, inability of learning, or other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of ecclesiastical cognizance, there the bishop must give notice to the patron of such his cause of refusal, who being usually a layman, is not supposed to have knowledge of it; else he cannot present by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a>; but if the cause be temporal, there he is not bound to give notice. If an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> at law be brought by the patron against the bishop for refusing his clerk, the bishop must assign the cause. If the cause be of a temporal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and the fact admitted, (as, for instance, outlawry), the judges of the king's courts must determine its validity, or whether it be sufficient cause of refusal: but if the fact be denied, it must be determined by a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURY">jury</a>. If the cause be of a spiritual nature, (as heresy, particularly alleged), the fact, if denied, shall also be determined by a jury: and if the fact be admitted or found, the court, upon consultation and advice of learned divines, shall decide its sufficiency. If the cause be want of learning, the bishop need not specify in what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> the clerk is deficient, but only allege that he is deficient; for the statute 9 Edw. II. li. i. c. 13, is express, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the fitness of a person presented to a benefice belongs to the ecclesiastical judge. But because it would be nugatory in this case to demand the reason of refusal from the ordinary, if the patron were bound to abide by his determination, who has already pronounced his clerk unfit; therefore if the bishop returns the clerk to be minus sufficiens in literatura, the court shall write to the metropolitan to re-examine him, and certify his qualifications; which certificate of the archbishop is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a>. If the bishop hath no objections, but admits the patron's presentation, the clerk so admitted is next to be instituted by him; which is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a> of the spiritual part of the benefice; for by institution, the care of the souls of the parish is committed to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the clerk. When a vicar is instituted, he (besides the usual forms) takes, if required by the bishop, an oath of perpetual residence; for the maxim of law is, that vicarius non habet vicariatum: and as the non-residence of the appropriators was the cause of the perpet- tual establishment of vicarages, the law judges it very improper for them to defeat the end of their constitution, and by absence to create the very mischief which they were appointed to remedy; especially as, if any profits are to arise from putting in a curate and living at a distance from the parish, the appropriator, who is the real parson, has undoubtedly the elder title to them. When the ordinary is also the patron, and confers the living, the presentation and institution are one and the same act, and are called a collation to a benefice. By institution or collation the church is full, so that there can be no fresh prestation till another vacancy, at least in the case of a common patron; but the church is not full against the king till induction: nay, even if a clerk is instituted upon the king's presentation, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> may revoke it before induction, and present another clerk. Upon institution also the clerk may enter on the parsonage-house and glebe, and take the tithes; but he cannot <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> or let them, or bring an action for them, till induction. See INDUCTION. For the rights of a parson or vicar, in his tithes and ecclesiastical dues, see TITHES. As to his duties, they are so numerous, that it is impracticable to recite them here with any tolerable conciseness or accuracy; but the reader who has occasion may consult Bp Gibson's Codex, and Burn's Ecclesiastical Law. We shall therefore only just mention the article of residence, upon the supposition of which the law doth style every parochial minister an incumbent. By statute 21 Hen. VIII. c. 13. persons willingly absenting themselves from their benefices, for one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> together, or two months in the year, incur a penalty of £1. to the king, and £1. to any person that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> sue for the same; except chaplains to the king, or others therein mentioned, during their attendance in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> of such as retain them: and also except all heads of houses, magistrates, and professors in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and all students under forty years of age residing there, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BONA">bona</a> fide, for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. Legal residence is not only in the parish, but also in the parsonage-house; for it hath been resolved, that the statute intended residence, not only for serving the cure and for hospitality, but also for maintaining the house, that the successor also may keep hospitality there. We have seen that there is but one way whereby one may become a parson or vicar: there are many ways by which one may cease to be so. 1. By death. 2. By cession, in taking another benefice; for by statute 21 Hen. VIII. c. 13. if any one having a benefice of £1. per annum, or upwards, in the king's books, (according to the present valuation), accepts any other, the first shall be adjudged void, unless he obtains a dispensation; which no one is entitled to have but the chaplains of the king and others therein mentioned, the brethren and sons of lords and knights, and doctors and bachelors of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and law, admitted by the universities of this realm. And a vacancy thus made for want of a dispensation, is called occlusion. 3. By consecration; for, as was mentioned before, when a clerk is promoted to a bishopric, all his other preferments are void the instant that he is consecrated. But there is a method, by the favour of the crown, of holding such livings in commendam. Commenda, or ecclesia commendata, is a living commended by the crown to the care of a clerk, to hold till a proper pastor is Parsonage, provided for it. This may be temporary for one, two, or three years, or perpetual, being a kind of dispensation to avoid the vacancy of the living, and is called a commenda retinere. There is also a commenda recipere, which is to take a benefice de novo in the bishop's own gift, or the gift of some other patron consenting to the same; and this is the same to him as institution and induction are to another clerk. 4. By resignation. But this is of no avail till accepted by the ordinary, into whose hands the resignation must be made. 5. By deprivation, either by canonical censures, or in pursuance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> penal statutes, which declare the benefice void, for some nonfeasance or neglect, or else some malefeasance or crime: as for simony; for maintaining any doctrine in derogation of the king's supremacy, or of the thirty-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> articles, or of the book of common-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>; for neglecting after institution to read the liturgy and articles in the church, or make the declarations against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">popery</a>, or take the abjuration-oath; for using any other form of prayer than the liturgy of the church of England; or for absenting himself 60 days in one year from a benefice belonging to a papish patron, to which the clerk was presented by either of the universities: in all which, and similar cases, the benefice is ipso facto void, without any formal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of deprivation.

PARSONAGE

Pages 382-382

a rectory, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, endowed with a glebe, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, lands, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a>, &c. for the maintenance of a minister, with cure of souls within such parish. See PARSON.

PARSONS

Pages 382-383
or PERSONS, (Robert), an eminent writer of the church of Rome, was born at Nether-Stowey, near Bridgewater, in Somersetshire, in 1546, and educated at Balliol college, Oxford, where he distinguished himself as a zealous Protestant and an acute disputant; but being charged by the society with incontinency and embezzling the college money, he went to Flanders, and declared himself a Catholic. After travelling to several other places, he effected the establishment of the English seminary at Rome, and procured father Allen to be chosen rector of it. He himself was appointed the head of the mission to England, in order to dethrone Queen Elizabeth, and if possible extirpate the Protestant religion. He accordingly came over to this kingdom in 1580, and took some bold steps towards accomplishing his purpose, in which he concealed himself with great art, travelling about the country to gentlemen's houses, disguised in the habit, sometimes of a soldier, sometimes of a gentleman, and at other times like a minister or an apparitor; but father Campian being seized and committed to prison, our author escaped out of England for fear of the same fate, and went to Rome, where he was made rector of the English seminary. He had long entertained the most sanguine hopes of converting to the papish faith the young king of Scots, which he considered as the best and most effectual means of bringing over his subjects to the same religious principles; but finding it impossible to succeed in his design, he published, in 1594, his celebrated book, under the feigned name of Doleman, in order to overthrow, as far as lay in his power, the title of that prince to the crown of England. He died at Rome in 1610, and was buried in the chapel of the English college. college. Besides the book already mentioned, he wrote, 1 A defence of the Catholic hierarchy. 2. The liturgy of the sacrament of the mails. 3. A memorial for the Reformation; and several other tracts.

PART

Pages 383-383

a portion of some whole, considered as divided <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> divisible. Aliquot Part, is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> which, being repeated any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of times, becomes equal to an integer. Thus 6 is an aliquot part of 24, and 5 an aliquot part of 30, &c. Aliquant Part, is a quantity which, being repeated any number of times, becomes always either greater or less than the whole. Thus 5 is an aliquant part of 17, and 9 an aliquant part of 10, &c. The aliquant part is resolvable into aliquot parts. Thus 15, an aliquant part of 20, is resolvable into 10, and 5 a fourth part of the same. Parts of speech, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, are all the sorts of words which can enter the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of a discourse. See Grammar.

PARTERRE

Pages 383-383

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of ground, which for the most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> faces the south, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> back <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and is generally furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">evergreens</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, &c. There are two kinds of these, the plain ones and the parterres of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>. Plain parterres are most valuable in England, because of the firmness of the English grass turf, which is superior to that of any other part of the world; and the parterres of embroidery are cut into shell and scroll <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, with alleys between them. An <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, is accounted the most proper <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> for a parterre; and a parterre should indeed be always twice as long as it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, because, according to the known laws of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, a long square always looks to a square; and an exact square always appears less than it really is. As to the breadth of a parterre, it is to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the front of the house; but less than 100 feet in breadth is too little. There should be on each side the parterre a terrace-walk raised for view, and the flat of the parterre between the terraces should never be more than 300 feet, at the utmost, in breadth, and about 140 feet in width, with twice and a half that in length, is esteemed a very good size and proportion.

PARTHIA

Pages 383-392

a celebrated empire of antiquity, bounded on the west by Media, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYRCANIA">Hyrcania</a>, on the east by Ariana, on the south by Carmania the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>; surrounded on every side by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which still serve as a boundary, though its name is now changed, having obtained that of Elyrac <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Arak; and, to distinguish it from Chaldea, that of Elyrac Agami. By <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> it is divided into five districts, viz. Caminice, or Gamifene, Parthyene, Choroane, Atticene, and Tabiene. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> geographers enumerate a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many cities in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Ptolemy in particular reckons 25 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cities; and it certainly must have been very populous, since we have accounts of 2000 villages, besides a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cities, in this district being destroyed by earthquakes. Its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> was named Hecatompolis, from the circumstance of its having 100 gates. It was a noble and magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and, according to some, it still remains under the name of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol9.html#article-ISPAHAN">Ispahan</a>, the capital of the present Persian empire. Parthia is by some supposed to have been first peopled by the Phetri or Pathri, often mentioned in Scripture, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> have the Parthians to be descended from Phratrum the son of Misraim. But however true this may be with regard to the ancient inhabitants, yet it is certain, that those Parthians who were so famous in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, descended from the Scythians, though from what tribe we are not certainly informed. The history of the ancient Parthians is totally lost. All that we know about them is, that they were first subject to the Medes, afterwards to the Persians, and lastly to Alexander the Great. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> fell to Seleucus Nicator, and was held by him and his successors till the reign of Antiochus Theus, about the year 250 before Christ. At this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the Parthians revolted, and chose one Arfaces for their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>. The immediate cause of this revolt was the treachery of Agathocles, to whom Antiochus had committed the care of all the provinces beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> made an infamous attempt on Terides, a youth of great <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; which so enraged his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Arfaces, that he excited his countrymen to revolt; and before Antiochus had leisure to attend to the rebellion, it became too powerful to be crushed. Seleucus Callinicus, the successor of Antiochus Theus, attempted to reduce Arfaces; but the latter having had so much time to strengthen himself, defeated, and drove his antagonist out of the country. Seleucus, however, in a short time, undertook another expedition against Arfaces; but was still more unfortunate than he had been in the former, being not only defeated in a great <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, but taken prisoner, and died in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> on which Arfaces gained this victory was ever after observed among the Parthians as an extraordinary festival. Arfaces being thus fully established in his new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, reduced Hyrcania, and some other provinces under his power; and was at last killed in a battle against Arearaches IV. king of Cappadocia. From this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> all the other kings of Parthia took the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Arfaces, as those of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> did that of Ptolemy from Ptolemy Soiter. Arfaces I. was succeeded by his son Arfaces II. who, entering Media, made himself <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of that country, while Antiochus the Great was engaged in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> with Ptolemy Euergetes king of Egypt. Antiochus, however, was no sooner disengaged from that war, than he marched with all his forces against Arfaces, and at first drove him quite out of Media. But he soon returned with an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 100,000 foot and 20,000 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, with which he put a stop to the further progress of Antiochus; and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> was soon after concluded, in which it was agreed, that Arfaces should remain master of Parthia and Hyrcania, upon condition of his assisting him in his wars with other nations. Arfaces II. was succeeded by his son Priapstius, who reigned 15 years, and left three sons, Phrahates, Conquettis <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a>, and Artabanus. Phrahates, the eldest, succeeded to the throne, and reduced under his subjection the Mardi, who had never been conquered by any but Alexander the Great. After him, his brother Mithridates was invested with the regal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. He reduced the Bactrians, Medes, Perians, Elamites, and overran in a manner all the east, penetrating beyond the boundaries of Alexander's conquests. Demetrius Nicator, who then reigned in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, endeavored... voured to recover those provinces; but his army was entirely destroyed, and himself taken prisoner, in which state he remained till his death; after which victory Mithridates made himself master of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a> and Mesopotamia, so that he now commanded all the provinces from between the Euphrates and the Ganges. Mithridates died in the 37th year of his reign, and left the throne to his son Phrahates II. who was scarce settled in his kingdom, when Antiochus Sideres marched against him at the head of a numerous army, under pretence of delivering his brother Demetrius, who was still in captivity. Phrahates was defeated in three pitched battles, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which he lost all the countries conquered by his father, and was reduced within the limits of the ancient Parthian kingdom. Antiochus did not, however, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> enjoy his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>; for his army, on account of their number, amounting to no fewer than 400,000, being obliged to separate to such distances as prevented them, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of any sudden attack, from joining together, the inhabitants, whom they had most cruelly oppressed, taking advantage of this separation, conspired with the Parthians to destroy them. This was accordingly executed; and the vast army of Antiochus, with the monarch himself, were slaughtered in one day, scarce a single person escaping to carry the news to Syria. Phrahates, elated with this success, proposed to invade Syria; but in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, happening to quarrel with the Scythians, he was by them cut off with his whole army, and was succeeded by his uncle Artabanus. The new king enjoyed his dignity but a very short time, being, a few days after his accession, killed in another battle with the Scythians. He was succeeded by Pacorus I. who entered into an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and by Phrahates III. This monarch took under his protection Tigranes the son of Tigranes the Great, king of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, gave him his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, and invaded the kingdom with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to place the son on the throne of Armenia; but on the approach of Pompey he thought proper to retire, and soon after solemnly renewed the treaty with the Romans. Phrahates was murdered by his children Mithridates and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORODES">Orodes</a>; and soon after, the former was put to death by his brother, who thus became sole master of the Parthian empire. In his reign happened the memorable war with the Romans under Crassus. This was occasioned not by any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of treaty on the side of the Parthians, but through the shameful avarice of Crassus. The whole Roman empire at that time had been divided between Caesar, Pompey, and Crassus; and by virtue of that partition, the eastern provinces had fallen to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of Crassus. No sooner was he invested with this dignity, than he resolved to carry the war into Parthia, in order to enrich himself with the spoils of that people, who were then looked upon to be very wealthy. Some of the tribunes opposed him, as the Parthians had religiously observed the treaty; but Crassus having, by the affluence of Pompey, carried every thing before him, left Rome in the year 55 B.C. and pursued his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a> to Brundusium, where he immediately embarked his troops, though the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blew very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and after a difficult passage, where he lost many of his ships, he reached the ports of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALATIA">Galatia</a>. From Galatia Crassus hastened to Syria, and passing through Judea, plundered the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>; the temple in his way. He then marched with as great expedition as he could to the river Euphrates, which he crossed on a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of boats; and, entering the Parthian dominions, began hostilities. As the enemy had not expected an invasion, they were quite unprepared for resistance, and therefore Crassus overran all Mesopotamia; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had taken advantage of the consternation which the Parthians were in, might have also reduced Babylonia. But instead of this, early in the autumn, he repassed the Euphrates, leaving only 7000 foot and 1000 horse to garrison the places he had reduced; and putting his army into winter-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> in Syria, gave himself totally up to his favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> of amassing <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Early in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, the Roman general drew his forces out of their winter-quarters, in order to pursue the war with vigour; but, during the winter, Orodes had collected a very numerous army, and was well prepared to oppose him. Before he entered upon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, however, the Parthian monarch sent ambassadours to Crassus, in order to expostulate with him on his injustice in attacking an ally of the Roman empire; but Crassus, without attending to what they said, only returned for answer, that "they should have his answer at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>." Orodes, finding that a war was not to be avoided, divided his army into two bodies. One he commanded in person, and marched towards Armenia, in order to oppose the king of that country, who had raised a considerable army to assist the Romans. The other he sent into Mesopotamia, under the command of Surena or Surenas, a most experienced general, by whose conduct all the cities which Crassus had reduced were quickly retaken. On this some Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> who had made their escape, and fled to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> of Crassus, filled the minds of his army with terror at the accounts of the number, power, and strength of the enemy. They told their fellow-soldiers, that the Parthians were very numerous, brave, and well disciplined; that it was impossible to overtake them when they fled, or escape them when they pursued; that their defensive weapons were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> against the Roman darts, and their offensive weapons so sharp, that no buckler was proof against them, &c. Crassus looked upon all this only as the effects of cowardice; but the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> soldiers, and even many of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> officers, were so disheartened, that Crassus, the same who afterwards conspired against Caesar, and most of the legionary tribunes, advised Crassus to suspend his march, and consider better of the enterprise before he proceeded farther in it. But Crassus obstinately persisted in his former <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, being encouraged by the arrival of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTABAZUS">Artabazus</a> king of Armenia, who brought with him 6000 horse, and promised to send 10,000 cuirassiers and 30,000 foot, whenever he should stand in need of them. At the same time, he advised him by no means to march his army through the plains of Mesopotamia, but to take his route over the mountains of Armenia. He told him, that as Armenia was a mountainous country, the enemy's cavalry, in which their main strength consisted, would there be entirely useless. useless; and besides, his army would there be plentifully supplied with all manner of necessaries: whereas, if he marched by the way of Mesopotamia, he would be perpetually harassed by the Parthian horse, and frequently be obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> his army thro' <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> deserts, where he would be distressed for want of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> and all other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. This salutary advice, however, was rejected, and Crassus entered Mesopotamia with an army of about 40,000 men. The Romans had no sooner crossed the Euphrates, than Cassius advised his general to advance to some of those <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in which the garrisons yet remained, in order to halt and refresh his troops; or if he did not choose to follow this advice, he said that his best way would be to march along the banks of the Euphrates to Seleucia; as by this method he would prevent the Parthians from surrounding him, at the same time that he would be plentifully supplied with provisions from his ships. Of this advice Crassus seemed to approve; but was dissuaded by Abgarus king of Edessa, whom the Romans took for an ally, but who was in reality a traitor sent by Surenas to bring about the destruction of the Roman army. Under the conduct of this faithless guide, the Romans entered a vast green plain divided by many rivulets. Their march proved very easy through this fine country; but the farther they advanced, the worse the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> became, insomuch, that they were at last obliged to climb up <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROCKY_MOUNTAINS">rocky mountains</a>, which brought them to a dry and sandy plain, where they could neither find food to satisfy their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, nor water to quench their thirst. Abgarus then began to be suspected by the tribunes and other officers, who earnestly intreated Crassus not to follow him any longer, but to retreat to the mountains; at the same time an express arrived from Artabazus, acquainting the Roman general that Orodes had invaded his dominions with a great army, and that he was obliged to keep his troops at home, in order to defend his own dominions. The same messenger advised Crassus in his master's name to avoid by all means the barren plains, where his army would certainly perish with hunger and fatigue, and by all means to approach Armenia, that they might join their forces against the common enemy. But all was to no purpose; Crassus, instead of hearkening either to the advice of the king or his own officers, first flew into a violent passion with the messengers of Artabazus, and then told his troops, that they were not to expect the delights of Campania in the most remote parts of the world. Thus they <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> their march for some days across a desert, the very sight of which was sufficient to throw them into the utmost despair; for they could not perceive, either near them or at a distance, the least tree, plant, or brook, not so much as an hill, or a single blade of grass; nothing was to be seen all around them, but huge heaps of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> sand. The Romans had scarcely got thro' this desert, when word was brought them by their scouts, that a numerous army of Parthians was advancing full march to attack them; for Abgarus, under pretence of going out on parties, had often conferred with Surenas, and concerted <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> with him for destroying the Roman army. Upon this advice, which occasioned great confusion in the camp, the Romans being quite exhausted and tired out with their long and troublesome march, Crassus drew up his men in battalia, following at first the advice of Cassius, who was for extending the infantry as wide as possible, that they might take up the more ground, and by that means prevent the enemy from surrounding them; but Abgarus assuring the proconsul, that the Parthian forces were not so numerous as was represented, he changed this disposition, and believing only the man who betrayed him, drew up his troops in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, which faced every way, and had on each side 12 cohorts in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a>. Near each cohort, he placed a troop of horse to support them, that they might <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> with the greater security and boldness. Thus the whole army looked more like one phalanx, than troops drawn up in manipuli, with spaces between them, after the Roman manner. The general himself commanded in the centre, his son in the left wing, and Cassius in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. In this order they advanced to the banks of a small river called the Balissus, the sight of which was very pleasing to the soldiers, who were much harassed with drought and excessive <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. Most of the officers were for encamping on the banks of this river, or rather rivulet, to give the troops time to refresh themselves after the fatigues of so long and painful a march; and, in the mean time, to procure certain intelligence of the number and disposition of the Parthian army; but Crassus, suffering himself to be hurried on by the inconsiderate ardour of his son, and the horse he commanded, only allowed the legions to take a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> standing; and before this could be done by all, he ordered them to advance, not slowly, and halting now and then, after the Roman manner, but as fast as they could move, till they came in sight of the enemy, who, contrary to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>, did not appear either so numerous or so terrible as they had been represented; but this was a stratagem of Surenas, who had concealed his men in convenient places, ordering them to cover their arms, lest their brightness should betray them, and, starting up at the first signal, of Carthae, to attack the enemy on all sides. The stratagem had the desired effect; for Surenas no sooner gave the signal, than the Parthians, rising as it were out of the ground, with dreadful cries, and a most frightful noise, advanced against the Romans, who were greatly surprized and dismayed at that sight; and much more so, when the Parthians, throwing off the covering of their arms, appeared in shining cuirasses, and helmets of burnished <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, finely mounted on horses covered all over with armour of the same metal. At their head appeared young Surenas, in a rich dress, and was the first who <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> the enemy, endeavouring, with his pikemen, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> through the first ranks of the Roman army; but finding it too <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and impenetrable, the cohorts supporting each other, he fell back, and retired in a seeming confusion; but the Romans were much surprized when they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> themselves suddenly surrounded on all sides, and galled with continual showers of arrows. Crassus ordered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-armed foot and archers to advance, and charge the enemy; but they were soon repulsed, and forced to cover themselves behind the heavy-armed foot. Then the Parthian horse, advancing near the Romans, discharged showers of arrows upon them, every one of which did execution, the legionaries being drawn up in such close close order, that it was impossible for the enemy to miss their aim. As their arrows were of an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and discharged with incredible force and impetuosity, nothing was proof against them. The two wings advanced in good order to repulse them, but to no effect; for the Parthians <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> their arrows with as great dexterity when their backs were turned, as when they faced the enemy; so that the Romans, whether they kept their ground, or pursued the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> enemy, were equally annoyed with their fatal arrows. The Romans, as long as they had any hopes that the Parthians, after having spent their arrows, would either betake themselves to flight, or engage them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to hand, stood their ground with great resolution and intrepidity; but when they observed, that there were a great many camels in their rear, loaded with arrows, and that those who emptied their quivers wheeled about to fill them anew, they began to lose courage, and loudly to complain of their general for suffering them thus to stand still, and serve only as a butt to the enemy's arrows, which, they well knew, would not be exhausted till they were all killed to a man. Hereupon Crassus ordered his son to advance, at all adventures, and attack the enemy with 1300 horse, 500 archers, and 8 cohorts. But the Parthians no sooner saw this choice body (for it was the flower of the army) marching up against them, but they wheeled about, and betook themselves, according to their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, to flight. Hereupon young Crassus, crying out as loud as he could, They fly before us, pushed on full speed after them, not doubting but he should <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a complete victory; but, when he was at a great distance from the main body of the Roman army, he perceived his mistake; for those who before had fled, facing about, charged him with incredible fury. Young Crassus ordered his troops to halt, hoping that the enemy, upon seeing their small number, would not be afraid to come to a close fight: but herein he was likewise greatly disappointed; for the Parthians, contenting themselves to oppose his front with their heavy-armed horse, surrounded him on all sides; and, keeping at a distance, discharged incessant showers of arrows upon the unfortunate Romans, thus surrounded and pent up. The Parthian cavalry, in wheeling about, raised so thick a dust, that the Romans could scarce see one another, much less the enemy: nevertheless, they found themselves wounded with arrows, tho' they could not perceive whence they came. In a short time, the place where they stood was all grown with dead bodies. Some of the unhappy Romans finding their entrails torn, and many overcome by the exquisite torments they suffered, rolled themselves on the sand with the arrows in their bodies, and expired in that manner. Others endeavouring to tear out by force the bearded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the arrows, only made the wounds the larger and increased their pain. Most of them died in this manner; and those who outlived their companions were no more in a condition to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>; for when young Crassus exhorted them to march up to the enemy, some shewed him their wounded bodies, others their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> nailed to their bucklers, and some their feet pierced through and pinned to the ground: so that it was equally impossible for them either to attack the enemy or defend themselves. The young commander, therefore, leaving his infantry to the mercy of the enemy, advanced at the head of the cavalry against their heavy-armed horse. The thousand Gauls whom he had brought with him from the west, charged the enemy with incredible boldness and vigour; but their lances did little execution on men armed with cuirasses, and horses covered with tried armour: however, they behaved with great resolution; for some of them taking hold of the enemies' spears, and closing with them, threw them off their horses on the ground, where they lay, without being able to stir, by reason of the great weight of their armour; others dismounting, crept under the enemy's horses, and thrusting their swords into their bellies, made them throw their riders. Thus the brave Gauls fought, tho' greatly harassed with heat and thirst, which they were not accustomed to bear, till most of their horses were killed, and their commander dangerously wounded. They then thought it advisable to retire to their infantry, which they no sooner joined, than the Parthians invested them anew, making a most dreadful havoc of them with their arrows. In this desperate condition, Crassus, spying a rising ground at a small distance, led the remains of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> thither, with a design to defend himself in the best manner he could, till succours should be sent him from his father. The Parthians pursued him; and having surrounded him in his new <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a>, continued showering arrows upon his men, till most of them were either killed or disabled, without being able to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of their arms, or give the enemy proofs of their valour. Young Crassus had two Greeks with him, who had settled in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Carrhae. These, touched with compassion, at seeing so brave a man reduced to such frights, pressed him to retire with them to the neighbouring city of Ichnes, which had declared for the Romans; but the young Roman rejected their proposal with indignation, telling them, that he would rather die a thousand times than abandon so many valiant men, who sacrificed their lives for his sake. Having returned this answer to his two Greek friends, he embraced and dismissed them, giving them leave to retire and shift for themselves in the best manner they could. As for himself, having now lost all hopes of being relieved, and seeing most of his men and friends killed round him, he gave way to his grief; and, not being able to make use of his arm, which was shot, he presented his young side to one of his attendants, and ordered him to put an end to his unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. His example was followed by Censorinus, a senator, by Megabacchus, an experienced and brave officer, and by most of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> who served under him. Five hundred common soldiers were taken prisoners, and the rest cut in pieces. The Parthians, having thus cut off or taken the whole detachment commanded by young Crassus, marched without delay against his father, who, upon the first advice that the enemy fled before his son, and were closely pursued by him, had taken heart, the more because those who had remained to make head against him, seemed to abate much of their ardour, the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of them having marched with the rest against his son. Wherefore, having encouraged his troops, troops, he had retired to a small hill in his rear, to wait there till his son returned from the pursuit. Young Crassus had dispatched frequent expressions to his father, to acquaint him with the danger he was in; but they had fallen into the enemy's hands, and been by them put to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>: only the last, who had escaped with great difficulty, arrived safe, and informed him that his son was lost; if he did not send him an immediate and powerful reinforcement. This news threw Crassus into the utmost consternation; a thousand affecting thoughts rose in his mind, and disturbed his reason to such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that he scarce knew what he was doing. However, the desire he had of saving his son, and so many brave Romans who were under his command, made him immediately decamp, and march to their assistance; but he was not gone far before he was met by the Parthians, who, with loud shouts, and songs of victory, gave, at a distance, the unhappy father notice of his misfortune. They had cut off young Crassus's head, and, having fixed it on the point of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCE">lance</a>, were advancing full speed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on the father. As they drew near, Crassus was struck with that dismal and affecting sight; but, on this occasion, behaved like an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERO">hero</a>: for tho' he was under the deepest concern, he had the presence of mind to stifle his grief, for fear of discouraging the army, and to cry out to the dismayed troops, "This misfortune is entirely mine; the loss of one man cannot affect the victory. Let us charge, let us fight like Romans: if you have any compassion for a father who has <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> now lost a son whose valour you admired, let it appear in your rage and resentment against these insulting barbarians." Thus Crassus strove to reanimate his troops; but his efforts were unsuccessful: their courage was quite sunk, as appeared from the faint and languishing shout which they raised, according to custom, before the action. When the signal was given, the Parthians, keeping to their old way of fighting, discharged <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> of arrows on the legionaries, without <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> near them; which did such dreadful execution, that many of the Romans, to avoid the arrows, which occasioned a long and painful death, threw themselves, like men in despair, on the enemy's heavy-armed horse, seeking from their spears a more quick and easy kind of death. Thus the Parthians continued plying them incessantly with their arrows till night, when they left the field of battle, crying out, that they would allow the father one night to lament the death of his son. This was a melancholy night for the Romans. Crassus kept himself concealed from the soldiery, lying not in the general's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENT">tent</a>, but in the open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and on the bare ground, with his head wrapped up in his paludamentum or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> cloak: and was, in that forlorn condition, says Plutarch, a great example to the vulgar, of the instability of fortune; to the wife, a still greater of the pernicious effects of avarice, temerity, and ambition. Octavius, one of his lieutenants, and Cassius, approached him, and endeavoured to raise him up and console him: but, seeing him quite sunk under the weight of his affliction, and deaf to all comfort, they summoned a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of war, composed of all the chief officers; wherein it was unanimously resolved, that they should decamp before break of day, and retire, without <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>, to the neighbouring city of Carrhae, which was held by a Roman garrison. Agreeable to this resolution, they began their march as soon as the council broke up; which produced dreadful outcry among the sick and wounded, who, perceiving that they were to be abandoned to the mercy of the enemy, filled the camp with their complaints and lamentations: but their cries and tears, though very affecting, did not stop the march of the others, which, indeed, was very slow, to give the stragglers time to come up. There were only 300 light horse, under the command of one Agnatus, who pursued their march, without stopping. These arriving at Carrhae about midnight, Agnatus, calling to the centinels on the walls, desired them to acquaint Coponius, governor of the place, that Crassus had fought a great battle with the Parthians; and, without saying a word more, or letting them know who he was, continued his march with all possible expedition to the bridge of Zeugma; which he passed, and by that means saved his troops, but was much blamed for abandoning his general. However, the message he sent to Coponius was of some temporary <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to Crassus. For that commander, wisely conjecturing, from the manner in which the unknown person had given him that intelligence, that some misfortune had befallen Crassus, immediately ordered his garrison to stand to their arms; and, marching out, met Crassus, and conducted him and his army into the city; for the Parthians, tho' informed of his flight, did not offer to pursue him, observing therein the superstitious custom which obtained among them and the Persians, not to fight in the night; but, when it was day, they entered the Roman camp, and, having put all the wounded, to the number of 4000, to the sword, dispersed their cavalry all over the plain, in pursuit of the fugitives. One of Crassus's lieutenants, named Vargunteius, having separated in the night from the main body of the army, with four cohorts, missed his way, and was overtaken by the enemy; at whose approach he withdrew to a neighbouring hill, where he defended himself with great valour, till all his men were killed, except 20, who made their way through the enemy sword in hand, and got safe to Carrhae: but Vargunteius himself lost his life on this occasion. In the mean time Surenas, not knowing whether Crassus and Cassius had retired to Carrhae, or chosen a different route; in order to be informed of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and take his measures accordingly, dispatched a messenger, who spoke the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, to the city of Carrhae, enjoining him to approach the walls, and acquaint Crassus himself, or Cassius, that the Parthian general was inclined to enter into a treaty with them, and demanded a conference. Both the proconsul and his quaestor Cassius spoke from the walls with the messenger; and, accepting the proposal with great joy, desired that the time and place for an interview might be immediately agreed upon. The messenger withdrew, promising to return quickly with an answer from Surenas: but that general no sooner understood that Crassus and Cassius were in Carrhae, than he marched thither with his whole army; and, having invested the place, acquainted the Romans, that, if they expected any favourable terms, they must deliver up Crassus and Cassius to him in chains. Hereupon a council of the chief chief officers being summoned, it was thought expedient to retire from Carrhae that very night, and seek for another <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>. It was of the utmost importance, that none of the inhabitants of Carrhae should be acquainted with their design till the time of its execution; but Crassus, whose whole conduct evidently shews that he was blinded, as Dio Cassius observes, by some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, imparted the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in confidence to one Andromachus, choosing him for his guide, and relying injudiciously on the fidelity of a man whom he scarce knew. Andromachus immediately acquainted Surenas with the design of the Romans; promising at the same time, as the Parthians did not engage in the night, to manage matters so, that they should not get out of his reach before day-break. Pursuant to his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, he led them through many windings and turnings, till he brought them into deep marshy grounds, where the infantry were up to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> in mire. Then Cassius, suspecting that their guide had led them into those bogs with no good design, refused to follow him any longer; and, returning to Carrhae, took his route towards Syria, which he reached with 500 horse. Octavius, with 5000 men under his command, being conducted by trusty guides, gained the mountains called by Plutarch and Appian Sinnaci, and there intrenched himself before break of day. As for Crassus, he was still entangled in the marshes, when Surenas, at the rising of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, overtook him, and invested him with his cavalry. The proconsul had with him four cohorts, and a small body of horse; and with these he gained, in spite of all opposition, the summit of another hill within 12 furlongs of Octavius; who, seeing the danger that threatened his general, flew to his assistance, first with a small number of his men, but was soon followed by all the rest, who, being ashamed of their cowardice, quitted their post, though very safe, and, charging the Parthians with great fury, disengaged Crassus, and obliged the enemy to abandon the hill. Upon the retreat of the enemy, they formed themselves into an hollow square; and placing Crassus in the middle, made a kind of rampart round him with their bucklers, resolutely protecting, that none of the enemy's arrows should touch their general's body, till they were all killed fighting in his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. Surenas, loth to let so fine a prey escape, surrounded the hill, as if he designed to make a new attack; but, finding his Parthians very backward, and not doubting but the Romans, when night came on, would pursue their march, and get out of his reach, he had recourse again to artifice; and declared before some prisoners, whom he soon after set at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, that he was inclined to treat with the proconsul of a peace; and that it was better to come to a reconciliation with Rome, than to sow the seeds of an eternal war, by shedding the blood of one of her generals. Agreeable to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>, Surenas, as soon as the prisoners were released, advanced towards the hill where the Romans were posted, attended only by some of his officers, and, with his bow unbent, and open arms, invited Crassus to an interview. So sudden a change seemed very suspicious to the proconsul; who therefore declined the interview, till he was forced, by his own soldiers, to intrust his life with an enemy whose treachery they had all experienced; for the legionaries flocking round him, not only abused him in an outrageous manner, but even menaced him if he did not accept of the proposals made him by the Parthian general. Seeing, therefore, that his troops were ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a>, he began to advance, without arms or guards, towards the enemy, after having called the gods and his officers to witness the violence his troops offered him; and intreated all who were present, but especially Octavius and Petronius, two of the chief commanders, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Rome their common mother, not to mention, after his death, the shameful behaviour of the Roman legionaries. Octavius and Petronius could not resolve to let him go alone; but attended him <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the hill, as did likewise some legionaries, keeping at a distance. Crassus was met at the foot of the hill by two Greeks; who, dismounting from their horses, saluted him with great respect; and desired him, in the Greek tongue, to send some of his attendants, who might satisfy him, that Surenas, and those who were with him, came without arms. Hereupon Crassus sent two brothers, of the Rolcian family; but Surenas, having caused them to be seized, advanced to the foot of the hill, mounted on a fine horse, and attended by the chief officers of his army. Crassus, who waited for the return of his two messengers, was surprized to see himself prevented by Surenas in person, when he least expected it.
