The lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANDES">Andes</a>, which are covered with snow a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the year, traversing the country from north to south, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is said to be much colder than in the north under the same parallels of latitude. Towards the north, it is said to be covered with wood, and stored with an inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; whereas, to the southward, not so much as a single tree fit for any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> purpose is to be seen: yet there is good pasture, and incredible numbers of wild horned cattle and horses, which were first brought hither by the Spaniards, and have increased amazingly. Fresh <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, we are told by some writers, is very scarce; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> that were really the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it is difficult to conceive how the present inhabitants, and such multitudes of cattle, could subsist. The east <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> is mostly low <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, with few or no good harbours: one of the best is Port St Julian. Patagonia is inhabited by a variety of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> tribes; as the Patagons, from which the country takes its name; the Pampas, the Coifares, &c. of whom we know very little. Only it appears, from the accounts of former voyagers, lately confirmed by commodore Byron and his crew, and the testimonies of other navigators, that some of them are of a gigantic stature, and clothed with skins; but it would seem that there are others who go almost quite naked, notwithstanding the inclemency of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. Some of them also, that live about the Straits, if we may <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> the navigators who have passed that way into the South Sea, are perfect savages: but those with whom commodore Byron and his people conversed, are represented as of a more gentle humane disposition; only, like other savages, they live on fish and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a>, and what the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> produces spontaneously. The Spaniards once built a fort upon the Straits, and left a garrison in it, to prevent any other European <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> passing that way into the South Sea: but most of the men perished by famine, whence the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> obtained the name of Port Famine; and no people have attempted to plant colonies here ever since. About the middle of the Strait is a promontory called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Frojard, which is the most southerly on the continent of South America. On the coasts of Patagonia <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, or clusters of islands. On the west coast are the islands Madre de Dios, Santa Trinidad, Santa Cruz, the isles of the Chunians and Huillans, the Sarmientos, and many others; to the number of 80 in all, as some say. Of those on the south coast, the most considerable are Terra del Fuego, and Staten Land. See these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>.

PATAN

Pages 407-407

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the same name, in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul; it is very little known. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 109. O. N. Lat. 27. 30.

PATANCE

Pages 409-409

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, flory at the ends; from which it differs only in this, that the ends, instead of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> like fleur-de-lis, are extended somewhat in the pattée form. See FLORY.

PATARA

Pages 407-407

(Livy, Mela); the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Lycia, to the east of the mouth of the river Xanthus; famous for a temple and oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, thence called Patareus, three syllables only; but Pataraeus, (Horace). For the six winter months, Apollo gave answers at Patara; and for the six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> at Delos, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Servius): these are the Lyciae Sortes of Virgil. The town was situated in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, called Lyciorum Cheroneus, (Stephanus).

PATAVINITY

Pages 407-407

among critics, denotes a peculiarity of Livy's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>; derived from Patavium <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>: but wherein this patavinity consists, they are by no means agreed.

PATAVIUM

Pages 407-407

(Tacitus, Strabo); a town of the Tranpadanae, situate on the left <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Medoacus <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>; founded by Antenor the Trojan, (Mela, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Seneca); Patavini, the people, (Livy); who himself was a native, and by Asinus Pollio <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATAVINITY">patavinity</a>. Now <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, in the territory and to the west of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 15. N. Lat. 45. 30.

PATAY

Pages 407-407

a town of France, in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Orleanais, remarkable for the defeat of the English in 1429, and where Joan of Arc did wonders. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 43. N. Lat. 48. 5.

PATEE

Pages 407-407
or PATEE, in heraldry, a cross small in the centre, and widening to the extremes, which are very broad.

PATELLA

Pages 407-407

the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMPET">Limpet</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of vermes testacea. It is an animal of the snail kind; the shell consists of one conical <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VALVE">valve</a> without any spiral. There are 36 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; principally distinguished by peculiarities in their shells.

PATENT

Pages 407-407

in general, denotes something that stand open <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> expanded: thus a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> is said to be patent, when it stands almost at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> with the stalk.

PATER NOSTER

Pages 407-408

the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRAYER">Prayer</a>, so called from the two first words thereof in Latin.

PATER PATRATUS

Pages 408-408

in Roman antiquity, an officer chosen by one of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of decemvirs out of their own body, to treat with an enemy on the subject of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> and peace. He derived his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> from a circumstance necessary to his enjoying it: for in order that he might be the more firmly interested in the fate of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he was to have both a father and a son living at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

PATERA

Pages 408-408

among antiquaries, a goblet <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> vessel used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in their sacrifices; wherein they offered their consecrated meats to the gods, and where-with they made libations. See SACRIFICE and LIBATION. The word is Latin, formed from pateo, "I am open;" quod pateat, "because it has a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> aperture;" in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to bottles, &c., which have only narrow necks, or whose aperture is less than the body of the vessel. On medals the patera is seen in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of several deities; and frequently in the hands of princes, to mark the sacrificial authority joined with the imperial, &c. Hence F. Joubert observes, that beside the patera, there is frequently an altar upon which the patera seems to be pouring its contents. The patera was of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, marble, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, glass, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and they used to inclose it in urns with the ashes of the deceased, after it had served for the libations of the wine and liquors at the funeral. The patera is an ornament in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, frequently seen in the Doric freeze, and the tympanum of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>.

PATERCULUS

Pages 408-409

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman historian, who flourished in the reign of Tiberius Caesar, was born in the year of Rome 735. His <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> were illustrious for their merit and their offices. His grandfather espoused the party of Tiberius Nero, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s father; but being old and infirm, and not able to accompany Nero when he retired from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, he ran himself through with his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. His father was a soldier of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and so was Paterculus himself. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> tribune when <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Caesar, a grandson of Augustus, had an interview with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Parthians, in an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the river <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, in the year 753. He commanded the cavalry in Germany under Tiberius; and accompanied that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years successively in all his expeditions. He received <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> rewards from him; but we do not find that he was preferred to any higher <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> than the praetorship. The praises he bestows upon Sejanus give some <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> to the conjecture, that he was looked upon as a friend of this favourite, and consequently that he was involved in his ruin. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is placed by Mr Dodwell in the year of Rome 784, when he was in his 50th year. He wrote an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in two books, which is very curious. His purpose was only to deduce things from the foundation of Rome to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> wherein he lived, but he began his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> with things previous to that memorable era: for, though Paterculus, the beginning of his first book is wanting, we yet find in what remains of it, an account of many cities more ancient than Rome. He promised a larger history; and no doubt would have executed it well: for during his military expeditions he had seen, as he tells us, the provinces of Thrace, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, Achaia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, and other more easterly regions; especially upon the shores of the Euxine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which had furnished his mind with much entertaining and useful knowledge. In the Abridgment which we have, many particulars are related that are nowhere else to be found; and this makes it the more valuable. The style of Paterculus, though miserably disguised through the carelessness of transcribers, and impossible to be restored to purity for want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, is yet manifestly worthy of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, which was the time of pure Latinity. The greatest excellence of this historian lies in his manner of commending and blaming those he speaks of; which he does in the finest terms and most delicate expressions. He is, however, condemned, and indeed with the greatest reason, for his partiality to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Augustus; and for making the most extravagant eulogies, not only upon Tiberius, but even upon his favourite Sejanus: whom, though a vile and cruel monster, Paterculus celebrates as one of the most excellent persons the Roman commonwealth had produced. Liphius, though he praises him in other respects, yet censures him most severely for his insincerity and partiality. "Velleius Paterculus (says he), raises my indignation: he represents Sejanus as endowed with all good qualities. The impudence of this historian! But we know, that he was born, and died, to the destruction of mankind. After many commendations, he concludes, that Livia was a woman more resembling the gods than men: and as to Tiberius, he thinks it a crime to speak otherwise of him than as of an immortal Jove. What sincere and honest mind can bear this? On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, how artfully does he everywhere conceal the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> qualities of Caesar Germanicus! how obliquely does he ruin the reputation of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRIPPINA">Agrippina</a> and others, whom Tiberius was thought to hate! In short, he is nothing but a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>-prostitute. You <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> say, perhaps, it was unsafe to speak the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> at those times: I <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> it; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he could not write the truth, he ought not to have written lies: none are called to account for silence." La Mothe le Vayer has made a very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> remark upon this occasion: "The same fault (says he) may be observed in many others, who have written the history of their own times, with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to be published while they lived." It is strange, that a work so elegant and worthy to be preserved, and of which, by reason of its shortness, copies might be so easily taken, should have been so near being lost. One manuscript only has had the luck to be found, as well of this author among the Latins, as of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HESYCHIUS">Hesychius</a> among the Greeks: in which, says a great critic of our own <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, "The faults of the scribes are found so numerous, and the defects so beyond all redress, that notwithstanding the pains of the learned and most acute critics for two whole centuries, these books still are, and are like to continue, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> heap of errors." No ancient author but Priscian makes mention of Paterculus: the moderns have done him infinitely more <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and have illustrated him with notes and and commentaries. He was first published, from the manuscript of Morbac, by Rhenanus, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> in 1520; afterwards by Lipsius at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1581; then by Gerard Vossius in 1639; next by Boeclerus at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a> in 1642; then by Thyssus and others; and, lastly, by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Burman at Leyden 1719, in 8vo. To the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> edition in 1693, 8vo, were prefixed the Annales Vellianiani of Mr Dodwell, which shew deep learning and a great knowledge of antiquity.

PATERNOSTER

Pages 408-408
islands of Asia, in the East Indian sea, so called because of the great number of rocks, which sailors have likened to the beads with which the Papists tell their pater-noster. They abound in corn and fruits, and are very populous.

PATHETIC

Pages 409-409

whatever relates to the passions, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> that is proper to excite or awake them. The word comes from the Greek πάθος, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>. See PASSION.

PATHOGNOMONIC

Pages 409-409

among physicians, an appellation for a symptom, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> concourse of symptoms that are inseparable from a distemper, and are found in that only, and in no other.

PATHOLOGY

Pages 409-409

that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of medicine which explains the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of diseases, their causes and symptoms. See MEDICINE.

PATIN

Pages 409-409

who made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in the world, and excelled in the knowledge of medals. He was born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1633; and made so surprising a progress, that he maintained theses in Greek and Latin, on all parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, in 1647. He studied the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> in compliance to an uncle, and was admitted an advocate in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Paris; but could not lay aside that of physic; for which he always had an inclination. He therefore quitted the law, and devoted himself to physic; in which, after taking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, he applied himself to practice, with great success. He afterwards travelled into Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, England, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. In 1676 he was appointed professor of physic in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>; and three years after was created a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of St Mark. He died in that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> in 1694. His works are many, and well known to the learned world. His wife too, and his daughters, were authoresses.

PATMOS

Pages 409-409

one of the Sporades (Dionysius); 30 miles in compass (Pliny); concerning which we read very little in authors. It was rendered famous by the exile of St John and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a> shewed him there. It is now in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Turks. It is considerable for its harbours; but the inhabitants derive little benefit from them, because the corsairs have obliged them to quit the town and retire to a hill on which St John's convent stands. This convent is a citadel, consisting of several <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> towers, and is a substantial <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> seated on a very steep rock. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is very barren, and without wood; however, it abounds with partridges, rabbits, quails, turtles, pigeons, and snipes. All their corn does not amount to 1000 barrels in a year. It is 18 miles in circumference; and there are scarce 300 men in it: but there are above 20 women to one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who expect that all strangers who <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> in the island should carry some of them away. To the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of St John, is an hermitage on the side of a mountain, where there is a chapel not above eight paces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Overhead they shew a chink in the rock, through which they pretend that the Holy Ghost dictated to St John. E. Long. 26. 40. N. Lat. 37. 20.

PATNA

Pages 409-409

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a territory of the same name, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, where the English have factories for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, and raw <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. It also produces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of opium. The town is large, but the houses are built at a distance from each other. It is seated in a fertile pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, 400 miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGRA">Agra</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 85. 40. N. Lat. 25. 25.

PATRANA

Pages 409-409
or Pastrana, a town of New Castile in Spain, with the title of a duchy. It is seated between the rivers Tajo and Tajuna, in E. Lon. 0. 15.

PATRAS

Pages 409-409

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and flourishing town of European <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, in the Morea, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>, with a Greek archbishop's see. It is pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous; and the Jews, who are one third <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the inhabitants, have four synagogues. There are several handsome mosques and Greek churches. The Jews carry on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, wax, and cheese. There are cypresses trees of a prodigious height, and excellent pomegranates, citrons, and oranges. It has been several times taken and retaken, and it is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> now in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Turks. It is seated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 21. 57. N. Lat. 38. 20.

PATRIARCH

Pages 409-410

Patriarcha, one of those first fathers who lived towards the beginning of the world, and who became famous by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of descendants. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, and his twelve sons, are the patriarchs of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; Seth, Enoch, &c. were antediluvian patriarchs. Patriarchs, among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, are <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> dig- Patriarchs dignitaries, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, so called from their paternal authority in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The power of patriarchs was not the same in all, but differed according to the different customs of countries, or the pleasures of kings and councils. Thus the patriarch of Constantinople grew to be a patriarch over the patriarchs of Ephesus and Caesarea, and was called the ecumenical and universal patriarch; and the patriarch of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> had some prerogatives which no other patriarch but himself enjoyed, such as the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of consecrating and approving every single bishop under his jurisdiction. PATRIARCHAL <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, is that where the shaft is twice crossed; the lower arms being longer than the upper ones.

PATRICA

Pages 409-409

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the territory of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> of Rome, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and eight miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OSTIA">Ostia</a>. About a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is a hill called Monte di Livano, which some have thought to be the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAVINIUM">Lavinium</a> founded by Æneas. PATRES CONSCRIPTI. See Conscript and Senator.

PATRICIAN

Pages 410-410

among the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> given to the descendents of the hundred, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, of the two hundred first senators chosen by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, and by him called patres, "fathers."

PATRICK

Pages 410-410

a very learned English bishop, was born at Gainborough in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a> in 1626. In 1644 he was admitted into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and entered into holy orders. After being for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> chaplain to Sir Walter St John, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at Battersea in Surry, he was preferred to the rectory of St Paul's, Covent-garden, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> all the time of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> in 1665 among his parishioners, to their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> comfort. In 1668 he published his Friendly Debate between a Conformist and a Non-conformist. This was answered by the Dissenters, whom he had much exasperated by it; but by his moderation and candour towards them afterwards, they were perfectly reconciled to him, and he brought over many of them to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the established church. In 1678 he was made <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of Peterborough, where he was much beloved. In 1682, Dr <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> de Moulin, who had been a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>-professor at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and written many bitter books against the church of England, sent for Dr Patrick upon his sick-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and made a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of his regret on that account, which he signed, and it was published after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. During the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> James, the dean's behaviour shewed that he had nothing more at heart than the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; for which he ventured all that was dear to him, by preaching, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> against the errors of the church of Rome. In 1687 he published a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> composed for that difficult time, when <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> was expected by all who stood firm to their religion. The year after the Revolution, the dean was appointed bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a>, and was employed with others of the new <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the affairs of the church in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. In 1691 he was translated to the see of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, in the room of the deprived bishop Turner. He died in 1707, after having published various works; among which the most distinguished are his Paraphrases and Commentaries on the holy scriptures, 3 volumes folio. These, with Lowth on the proverbs, Arnold on the Apocrypha, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITBY">Whitby</a> on the New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, make a regular Patrimony continued <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> in English on all the sacred books.

PATRIMONY

Pages 410-410

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> estate inherited by a person from his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> patrimony has been also given to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-estates or revenues; in which some authors still say, the patrimony of the church of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIMINI">Rimini</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, &c. The church of Rome hath patrimonies in France, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and many other countries. To create the greater respect to the estates belonging to the church, it was usual to give their patrimonies the names of the saints they held in the highest veneration: thus the estate of the church of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a> was called the patrimony of St Apollinaris; that of Milan, the patrimony of St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a>; and the estates of the Roman church were called the patrimony of St <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> in Abruzzo, the patrimony of St Peter in Sicily, and the like. What is now called St Peter's patrimony is only the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Castro, and the territory of Orvietto. See CASTRO, &c.

PATRIPASSIANS

Pages 410-410

PATRIPASSIANI, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, who appeared about the latter end of the 2d century; so called, from their afflicting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> to the Father; for they affected the unity of God in such a manner as to destroy all distinctions of persons, and to make the Father and Son precisely the same; in which they were followed by the Sabellians and others. The author and head of the Patripassians was Praxeas, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>.

PATROL

Pages 410-410

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, a round <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a> made by the guards or watch in the night-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, to observe what passes in the streets, and to secure the peace and tranquillity of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. The patrol generally consists of a body of five or six men, detached from a body on <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, and commanded by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a>. They go every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the night, from the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> of the tattoo until the reveille: they are to walk in the streets in garrisons, and all over the camp in the field, to prevent disorders, or any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people from assembling together: they are to see the lights in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a> put out, and to take up all the soldiers they find out of their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. Sometimes patrols consist of an officer and 30 or 40 men, as well infantry as cavalry; but then the enemy is generally near at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and consequently the danger greater.

PATRON

Pages 410-411

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was an appellation given to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> who had freed his slave. As soon as the relation of master expired, that of patron began: for the Romans in giving their slaves their freedom, did not despoil themselves of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges in them; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> still subjected them to considerable services and duties towards their patrons, the neglect of which was very severely punished. Patron was also a name which the people of Rome gave to some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, under whose protection they usually put themselves; paying him all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and respect, and denominating themselves his clients; while the patron, on his side, granted them his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> and protection. Patron, in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, a saint, whose name a person bears, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> under whose protection he is put, and whom he takes particular care to invoke: or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRONAGE">Patronage</a>, a saint, in whose name a church or order is founded. Patron, in the canon and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, is a person, who having the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ADVOWSON">advowson</a> of a parsonage, vicarage, or the like spiritual promotion, belonging to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>, hath, on that account, the gift and disposition of the benefice, and may present to it whenever it becomes vacant. The patron's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of disposing of a benefice, originally arises either from the patron, or his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, &c., being the founders or builders of the church; from their having given lands for the maintenance thereof; or, from the church's being built on their ground; and frequently from all three together.

PATRONAGE

Pages 411-411
or ADVOWSON, a sort of incorporeal hereditament, consisting in the right of presentation to a church or ecclesiastical benefice. Advowson, advocatio, signifies in clientela recipere, the taking into protection; and therefore is synonymous with patronage, patronatus: and he who has the right of advowson is called the patron of the church. For, when lords of manors first built churches on their own demesnes, and appointed the tithes of those manors to be paid to the officiating ministers, which before were given to the clergy in common (from whence arose the division of parishes), the lord, who thus built a church, and endowed it with glebe or land, had of common right a power annexed of nominating such minister as he pleased, (provided he were canonically qualified), to officiate in that church, of which he was the founder, endower, maintainer, or, in one word, the patron. Advowsons are either advowsons appendant, or advowsons in gross. Lords of manors being originally the only founders, and of course the only patrons, of churches, the right of patronage or presentation, so long as it continues annexed to the possession of the manor, as some have done from the foundation of the church to this day, is called an advowson appendant: and it will pass, or be conveyed, together with the manor, as incident and appendant thereto, by a grant of the manor only, without adding any other words. But where the property of the advowson has been once separated from the property of the manor, by legal conveyance, it is called an advowson in gross, or at large, and never can be appendant any more; but is for the future annexed to the person of its owner, and not to his manor or lands. Advowsons are also either presentative, collative, or donative. And advowson presentative is where the patron hath a right of presentation to the bishop or ordinary, and moreover to demand of him to institute his clerk if he finds him canonically qualified; and this is the most usual advowson. An advowson collative is where the bishop and patron are one and the same person: in which case the bishop cannot present to himself; but he does, by the one act of collation, or conferring the benefice, the whole that is done in common cases, by both presentation and institution. An advowson donative is when the king, or any subject by his licence, doth found a church or chapel, and ordains that it shall be merely in the gift or disposal of the patron; subject to his visitation only, and not to that of the ordinary; and vested absolutely in the clerk by the patron's deed of donation, without presentation, institution, or induction. This is said to have been anciently the only way of conferring Patronage, ecclesiastical benefices in England; the method of institution by the bishop not being established more early than the time of archbishop Becket in the reign of Henry II. and therefore, though pope Alexander III. in a letter to Becket, severely inveighs against the prava consuetudo, as he calls it, of investiture conferred by the patron only, this however shews what was then the common usage. Others contend, that the claim of the bishops to institution is as old as the first planting of Christianity in this island; and in proof of it they allege a letter from the English nobility to the pope in the reign of Henry the third, recorded by Matthew Paris, which speaks of presentation to the bishop as a thing immemorial. The truth seems to be, that, where the benefice was to be conferred on a mere layman, he was first presented to the bishop in order to receive ordination, who was at liberty to examine and refuse him: but where the clerk was already in orders, the living was usually veiled in him by the sole donation of the patron; till about the middle of the 12th century, when the pope and his bishops endeavoured to introduce a kind of feudal dominion over ecclesiastical benefices, and, in consequence of that, began to claim and exercise the right of institution universally, as a species of spiritual investiture. However this may be, if, as the law now stands, the true patron once waives this privilege of donation, and presents to the bishop, and his clerk is admitted and instituted, the advowson is now become for ever presentative, and shall never be donative any more. For these exceptions to general rules and common right, are ever looked upon by the law in an unfavourable view, and construed as strictly as possible. If therefore the patron, in whom such peculiar right resides, does once give up that right, the law, which loves uniformity, will interpret it to be done with an intention of giving it up for ever; and will therefore reduce it to the standard of other ecclesiastical livings. See further, Law, Part III. No clix. 5.—9. Arms of PATRONAGE, in heraldry, are those on the top of which are some marks of subjection and dependence: thus the city of Paris bears the fleurs de lis in chief, to show her subjection to the king; and the cardinals, on the top of their arms, bear those of the pope, who gave them the hat, to show that they are his creatures.

PATRONYMIC

Pages 411-412

among grammarians, is applied to such names of men <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> women as are derived from those of parents or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. Patronymics are derived, 1. From the father; as Pelides, i.e. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a> the son of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELEUS">Peleus</a>. 2. From the mother; as Philyrides, i.e. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIRON">Chiron</a> the son of Philyra. 3. From the grandfather on the father's side; as Æscides, i.e. Achilles the grandson of Æacus. 4. From the grandfather by the mother's side; as Atlaniades, i.e. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> the grandson of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>. And, 5. From the kings and founders of nations; as Romulide, i.e. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> from their founder <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>. The termination of Greek and Latin patronymics are chiefly four, viz. des, of which we have examples above; as, as Thaumantias, i.e. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRIS">Iris</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Thamaus; is, as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLANTIS">Atlantis</a>, i.e. Electra the daughter of Atlas; and ne, as Nerine, the daughter of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEREUS">Nereus</a>.

PATROS

Pages 412-412

(Jeremiah, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a>), appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEXT">context</a> to be meant of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. Bochart thinks it denotes the Higher Egypt: the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> translate it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Pathure; in Pliny we have the Nomos Phaturites in the Thebais; in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Pathyris, probably the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. From the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> appellation Patros comes the gentilious name Pathurism, Moses.

PATRU

Pages 412-412

a counsellor in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of the French academy, was born at Pairs in 1604. He had an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> both of speaking and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. Upon his admission into the French academy in 1640, he made an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> of thanks, that gave rise to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of admittance speeches, which are still in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. Mr de Vauglas owns himself much indebted to him for his assistance in composing his Remarks on the French tongue, of which he was by far the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in France; so that he was consulted as an oracle by all the best writers of that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. Patru was estimable for the qualities of his heart, as well as for those of the head: was honest, generous, sincere; and preserved a gayness of character, which no ill-fortune could alter <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> affect. For this famous advocate, in spite of all his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> talents, lived almost in a state of indigence. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of the belles lettres made him neglect the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and the barren <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of being an oracle to the best French writers had more charms for him, than all the profits of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>. Hence he became so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, as to be reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of selling his books, which seemed dearer to him than his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and would actually have sold them for an under-price, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Boileau had not generously advanced him a larger sum, with this further privilege, that he should have the use of them as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he lived. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was preceded by a tedious illness, during which he received a present of 500 crowns from Colbert, as a mark of the esteem which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> had for him. He died the 16th of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1681. The prodigious care and exactness with which he retouched and finished every thing he wrote, did not permit him to publish much. His miscellaneous works were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1670, 4to; the third edition of which, in 1714, 4to, was augmented with several pieces. They consist of Pleadings, Orations, Letters, Lives of some of his friends, Remarks upon the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, &c.

PAUL

Pages 412-413

was born at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1552. He was educated by his uncle Ambrosio Morelli, and soon made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in learning. He was remarkable for two qualities, which seldom meet in the same person; a strong <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, and clear judgment. He took upon him the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of the Servites in 1566. Upon entering into this order, he changed his name of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Sarpi for that of Paul. He was afterwards chaplain chaplain to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, and reader of positive and casuistical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and canon <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>. So he became a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> and of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; but shewed the utmost contempt for judicial astrology. When weary of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he returned to his convent at Venice; and fo intently applied himself to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, that he injured his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> by it. He was chosen <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> of his order for the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Venice at 26 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and discharged this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a> with such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, that 1759 he was appointed, with two others, to draw up new regulations and statutes for his order. This he executed with great success; and when his office of provincial was expired, he retired for three years to the study of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental <a class="</a>xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and anatomy, in which he is said to have made some useful discoveries. He was then chosen procurator-general of his order; and during his residence at Rome was greatly esteemed by pope Sixtus V. and contracted an intimate friendship with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> Bellarmine and other eminent persons. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, he was accused of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>; and brought into a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of troubles, which he supported with exemplary <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>; till at length, growing extremely odious to the pope's party, he was assassinated, and left for dead, by five ruffians, who retired to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the pope's nuncio in Venice, from whence they escaped to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>. These circumstances discovered who were concerned in this attempt. He recovered, however, of his wounds; and retired to a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of security, where he wrote his history of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, which he compiled principally for the sake of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> James I. of England, with whom he corresponded. His name, ever since the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERDICT">interdict</a>, was become famous all over <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and two kings made him very advantageous offers to reside in their dominions. He died as he had lived, with piety and resignation, in 1623. He was a good controversial writer, a judicious and elegant historian.

PAULICIANS

Pages 413-413

Christian heretics of the seventh century, disciples of one Constantine a native of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, and a favourer of the errors of Manes; who, as the name Manichee was become odious, gave thole of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> the name of Paulicians, on the pretence that they followed only the doctrine of St Paul.

PAULIONISTS

Pages 413-413

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, Christian heretics of the third century, disciples of Paul Samotraensis bishop of Antioch, who denied Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; maintaining, that, when we call him the Son of God, we do not therefore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> that he is truly and really God; but only that he was so perfect a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and so superior in virtue to all others, that he had this name given him by way of eminence.

PAUSANIA

Pages 413-413

in Grecian antiquity, a festival in which were solemn games, wherein nobody contended but free-born Spartans; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Pausanias the Spartan general, under whom the Greeks overcame the Perians in the famous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Platæa.

PAUSANIAS

Pages 413-413

a learned Greek historian and orator, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, under the reign of Antoninus the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Herodus Atticus. He lived for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; and afterwards went to Rome, where he died at a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He wrote an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a> of Greece, in ten books; in which we find not only the situation of places, but the antiquities of Greece, and everything most curious and worthy of knowledge. Abbé Gedoin has given a French translation of it, in 2 vols 4to.

PAUSE

Pages 413-413

a stop <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> cessation in speaking, singing, playing, or the like. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> pointing in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> is to make proper pauses, in certain places. There is a pause in the middle of each <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; in an hemistich, it is called a refi or refiée. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, n° 118, &c. and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">Reading</a>, n° xi.

PAVIA

Pages 412-412

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and celebrated town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Pavese, with an university and bishop's see. It is defended by strong walls, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ditches, good ramparts, excellent bastions, and a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river Tafin. In the centre of the town is a strong castle, where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Milan was wont to reside. There are a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of magnificent castles, and some colleges. It was taken by the duke of Savoy in 1706; by the French in 1733; by the French and Spaniards in 1745; but retaken by the Austrians in 1746. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 5. N. Lat. 45. 10.

PAVILION

Pages 412-412

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, denotes a covering in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENT">tent</a>, which invests <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> wraps up the armories of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> kings and sovereigns, depending only on God and their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. The pavilion consists of two parts; the top, which is the chapeau, or coronet; and the curtain, which makes the mantle. None but sovereign monarchs, according to the French heralds, may bear the pavilion entire, and in all its parts. Those who are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a>, or have any dependence, say the heralds, must take off the head, and retain nothing but the curtains. Pavilions, among jewellers, the undersides and corners of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRILLIANTS">brilliants</a>, lying between the girdle and the collet. PAUL (St) the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>, was born at Tarshis in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, of Jewish parents. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TARSUS">Tarsus</a>; which, as Strabo informs us, excelled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, and Rome itself, for polite learning. Thence he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> under Gamaliel. Here he became a Pharisee, and engaged in a violent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>; but was wonderfully converted in his way to Damascus. After which he preached the gospel in various parts, until he was at last sent to Rome, where he is said to have converted Poppea Sabina, Nero's concubine; for which Nero being enraged against him, commanded him to be beheaded.

PAVO

Pages 413-413

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>; a genus belonging to the order of gallinae. The head is covered with feathers which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> backwards; the feathers of the tail are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and beautifully variegated with eyes of different colours. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. 1. The cristatus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> peacock of English authors, has a compressed crest and solitary spurs. It is a native of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>; and we are assured, that they are still found in a wild state in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Ceyland and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>. So beautiful a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> could not long be permitted to be a stranger in the more distant parts; for so early as the days of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, we find, among the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> imported in his Tarshish navies, apes and peacocks. A monarch so conversant in all branches of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, "who spoke of trees, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a> of Lebanon, even unto the hyssop that springeth out of the wall; who spoke also of beasts and of fowl," would certainly not neglect furnishing his officers with instructions for collecting every curiosity in the countries they voyaged to, which gave him a knowledge that distinguished him from all the princes of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Athen relates, that they were brought into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> from some barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and that they were held in such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem, that a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> were valued at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> at 1000 drachmas, or 32 l. 5 s. 10 d. Their next step might be to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a>; where they were preferred about the temple of Juno, being the birds sacred to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>; and Gellius, in his Notae Atticae, c. 16, commends the excellency of the Samian peacocks. It is therefore probable, that they were brought here originally for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, and afterwards cultivated for the uses of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>. We are also told, when Alexander was in India, he found vast numbers of wild ones on the banks of the Hyarotis; and was so struck with their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, as to appoint a severe <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> on any person that killed them. Peacock's <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times, were among the ornaments of the kings of England. Ernald de Aclent was fined to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> John in 140 palfreys, with jacks, butts, lorains, gilt spurs, and peacock's crests, such as would be for his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. 2. The bicalcaratas has a small crest and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> spurs. It is a native of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. 3. The muticus has a sharp-pointed crest, and no spurs; the orbits of the eyes are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>. It is found in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>.

PEAK OF DERBYSHIRE

Pages 414-414

a chain of very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a> in England, famous for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> they contain, and for their remarkable caverns. The most remarkable of these are Pool's-hole and Elden-hole. The former is a cave at the foot of a high hill called Coitmoor, so narrow at the entrance that passengers are obliged to creep on all-fours; but it soon opens to a considerable height, extending to above a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> somewhat resembling that of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>. By the petrifying <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> continually dropping in many parts of the cave are formed a variety of curious figures and representations of the works both of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> here as clear as alabaster, which is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> of Scots Pillar, because Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> is said to have proceeded thus far when she visited the cavern. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a pistol is fired by this pillar, it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> make a report as loud as a cannon. Near the extremity there is a hollow in the roof, called the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEEDLE">Needle</a>'s eye; in which if a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> is placed, it will represent a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a> in the firmament to those who are below. At a little distance from this cave is a small clear stream consisting of hot and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water, so near each other, that the finger and thumb of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> may be put, the one into the hot water, and the other into the cold. Elden-hole is a dreadful chasm in the side of a mountain; which, before the latter <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the last century, was thought to be altogether unfathomable. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of queen <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> was let <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into it for 200 yards; but he was drawn up in a frenzy, and soon after died. In 1682, it was examined by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Collins, and in 1699 by Captain Sturmy, who published their accounts in the Philosophical Transactions. The latter descended by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> fixed at the top of an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>-ore pit, four fathoms almost perpendicular, and from thence three fathoms more obliquely, between two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rocks. At the bottom of this he found an entrance into a very spacious cavern, from whence he descended along with a miner for 25 fathoms perpendicular. At last they came to a great river <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> water, which he found to be 20 fathoms <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and eight fathoms deep. The miner who accompanied him, insisted that this water ebbed and flowed with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; but the Captain disproved this assertion by remaining in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> from three hours <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> to two hours ebb, during which time there was no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the height of the water. As they walked by the side of this water, they observed a hollow in the rock some feet above them. The miner went into this place, which was the mouth of another cavern; and walked for about 70 paces in it, till he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> lost sight of the Captain. He then called to him, that he had found a rich mine; but immediately after came running out and crying, that he had seen an evil spirit; neither could any persuasions induce him to return. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of these caverns is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> enamelled with lead ore, and the roofs are encrusted with shining <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAR">spar</a>. On his return from this subterraneous journey, Captain Sturmy was seized with a violent head-ach, which, after continuing four days, terminated in a fever, of which he died in a short time. A few years ago this cavern was visited by the late Mr James Ferguson: who tells us, that it consists of two hollows one over another; but that the mouth of the lowermost is now stopped up by planks of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> laid across it, on which are a heap of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> thrown in at the upper mouth with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to fill up the cavern entirely; which, however, will probably be never accomplished on account of its vast size.

PEARCE

Pages 414-415
lord bishop of Rochester, was the son of a distiller in High Holborn. He married Miss Adams, the daughter of a distiller in the same neighbourhood, with a considerable fortune, who lived with him 52 years in the highest degree of connubial happiness. He had his education in Westminster school, where he was distinguished by his merit, and elected one of the king's scholars. In 1710, when he was 20 years old, he was elected to Trinity College, Cambridge. During the first years of his residence at the university, he sometimes amused himself with lighter compositions, some of which are inserted in the Guardian and Spectator. In 1716, he published his edition of Cicero de Oratore, and, at the desire of a friend, luckily dedicated it to Lord Chief Justice Parker, (afterwards Earl of Macclesfield,) to whom he was a stranger. This incident laid the foundation of his future fortune: for Lord Parker soon recommended him to Dr Bentley, master of Trinity, to be made one of the fellows; and the doctor consented to it on this condition, that his lordship would promise to unmak him again as soon as it lay in his power to give him a living. In 1717, Mr Pearce was ordained at the age of 27; having taken time enough, as he thought, to attain a sufficient knowledge of the sacred office. In 1718, Lord Parker was appointed chancellor, and invited Mr Pearce to live with him in his house as chaplain. In 1719, he was instituted into the rectory of Stapleford Abbots, in Essex; and in 1720, into that of St Bartholomew, behind the Royal Exchange, worth 400l. per annum. In 1723, the lord chancellor presented him to St Martin's in the Fields. His Majesty, who was then at Hanover, was applied to in favour of St Claget, who was then along with him; and the doctor actually kissed hands upon the occasion: but the chancellor, upon the king's return, disputed the point, and was permitted to present Mr Pearce.—Mr Pearce soon attracted the notice and esteem of persons in the highest stations and of the greatest abilities. Beside Lord Parker, he could reckon amongst his patrons or friends, Lord Macclesfield, Mr Pulteney (afterwards Earl of Bath), archbishop Potter, Lord Hardwicke, Sir Isaac Newton, and other illustrious personages.—In 1724, the degree of doctor of divinity was conferred on him by archbishop Wake. The same year he dedicated to his patron, the Earl of Macclesfield, his edition of Longinus on the Sublime, with a new Latin version and notes. When the church of St Martin's was rebuilt, Dr Pearce preached a sermon at the consecration, which he afterwards printed, and accompanied with an essay on the origin and progress of temples, traced from the rude stones which were first used for altars, to the noble structure of Solomon, which he considers as the first temple completely covered. His observations on that building, which is called the temple of Dagon, removes part of the difficulty which presents itself in the narration of the manner in which Samson destroyed it. The deanery of Winchester becoming vacant, Dr Pearce was appointed dean in 1739; and in the year 1744 he was elected prolocutor of the lower house of convocation for the province of Canterbury. His friends now began to think of him for the episcopal dignity; but Mr Dean's language rather delayed it. However, after several difficulties had been started and removed, he consented to accept the bishopric of Bangor, and promised Lord Hardwicke to do it with a good grace. He accordingly made proper acknowledgments of the royal goodness, and was consecrated Feb. 12, 1748. Upon the declining state of health of Dr Wilcocks, bishop of Rochester, the bishop of Bangor was several times applied to by archbishop Herring to accept of Rochester, and the deanery of Westminster, in exchange for Bangor; but the bishop then first signified his desire to obtain leave to resign and retire to a private life. His lordship, however, upon being pressed, suffered himself to be prevailed upon.—"My Lord," said he to the Duke of Newcastle, "your grace offers these dignities to me in so generous and friendly a manner, that I promise you to accept them." Upon the death of bishop Wilcocks he was accordingly promoted to the see of Rochester and deanery of Westminster in 1756. Bishop Sherlock died in 1761, and Lord Bath offered his interest for getting the bishop of Rochester appointed to succeed him in the diocese of London; but the bishop told his lordship, that he had determined never to be bishop of London or archbishop of Canterbury. In the year 1763, his lordship being 73 years old, and finding himself less fit for the business of his stations as bishop and dean, informed his friend lord Bath of his intention to resign both, and live in a retired manner upon his private fortune. Lord Bath undertook to acquaint his majesty; who named a day and hour, when the bishop was admitted alone into the closet. He told the king, that he wished to have some interval between the fatigues of business and eternity; and desired his majesty to consult proper persons about the propriety and legality of his resignation. In about two months the king informed him, that Lord Mansfield saw no objection; and that Lord Northington, who had been doubtful, on farther consideration thought that the request might be complied with. Unfortunately for the bishop, lord Bath applied for bishop Newton to succeed. This alarmed the ministry, who thought that no dignities should be obtained but through their hands. They therefore opposed the resignation; and his majesty was informed that the bishops disliked the design. His majesty sent him again; and at a third audience told him, that he must think no more of resigning. The bishop replied, "Sir, I am all duty and submission;" and then retired. In 1768 he obtained leave to resign the deanry; in 1773, he lost his lady; and after some months of lingering decay, he died at Little Ealing, June 29, 1774. This eminent prelate distinguished himself in every part of his life by the virtues proper to his station. His literary abilities, and application to sacred and philological learning, appear by his works; the principal of which are, A letter to the clergy of the church of England, on occasion of the bishop of Rochester's commitment to the Tower, 2d ed. 1722. Miracles of Jesus vindicated, 1727 and 1728. A review of the text of Milton, 1733. Two letters against Dr Middleton, occasioned by the doctor's letter to Waterland, on the publication of his treatise, intitled Scripture Vindicated, 3d edit. 1752. And since his death, a commentary with notes on the four Evangelists and the Acts of the Apostles, together with a new translation of St Paul's first Epistle to the Corinthians, with a paraphrase and notes, have been published, with his life prefixed, from original MSS. in 2 vols 4to.

PEARCH

Pages 415-416

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>. See PERCA. The perch affords good sport for the angler. The best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> for their biting is when the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> is over, and before the heats of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> come on. At this time they are very greedy; and the angler, with good management, may take at one standing all that are in the hole, be they ever so many. The proper baits are a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINNOW">minnow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> young frog; but the worm called the brandling, well flowered, is also excellent at all times of the year. When the perch bites, he should always have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of time allowed him to swallow the bait. The perch <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> bite all <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> be cloudy; but the best time is from eight to ten in the morning, and from three till six in the afternoon. The perch is very abstemious in winter, and will seldom bite in this season of the year; if he does at all, it is in the middle of the day: at which time indeed all fish bite best at that season.
