If the bait be a minnow, which is the bait that affords most diversion to the angler, it must be fastened to the hook alive, by putting the hook through the upper lip or back-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIN">fin</a>; it must be kept at about mid-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and the float must be a quill and a cork, that the minnow alone may not be able to sink it. The line must be of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and strong; and the hook armed with a small and fine wire, that if a pike should take the bait, as is not unfrequently the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, he may be taken. The way to carry the minows or small gudgeons alive for baits is this: A tin-pot is to be provided, with holes in the lid, and filled with water; and the fish being put in this, the water is to be changed once in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> by the holes, without taking off the lid at any time, except when the bait is to be taken out. A small casting-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NET">net</a>, made for these little fish, should be taken out with the perch-tackle; and one or two casts of this will take baits enough for the day, without any farther trouble. When the bait is a frog, the hook is to be fastened to the upper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the leg. The best <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> for perch is in the turn of the water near some gravelly scour. A place of this kind being pitched upon, it should be baited over-night with lobworms chopped to pieces; and in the morning, on going to it, the depth is to be regularly plumbed, and then the hook is to be baited with the worm or other bait; and as it drags along, the perch will soon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> upon it. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEARL">PEARL</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GLUE">Glue</a>, the name of a kind of glue, of remarkable strength and purity, made from the skins of peaches.

PEARL

Pages 416-417

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a hard, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, shining body, usually roundish, found in a teffaceous fish resembling an oyster. Pearls, though esteemed of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of gems by our jewellers, and highly valued, not only at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, but in all ages, proceed only from a distemper in the creature that produces them, analogous to the bezoars, and other stony concretions in several animals of other kinds. The fish in which these are usually produced is the East-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> pearl-oyster, as it is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called. Besides this shell, there are many others that are found to produce pearls; as the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> oyster, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MULE">mule</a>, and several others; the pearls of which are often very good; but those of the true Indian berberi, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> pearl-oyster, are in general superior to all. The small or seed-pearls, also called ounce-pearls, from their being sold by the ounce and not by tale, are vastly the most numerous and common; but, as in diamonds, among the multitudes of small ones, there are smaller numbers and larger found, so in pearls there are larger and larger kinds; but as they increase in size, they are proportionably less frequent; and this is one reason of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> price. We have Scotch pearls frequently as big as a little tare, some as big as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>, and some few of the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-bean; but there are usually of a bad shape, and of little value in proportion to their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> had a pearl perfect in its shape and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and of the size of a pigeon's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a>. The finest, and what is called the true shape of the pearl, is a perfect round; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> pearls of a considerable size, are of the shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, as is not unfrequently the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, they are not less valued, as they serve for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>-rings and other ornaments. Their colour ought to be a pure white; and that not a dead and lifeless, but a clear and brilliant one; they must be perfectly free from any foulness, spot, or flaw; and their surfaces must be naturally smooth and glossy; for they bring their natural polish with them, which art is not able to improve. All pearls are formed of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of the shell, and consist of a number of coats spread with perfect regularity one over another, in the manner of the several coats of an onion, or like the several <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> found in the bladders or stomachs of animals, only much thinner. Manner of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> for Pearls in the East Indies. There are two seasons for pearl-fishing: the first is in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> and April, and the last in August and September; and the more <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> there falls in the year, the more plentiful are these <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>. At the beginning of the season there are sometimes 250 barks on the banks; the larger barks have two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a>, and the smaller one. As soon as the barks arrive at the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the fish <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a>, and have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, each diver binds a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, six inches thick and a foot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, under his body; which serves him as ballast, prevents his being driven away by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and enables him to walk more steadily under the waves. They also tie another very heavy stone to one foot, by which they are very speedily sent to the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and as the oysters are usually firmly fastened to the rocks, they arm their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> mittens, to prevent their being wounded in pulling them violently off; but this task some perform with an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a>. In the last place, each diver carries <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with him a large <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NET">net</a> in the manner of a sack, tied to his neck by a long <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, the other end of which is fastened to the side of the bark. This net is to hold the oysters gathered from the rock; and the cord is to pull up the diver when his bag is full, or he wants <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>. In this equipage he sometimes precipitates himself sixty feet under water; and as he has no time to lose, he no sooner arrives at the bottom, than he begins to run from side to side, tearing up all the oysters he meets with, and cramming them into his budget. At whatever depth the divers are, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> is so great, that they easily see whatever passes in the sea; and, to their great consternation, sometimes perceive monstrous fishes, from which all their addresses in muddying the water, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> them, but they unhappily become their prey: and of all the dangers of the fishery, this is one of the greatest and most usual. The best divers will keep under water near half an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, and the rest do not stay less than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. During this time they hold their breath without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of oils or any other liquors; only acquiring the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> by long practice. When they find themselves straitened, they pull the rope to which the bag is fastened, and hold fast by it with both hands; when those in the bark, taking the signal, heave them up into the air, and unload them of their fish; which is sometimes 500 oysters, and sometimes not above 50. Some of the divers need a moment's respite to recover breath; others jump in again instantly, continuing this violent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> without intermission for several hours. On the shore they unload their barks, and lay their oysters in an infinite number of little pits dug in the sand four or five feet <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, raising heaps of sand over them to the height of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and in this condition they are left till the rain, <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, have obliged them to open, which soon kills them: upon this the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> rots and dries, and the pearls, thus disengaged, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the pit, on their taking out the shells. After clearing the pits of the groffier filth, they sift the sand several times in order to find the pearl; but, whatever care they take, they always lose a great many. After cleaning and drying the pearls, they are passed through a kind of sieve, according to their sizes; the smallest are then sold as seed-pearls, and the rest put up to auction, and sold to the highest bidder. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">Artificial</a> Pearls. Attempts have been made to take out stains from pearls, and to render the foul opaque-coloured ones equal in lustre to the oriental. Abundance of processes are given for this purpose in books of secrets and travels; but they are very far from answering what is expected from them. Pearls may be cleaned indeed from any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> foulnesses by washing and rubbing them with a little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> and warm water, or with ground <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STARCH">starch</a> and powder-blue, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, coral, white vitriol and tartar, cuttle-bone, pumice-stone, and other similar substances; but a stain that reaches deep into into the substance of the pearls is impossible to be taken out. Nor can a number of small pearls be united into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> similar to an entire natural one, as some pretend. There are, however, methods of making artificial pearls, in such manner as to be with difficulty distinguished from the best oriental. The ingredient used for this purpose was long kept a secret; but is now discovered to be a fine silver-like substance found upon the under side of the scales of the blay or bleak fish. The scales, taken off in the usual manner, are washed and rubbed with fresh parcels of fair water, and the several liquors suffered to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a>: the water being then poured off, the pearly matter remains at the bottom, of the confluence of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, called by the French essence d'orient. A little of this is dropped into a hollow bead of bluish glass, and shaken about so as to line the internal surface; after which the cavity is filled up with wax, to give solidity and weight. Pearls made in this manner are indistinguishable from the natural only by their having fewer blemishes. Mother-of-Pearl is the shell, not of the pearl oyster, but of another sea-fish of the oyster kind. This shell, on the inside, is extremely smooth, and of the whiteness and water of pearl itself: it has also the same lustre on the outside after the external laminae have been taken off by aquafortis and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAPIDARY">lapidary</a>'s mill. Mother-of-pearl is used in inlaid works, and in several toys, as snuff-boxes, &c.

PEARSON

Pages 417-417

a very learned English bishop in the 17th century, was born at Snoring in 1613. After his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ETON">Eton</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, he entered into holy orders in 1639, and was the same year collated to the prebend of Netherhaven in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Sarum. In 1640 he was appointed chaplain to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> keeper Finch, and by him presented to the living of Torrington in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>. In 1650 he was made minister of St Clement's, Eastcheap, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. In 1657, he and Mr Gunning had a dispute with two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, upon the subject of schism; a very unfair account of which was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1658. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, he published his Exposition of the Creed, and several other works. After various preferments, he was advanced in 1672 to the see of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>; where he died, in 1686.

PEAT

Pages 417-417

a kind of turf used for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> in several countries. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, no 516. There are very considerable differences in peat, proceeding perhaps wholly from different mineral admixtures; for the substance of the peat is plainly of vegetable origin, whence it is found to answer for the smelting of ores, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of metallic calces, nearly in the same manner as the coals of wood. Some sorts yield in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> a very disagreeable smell, which extends to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance; whilst others are inoffensive. Some burn into grey <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and others into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> ashes. The ashes yield, on elixation, a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of alkaline <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, with sometimes one and sometimes another salt of the neutral kind. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of peat does not preserve or harden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> like that of wood; and the foot, into which it condenses, is more disposed to liquefy in moist <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. On distilling peat in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> vessels, there arises a clear infusible phlegm, an acid liquor, which is succeeded by an alkaline one, and a dark coloured <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. The oil has a very pungent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; and an empyreumatic smell, less fetid than that of animal substances, more so than that of mineral bitumens: it congeals in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> into a pitchy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, which liquefies in a small <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>: it readily catches fire from a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, but burns less vehemently than other oils, and immediately goes out upon removing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>: it dissolves almost totally in rectified spirit of wine into a dark brownish red liquor.

PEBBLES

Pages 417-417

the name of a genus of fossils, distinguished from the flints and homochroa by their having a variety of colours. These are defined to be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> composed of a crystalline <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> debased by earths of various kinds in the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, and then subject to veins, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, and other variegations, usually formed by incrustation round a central nucleus, but sometimes the effect of a simple concretion; and veined like the agates, by the disposition which the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the fluid they were formed in gave their differently coloured substances. The variety of pebbles is so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that an hasty describer would be apt to make almost as many species as he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> specimens. A careful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> teach us, however, to distinguish them into a certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of essentially different species, to which all the rest may be referred as accidental varieties. When we find the same colours, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> those resulting from a mixture of the same, such as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> frequently makes in a number of stones, we shall easily be able to determine that these are all of them the same species, though of different appearances; and that whether the matter be disposed of in one or two, or in 20 crusts, laid regularly round a nucleus; or thrown irregularly, without a nucleus, into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; or lastly, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> blended into an uniform <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. These are the three states in which every pebble is found; for if it has been naturally and regularly formed by incrustation round a certain nucleus, we find that always the same in the same species, and the crusts not less regular and certain. If the whole has been more hastily formed, and the result only of one simple concretion, if that has happened while its different substances were all moist and thin, they have blended together and made a mixed mass of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of them all. But if they have been something harder when this has happened, and too far concreted to diffuse wholly among one another, they are found thrown together into irregular veins. These are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> differences of all the pebbles; and having regard to these in the several variegations, all the known pebbles may be reduced to 34 species.

PECCANT

Pages 417-417

in medicine, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> used for those humours of the body which offend either by their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>.

PECORA

Pages 417-417

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, the fifth order of the class <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a>, in the Linnean system. See Zoology.

PECTEN

Pages 417-418

the Scallop; a genus of shell-fish, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are these: The animal is a tethys; the shell bivalve and unequal; the hinge toothless, having a small ovated hollow. This shell-fish is one of the spinners, having the power of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> threads like the mucus. muscle; but they are much shorter and coarser than even those of that fish; so that they can never be wrought into any kind of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> like the longer and finer threads of the pinna marina. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the threads which are spun by the scallop is to fix the creature to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body near its shell. All these proceed, as in the muscle, from one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>. It is an evident <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that the fish has a power of fixing itself at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to any solid body by means of these threads, that after storms the scallops are often found tossed upon rocks, where there were none the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> before; and yet these are fixed by their threads, as well as those which had remained ever so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. They form their threads in the very same manner with the muscle; only their organ which serves for spinning is shorter, and has a wider hollow, whence the threads are necessarily thicker and shorter. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this genus is, The maximus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> scallop, with 14 rays, very prominent and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; striated lengthwise above and below. These grow to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> size; are found in beds by themselves; are dredged up, and barrelled for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> say that they have a power of removing themselves from place to place by vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> or leaps. This shell was called by the Greeks xrioe, by the Latins pecten; and was used by both as a food. When dressed with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a> and cummin, it was taken medicinally. The scallop was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> worn by pilgrims on their hat, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> of their coat, as a mark that they had crossed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in their way to the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">Land</a>, or some distant object of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>.

PECTORAL

Pages 418-418

an epithet for medicines good in diseases of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> and lungs.

PECTULUM

Pages 418-418

the stock <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> estate which a person, in the power of another, as a slave, may acquire by his industry. In the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, peculum denotes the goods which each <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> reserves and possesses to himself.

PECULATE

Pages 418-418

in civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the crime of embezzling the public <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, by a person intrusted with the receipt, management, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> custody thereof. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> is also used by civilians for a theft, whether the thing be public, fiscal, sacred, or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>.

PECULIAR

Pages 418-418

in the canon <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies a particular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> that has jurisdiction within itself for granting probates of wills and administrations, exempt from the ordinary or bishop's courts. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s chapel is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> peculiar, exempt from all spiritual jurisdiction, and referred to the visitation and immediate <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the king himself. There is likewise the archbishop's peculiar, for it is an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> privilege of the see of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, that wherever any manors or advowsons belong to it, they forthwith become exempt from the ordinary, and are reputed peculiars: there are 57 such peculiars in the see of Canterbury. Besides these, there are some peculiars belonging to deans, chapters, and prebendaries, which are only exempted from the jurisdiction of the archdeacon: these are derived from the bishop, who may visit them, and to whom there lies an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>.

PECULIARS

Pages 418-418

is a branch of, and annexed to, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. It has a jurisdiction over all those parishes dispersed through the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> in the midst of other dioceses, which are exempt from the ordinary's jurisdiction, and subject to the metropolitan only. All <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> causes, arising within these peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> exempt jurisdictions, are originally cognizable by this court; from which an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> lay formerly to the pope, but now by the stat. 25 H.VIII. c. 19, to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>.

PEDAGOGUE

Pages 418-418
or Pedagogue, a tutor or master, to whom is committed the discipline and direction of a scholar, to be instructed in grammar and other arts. The word is formed from the Greek παιδαγωγος, παιδαγωγος διδασκαλος, "leader of boys." M. Fleury observes, that the Greeks gave the name pedagogus to slaves appointed to attend their children, lead them, and teach them to walk, &c. The Romans gave the same denomination to the slaves who were intrusted with the care and instruction of their children.

PEDALS

Pages 418-418

the largest <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> of an organ, so called because played and stopped with the foot. The pedals are made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and of wood; they are usually 13 in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. They are of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, and serve to carry the sounds of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a> deeper than the rest. See Organ.

PEDANT

Pages 418-418

a school-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> pedagogue, who professes to instruct and govern youth, teach them the humanities, and the arts. See Pedagogue. Pedant is also used for a rough, unpolished <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of letters, who makes an impertinent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the sciences, and abounds in unseasonable criticisms and observations. Dacier defines a pedant, a person who has more <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a> than good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. See Pedantry. Pedants are people ever armed with quibbles and syllogisms; breathe nothing but disputation and chicanery, and pursue a proposition to the last limits of logic. Malebranche describes a pedant as a man full of false erudition, who makes a parade of his knowledge, and is ever quoting some Greek or Latin author, or hunting back to a remote <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a>. St Evremon says, that to paint the folly of a pedant, we must represent him as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> all conversation to some one science or subject he is best acquainted withal. There are pedants of all conditions, and all robes. Wicquefort says, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, always attentive to formalities and decorums, is nothing else but a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> pedant.

PEDANTRY

Pages 418-418
or Pedantism, the quality or manner of a pedant. See Pedant. To swell up little and low things, to make a vain show of science, to heap up Greek and Latin without judgment, to tear those to pieces who differ from us about a passage in Suetonius or the etymology of a word, to stir up all the world against a man for not admiring Cicero enough, to be interested for the reputation of an ancient as if he were our next of kin, is what we properly call pedantry.

PEDARIAN

Pages 418-418

in Roman antiquity, those senators who signified their votes by their feet, not their tongues; that is, such as walked over to the side of those whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> they approved of, in divisions of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>.

PEDESTAL

Pages 418-419

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of an an order of columns, being that part which sustains the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, and serves it as a foot <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> stand. See Column.

PEDICLE

Pages 419-419

among botanists, that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of a stalk which immediately sustains the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of a flower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a fruit, and is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called a footstalk.

PEDICULUS

Pages 419-420

the Louse, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of aptera. It has six feet, two eyes, and a sort of sting in the mouth; the feelers are as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the thorax; and the belly is depressed and sublobated. Many animals both of the quadruped and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> kinds are subject to <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a>; but these are of peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> on each animal, and are not at all like those which infest the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body. Nay, even insects are infested with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> which feed on and torment them. Several kinds of beetles are subject to lice; but particularly that kind called thence the lousy beetle. The lice on this are very numerous, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be shook off. The earwig is often infested with lice, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> at the setting on of its head; these are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and shining like mites, but they are much smaller; they are round-backed, flat belled, and have long legs, particularly the foremost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a>. Snails of all kinds, but especially the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> naked sorts, are very subject to lice; which are continually seen running about them, and devouring them. Numbers of little <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> lice, with a very small head, and in shape resembling a tortoise, are often seen about the legs of spiders, and they never leave the animal while he lives; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he is killed, they almost instantly forsake him. A sort of whitish lice is found on humble-bees: they are also found upon ants; and fishes are not let subject to them than other animals. Kircher tells us, that he found lice also on flies, and M. de la Hire has given a curious account of the creature which he found on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fly. Having occasion to view a living fly with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, he observed on its head, back, and shoulders, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small animals crawling very nimbly about, and often climbing up the hairs which grow at the origin of the fly's legs. He with a fine <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> took up one of these, and placed it before the microscope used to view the animalcules in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>. It had eight legs; four on each side. These were not placed very distant from each other; but the four towards the head were separated by a small space from the four towards the tail. The feet were of a particular structure, being composed of several fingers, as it were, and fitted for taking fast hold of any thing; but the two nearest the head were also more remarkable in this particular than those near the tail; the extremities of the legs for a little way above the feet were dry and void of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> like the legs of birds, but above this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> they appeared plump and fleshy. It had two small houses upon its head, formed of several hairs arranged closely together; and there were some other clutters of hairs by the side of these horns, but they had not the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; and towards the origin of the hinder legs there were two other such clutters of hairs which took their origin at the middle of the back. The whole creature was of a bright yellowish red; the legs, and all the body, except a large spot in the centre, were perfectly transparent. In size, he computed it to be about \(\frac{1}{400}\)th part of the head of the fly; and he observes, that such kind of vermin are rarely found on flies. The louse which infests the human body makes a Pediculus very curious appearance through a microscope. It has such a transparent shell <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> skin, that we are able to discover more of what passes within its body than in most other living creatures. It has naturally three divisions, the head, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, and the tail part. In the head appear two fine <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> eyes, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a> that has five <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, and is surrounded with hairs standing before each eye; and from the end of the nose or snout there is a pointed projecting part, which serves as a sheath or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> to a piercer or sucker, which the creature thrusts into the skin to draw out the blood and humours which are its destined food; for it has no mouth that opens in the common way. This piercer or sucker is judged to be 700 times smaller than a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and is contained in another case within the first, and can be drawn in or thrust out at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. The breast is very beautifully marked in the middle; the skin is transparent, and full of little pits; and from the under part of it proceed six legs, each having five joints, and their skin all the way resembling <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHAGREEN">shagreen</a>, except at the ends where it is smoother. Each leg is terminated by two claws, which are hooked, and are of an unequal length and size. These it uses as we would a thumb and middle finger; and there are hairs between these claws as well as all over the legs. On the back part of the tail there may be discovered some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>-like divisions, and a sort of marks which look like the strokes of a rod on the human skin; the belly looks like shagreen, and towards the lower end it is very clear, and full of pits; at the extremity of the tail there are two semicircular parts all covered over with hairs, which serve to conceal the anus. When the louse moves its legs, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the muscles, which all unite in an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> dark spot in the middle of the breast, may be distinguished perfectly, and so may the motion of the muscles of the head when it moves its horns. We may likewise see the various ramifications of the veins and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a>, which are white, with the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> regularly <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> in the arteries. But the most surprising of all the sights is the peristaltic motion of the guts, which is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> all the way from the stomach <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the anus. If one of these creatures, when hungry, be placed on the back of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, it will thrust its sucker into the skin, and the blood which it sucks may be seen passing in a fine stream to the fore-part of the head; where, falling into a roundish cavity, it passes again in a fine stream to another circular receptacle in the middle of the head; from thence it runs thro' a small vessel to the breast, and then to a gut which reaches to the hinder part of the body, where in a curve it turns again a little upward; in the breast and gut the blood is moved without intermission, with a great force; especially in the gut, where it occasions such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the gut as is very surprising. In the upper part of the crooked ascending gut above mentioned, the propelled blood stands still, and seems to undergo a separation, some of it becoming clear and watery, while other black particles are pushed forward to the anus. If a louse is placed on its back, two bloody darkish spots appear; the larger in the middle of the body, the lesser towards the tail; the motions of which are followed by the pulsation of the dark bloody spot, in or over which the white bladder Pediculus, seems to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a>. This motion of the systole and diastole is best seen when the creature begins to grow weak; and on pricking the white bladder, which seems to be the heart, the creature instantly dies. The lower dark spot is supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCREMENT">excrement</a> in the gut. Lice have been supposed to be hermaphrodites; but this is erroneous; for Mr Lieuwenhoek observed, that the males have flings in their tails, which the females have not. And he supposes the smarting pain, which those creatures sometimes give, to be owing to their flinging with these flings when made uneasy by pressure or otherwise. He says, that he felt little or no pain from their suckers, though six of them were feeding on his hand at once. In order to know the true <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and manner of breeding of these creatures, Mr Lieuwenhoek put two <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> lice into a black <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a>, which he wore night and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>. He found on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> that, in six days one of them had laid above 50 eggs; and, upon dissecting it, he found as many yet remaining in the ovary: whence he concludes, that in 12 days it would have laid 100 eggs. These eggs naturally <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HATCH">hatch</a> in six days, and would then probably have produced 50 males, and as many females; and these females coming to their full growth in 18 days, might each of them be supposed after 12 days more to lay 100 eggs; which eggs, in six days more, might produce a young brood of 5000; so that in eight weeks, one louse may see 5000 of its own descendents. Signior Rhedi, who has more attentively observed these animals than any other author, has given several engravings of the different species of lice found on different animals. Men, he observes, are subject to two kinds; the common louse, and the crab-louse. He observes also, that the size of the lice is not at all proportioned to that of the animal which they infest; since the starling has them as large as the swan. Some kinds of constitutions are more apt to breed lice than others; and in some places of different degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, they are certain to be destroyed upon people who in other climates are overrun with them. It is an observation of Oviedo, that the Spanish sailors, who are generally much afflicted with lice, always lose them in a certain <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude in their voyage to the East Indies, and have them again on their returning to the same degree. This is not only true of the Spaniards, but of all other people who make the same voyage; for though they set out ever so lousy, they have not one of those creatures by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> they come to the tropic. And in the Indies there is no such thing as a louse about the body, though the people be ever so nasty. The sailors continue free from these creatures till their return; but in going back, they usually begin to be lousy after they arrive at the latitude of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> sweats, which the working people naturally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into, between the latitude of Madeira and the Indies, drown and destroy the lice; and have the same effect as the rubbing over the lousy heads of children with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. The sweat, in these hot climates, is not <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> as in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and therefore it is not apt to breed lice; but where people return into latitudes where they sweat rank again, their nastiness subjects them to the same visitations of these vermin as before. The people in general in the Indies are very subject to lice in their heads, tho' free from them on their bodies. The reason Pediluvium of this is, that their heads sweat less than their bodies, and they take no care to comb and clean them. The Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> wash their heads thoroughly once every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, to prevent their being lousy. This makes them escape much better than the other negroes who are slaves there; for the lice grow so numerous in their heads, that they often eat large holes in them.

PEDILUVIUM

Pages 420-421
or Bathing of the Feet. The uses of warm bathing in general, and of the pediluvium in particular, are so little understood, that they are often preposterously used, and sometimes as injudiciously abstained from. In the Edinburgh medical essays, we find an ingenious author's opinion of the warm pediluvium, notwithstanding that of Borelli, Boerhaave, and Hoffman, to the contrary, to be, That, the legs becoming warmer than before, the blood in them is warmed; this blood rarefying, dilutes the vessels; and in circulating imparts a great degree of warmth to the rest of the mass; and as there is a portion of it constantly passing through the legs, and acquiring new heat there, which heat is in the course of circulation communicated to the rest of the blood, the whole mass rarefying, occupies a larger space, and of consequence circulates with greater force. The volume of the blood being thus increased, every vessel is distended, and every part of the body feels the effects of it; the distant parts a little later than those first heated. The benefit obtained by a warm pediluvium is generally attributed to its making a derivation into the parts immersed, and a revulsion from those affected, because they are relieved; but the cure is performed by the direct contrary method of operating, viz. by a greater force of circulation through the parts affected, removing what was stagnant or moving too sluggishly there. Warm bathing is of no service where there is an irreducible obstruction, though, by its taking off from a spasm in general, it may seem to give a moment's ease: nor does it draw from the distant parts, but often hurts by pushing against matter that will not yield with a stronger impetus of circulation than the stretched and diseased vessels can bear: so that where there is any suspicion of scirrhus, warm bathing of any sort should never be used. On the other hand, where obstructions are not of long standing, and the impacted matter is not obstinate, warm baths may be of great use to resolve them quickly. In recent colds, with slight humoral peripneumonies, they are frequently an immediate cure. This they effect by increasing the force of the circulation, opening the skin, and driving freely through the lungs that lentor which stagnated or moved slowly in them. As thus conducing to the resolution of obstructions, they may be considered as short and safe fevers; and in using them we imitate nature, which by a fever often carries off an obstructing cause of a chronic ailment. Borelli, Boerhaave, and Hoffman, are all of opinion, that the warm pediluvium acts by deriving a larger quantity of blood into the parts immersed. But arguments must give way to facts: the experiments related in the Medical Essays seem to prove a demonstration, that the warm pediluvium acts by rarifying the blood. A warm pediluvium, when rightly tempered, may be Pediment used as a safe cordial, by which circulation can be roused, or a gentle fever raised; with this advantage over the cordials and sudorifics, that the effect of them may be taken off at pleasure. Pediluvia are sometimes used in the small-pox; but Dr Stevenson thinks their frequent tumultuous operations render that suspected, and at best of very doubtful effect; and he therefore prefers Monf. Martin of Lausanne's method of bathing the skin, not only of the legs, but of the whole body, with a soft cloth dipped in warm water, every four hours, till the eruption; by which means the pustules may become universally higher, and consequently more safe. PEDIMENT. See Architecture, n° 77.

PEDLAR

Pages 421-421

a travelling foot-trader. See Hawker. Among the British and French the pedlars are despised; but it is otherwise in certain countries. In Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, the business is so profitable, that it is thought by no means dishonourable; and there are many gentlemen in Old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, who, when their circumstances are declining, send their sons to the Indies to retrieve their fortunes in this way. Almost all the commodities of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> are distributed through the southern continent of America by means of these pedlars. They come from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAITA">Paita</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from the port last mentioned, they make Peura their first voyage to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIMA">Lima</a>. Some take the road through Caxamalia; others through <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-TRUXILLO">Truxillo</a>, along shore from Lima. They take their passage back to Panama by sea, and perhaps take with them a little cargo of brandy. At Panama they again stock themselves with European goods, returning by sea to Paita, where they are put on shore; there they hire mules and load them, the Indians going with them in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them back. Their travelling expenses are next to nothing; for the Indians are brought under such subjection, that they find lodging for them, and provender for their mules, frequently thinking it an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> done them for their guests to accept of this for nothing, unless the stranger now and then, out of generosity <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> compassion, makes a small recompence. In <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, where there are few or no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, almost all the merchandise is carried on by pedlars, who are said to be generally Scotsmen, and who, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., are said to have amounted to no fewer than 53,000.

PEEBLES

Pages 421-421
or Tweedale, a county of Scotland, extending 25 miles in length, and 18 in breadth. It is bounded on the east by Ettrick Forest, on the south by Annandale, on the west by Clydendale, and on the north by Mid Lothian. Tweedale is a hilly country, well watered with the Tweed, the Yarrow, and a great number of smaller streams that fertilize the valleys, which produce good harvests of oats and barley, with some proportion of wheat. All the rivers of any consequence abound with trout and salmon. The lake called Wigt-Water Loch swarms with a prodigious number of eels. In the month of August, when the west wind blows, they tumble into the river Yarrow in such shoals, that the people who wade in to catch them run the risk of being overturned. There is another lake on the borders of Annandale, called Lech- gennen, which forms a cataract over a precipice 250 paces high: here the water falls with such a momentum as to kill the fish underneath. About the middle of this country is the hill or mountain of Braidalb, from the top of which the sea may be seen on each side of the island. Tweedale abounds with limestone and freestone. The hills are generally as green as the downs in Sussex, and feed innumerable flocks of sheep, that yield great quantities of excellent wool. The country is well shaded with woods and plantations, abounds with all the necessaries of life, and is adorned with many fine seats and populous villages. The earls of March were hereditary sheriffs of Tweedale, which beftows the title of marquis on a branch of the ancient house of Hay, earls of Errol, and hereditary high constables of Scotland. The family of Tweedale is, by the female side, descended from the famous Simon de Fraser, proprietor of great part of this country, who had a great share in obtaining the triple victory at Rossin. The chief, and indeed the only town of consequence in Tweedale, is Peebles, a small inconsiderable royal borough, and seat of a prebendary, pleasantly situated on the banks of the Tweed, over which there is at this place a stately stone bridge of five arches. In the neighbourhood of Peebles, near the village of Romana, on the river Lene, we see the vestiges of two Roman castella, or stationary forts; and a great many terraces on the neighbouring hills, which perhaps have served as itinerary encampments. In the thire of Tweedale there are many ancient and honourable families of the gentry. Among these, Douglas of Cavers, who was hereditary sheriff of the county, still preserves the standard and the iron mace of the gallant lord Douglas, who fell in the battle of Otterburn, just as his troops had defeated and taken Henry Percy, surnamed Hotspur. In the churchyard of Drumelzier, belonging to an ancient branch of the Hay-family, the famous Merlin is supposed to lie buried. There was an old traditional prophecy, that the two kingdoms should be united, when the waters of the Tweed and the Panfil should meet at his grave. Accordingly, the country people observe that this meeting happened in consequence of an inundation at the accession of James VI. to the crown of England.

PEEK

Pages 421-421

in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is a word used in various senses. Thus the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> is said to be a-peek, when the ship being about to weigh comes over her anchor in such a manner that the cable hangs perpendicularly between the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAWSE">hawse</a> and the anchor. To have a-peek is to bring the peck so as that the anchor may hang a-peek. A ship is said to ride a-peek, when lying with her main and fore yards hoisted up, one end of her yards is brought <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the shrouds, and the other raised up an end; which is chiefly done when she lies in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, lest other ships falling foul of the yards should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> them. Riding a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> peck, denotes much the same, excepting that the yards are only raised to half the height. Peek is also used for a room in the hold, extending from the bitts forward to the stem; in this room men of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> keep their powder, and merchant-men their victuals.

PEER

Pages 421-422

in general, signifies an equal, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> one of the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and station: hence in the acts of some coun- Peer, we find these words, with the consent of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, abbots, &c. Afterwards the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> was applied to the vassals or tenants of the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, who were called peers, because they were all equal in condition, and obliged to serve and attend him in his courts; and peers in fiefs, because they all hold fiefs of the same lord. The term peers is now applied to those who are impannelled in an inquest upon a person for convicting or acquitting him of any offence laid to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>: and the reason why the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURY">jury</a> is so called, is because by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, every person is to be tried by his peers or equals; a lord by the lords, and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> by commoners. See the article Jury. Peer of the Realm, a noble lord who has a seat and vote in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Lords, which is also called the House of Peers. These lords are called peers, because though there is a distinction of degrees in our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, yet in public actions they are equal, as in their votes in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and in trying any nobleman or other person impeached by the commons, &c. See Parliament. House of Peers, or House of Lords, forms one of the three estates of parliament. See Lords and Parliament. In a judicative capacity, the house of peers is the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the kingdom, having at present no original jurisdiction over causes, but only upon appeals and writs of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>; to rectify any injustice or mistake of the law committed by the courts below. To this authority they succeeded of course upon the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the Aula Regia. For as the barons of parliament were constituent members of that court, and the rest of its jurisdiction was dealt out to other tribunals, over which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> officers who accompanied those barons were respectively delegated to preside, it followed, that the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of receiving appeals, and superintending all other jurisdictions, still remained in that noble <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, from which every other great court was derived. They are therefore in all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>, from whose judgment no farther <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> is permitted; but every subordinate tribunal must conform to their determinations: The law repaying an entire confidence in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> of the noble persons who compose this important assembly, that they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> make themselves masters of those questions upon which they undertake to decide; since upon their decision all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> must finally depend. See Lords. Peers of France, are twelve great lords of that kingdom; of which six are dukes and six counts; and of these, six are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> and six laymen: thus the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>, and the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAON">Laon</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGRES">Langres</a>, are dukes and peers; and the bishops of Chalon on the Marn, Noyons, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUVAIS">Beauvais</a>, are counts and peers. The dukes of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, Normandy, and Aquitain, are lay peers and dukes; and the counts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, Champaign, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a>, lay peers and counts. These peers still assist at the coronation of kings, either in person or by their representatives, where each performs the functions attached to his respective <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>: but as the six lay peerages are all at present united to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, except that of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Flanders, six lords of the first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> are chosen to represent them: but the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> peers usually assist in person. At present the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of peer is bestowed on every lord whose estate is erected into a peerage; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of which is uncertain, as it depends entirely on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>. Peeress, a woman who is noble by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a peeress, by descent or creation, marries a person under the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of nobility, she still continues noble: but if she obtains that dignity only by marriage, she loses it, on her afterwards marrying a commoner; yet by the courtesy of England, she always retains the title of her nobility.

PEGASUS

Pages 422-422

among the poets, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> imagined to have wings; being that whereon Bellerophon was fabled to be mounted when he engaged the chimera. See CHIMERA. The opening of the fountain Hippocrene on mount <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HELICON">Helicon</a>, is ascribed to a blow of Pegasus's hoof. It was feigned to have flown away to heaven, where it became a constellation. Hence Pegasus, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, the name of a constellation of the northern hemisphere, in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> horse. See ASTRONOMY, No 206.

PEGU

Pages 422-426

a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, beyond the Ganges. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> properly so called is but about 350 miles in length from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, and as much in breadth from east to west. It is bounded, on the north by the kingdoms of Arrakan and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AVA">Ava</a>; on the east, by the Upper and Lower <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>; on the south, by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Siam and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and on the west, by the sea and part of Arrakan. Considered in a larger <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> however, as augmented by the conquests of its Barma kings, it extends as far north as the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Yunan in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, comprehending almost all the farther <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. The kingdom of Pegu is said to have been founded about 1100 years ago. Its first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> was a seaman; concerning whom and his successors we know nothing till the discovery of the East Indies by the Portuguese in the beginning of the 16th century. In 1518 the throne of Pegu was possessed by one Bressagukan, with whom Antony Correa the Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> solemnly concluded a peace in 1519. This monarch was possessed of a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and rich empire, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> kingdoms being in subjection to him, whose revenues amounted to three millions of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. We hear no farther account of his transactions after the conclusion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with the Portuguese. In 1539 he was murdered on the following occasion: Among other princes who were his tributaries was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARA">Para</a> Mandera, king of the Barmas. These people inhabited the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> lands called Pangavirau, to the northward of the kingdom of Pegu. Their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, by one of the terms of his vassalage, was obliged to furnish the king of Pegu with 30,000 Barmas, to labour in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> and other public works. As the king used frequently to go and see how his works went forward, and in these journeys took along with him none but his women, the Barmas observing these visits frequently repeated, formed a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of robbing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> and all the concubines of their jewels; and pursuant to this design, the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the king visited the works, they murdered him, and having stripped the ladies fled to their own country. By this enormity all Pegu was thrown into confusion; but, instead of revenging the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of their king, the people divided everywhere into factions; so that Dacha Rupi, the lawful heir to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, found himself unable to maintain his authority. Of these commotions, the king of the Barmas taking the advantage, not only shook off the yoke, but formed a design of conquering the kingdom of Pegu itself. With this view he invaded the country with an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of more than a million of foot, and 5000 elephants; besides a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fleet which he sent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the river Ava towards Bagou, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Pegu, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the empire; while he himself marched thither by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">Just</a> at this time Ferdinand de Mirales arrived at Pegu from Goa with a large galleon richly laden on account of the king of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. As soon as Dacha Rupi heard of his coming, he sent to desire his assistance against the enemy. This he obtained by great presents and promises; and Mirales, setting out in a galliot, joined the king's ships. Had the numbers been anything near an equality, the superior skill of Mirales would undoubtedly have gained the victory: But the fleet of the Barmas covered the whole river though as large as the Ganges, while that of Dacha Rupi could scarce be observed in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with them. Mirales did every thing that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> could do, and even held out alone after the natives had deserted him; but at last, oppressed and overwhelmed with numbers, he was killed, with all his men. Thus Para <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANDARA">Mandara</a> became <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all Pegu; after which he attacked the tributary kingdoms. In 1544 he besieged Martavan, the capital of a kingdom of the same name, then very great and flourishing. The land-forces which he brought against it consisted of 700,000 men, while by sea he attacked it with a fleet of 1700 sail; 100 of which were large galleys, and in them 700 Portuguese commanded by John Cayero, who had the reputation of being a valiant and experienced officer. The siege, however, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months, during which time the Barmas lost 120,000 men; but at last the beleagued king, finding himself starved for want of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and unable to withstand so great a power, offered terms of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>. The besiegers would admit of no terms, upon which the distressed king applied to the Portuguese in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of his enemy; for by their assistance he doubted not to be able to drive away the Barmas. Accordingly he sent one Seixas to Cayero, intreating him to receive himself, his family, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, on board the four ships he had under his command; offering, on that condition, to give half his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> to the king of Portugal, to become his vassal, and pay such tribute as should be agreed upon. Cayero consulted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers, and in their presence asked Seixas what he thought the treasure might amount to. Seixas answered, that out of what he had seen, for he had not seen all, two ships might be loaded with gold, and four or five with silver. This proposal was too advantageous to be slighted; but the rest of the officers envying the great fortune which Cayero would make, threatened to discover the whole to the king of Barma <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he did not reject it. The unhappy king of Martavan had now no other resource but to set fire to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, make a sally, and die honourably with the few men he had with him; but even here he was disappointed; for by the desertion of 4000 of his troops the enemy were apprised of his design, and prevented it. Thus betrayed, he capitulated with the Barma king for his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and the lives of his wife and children, with leave to end his days in retirement. All this was readily granted, but the conqueror intended to perform no part of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>. The city was plundered and burnt, by which above 60,000 persons perished, while at least an equal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> were carried into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. Six thousand cannon were found in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; 100,000 quintals of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, and an equal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of other spices. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> after this destruction, 21 gibbets were erected on an hill adjoining to the city; on which the queen, her children and ladies, were executed, by hanging them up alive by the feet: however, the queen expired with anguish before she suffered such a cruel indignity. The king, with 50 of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> lords, was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into the sea, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> about their necks. This monstrous cruelty so provoked the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, that they mutinied, and he was in no small danger of suffering for it; however, he found means to pacify them; after which he proceeded to besiege Prom, the capital of another kingdom. Here he increased his army to 900,000 men. The queen by whom it was governed offered to submit to be his vassal; but nothing would satisfy the Barma monarch less than her surrender at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, and putting all her treasure into his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. This she, who knew his perfidy, refused to do; on which the city was fiercely assaulted, but greatly to the disadvantage of the Barmas, who lost near 100,000 men. However, the city was at last betrayed to him, when Mandara behaved with his usual cruelty. Two thousand children were slain, and their bodies cut in pieces and thrown to the elephants; the queen was stripped naked, publicly whipped, and then tortured till she died; the young king was tied to her dead body, and both together cast into a river, as were also 300 other people of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. While the tyrant was employed in fortifying the city, he was informed, that the prince of Ava had failed down the river Queytor with 400 rowing vessels having 30,000 soldiers on board; but that, hearing of the queen's distress, he stood at Meletay a strong fortress about 12 leagues north of Prom, where he waited to be joined by his father the king of Ava with 80,000 men. On this news the Barma king sent his foster-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Chaumigrem along the river-side with 200,000 men, while he himself followed with 100,000 more. The prince in this emergency burnt his barks, forming a vanguard of the mariners; and, putting his small army in the best position he could, expected the enemy. A most desperate engagement ensued, in which only 800 of the prince's army were left, and 115,000 out of 200,000 Barmas who opposed him were killed. The 800 Avans retired into the fort: but Mandara coming up soon after, and being enraged at the terrible havoc made in his army, attacked the fortress most violently for seven days; at the end of which time, the 800, finding themselves unable to hold out any longer, rushed out in a dark and rainy night, in order to sell their lives at as dear a rate as possible. This last effort was so extremely violent, that they broke through the enemy's troops in several places, and even pressed so hard on the king himself that he was forced to jump into the river. However, they were at last all cut off, but not before they had destroyed 12,000 of their enemies. Mandara having thus become master of the fort, commanded it to be immediately repaired; and sailed up the river to the port of Ava, about a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> from the capital, where he burnt between 2000 and 3000 vessels, and lost in the enterprise about 8000 men. The city itself he did not think proper to invest, as it had been newly fortified, was defended by a numerous garrison, and an army of 80,000 men was advancing to its relief. The king also, apprehensive of Mandara's power, had implored the protection of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Siam; offering to become his tributary on condition that he would assist him with his forces in recovering the city of Prom. To this the emperor readily assented; which news greatly alarmed the Barma monarch, so that he dispatched ambassadors to the Kalamingham or sovereign of a large territory adjacent, requesting him to divert the emperor from his purpose. On the ambassadors return from this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> it appeared that the treaty had already taken effect; but as the season was not yet arrived for invading Ava, Chaumigren the king's foster-brother was sent with 150,000 men to reduce Sebadi or Savadi the capital of a small kingdom about 130 leagues north-east from Pagu. The general, however, failed in his attempt; and afterwards endeavouring to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> himself on a town in the neighbourhood, he was surprised by the enemy and put to flight. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time the empire of Siam fell into great distractions; the king together with the heir to the crown were murdered by the queen, who had fallen in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with an officer, whom she married after her husband's death. However, both of them were soon after killed at an entertainment; and the crown was given to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> brother of the late king, but a coward and a tyrant. On this Mandara resolved to invade the country; and, his principal courtiers concurring in the scheme, he collected an army of 800,000 men, with no fewer than 20,000 elephants. In this army were 1000 Portuguese, commanded by one James Suarez, who already had a pension of 200,000 ducats a-year from the king of Pegu, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of his brother, and governor of the kingdom. With this formidable army he set out in April 1548. His first achievement was the taking of a fortress on the borders of the enemy's country; before which, being several times repulsed, and having lost 3000 of his men, he revenged himself by putting all the women to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>.
