He next besieged the capital of itself; but though the siege was continued for five months, during which time the most violent attacks were made upon it, the assailants were constantly repulsed with great loss. However, it was still resolved to continue the siege; and a mound of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> was raised, on which were placed 40 pieces of cannon ready to batter it anew, when, in October, advice was received of a rebellion having broken out in Pegu. The person who headed the rebels on the present occasion was Shoripam Shay, near akin to the former monarch slain twelve years before. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> person, of great understanding, and esteem; a saint. As he was a famous preacher, he made a sermon, in which he set forth the tyranny of the Barmas in such a manner, that he was immediately taken out of the pulpit and proclaimed king by the people, who, as a token of sovereignty, gave him the title of Shemindoo. The first <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of sovereignty which he exerted was to cut in pieces 15,000 Barmas, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> on the treasure; and so agreeable was this change of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to all ranks of people, that in three weeks time all the strong-holds of Pegu fell into his hands. On this news the king immediately raised the siege in which he was engaged, and in 17 days got to Martavan. Here he was informed, that Shemindoo had posted 500,000 men in different places, in order to intercept his passage; at the same time that he had the mortification to find 50,000 of his best troops deserted. To prevent a greater desertion, after 14 days stay, he departed from Martavan, and soon met Shemindoo at the head of 600,000 men. A desperate engagement followed; in which Shemindoo was entirely defeated, with the loss of 300,000 men. Of the Barma troops were slain 60,000; among whom were 280 Portuguese. The morning after this victory, the tyrant marched to the city; the inhabitants of which surrendered, on condition of having their lives and effects spared. The kingdom being thus again brought under his subjection, his next step was to punish the principal persons concerned in the rebellion: their heads he cut off; and confiscated their estates, which amounted to no less than ten millions of gold. Others say, that he put all without distinction to the sword, excepting only 12,000, who took shelter in James Suarez's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; that alone affording an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> from the general slaughter. The plunder was incredible, Suarez alone getting three millions. All these cruelties, however, were insufficient to secure the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> of the tyrant's subjects: for in less than three months news was brought that the city of Martavan had revolted; and that the governor had not only declared for Shemindoo, but murdered 2000 Barmas. Mandara then summoned all the lords of the kingdom to meet him with their force, within 15 days, at a place called Mouchau, not far from his capital, whither he himself went with 300 men, to wait their arrival. But in the meantime he received intelligence that the shemin or governor of Zatan, a city of some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, had submitted to Shemindoo, and also <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENT">lent</a> him a large sum of gold. The shemin was immediately sent for in order to be put to death: but he, suspecting Mandara's design, excused himself by pretending sickness; after which, having consulted with his friends, he drew together about 600 men; and having with these privately advanced to the place where the king was, he killed him, with the few attendants that were about him at the time. The guards in the court being alarmed with the noise, a skirmish ensued with the shemin's men, in which about 800 were slain on both sides, most of them Barmas. The shemin then retreated to a place called Pontel; whither the people of the country, hearing of the death of the king, who was universally hated, resorted to him. When he had assembled about 5000 men, he returned to seek the troops which the late king had with him; and finding them dispersed in several places, easily killed them all. With the Barmas were slain 80 out of 300 Portuguese. The remainder surrendered, with Suarez their leader; and were spared, on condition of their remaining remaining in the service of the shemin. The shemin now finding his forces daily increase, assumed the title of king; and, to render himself the more popular, gave out, that he would exterminate the Barmas so effectually, as not to leave one in all the kingdom. It happened, however, that one of those who were with the late king at the time he was murdered, escaped the general slaughter; and, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> over the river, informed Chaumigrem of the king's death. He had with him 180,000 men, all of them natives of Pegu, excepting 30,000 Barmas. He knew very well, that if the natives had known that the king was dead, he and all his Barmas would have instantly been put to the sword. Pretending therefore that he had received orders to put garrisons into several places, Chaumigrem dispatched all the natives into different parts; and thus got rid of those whom he had so much cause to fear. As soon as they were marched, he turned back upon the capital, and seized the king's treasure, together with all the arms and ammunition. He then set fire to the magazines, arsenals, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, some of whose apartments were cased with gold, and 2000 rowing vessels which were on the river. Then, destroying all the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, he fled with the 30,000 Barmas to his own country, being pursued in vain by the natives of Pegu. Thus the shemin of Zatan was left in quiet possession of the kingdom; but, by his repeated acts of tyranny and cruelty, he so disgusted his subjects, that many fled to foreign countries, while others went over to Shemindoo, who began now to gather strength again. In the mean time, James Suarez, the Portuguese whom we have often mentioned, lost his life by attempting to ravish a young woman of distinction; the shemin being unable to protect him, and obliged to give him up to the mob, who stoned him to death. The shemin himself did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> survive him; for, being grown intolerable by his oppressions, most of his followers abandoned him, and he was besieged in his capital by Shemindoo with an army of 200,000 men, and soon after slain in a sally; so that Shemindoo now seemed to be fully established in the throne. But in the mean time Chaumigrem, the foster-brother to the deceased king, hearing that Pegu was very ill provided with the means of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, invaded the kingdom with an army of 300,000 men. Shemindoo met him with three times their number; but his men, being all natives of Pegu, were inferior in strength, notwithstanding their numbers, to the enemy. The consequence was, that Shemindoo was defeated with prodigious slaughter, and Chaumigrem caused himself to be proclaimed king of Pegu. Shortly after, Shemindoo himself was taken; and, after being treated with the utmost of cruelty, was beheaded. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Chaumigrem is very imperfect. However, we know that he was a very great conqueror, and not at all inferior in cruelty to his predecessors. He reduced the empire of Siam and Arrakan, and died in 1583; being succeeded by his son named Pranjinok, then about 50 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. When this prince ascended the throne, the kingdom of Pegu was in its greatest height of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>; but by his tyranny and obstinacy he lost all that his father had gained. He died in 1599, and after his death the kingdom of Pegu became subject to Arrakan; nor have we any farther distinct history of it. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> of Pegu is very healthy, and presently recovers sick strangers. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> also is very rich and fertile in corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, fruit, and roots; being enriched by the inundations of the river Pegu, which are almost incredible, extending above 30 leagues beyond its channel. It produces also good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> of several kinds. The country abounds with elephants, buffaloes, goats, hogs, and other animals, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a>; and deer is so plenty in September and October, that one may be bought for three or four pence: they are very fleasy, but have no fat. There is store of good <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>; the cocks are vastly large, and the hens very beautiful. As for fish, there are many sorts, and well tasted. In Pegu are found mines, not only of gold, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, tin, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, or rather a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, or mixture of copper and lead, but also of rubies, diamonds, and sapphires. The rubies are the best in the world; but the diamonds are small, and only found in the craws of poultry and pheasants. Besides, only one family has the privilege of selling them; and none dare open the ground to dig for them. The rubies are found in a mountain in the province of Kablan, or Kapelan, between the city of Pegu and the port of Sirian. The inhabitants are of an olive, or rather a tawny <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. The women are branded by some travellers, as having shook off all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, on account of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> some parts of their bodies which ought to be concealed from sight. Some also tell us, that the men wear bells, which at a certain age, viz. 25 or 30, or, according to others, when they are capable of making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of women, are inserted on each side the virile member between the skin and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, which is opened for that purpose, and healed in seven or eight days. The Peguers may be ranked among the most superstitious of all mankind. They maintain and worship crocodiles; and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> drink nothing but the waters of the ditches where those monstrous animals harbour. By thus exposing themselves to the manifest hazard of their lives, they have frequently the misfortune to be devoured. They have five principal festivals in the year, called japans, which they celebrate with extraordinary magnificence. In one of them the king and queen make a pilgrimage about 12 leagues from the city, riding on a triumphal car, so richly adorned with jewels, that it may be said without an hyperbole, that they carry about with them the value of a kingdom. This prince is extremely rich; and has in the chapel of his palace, idols of incalculable value, some of them being of maffy gold and silver, and adorned with all sorts of precious stones. The talapins, or priests of this country, have no possessions; but such is the respect paid them by the people, that they are never known to want. They preach to them every Monday, not to commit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>; to take from no person anything belonging to him; to do no hurt; to give no offence; to avoid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPURITY">impurity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; but above all, not to worship the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>: but these discourses have no effect in the least respect. The people, attached to manicheism, believe, that all good comes from God, that the devil is the author of all the evil that happens to men; and that therefore they ought to worship him, that he may not afflict them. This is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> notion among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> idolaters. The inhabitants of Pegu are accused by some authors with being slovenly in their houses, and nasty in their diet, on account of their seasoning their viands with fidal, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> made of stinking fish, reduced to a consistency like mustard, so nauseous and offensive, that none but themselves can endure the smell of it. Balbi says, he could sooner bear the scent of stinking carrion; and yet with this they season their rice, and other soups, instead of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>. As they have no wheat in this country, their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> is rice made into cakes. Their common drink is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or a liquor distilled from cocoanut water. The men here, as in most eastern countries, buy their wives, or pay their parents a dowry for them. They have an odd <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>; which is to offer their daughters to strangers, and hire them out for a time: some say they hire out their wives in the same manner. These marriages for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> are well regulated, and often prove very beneficial to the occasional husband. Most of the foreigners who trade hither, marry a wife for the time of their stay. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a separation, the father is obliged to take care of the boys, and the mother of the girls. We are told that no woman is looked upon the worse, but rather the better, for having had several European husbands: nay, we are told, that no person of fashion in Pegu, from the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> to the king, will marry a maiden, till some acquaintance or stranger has had the first night's lodging with her. In Pegu, the inheritance of all land is in the king: he is likewise the heir of all his subjects who die without issue; but in case they have children, two-thirds go to them, and the rest to his majesty. When a person falls sick, we are told that they generally make a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOW">vow</a> to the devil, from whom they believe all evil comes. Then a scaffold is built, and victuals are spread on the top of it to solace Old Nic, and render him propitious. This feast is accompanied with lighted candles and music; and the whole is managed by an undertaker called the devil's father. The commodities exported from this country are gold, silver, rubies, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>, benjamin, long-pepper, tin, lead, copper; lakka, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-lac, whereof they make hard wax; rice; rice-wine; and some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes, of which they would have plenty, but that the elephants eat them. It may be observed, that under the name of rubies, the Peguers comprise topazes, sapphires, amethysts, and other stones; which they distinguish by saying the blue, the violet, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> rubies. The true <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RUBY">ruby</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, transparent, or sparkling, inclining near the surface, to the violet of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMETHYST">amethyst</a>. Cotton cloths from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> and Coromandel, with some striped silks, are best for the Pegu market, and silver of any sort will go off there; for the king, in return for his eight and a half per cent. duty on it, allows the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> to melt it down, and put what copper alloy they please in it. They wear none of our European commodities in Pegu but <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a> and ribbons. The gentry will give extravagant prices for fine beaver hats, which they wear without any coaks. They are not less fond of ribbons flowered with gold and silver, which they wear round their hats. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the Peguers, it is the same at bottom with that which prevails over the rest of India and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIBET">Tibet</a>; only varies in dress somewhat in different countries, according to the humour or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the priests. They hold the existence of one supreme God, of whom they make no image; but they have many inferior created gods, whose images are set up in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> to worship. Not content with these, we are told they worship the devil also. Many are seen to run about the streets every morning, with rice in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and a torch in the other, crying aloud, that they are going to give the devil his breakfast, that he may not hurt them all the day. Besides the manichean doctrine of two principles, one the author of good, and the other of evil, from whence their worshipping the devil has its rise, they believe an eternal succession of worlds without <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. The Peguers hold the doctrine of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METEMPSYCHOSIS">Metempsychosis</a>, or transmigration of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, which, after passing through the bodies of various animals, shall attain to the perfection and felicity of their gods; which in effect is no other than a state of annihilation. They have a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the sanctity of apes and crocodiles, inasmuch that they believe the persons to be perfectly happy that are devoured by them. Their temples are of a conic form, and some of them a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> round. They observe a great many festivals, some of which are called <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>. The images of their inferior gods are in a sitting posture, with their legs across, and toes of equal length: their arms and hands very small in proportion to their bodies; their faces longer than human; their ears long, and the lappets very thick. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> bow to them when they come in and when they go out; and that is all the worship which they pay to them. The priests of Pegu, called talapins, are a sort of medican friars. They observe celibacy; and eat but once a-day; living in the woods, in a fort of nets or cages built on the tops of trees for fear of the tygers. They preach frequently, lead very innocent lives, and are very hospitable and humane. The king of Pegu's revenues arise chiefly from the rent of lands, of which he is the sole proprietor. Another branch of it are the duties paid for the commodities imported or exported. In a word, he is judged the richest monarch in the world, next to the emperor of China.

PEINE FORT ET DURE

Pages 426-426

(Lat. poena fortis et dura), signifies a special <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> inflicted on those who, being arraigned of felony, refuse to put themselves on the ordinarily <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, but stubbornly stand <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">mute</a>; it is vulgarly called preying to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. See ARR AIGNMENT.

PEIRCE

Pages 426-427

an eminent dissenting minister, was born at Wapping, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in the year 1674, and was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>; after which he spent some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, in order to enjoy the benefit of frequenting the Bodleian library. He then for two years preached the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>-evening's lecture at the meeting-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Miles-Lane, London, and then settled at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. In 1713, he was removed to a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the year 1718: when the Calvinists among the dissenters proposing a subscription to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> to be signed by all the dissenting ministers in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, several articles were proposed to him and Mr John Hallet, another dissenting minister at Exeter, in order to their subscribing them, they both refused, imagining this proceeding of their dissenting brethren to be an unworthy imposition on <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> and private judgment; for which they were ejected from their congregation. Upon this, a new meeting was opened for them at Exeter, of which Mr. Pierce continued minister till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in 1726. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of the strictest virtue, exemplary piety, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning. He wrote, 1. *Exercitatio philosophica de Homemeria Anaxagorae.* 2. Thirteen pieces on the Controversy between the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> of England and the Dissenters. 3. Ten pieces on the Controversy about the Ejection at Exeter. 4. Six pieces on the Doctrine of the Trinity. 5. A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARAPHRASE">Paraphrase</a> and Notes on the Epistles of St. Paul to the Colossians, Philippians, and Hebrews. 6. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> in favour of giving the Eucharist to Children. 7. Fourteen Sermons.

PEKIN

Pages 427-427

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the empire of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> generally resides. It is an exact <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and divided into two parts; namely, that which contains the emperor's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, which is in the new city, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the Tartars city, because it is inhabited by Tartars ever since they conquered this empire; the other, called the Old City, is inhabited by the Chinese. The circuit of both these together is 52 Chinese li, each of which contains 240 geometrical paces. The gates of this city are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and well arched, supporting buildings of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> stories high; the lowest of which is for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> when they come off <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>. The gates are nine in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; and before each is an open space, which serves for a parade. The streets are as straight as a line, most of which are three miles in length, and about 120 feet wide, with shops on both sides; but the houses are poorly built, and have only a ground-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>. It is surprising to see what numbers of people there are in the streets, and not one woman among them; there is always a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> confusion, occasioned by the vast numbers of horses, camels, mules, asses, waggons, carts, and chairs, without reckoning the several mobs which gather about jugglers, ballad-singers, and the like. Persons of distinction have always a horseman, who goes before them to clear the way. All the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> and merchandises of the empire are continually pouring into this city. There are always <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HACKNEY">hackney</a>-horses and chairs in various parts, which stand ready to be hired for a trifle; and the owners of them know every street and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> where any considerable person lives. All the great streets are guarded by soldiers, who patrol night and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> with swords by their sides, and whips in their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, to chastise those who make any disturbance, or take them into custody. The little streets have lattice-gates at their entrance into the great streets, which are shut up at nights, and guarded by soldiers, who suffer no assemblies in the streets at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and examine all that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> along. The emperor's palace is of vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and surrounded with a brick wall, with pavilions at each corner, encompassed by galleries supported by columns. But it would be endless to give an account of the different apartments, with their ornaments and furniture, as well as of the different magazines, and rich commodities kept therein; not to mention the supreme courts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, which are six in number, and are only to be controled by the emperor and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. Those who have computed the compass of this city a different way, observe, that it is 20 miles in circumference, and that the number of inhabitants is at least 2,000,000; that the walls are so high that they cover the town, and are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> enough for several horsemen to ride abreast; and there are strong towers a bow-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> distant from each other. The walls of the emperor's palace, including that and the gardens, are about two miles in length; and the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> of the structures entirely different from that of the Europeans, for they are covered with tiles of a shining beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> and the towers of this city are so numerous, that it is difficult to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> them. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about it is plain, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, and not very fruitful; yet <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> of all kinds are exceeding plentiful, they being, as well as the merchandises, brought from other parts by means of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> cut from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and always crowded with vessels of different sizes. An earthquake which happened here in 1731 buried above 100,000 persons in the ruins of the houses, which were thrown <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 116. 41. N. Lat. 39. 54.

PELAGIANS

Pages 427-427

a Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> who appeared about the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> end of the fourth century. They maintained the following doctrines. 1. That <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> was by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> mortal, and whether he had sinned or not, would certainly have died. 2. That the consequences of Adam's sin were confined to his own person. 3. That new-born <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> are in the same situation with Adam before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. 4. That the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> qualified men for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of heaven, and was founded upon equal promises with the gospel. 5. That the general <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of the dead does not follow in virtue of our Saviour's resurrection. 6. That the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> of God is given according to our merits. 7. That this grace is not granted for the performance of every moral <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and information in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of duty, being sufficient, &c. The founder of this sect was

PELAGIUS

Pages 427-428

a native of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; but whether of England, Scotland, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, is as uncertain as it is immaterial. He was born towards the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the fourth century, and educated in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Banchory, in Wales, of which he became a monk, and afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>. In the early <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he went over to France, and thence to Rome, where he had the influence to promulgate certain opinions somewhat different from those of the infallible <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. His morals being irreproachable, he gained many disciples; and the dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> made so rapid a progress, that, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> of souls, it became necessary for the pope to exert his power. Pelagius, to avoid the danger, in the year 409, passed over to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, attended by his friend and pupil <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CELESTIUS">Celestius</a>. In 411 they landed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> at Hippo, and were present at the famous conference between the Catholics and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DONATISTS">Donatists</a> which was held at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a> in 412. From thence they travelled to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; and from Egypt, in 415, to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, where they were graciously received by John bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. In the same year, Pelagius was cited to appear before a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of seventeen <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, held at Diospolis. They were satisfied with his creed, and absolved him of heresy. The African bishops, however, being displeased with their proceedings, appealed to the Roman pontiff; he first approved, and afterwards condemned the opinions of Pelagius, who, with his pupil Celestius, was publicly excommunicated; and all the bishops who refused to subscribe the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> of the Pelagian heresy were immediately deprived. What became of him after this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, is entirely unknown; known; but it seems very probable that he retired to Panchor, and died abbot of that monastery. He wrote, 1. Expositionum in epist. Paulinas lib. xiv. 2. Epistolae <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> Demetriadeum de virginitate. 3. Ex- planationis symboli ad Damascum. 4. Epistle ad vidu- am dua. 5. De libero arbitrio. These and many other fragments are scattered among the works of St Jerom. They are also collected by Garnierius, and published in Append. op. Mercatoris, p. 373. Cave. PELASGL. See PELASGIOTIS.

PELASGIA

Pages 428-428

(Pliny); the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of Le- <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOS">bos</a>; so called from the Pelasgi, its first inhabitants, (Diodorus Siculus). Also the ancient name of Pe- lonneus, from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PELAGIUS">Pelagius</a>, a native of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, (Nicolaus Damascenus, Ephorus).

PELASGICUM

Pages 428-428

(Pausanias, Pliny); the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> wall of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>; so called from the builders, the Pe- lasgi. There was an exorcism pronounced on any that should build houses under this wall; because the Pelasgi, while dwelling there, entered into a conspira- cy against the Athenians, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a>).

PELASGIOTIS

Pages 428-428

a third <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Thessaly, (Strabo); so called from a very <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> people, the Pelas- gi, called Pelagiota, (<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); who formerly, to- gether with the Æolians, occupied Thessaly, and thence that part was called Pelagium <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>; besides many other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. Their name Pelagi, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Pelargi, denoting storks, was given them from their wandering roving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, (Strabo). The poets extend the appellation to Greeks in general. Pelagus, the epithet. Some of the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> were called Pelagi, (<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>); who thus also calls the neigh- bouring people to the Cilicians in Troas. The Pelagi were originally of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, (<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>); but Æs- chylus makes Argos, near Mycenæ, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The Pelasgians were situated between Pieria and Macedo- nia to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and west, Thessalotis to the south, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNESIA">Magnesia</a> to the east, (Strabo, Pliny).

PELEPOPE

Pages 437-437

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICARUS">Icarus</a>, married Ulysses, by whom she had <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-TELEMACHUS">Telemachus</a>. During the absence of Ulysses, who was gone to the siege of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, and who laid 20 years from his dominions, several princes, charmed with Penelope's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, told her that Ulysses was dead, offered to marry her, and pressed her to declare in their favour. She promised compliance on condition they would give her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to finish a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a> she was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a>; but at the same time she undid in the night what she had done in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and by this artifice eluded their importunity till Ulysses's return.

PELETHRONIUM

Pages 428-428

(Nicander and Scholiast); a town of Thessaly, situate in a flowery <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of mount Pelios; and hence the appellation throna, signifying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. Pelethronii, the people, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>); the Lapi- thæ so called, who first broke horses. Lucan says the Centaurs were natives of that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; to whom Vir- gil assigns mount Othrys. Most authors, however, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the breaking of horses to the Centaurs. Some make the Lapithæ and Centaurs the same; others a different people; allowed however to be both of Thes- saly. Their story is greatly involved in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>.

PELETS

Pages 434-434

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, those roundels that are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; called also agrettes and gunstones, and by the French torteaux de sable.

PELICAN

Pages 428-428

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>. See PELICANUS. Pelican, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, is a glass alembic con- sisting of one piece. It has a tubulated <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, from which two opposite and crooked beaks <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> out, and enter again at the belly of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUCURBIT">cucurbit</a>. This vessel has been contrived for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> and co- hobation, which chemists call circulation. The volatile parts of substances put into this vessel rise into the ca- pital, and are obliged to return through the crooked beaks into the cucurbit; and this without interruption, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> luting and unluting the vessels. Although the pelican seems to be a very convenient <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, it is nevertheless little used, and even Pelicanus, much neglected at present; either because the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> chemists have not so much <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> as the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> che- mists had for making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> experiments; or because they find that two matresses, the mouth of one of which is inserted into the mouth of the other, produce the same effect.

PELICANUS

Pages 428-434

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of auers. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> is stout, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and crooked at the point; the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> is naked, and the feet are palmated. There are eight <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, principally distinguished by the shape of their tails. The most remarkable are, 1. The carbo, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> corvornant, sometimes exceeds <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> pounds in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; the length three feet four; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> four feet two; the bill dusky, five inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, destitute of nostrils; the base of the lower mandible is covered with a naked <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> skin, that extends under the chin, and forms a sort of pouch; a loose skin of the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> reaches from the upper mandible round the eyes and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of the mouth; the head and neck are of a footy blackness; but under the chin of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> the feathers are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; and the head in that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a> is adorned with a short loose pendant crest; in some the crest and hind-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the head are streaked with white. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COVERT">covert</a> of the wings, the scapulars, and the back, are of a deep green, edged with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and glowed with blue; the quill-feathers and tail dusky; the legs are short, strong, and black; the middle claw ferrated on the inside; the irises are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> ash- colour. These birds occupy the highest parts of the cliffs that impend over the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>: they make their nests of sticks, sea-tang, grass, &c. and lay six or seven white eggs of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> form. In winter they disperse a- long the shores, and visit the fresh waters, where they make <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> havoc among the fish. They are remark- ably voracious, having a most sudden digestion, pro- moted by the infinite <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of small <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> that fill their intestines. The corvornant has the rankest and most disagreeable smell of any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, even when alive. Its form is disagreeable; its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> hoarse and croaking, and its qualities base. These birds, however, have been trained to fish like falcons to fowl. Whitelock tells us, that he had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of them manned like hawks, and which would come to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. He took much <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLEA">plea</a>- sure in them; and relates, that the best he had was one presented him by Mr Wood, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the corvornants to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. It is well known that the Chinese make great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of these birds, or a congene- rous sort, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>; and that not for amusement, but profit. 2. The graculus, or shag, called in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRANE">crane</a>, is much inferior in size to the cor- vornant: the length is 27 inches; the breadth three feet six; the weight three pounds three <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. The bill is four inches long, and more slender than that of the preceding: the head is adorned with a crest two inches long, pointing backward; the whole plumage of the upper part of this bird is of a fine and very shin- ing green; the edge of the feathers a purplish black; but the lower part of the back, the head, and neck, wholly green; the belly is dusky; the tail of a dusky hue, tinged with green; the legs are black, and like those of the corvornant. Both these kinds agree in their manners, and breed in the same places; and, what is very strange in webbed-footed birds, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> perch and build in trees: both swim with their head quite erect, and are very difficult to be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>; for, like the grebes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a>, as soon as they see the flash of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, they pop under <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and never rise but at a considerable distance. 3. The bassanous, gannet, or solan goose, weighs seven pounds; the length is three feet one inch; the breadth six feet two inches. The bill is six inches long, strait almost to the point, where it inclines <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; and the sides are irregularly jagged, that it may hold its prey with more security: about an inch from the base of the upper mandible is a sharp <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> pointing forward; it has no nostrils; but in their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> a long surrow, that reaches almost to the end of the bill: the whole is of a dirty white, tinged with ash-colour. The tongue is very small, and placed low in the mouth; a naked skin of a fine blue surrounds the eyes, which are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> yellow, and are full of vivacity: this bird is remarkable for the quickness of its flight. Martin tells us, that solan is derived from an Irish word expressive of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. From the corner of the mouth is a narrow slip of black bare skin, that extends to the hind-part of the head; beneath the chin is another, that, like the pouch of the Pelican, is dilatable, and of size sufficient to contain five or six entire herrings; which in the breeding season it carries at once to its mate or young. The young birds, during the first year, differ greatly in colour from the old ones; being of a dusky hue, speckled with numerous triangular white spots; and at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> resemble in colours the speckled diver. Each bird, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> left undisturbed, would only lay one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a> in the year; but if that be taken away, they will lay another; if that is also taken, then a third; but never more that season. Their egg is white, and rather less than that of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> goose; the nest is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and formed of any thing the bird finds floating on the water, such as grass, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-SEA_PLANTS">sea-<a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, shavings, &c. These birds frequent the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Alisa, in the frith of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>; the rocks adjacent to St Kilda; the Stack of Souliferry, near the Orkneys; the Skellig Isles, off the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KERRY">Kerry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">Bass</a> Isle, in the frith of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>: the multitudes that inhabit these places are prodigious. Dr Harvey's elegant account of the latter will serve to give some idea of the numbers of these, and of the other birds that annually migrate to that little spot. "There is a small <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, called by the Scotch Bass Island, not more than a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in circumference; the surface is almost wholly covered during the months of May and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> with nests, eggs, and young birds; so that it is scarcely possible to walk without treading on them; and the flocks of birds in flight are so prodigious, as to darken the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> like <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>; and their noise is such, that you cannot without difficulty hear your next neighbour's voice. If you look down upon the sea from the top of the precipice, you will see it on every side covered with infinite numbers of birds of different kinds, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> and hunting for their prey: if in failing round the island you survey the hanging cliffs, you may see in every crag or fissure of the broken rocks innumerable birds of various sorts and sizes, more than the stars of heaven when viewed in a serene night: if from afar you see the distant flocks, either Pelicanus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> to or from the island, you would imagine them to be a vast swarm of bees." Nor do the rocks of St Kilda seem to be less frequented by these birds; for Martin assures us, that the inhabitants of that small island consume annually no less than 22,600 young birds of this species, besides an amazing quantity of their eggs, these being their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> support throughout the year: they preserve both eggs and fowls in pyramidal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> buildings, covering them with turf-ashes to preserve them from moisture. This is a dear-bought food, earned at the hazard of their lives, either by climbing the most difficult and narrow paths, where (to appearance) they can barely cling, and that too at an amazing height over the raging sea; or else, being lowered down from above, they collect their annual provision, thus hanging in midway air; placing their whole dependance on the uncertain footing of one person, who holds the rope by which they are suspended at the top of the precipice. The young birds are a favourite <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISH">dish</a> with the North Britons in general: during the season, they are constantly brought from the Bass Isle to Edinburgh, sold at 20d. a-piece, are roasted, and served up a little before dinner as a whet. The gannets are birds of passage. Their first appearance in those <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> is in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>; their continuance there till August or September, according as the inhabitants take or leave their first egg; but, in general, the time of breeding, and that of their departure, seems to coincide with the arrival of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERRING">herring</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a> of that fish (which is their principal food) out of those seas. It is probable that these birds attend the herring and pilchard during their whole circuit round the British islands; the appearance of the former being always esteemed by the fishermen as a sure preage of the approach of the latter. It migrates in quest of food as far south as the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a>, being frequently seen off <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a> during the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of September, plunging for sardine, fish resembling, if not the same with our pilchard. In the month of August Mr Pennant has observed in Cathness their northern migrations: he has seen them passing the whole <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> in flocks, from five to fifteen in each: in calm <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> they fly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; in storms they fly low and near the shore; but never <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> over the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, even when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> with promontories intervenes, but follow, at an equal distance, the course of the bay, and regularly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">cape</a>. Many of the parties made a sort of halt for the sake of fishing: they soared to a vast height, then darting headlong into the sea, made the water foam and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> up with the violence of their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>; after which they pursued their route. Our author inquired whether they ever were observed to return southward in the spring, but was answered in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>; so it appears that they annually encircle the whole island. They are well known on most of the coasts of England, but not by the name of the Solan goose. In Cornwall and in Ireland they are called gannets; by the Welsh, gan. Mr Ray supposed the Cornish gannet to be a species of large gull: a very excusable mistake; for during his six months residence in Cornwall, he never had an opportunity of seeing that bird, except flying; and in the air it has the appearance of Pelicanus, a gull. On that supposition he gave our skua the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of *catacalo*, a name borrowed from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, and which admirably expresses the rapid descent of this bird on its prey. Mr Moyle first detected this mistake; and the Rev. Dr William Borlase, by presenting us with a fine specimen of this bird, confirms the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Mr Moyle; at the same time giving the following <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the bird. "The gannet comes on the coasts of Cornwall in the latter end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, or beginning of autumn; hovering over the shoals of pilchards that come down to us through St George's Channel from the northern seas. The gannet seldom comes near the land, but is constant to its prey, a sure sign to the fishermen that the pilchards are on the coasts; and when the pilchards retire, generally about the end of November, the gannets are seen no more. The bird now sent was killed at Chandour, near Mounts Bay, Sept. 30, 1762, after a long struggle with a water-spaniel, assisted by the boatmen; for it was strong and pugnacious. The person who took it observed that it had a transparent membrane under the eye-lid, with which it covered at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> the whole eye, without obscuring the sight or shutting the eye-lid; a gracious provision for the security of the eyes of so weighty a creature, whose method of taking its prey is by darting headlong on it from a height of 150 feet or more into the water. About four years ago, one of these birds flying over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENZANCE">Penzance</a>, (a thing that rarely happens), and seeing some pilchards <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on a fir-plank, in a cellar used for curing fish, darted itself down with such violence, that it struck its bill quite through the board, (about an inch and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> thick), and broke its neck." These birds are sometimes taken at sea by a deception of the like kind. The fishermen fasten a pilchard to a board, and leave it floating; which inviting bait decoys the unwary gannet to its own destruction. In the *Cataracta* of Juba may be found many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of this bird: he says, that the bill is toothed; that its eyes are fiery; and that its colour is white; and in the very name is expressed its furious descent on its prey. The rest of his accounts favour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>. —We are uncertain whether the gannet breeds in any other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> besides our own islands; except (as Mr Ray inspects, the fula, described in Clusius's Exotics, which breeds in Ferroe Isles) be the same bird. 4. The fula, or booby, is somewhat less than a goose; the basis of the bill yellow, and of bare feathers; the eyes of a light-grey colour; the lower part of the bill of a light <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. The colours of the body are brown and white; but varied so in different individuals, that they cannot be described by them. Their wings are very long; their legs and feet pale yellow, shaped like those of corvoraits. They frequent the Bahama islands, where they breed all months in the year, laying one, two, or three eggs on the bare rock. While young, they are covered with a white down, and continue so till they are almost ready to fly. They feed on fish like the rest of this genus; but have a very troublesome enemy of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> bird, which lives on the spoils obtained from other sea-birds, particularly the booby. As soon as this rapacious enemy perceives that the booby has taken a fish, he flies furiously at him, upon which the former Pelicanus, dives to avoid the blow; but as he cannot swallow his prey below water, he is soon obliged to come up again with the fish in his bill as before, when he suffers a new assault; nor does his enemy cease to persecute him till he lets go the fish, which the other immediately carries off. 5. The great booby, by Linnæus called *pelicanis Basilani puffus*, frequents the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and sea-coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>, pursuing and devouring fishes like others of the genus. Mr Catesby informs us, that he has several times found them disabled, and sometimes dead, on the shore; whence he thinks that they meet with sharks or other voracious fishes, which destroy them. The bird is about the size of a goose; the head and neck remarkably prominent; the back of a brown colour; the belly dusky white; the feet black, and shaped like those of a corvoraits; the head elegantly spotted with white; the wings extend six feet when spread. Both this species and the last have a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> in the upper mandible of the bill, by which they can raise it considerably from the lower one without opening the mouth. 6. The oncorotulus, or pelican of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; though Linnæus thinks that the pelican of America may possibly be a distinct variety. This creature, in Africa, is much larger in the body than a swan, and somewhat of the same shape and colour. Its plate four toes are all webbed together; and its neck in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> resembles that of a swan; but that singularity in which it differs from all other birds is in the bill and the great pouch underneath. This enormous bill is 15 inches from the point to the opening of the mouth, which is a good way back behind the eyes. At the base the bill is somewhat greenish, but varies towards the end, being of a reddish blue. It is very thick in the beginning, but tapers off to the end, where it hooks downwards. The under-chap is still more extraordinary; for to the lower edges of it hang a bag, reaching the whole length of the bill to the neck, which is said to be capable of containing 15 quarts of water. This bag the bird has a power of wrinkling up into the hollow of the under-chap; but by opening the bill, and putting one's hand down into the bag, it may be distended at pleasure. The skin of which it is formed will then be seen of a bluish ash-colour, with many fibres and veins running over its surface. It is not covered with feathers, but a short downy substance as smooth and as soft as latin, and is attached all along the under edges of the chap, to be fixed backward to the neck of the bird by proper ligaments, and reaches near half way down. When this bag is empty it is not seen; but when the bird has fished with success, it is then incredible to what an extent it is often seen dilated. For the first thing the pelican does in fishing is to fill up the bag; and then it returns to digest its burden at leisure. When the bill is opened to its widest extent, a person may run his head into the bird's mouth, and conceal it in this monstrous pouch, thus adapted for very singular purposes. Yet this is nothing to what Ruyfch assures us, who avers that a man has been seen to hide his whole leg, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOOT">boot</a> and all, in the monstrous jaws of one of these animals. At first appearance this would seem impossible, as the sides of the under chap, from which the bag depends, are not Pelicanus, not above an inch asunder when the bird's bill is first opened; but then they are capable of great separation; and it must necessarily be so, as the bird preys upon large fishes, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> them by dozens in its pouch. Tertre affirms, that it will hide as many fish as will serve 60 hungry men for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>. The pelican was once also known in Europe, particularly in Russia; but it seems to have deserted our coasts. This is the bird of which so many fabulous accounts have been propagated; such as its feeding its young with its own blood, and its carrying a provision of water for them in its great reservoir in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. But the absurdity of the first account answers itself; and as for the latter, the pelican uses its bag for very different purposes than that of filling it with water. Its amazing pouch may be considered as analogous to the crop in other birds; with this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that as theirs lies at the bottom of the gullet, so this is placed at the top. Thus, as pigeons and other birds macerate their food for their young in their crops, and then supply them; so the pelican supplies its young by a more ready contrivance, and macerates their food in its bill, or stores it for its own particular sustenance. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were particularly fond of giving this bird admirable qualities and parental affections: struck, perhaps, with its extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, they were willing to supply it with as extraordinary appetites; and having found it with a large reservoir, they were pleased with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> it to the most tender and parental uses. But the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, the pelican is a very heavy, sluggish, voracious bird, and very ill fitted to take those flights, or to make those cautious <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> for a distant time, which we have been told they do. The pelican, says Labat, has strong wings, furnished with thick plumage of an ash-colour, as are the rest of the feathers over the whole body. Its eyes are very small, when compared to the size of its head; there is a sadness in its countenance, and its whole air is melancholy. It is as dull and reluctant in its motions as the flamingo is frightfully and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>. It is slow of flight; and when it rises to fly, performs it with difficulty and labour. Nothing, as it would seem, but the spur of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> could make these birds change their situation, or induce them to ascend into the air: but they must either starve or fly. They are torpid and inactive to the last <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, so that nothing can exceed their indolence but their gluttony; it is only from the stimulations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> that they are excited to labour; for otherwise they would continue always in fixed repose. When they have raised themselves about 30 or 40 feet above the surface of the sea, they turn their head with one eye downwards, and continue to fly in that posture. As soon as they perceive a fish sufficiently near the surface, they dart down upon it with the swiftness of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> it with unerring certainty, and store it up in their pouch. They then rise again, though not without great labour, and continue hovering and fishing, with their head on one side as before. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> they continue with great effort and industry till their bag is full, and then they fly to land to devour and digest at leisure the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of their industry. This, however, it would appear, they are not long performing; for towards night they have another hungry call; and they again reluctantly go to labour. At Pelicanus' night, when their fishing is over, and the toil of the day crowned with success, these lazy birds retire a little way from the shore; and, though with the webbed feet and clumsy figure of a goose, they will be contented to perch nowhere but upon trees among the light and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> tenants of the forest. There they take their repose for the night; and often spend a great part of the day, except such times as they are fishing, sitting in dismal solemnity, and, as it would seem, half asleep. Their attitude is with the head resting upon their great bag, and that resting upon their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. There they remain without <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, or once changing their situation, till the calls of hunger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> their repose, and till they find it indispensably necessary to fill their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> for a fresh meal. Thus their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is spent between sleeping and eating; and our author adds, that they are as foul as they are voracious, as they are every moment voiding excrements in heaps as large as one's fist. The same indolent habits seem to attend them even in preparing for incubation, and defending their young when excluded. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> makes no <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> for her nest, nor seems to choose any place in preference to lay in; but drops her eggs on the bare ground to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of five or six, and there continues to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HATCH">hatch</a> them. Attached to the place, without any desire of defending her eggs or her young, she tamely sits and suffers them to be taken from under her. Now and then she <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> ventures to peck, or to cry out when a person offers to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> her off. She feeds her young with fish macerated for some time in her bag; and when they cry flies off for a new supply. Labat tells us, that he took two of these when very young, and tied them by the leg to a pole stuck into the ground, where he had the pleasure of feeding the old one for several days come to feed them, remaining with them the greatest part of the day, and spending the night on the branch of a tree that hung over them. By these means they were all three become so familiar, that they suffered themselves to be handled; and the young ones very kindly accepted whatever fish he offered them. These they always put first into their bag, and then swallowed at their leisure. It seems, however, that they are but disagreeable and useless domestics; their gluttony can scarcely be satisfied; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> smells very rancid; and tastes a thousand times worse than it smells. The native Americans kill vast numbers; not to eat, for they are not fit even for the banquet of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>; but to convert their large bags into purses and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>-pouches. They bestow no small pains in dressing the skin with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and ashes, rubbing it well with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and then forming it to their purpose. It thus becomes so soft and pliant, that the Spanish women sometimes adorn it with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a> to make work-bags of. Yet, with all the seeming hebetude of this bird, it is not entirely incapable of instruction in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> state. Father Raymond assures us, that he has seen one so tame and well educated among the native Americans, that it would go off in the morning at the word of command, and return before night to its master, with its great paunch distended with plunder; a part of which the savages would make it disgorge, and and a part they would permit it to reserve for itself. "The pelican," as Faber relates, "is not destitute of other qualifications. One of those which was brought alive to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, where it lived 40 years, seemed to be possessed of very uncommon sensations. It was much delighted in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> and conversation of men, and in music both vocal and instrumental; for it would willingly stand," says he, "by those that sung or sounded the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>; and stretching out its head, and turning its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a> to the music, listened very attentively to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>, though its own voice was little pleasanter than the braying of an ass." Gefner tells us, that the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Maximilian had a tame pelican which lived for above 80 years, and that always attended his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> on their march. It was one of the largest of the kind, and had a daily allowance by the emperor's orders. As another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the great <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> to which the pelican lives, Aldrovandus makes mention of one of these birds that was kept several years at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MECHLIN">Mechlin</a>, and was verily believed to be 50 years old.—We often see these birds at our <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> about town.

PELICCLE

among physicians, denotes a thin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILM">film</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> fragment of a membrane. Among chemists it signifies a thin surface of crystals uniformly spread over a saline liquor evaporated to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>.

PELION

Pages 434-434

(Diodorus Siculus, &c.) Pelios, monte undertood, (Mela, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Horace, Seneca), a mountain of Thessaly near Olla, and hanging over the Sinus Pelaigicus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Pagacius; its top covered with pines, the sides with oaks, (Ovid). Said also to abound in wild ash, (Val. Flaccus). From this mountain was cut the spear of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>, called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELIAS">pelias</a>; which none but himself could wield, (<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>). Dioclearchus, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s scholar, found this mountain 1250 paces higher than any other of Thessaly, (Pliny). Pelius, Cicero; Peliacus, (Catullus), the epithet.

PELLA

Pages 434-434

(an. geogr.) a town situate on the confines of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMATHIA">Emathia</a>, a district of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, (<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); and therefore <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> allots it to Bottiza, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> district on the Sinus Thermaicus. It was the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence, situate on an eminence, verging to the south-west, encompassed with impassable marshes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> and winter: in which, next the town, a citadel like an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> rises, placed on a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a>, a prodigious <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, both supporting the wall and securing it from any hurt by means of the circumfluent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. At a distance, it seems <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the town, but is separated from it by the Ludias, running by the walls, and joined to it by a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, (Livy): distant from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> 120 stadia, the Ludias being so far navigable, (Strabo). Mela calls the town Pelle, though most Greek authors write Pella. The birth-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, who enlarged it; and afterwards of Alexander, (Strabo, Mela). <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">Continued</a> to be the royal residence <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to Perseus, (Livy). Called Pella Colonia, (Pliny); Colonia Julia Augusta, (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">Coin</a>). It afterwards came to decline, with but few and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> inhabitants, (Lucian). It is now called Τα Παλαιά, the Little <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">Palace</a>, (Holstenius). Pellaeus, both the gentilissimus name and the epithet, (Lucian, Juvenal, Martial).—Another Pella, (Polybius, Pliny); a town of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECAPOLIS">Decapolis</a>, on the other side the Jordan; abounding in water, like its cognominal town in Macedonia; built by the Macedonians, (Strabo); by Seleucus, (Eusebius); anciently called Butii, (Stephanus); Apamea, (Strabo); situate 35 miles to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Gerasa, (Ptolemy). Thither the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> before the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> by Titus, were divinely admonished to fly, (Eusebius). It was the utmost boundary of the Paræa, or Transjordan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to the north, (Josephus).

PELLANDRIUM

Pages 646-646
WATER HEMLOCK, a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the pentandria clas of plants. There are two species; one of which, viz. the aquaticum, is a native of Britain. This grows in ditches and ponds, but is not very common. The stalk is remarkably thick and dichotomous, and grows in the water. It is a poison to horses, bringing upon them, as Linnaeus informs us, a kind of paltry; which, however, he supposes to be owing not so much to the noxious qualities of the plant itself, as to those of an insect which feeds upon it, breeding within the stalks, and which he calls curculio paraplecticus. The Swedes give swine's dung for the cure. The seeds are sometimes given in intermittent fevers, and the leaves are by some added to difficult cataplasms. In the winter, the roots and stem, affected by the influence of the weather, afford a very curious skeleton or network. Horses, sheep, and goats, eat the plant; swine are not fond of it; cows refuse it. PHENICIA. See Phoenicia.

PELLETIER

Pages 434-434

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic, and an eminent mathematician, was born in 1517. He was an excellent Latin and French poet, a good orator, physician, and grammarian. He wrote, Œuvres Poétiques, Commentaires Latins sur Euclide, &c.

PELLISON

Pages 434-434
or PELLISON FONTANIER, (Paul), one of the finest geniuses of the 17th century, was the son of James Pellison counsellor at Castras. He was born at Beziers in 1624, and educated in the Protestant religion.
