He studied with success the Latin, Greek, French, Spanish, and Italian tongues, and applied himself to the reading the best authors in these languages; after which he studied the law at Castras with reputation. In 1652 he purchased the post of secretary to the king; and, five years after, became first deputy to M. Fouquet. He suffered by the disgrace of that minister; and in 1661 was confined in the Bastile; from whence he was not discharged till four years after. During his confinement he applied himself to the study of controversy; and in 1670 abjured the Protestant religion. Lewis XIV. bestowed upon him an annual pension of 2000 crowns; and he likewise enjoyed several posts. In 1676 he had the abbey of Giment, and some years after the priory of St Orens at Auch. He died in 1693. His principal works are, 1. The History of the French Academy. 2. Reflections on religious Disputes, &c. in 4 vols 12mo. 3. The History of Lewis XIV. 4. Historical Letters and Miscellanies, in 3 vols 12mo.

PELOPONNESUS

Pages 434-434

(Dionysius); a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, to the south of the rest of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; called, as it were, Pelopis nefus <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> insula, though properly not an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, but a peninsula; yet wanting but little to be one, viz. the isthmus of Corinth, ending in a point like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of the Platane or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>-tree. Anciently called Apià and Pelagia; a peninsula <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> to no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> for noblenes; situate between two seas, the Egean and Ionian, and resembling a platane-leaf, on account of its angular recesses or bays, (Pliny, Strabo, Mela). Strabo adds from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, that one of its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> names was <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, with the epithet Achaicum, to distinguish it from Thessaly, called Pelaigicum. Divided into six parts; namely, Argolis, Laconica, Messenia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>, Achaia, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, (Mela). Now called the Morea.

PELOPS

Pages 434-434

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TANTALUS">Tantalus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, went into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>, where he married Hippodamia the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of OEnomaus, king of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and became so powerful, that all the territory which lies beyond the Isthmus, and composes a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, was called <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>; that is, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Pelops, from his name, and the word Nisos.

PELUSIUM

Pages 434-435

(anc. geogr.); a noble and strong <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, without the Delta, distant 20 stadia from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; situate amidst marshes; and hence its name name and its strength. Called the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEY">key</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> inlet of Egypt, (Diodorus, Hirtius); which being taken, the rest of Egypt lay quite open and exposed to an enemy. Called Sin, (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a>). Pelysiacus, the epithet, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Diodorus). From its ruins arose Damietta. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 32° N. Lat. 31°.

PEMBROKESHIRE

Pages 435-435

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, bounded on all sides by the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, except on the east, where it joins to Caerphillyshire, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east to Cardiganshire. It lies the nearest to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> of any county in Wales. Its length is 26 miles, its breadth 20, and its circumference 93; within which it contains about 420,000 acres, 145 parishes, 7 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, 1 <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, 9 market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 2 forests, and about 26,000 inhabitants. This county lies in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s, and sends three members to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, viz. one for the shire, one for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAVERFORDWEST">Haverfordwest</a>, and one for the town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> of Pembroke, considering its situation, is good; but it is in general better the farther from the sea. As there are but few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is generally fruitful, especially on the sea-coasts; nor are its mountains altogether unprofitable, but produce pasture sufficient to maintain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of sheep and goats. Its other commodities are corn, cattle, pit-coal, marle, flint, and fowl. Among these last are falcons, called here peregrins. The inhabitants of this county make a very pleasant durable fire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CULM">culm</a>, which is the dust of coal made up into balls, with a third <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of mud. The county is well watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Clethy, Dougledy, Cledhew, and Teive; which last parts it from Cardiganshire. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the county styled Rhos in the Welsh, by which is meant a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> green plain. This is inhabited by the descendants of the Flemings, placed there by Henry I. to curb the Welsh, who were never able to expel them, though they often attempted it. On the coals of this county, as well as on those of Glamorganshire and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a> Sea, is found the lactuca marina of Cambden, being a marine plant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> weed, which, when dressed in a certain manner, is eaten by the inhabitants, and called laver, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>.

PEN

Pages 435-435

a little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, usually formed of a quill, serving to write withal. Pens are also sometimes made of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. Dutch Pens, are made of quills that have passed through hot ashes, to take off the grosser fat and moisture, and render them more transparent. Fountain Pen, is a pen made of silver, brass, &c., contrived to contain a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INK">ink</a>, and let it flow out by gentle degrees, so as to supply the writer a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> without being under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of taking fresh ink. The fountain-pen is composed of several pieces, as in Plate CCXXXII. fig. 3. where the middle piece F carries the pen, which is screwed into the inside of a little pipe, which again is soldered to another pipe of the same bigness as the lid G; in which lid is soldered a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> screw, for screwing on the cover, as also for stopping a little hole at the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and hindering the ink from passing through it. At the other end of the piece F is a little pipe, on the outside of which the top-cover H may be screwed. In the cover there goes a port-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRAYON">crayon</a>, which is to be screwed into the last-mentioned pipe, in order to stop the end of the pipe, into which the ink is to be poured by a funnel. To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the pen, the cover G must be taken off, and the pen a little shaken, to make the ink run more freely. Pen, or Penhook. See PENSTOCK.

PENANCE

Pages 435-435

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, either voluntary <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> imposed by authority, for the faults a person has committed. Penance is one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sacraments of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Besides fasting, alms, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a>, and the like, which are the general conditions of penance, there are others of a more particular kind; as repeating a certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ave-marys, paternosters, and credos, wearing a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>-shirt, and giving oneself a certain number of stripes. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> it is usual to see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> almost naked, loaded with chains and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, and lashing themselves at every step.

PENATES

Pages 435-435

in Roman antiquity, a kind of tutelar deities, either of countries <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> particular houses; in which last <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> they differed in nothing from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LARES">lares</a>. See LARES. The penates were properly the tutelar gods of the Trojans, and were only adopted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who gave them the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of penates.

PENCIL

Pages 435-436

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used by painters for laying on their colours. Pencils are of various kinds, and made of various materials; the larger sorts are made of boars bristles, the thick ends of which are bound to a stick, bigger <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> less, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; they are designed for: these, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, are called brushes. The finer sorts of pencils are made of camels, badgers, and squirrels <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> of swans; these are tied at the upper end with a piece of strong thread, and inclosed in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> of a quill. All good pencils, on being drawn between the lips, come to a fine point. Pencil, is also an instrument used in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, &c. made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK_LEAD"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>-chalk, placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> cut in a slip of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>; on which other pieces of cedar being glued, the whole is planed round; and one of the ends being cut to a point, it is fit for use. Black-lead in fine powder, stirred into melted sulphur, unites with it so uniformly, and in such <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, in virtue perhaps of its abounding with sulphur, that though the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> remains fluid enough to be poured into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>, it looks nearly like the coarser sorts of black-lead itself. Probably the way which <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> Rupert is said to have had, mentioned in the third volume of Dr Birch's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, of making black-lead run like a metal in a mould, so as to serve for black-lead again, consisting in mixing with it sulphur or sulphureous bodies. On this principle the German black-lead pencils are said to be made; and many of those which are hawked about by certain persons among us are prepared in the same manner: their melting or softening, when held in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, or applied to a red-hot <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and yielding a bluish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, with a strong smell like that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> brimstone, betrays their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>; for black-lead itself yields no smell or fume, and suffers no Pendant apparent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. Pencils made with such additions are of a very bad kind; they are hard, brittle, and do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> or make a mark freely either on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> or wood, rather <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> or scratching them than leaving a coloured stroke. The true English pencils (which Vogel in his mineral system, and some other foreign writers, imagine to be prepared also by melting the black-lead with some additional substances, and casting it into a mould) are formed of black-lead alone, sawed into slips, which are fitted into a groove made in a piece of wood, and another slip of wood glued over them: the softest wood, as cedar, is made choice of, that the pencil may be the easier cut; and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> at one end, too short to be conveniently used after the rest has been worn and cut away, is left unfilled with the black-lead, that there may be no waste of so valuable a commodity. These pencils are greatly preferable to the others, though seldom so perfect as could be wished, being accompanied with some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the same inconveniences, and being very unequal in their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, on account of different sorts of the mineral being fraudulently joined together in one pencil, the fore-part being <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> pretty good, and the rest of an inferior kind. Some, to avoid these imperfections, take the finer pieces of black-lead itself, which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> into slips, and fix for use in port-crayons: this is doubtless the surest way of obtaining black-lead crayons, whose good uses can be depended on.

PENDANT

Pages 436-436

an ornament hanging at the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, frequently composed of diamonds, pearls, and other jewels.

PENDANTS

Pages 436-436

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, parts hanging <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the label, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of three, four, five, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> six at most, resembling the drops in the Doric freeze. When they are more than three, they must be specified in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLAZONING">blazoning</a>. PENDANTS of a Ship, are those streamers, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> colours, which are split and divided into two parts, ending in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, and hung at the head of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, or at the yard-arm ends.

PENDICULAR

Pages 454-454

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, a line falling directly on another line, so as to make equal <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> on each side. See Geometry.

PENDULOUS

Pages 436-436

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to any thing that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> hangs downwards.

PENDULUM

Pages 436-437

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, denotes any heavy body, so suspended as that it may vibrate <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> swing, backwards and forwards, about some fixed point, by the force of gravity. The vibrations of a pendulum are called its oscillations. A pendulum, therefore, is any body, B, (fig. 2.) suspended upon, and moving about, a fixed point, A, as a centre. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a pendulum consists in the following particulars: 1. The times of the vibrations of a pendulum, in very small <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, are all equal. 2. The velocity of the bob, in the lowest point, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be nearly as the length of the chord of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> which it describes in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>. 3. The times of vibration in different pendulums, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a>, AC, are as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> roots of the times of their vibrations. 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of one vibration is to the time of the descent, through half the length of the pendulum, as the circumference of a circle to its diameter. 5. Whence the length of a pendulum, vibrating seconds, will be found 39.2 inches nearly; and that of an half-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> pendulum 9.8 inches. 6. An uniform homogeneous body BG, Pendulum, (ibid. n° 2.) as a rod, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, &c., which is one-third <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> longer than a pendulum <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">AD</a>, will vibrate in the same time with it. From these properties of the pendulum we may discern its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> as an universal chronometer, or regulator of time, as it is used in clocks, and such like <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>. By this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> also we can <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the distance of a ship, by measuring the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of time between the fire and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a>; also the distance of a cloud, by numbering the seconds or half-seconds between the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>. Thus, suppose between the lightning and thunder, we <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> 10 seconds; then, because sound passes through 1142 feet in one second, we have the distance of the cloud equal to 11420 feet. Again, the height of any room, or other object, may be measured by a pendulum vibrating from the top thereof. Thus, suppose a pendulum from the height of a room vibrates once in three seconds; then say, as 1 is to the square of 3, viz. 9, so is 39.2 to 352.8 feet, the height required. Lastly, by the pendulum we discover the different force of gravity on diverse parts of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>'s surface; and thence the true <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the earth. When pendulums were first applied to clocks, they were made very short: and, the arches of the circle being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, the time of vibration through different arches could not in that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> be equal; to effect which, the pendulum was contrived to vibrate in the arch of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYCLOID">cycloid</a>, by making it play between two semi-cycloids, CB, CD, (ibid. n° 3.) whereby it describes the cycloid BE, AD; the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of which curve is, that a body vibrating in it will describe all its arches, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> or small, in equal times. In all that has been hitherto said, the power of gravity has been supposed constantly the same. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the said power varies, the lengths of pendulums must vary in the same proportion, in order that they may vibrate in equal times; for we have shewn, that the ratio of the times of vibration and descent through half the lengths is given, and consequently the times of vibration and descent through the whole length is given: But the times of vibration are supposed equal, therefore the times of descent through the lengths of the pendulum are equal. But bodies descending through unequal spaces, in equal times, are impelled by powers that are as the spaces described, that is, the powers of gravity are as the lengths of the pendulums. The greatest inconvenience attending this most useful instrument is, that it is constantly liable to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of its length, from the effects of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, which very sensibly expand and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> all metallic bodies. To remedy this inconvenience, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> method is by applying the bob of the pendulum with a screw; so that it may be at any time made longer or shorter, according as the bob is screwed downwards or upwards, and thereby the time of its vibrations kept always the same. Again, if a glass or metallic tube, uniform throughout, filled with quicksilver, and 58.8 inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, were applied to a clock, it would vibrate seconds for $39.2 = \frac{3}{4}$ of 58.8); and such a pendulum admits of a twofold expansion and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a>, viz. one of the metal and the other of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>; and these will be at the same time contrary, and therefore will Pendulum correct each other. For by what we have shewn, the metal will extend in length with heat, and so the pendulum will vibrate slower on that account. The mercury also will expand with heat; and since by this expansion it must extend the length of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> upward, and consequently raise the centre of oscillation; so that by this means its distance from the point of suspension will be shortened, and therefore the pendulum on this account will vibrate quicker; wherefore, if the circumstances of the tube and mercury are skillfully adjusted, the time of the clock might by this means, for a long course of time, continue the same, without any sensible <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> or loss. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the late ingenious Mr Graham, in the year 1721, who made a clock of this sort, and compared it with one of the best of the common sort for three years together, and found the errors of the former but about \( \frac{1}{3} \) part of the latter; of which the reader may see a farther account in Phil. Trans. no. 393. It is what is now called Mr Graham's quicksilver pendulum. In the 47th volume of the Phil. Trans. Mr Short gives us an account of other inventions to remedy the same inconvenience. Mr John Harrison of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, famous for his invention of a clock to find the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, without having the least knowledge of what Mr Graham had done before him, made several experiments upon wires of different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, in order to find their different degrees of expansion and contraction. He thought, that by a proper <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of wires of two different metals, differing considerably in their expansion and contraction, he might be enabled to keep the centre of oscillation of a pendulum always at the same distance from the point of suspension. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of these experiments, he made a pendulum consisting of one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>-wire, at the end of which is the bob or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; and on each side of this wire, four wires, alternately <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> and steel, so disposed and contrived as to raise the pendulum by the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> that it is lengthened by heat, and to let <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the pendulum in the same proportion as it is raised by cold. Mr Harrison, in his first machine for measuring time at sea, likewise applied this combination of wires of brass and steel, to prevent any alterations by heat and cold. And in the two machines or clocks he has since made for the same purpose, a like method of guarding against the irregularities arising from this cause is used. Mr Graham also made a pendulum consisting of three bars, one of steel between two of brass; and the steel <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> acted upon a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVER">lever</a>, so as to raise the pendulum, when lengthened by heat, and to let it down, when shortened by cold; but he found this clock liable to sudden starts and jerks in its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. The ingenious Mr Ellicott, in the same volume of the Transactions, describes a pendulum of his invention, composed of brass and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, with the method of applying it, so as to avoid the many jerks to which the machine might be liable. But besides the irregularities arising from heat and cold, pendulum-clocks are liable to others from friction and foulness; to obviate which, Mr Harrison has several excellent contrivances, whereby his clocks are almost entirely free from friction, and never need to be cleaned.

PENESTICA

Pages 437-437

(Antonine), a town of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELVETII">Helvetii</a>, situated between the Lacus Lanfonus and Salodurum; called Petenifca by Peutinger. Thought now to be Biel, (Cloverius); the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a small territory in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>.

PENETRALE

Pages 437-437

in Roman antiquity, properly denoted the chapel, consecrated to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENATES">penates</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> gods.

PENEUS

Pages 437-437

(Strabo); a river running through the middle of Thessaly, from west to east, into the Siuss Thermaicus, between Olympus and Ossa, near <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEMPE">Tempe</a> of Thessaly, rising in mount Pindus, (Ovid, Val. Flaccus).

PENICILLUS

Pages 437-437

among surgeons, is used for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENT">tent</a> to be put into wounds <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> ulcers.

PENINSULA

Pages 437-437

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, a portion <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> joining to the continent by a narrow neck or isthmus, the rest being encompassed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. See Plate CXVI.

PENITENTIAL

Pages 438-438

an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> book retained among the Romanists; in which is prescribed what relates to the imposition of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a> and the reconciliation of penitents. See PENANCE. There are various penitentials, as the Roman penitential, that of the venerable Bede, that of pope Gregory III, &c.

PENITENTIARY

Pages 438-438

is also an officer, in some cathedrals, vested with power from the bishop to absolve, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> referred to him. The pope has at present his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> penitentiary, who is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the other penitentiary priests established in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, who consult him in all difficult cases. He presides in the penitentiary, dispatches dispensations, absolutions, &c. and has under him a regent and 24 proctors, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> of the sacred penitentiary.

PENITENTS

Pages 437-438

an appellation given to certain fraternities of penitents distinguished by the different shape and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of their habits. These are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, who have their rules, statutes, and churches, and make public processions under their particular crosses <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> banners. Of these there are more than a hundred, the most considerable of which are as follows: the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> penitents, of which there are several different sorts at Rome, the most <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> of which was constituted in 1264; the brethren of this fraternity every year give portions to a certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of young girls, in order to their being married: their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> is a kind of white fackcloth, and on the shoulder is a circle, in the middle of which is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> and white <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> penitents, the most considerable of which are the brethren of mercy, instituted in 1488, by some Florentines, in order to assist criminals during their imprisonment, and at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>: on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of execution, they walk in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> before them, singing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENITENTIAL">penitential</a> psalms and the litanies; and after they are dead, they take them <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the gibbet and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURY">bury</a> them: their habit is black fackcloth. There are others whose business it is to bury such persons as are found dead in the streets: these wear a death's head on one side of their habit. There are also blue, grey, red, green, and violet penitents; all which are remarkable for little else besides the different colours of their habits. Mabillon tells us, that at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a> there are a set of penitents kept in pay to walk through the streets in procession, Penitential cession, and cut their shoulders with whips, &c.

PENN

Pages 438-439

an eminent writer among the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, and the planter and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>, was the son of the above Sir William Penn, and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1644. In 1660, he was entered a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> of Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; but having before received an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> from the preaching of one Thomas Loe a Quaker, withdrew with some other students from the national worship, and held private meetings, where they preached and prayed amongst themselves. This giving <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> offence to the heads of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, Mr Penn, though but 16 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was fined for nonconformity; and continuing his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> exercises, was at length expelled his college. Upon his return home, he was, on the same account, treated with great severity by his father, who at last turned him out of doors; but his resentment afterwards abating, he sent him to France in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with some persons of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; where he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and returned not only well skilled in the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, but a polite and accomplished gentleman. About the year 1666, his father committed to his care a considerable estate in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. Being found in one of the Quakers meetings in Cork, he, with many others, was thrown into prison; but on his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORRERY">Orrery</a>, was soon discharged. However, his father being informed he still adhered to his opinions, sent for him to England, and finding him inflexible to all his arguments, turned him out of doors a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time. About the year 1668, he became a public preacher among the Quakers; and that year was committed <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> prisoner to the Tower, where he wrote several treatises. Being discharged after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months imprisonment, he went to Ireland, where he also preached amongst the Quakers. Returning to England, he was, in 1670, committed to Newgate for preaching in Gracechurch-street meeting-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, London; but being tried at the sessions-house in the Old Bailey, he was acquitted. In September the same year, his father died; and being perfectly reconciled to him, left him both his paternal blessing and a plentiful estate. But his persecutions were not yet at an end; for, in 1671, he was committed to Newgate for preaching at a meeting in Wheeler-street, London; and during his imprisonment, which continued six months, he also wrote several treatises. After his discharge, he went into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> and Germany; and in the beginning of the year 1672, married and settled with his family at Rickmanworth in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>. The same year he published several pieces; and particularly one against Reeve and Muggleton. In 1677, he again travelled into Holland and Germany in order to propagate his opinions; and had frequent conversations with the princess <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and sister to the princess Sophia, mother to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Geo. I. In 1681, king <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II, in consideration of the services of Mr Penn's father, and several debts due to him from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> at the time of his decease, granted Mr Penn and his heirs the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> lying on the west side of the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, which from thence obtained the name of Pennsylvania. Upon this Mr Penn published a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> account of that province, with the king's patent; and proposing an easy purchase of lands, and good terms of settlement for such as were inclined to remove thither, many went over. These having made and improved their plantations to good advantage, the governor, in order to secure the planters from the native Indians, appointed commissioners to purchase the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> he had received from the king of the native Indians, and concluded a peace with them. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a> was planned and built; and he himself drew up the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> constitutions of Pennsylvania in 24 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. In 1681, he was elected a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>; and the next year he embarked for Pennsylvania, where he continued about two years, and returned to England in August 1684. Upon the accession of king James to the throne, he was taken into a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of favour with his Majesty, which exposed him to the imputation of being a Papist; but from which he fully vindicated himself. However, upon the Revolution, he was examined before the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, in 1688, and obliged to give security for his appearance on the first <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of next <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>, which was afterwards continued. He was several times discharged and examined; and at length warrants being issued out against him, he was obliged to conceal himself. self for two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> three years. Being at last permitted to appear before the king and council, he represented his innocence so effectually that he was acquitted. In August 1699, he, with his wife and family, embarked for Pennsylvania; whence he returned in 1701, in order to vindicate his proprietary <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, which had been attacked during his absence. Upon queen <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s accession to the crown, he was in great favour with her, and was often at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>. But, in 1707, he was involved in a lawsuit with the executors of a person who had been formerly his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>; and, though many thought him aggrieved, the court of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> did not think proper to relieve him; upon which account he was obliged to live within the rules of the Fleet for several months, till the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in dispute was accommodated. He died in 1718. Mr Penn's friendly and pacific manner of treating the Indians produced in them an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> for him and his people; so that they have maintained a perfect amity with the English in Pennsylvania ever since. He was the greatest bulwark of the Quakers; in whose <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> he wrote numberless pieces. Besides the above works, he wrote a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of others; the most esteemed of which are, 1. His Primitive Christianity revived. 2. His Defence of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, intitled Gospel Truths, against the Exceptions of the Bishop of Cork. 3. His Persuasion to Moderation. 4. His Good Advice to the Church of England, Roman Catholic, and Protestant dissenters. 5. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">Sandy</a> Foundation shaken. 6. No Crofs, no Crown. 7. The great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">Case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">Liberty</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">Conscience</a> debated. 8. The Christian Quaker and his Testimony stated and vindicated. 9. A Discourse of the general Rule of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a> and Practice, and Judge of Controversy. 10. England's Present <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">Interest</a> considered. 11. An <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">Address</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. 12. His Reflections and Maxims. 13. His Advice to his Children. 14. His Rise and Progress of the People called Quakers. 15. A Treatise on <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-OATHS">Oaths</a>. Most of these have passed several editions, some of them many. The letters between William Penn and Dr Tilloton, and William Penn and William Popple, Esq; together with Penn's letters to the princess Elizabeth of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> and the countess of Hornes, as also one to his wife on his going to Pennsylvania, are inserted in his works, which were first collected and published in 2 vols folio; and the parts since selected and abridged into 1 vol. folio, are very much and deservedly admired for the good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> they contain.

PENNI

Pages 439-439

born at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in 1488, was the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Raphael, who observing his genius and integrity, intrusted his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> concerns entirely to his management; by which means he got the appellation of il fattore, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the "<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>," which he retained ever after. The genius of Penni was universal; but his greatest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> was in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> landscapes and buildings: he was an excellent designer, and coloured extremely well in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, distemper, and fresco. He painted portraits in an exquisite style, and had such happy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> talents, that Raphael left him heir to his fortune in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> with Julio Romano his fellow-disciple. After Raphael's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, Penni painted many pictures at Rome, particularly in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Chigi, so exactly in the style of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, that they might not undeservedly have been imputed to him: he finished, in conjunction with Julio and Pierino del Vaga, the celebrated designs of the battles of Constantine, and others, which Raphael had left imperfect; but differing with them about a copy of the transfiguration, which the pope intended for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of France, they separated. Penni went to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> disagreeing with his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, he died soon after in 1528. He had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a> Penni, who worked at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a> and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in conjunction with Pierino del Vaga, who married his sister; he went thence to England, where he worked for Henry VIII. and for several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; was employed by Francis I. at Fontainbleau; but at last quitted the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, and devoted himself to engraving.

PENNSILVANIA

Pages 440-441

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> British colonies in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, had its name from the famous Quaker William Penn, son of Sir William, commander of the English fleet in Oliver Cromwell's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and in the beginning of Ch. II.'s reign, who obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of it in the year 1679; is bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> and river, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>; on the north by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Iroquois, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> five nations; and on the south and west by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARYLAND">Maryland</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, from north to south, is about 200 miles; but its breadth varies greatly, from 15, and even less, to near 200. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a> is sweet and clear. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, or autumn, begins about the 20th of October, and lasts till the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, when the winter sets in, which continues till <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, and is sometimes extremely <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and severe; but the air is then generally dry and healthy. The river Delaware, though very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, is often frozen over. From March to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, that is, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> is more inconstant than in the other seasons. In the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, August, and September, the heats would be almost intolerable, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were not mitigated by frequent cool breezes. The <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, is generally south-west; but in the winter blows for the most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> from the north-west, over the snowy frozen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a>, which occasions the excessive cold during that season. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> of this country, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, like the adjacent colonies, it is flat, but rises gradually to the Appalachian mountains on the west. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are three, Delaware, Susquehanna, and Skookum. The Delaware, rising in the country of the Iroquois, takes its course southward; and after dividing this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> from that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_JERSEY">New <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>, falls into the Atlantic ocean between the promontories or capes May and Henlopen, forming at its mouth a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bay, called, from the river, Delaware Bay. This river is navigable above 200 miles. The Susquehanna rises also in the country of the Iroquois, and running south through the middle of the province, falls into the bay of Chesapeake, being navigable a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> way for large ships. The Skookum has its source in the same country as the other two, and also runs Pennsylvania south, almost <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to them; till at length <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> to the eastward, it falls into the Delaware at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>. It is navigable for boats above 100 miles. These rivers, with the numerous creeks and harbours in Delaware bay, capable of containing the largest fleets, are extremely favourable to the trade of this province. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, produce, and traffic of Pennsylvania, we refer the reader to what has been said on these heads under New-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a> and the Jerseys, which is equally applicable to this province; and if there is any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, it is on the side of this province. They have some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> here, but no great quantities; and some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, but it is not equal to that of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>. From the premiums offered by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of arts in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, it appears that the soil and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of this province are looked upon as proper for the cultivation of some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of vines. The trade carried on from hence and the other colonies to the French and Dutch <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> and Surinam, was greatly to the disadvantage of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and very destructive to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-colonies; for they take molasses, rum, and other spirits, with a great many European goods, from these foreigners; carrying them horses, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and lumber in return, without which the French could not carry on their sugar-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> to that advantage they do. New-York, the Jerseys, and Pennsylvania, were discovered, with the rest of the continent of North America, in the reign of Henry VII. by Sebastian Cabot, for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England; but Sir Walter Raleigh was the first adventurer that attempted to plant colonies on these shores, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; and, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of that princess, gave all the eastern coast of North America the name of Virginia. Mr Hudson, an Englishman, sailing to that part of the coast which lies between Virginia and New England, in the beginning of the reign of James I. and being about to make a settlement at the mouth of Hudson's river, the Dutch gave him a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to dispose of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in this country to them. In the year 1608 they began to plant it; and, by virtue of this purchase, laid claim to all those countries which are now denominated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEW_YORK">New York</a>, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania; but there remaining some part of this coast which was not planted by the Hollanders, the Swedes sent a fleet of ships thither, and took possession of it for that crown; but the Dutch having a superior force in the neighbourhood, compelled the Swedes to submit to their dominion, allowing them, however, to enjoy the plantations they had settled. The English not admitting that either the Dutch or Swedes had any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to countries first discovered and planted by a subject of England, and part of them at that time possessed by the subjects of Great Britain, under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> from Queen Elizabeth and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> James I., king <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., during the first Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> in 1664, granted the countries of New York, the Jerseys, and Pennsylvania, of which the Dutch had usurped the possession, to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> James <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of York; and Sir Robert Carr being sent over with a squadron of men of war and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>-forces, and summoning the Dutch governor of the city of New <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, now New York, to surrender, he thought fit to obey the summons, and yield that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> to the English: the rest of the places in the possession of the Dutch and Swedes followed. Pennsylvania, followed his example; and these countries were confirmed to the English by the Dutch at the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of peace between the two nations. The Duke of York afterwards parcelled them out to under proprietors; selling, in particular, to William Penn the elder, in 1683, the town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, alias Delaware, and a district of twelve miles round the same; to whom, his heirs and assigns, by another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> of the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a>, he made over all that tract of land from 12 miles south of Newcastle to the Whore-hills, otherwise called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Henlopen, now divided into the two counties of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, which, with Newcastle district, are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known by the name of the Three Lower counties upon Delaware River. All the rest of the under-proprietors, some time after, surrendered their charters to the crown; whereby New York and the Jerseys became <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> governments; but Penn retained that part of the country which had been sold him by the Duke of York, together with what had been granted to him before in 1680-1, which now constitutes the province of Pennsylvania. As soon as Penn had got his patent, he began to plant the country. Those who went over from England were generally dissenters and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUAKERS">quakers</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is established by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> here, but with a toleration of all other protestant sects. The Dutch and Swedes, who were settled here before Mr Penn became proprietor, choosing still to reside in this country, as they did in New York and the Jerseys, obtained the same privileges as the rest of his majesty's subjects; and their descendents are now in a manner the same people with the English, speaking their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and being governed by their laws and customs. Mr Penn, however, not satisfied with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> granted him by king Charles II. and his brother, bought the lands also of the Indians for a valuable consideration, or what they deemed such, (though 20 miles were purchased, at first, for less than an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> about Philadelphia would pay now), paying them in cloth, tools, and utensils, to their entire satisfaction; for they had not <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> to cultivate the hundredth part of their lands, and if they could have raised a product, there was nobody to buy: the purchase, therefore, was all clear <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> to them; and, by the coming of the English, their peltry trade became so profitable, that they soon found their condition much altered for the better; and are now as well clothed and fed as the European peasantry in many places. Pennsylvania is one of the most flourishing colonies in North America, having never had any quarrel with the natives. Whenever they desire to extend their settlements, they purchase new lands of the sachems, never taking any by force; but the Indians now set a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> price upon their lands, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of what they did at first, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> hardly part with them at any rate. In an estimate of the proprietary estate of the province, published above thirty years ago, we find, that the proprietaries, who alone can purchase lands here from the natives, had bought <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> millions of acres for no more than 750l. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>, which the proprietaries afterwards sold at the rate of 15l. for every 100 acres. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> at Onandago, however, disapproved of their deputies parting with so much land; and, in the year 1755, obliged the proprietaries to re-convey great part of the same to the Indians. A dispute subsisted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time between the proprietaries of this province and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALTIMORE">Baltimore</a>, proprietary of Maryland, about the right to certain lands; which was at last amicably adjusted, though greatly in favour of the Penns. About the year 1704 there happened some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the province. The establishment that took <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and subsisted till the present troubles broke out, consisted of a governor, council, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, each with much the same power and privileges as in the neighbouring colony of New York. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-governor and council were appointed by the proprietaries Thomas and Richard Penn, with his majesty's approbation; but if the laws enacted here were not repealed within six months after they had been presented to the king for his approbation or disallowance, they were not repealable by the crown after that time. Pennsylvania is divided into seven counties; four of which are called the Upper, and three the Lower. Of the upper, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>, Philadelphia, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, the three first are the lands included in king Charles II.'s grant, and designed Pennsylvania; the lower, viz. those of Newcastle, Kent, and Sussex, were called Nova Belgia before the duke of York sold them, as we observed above, to Mr Penn. The upper counties end at Marcus Hook, four miles below Chester Town, where the lower begin, and run along the coast near 100 miles. Each of these counties had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, with a quarterly and monthly session, and assizes twice a-year.

PENNY

Pages 439-439
or PENY, in commerce, an ancient English coin, which had formerly considerable course; but is now generally dwindled into an imaginary money, or money of account. Camden derives the word from the Latin pecunia, "money." The ancient English penny, penig, or pening, was the first silver coin struck in England; nay, and the only one current among our Saxon ancestors: as is agreed by Camden, Spelman, Dr Hicks, &c. The penny was equal in weight to our three-pence; five of them made one shilling, or sciling Saxon; 30 a mark or mancuse, equal to our 7s. 6d. Till the time of king Edw. I. the penny was struck with a crofs, so deeply indented in it that it might be easily broke, and parted, on occasion, into two parts, thence called half-pennies; or into four, thence called fourthings, or farthings.—But that prince coined it without indenture; in lieu of which, he first struck round half-pence and farthings. He also reduced the weight of the penny to a standard; ordering that it should weigh 32 grains of wheat, taken out of the middle of the ear.—This penny was called the penny sterling.—Twenty of these pence were to weigh an ounce; whence the penny became a weight as well as a coin. See Sterling and Penny-Weight. The penny sterling is now nigh diluted as a coin; and scarce subsists, but as a money of account, containing the 12th part of a shilling, or the 140th part of a pound. Penny, in ancient statutes, &c. is used for all silver money. And hence the sword-penny, aver-penny, hundred-penny, tithing-penny, and brothal-penny. Penny-Weight, a Troy weight, containing 24 grains; each grain weighing a grain of wheat gathered out of the middle of the ear, well dried. The name took its rise hence, that this was anciently the weight of one of our ancient silver pennies. See Penny. Twenty of these penny-weights make an ounce Troy.

PENRITH

Pages 439-440

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> in England, seated under a hill called Penrith-Fell, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Eamont and Lowther. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> thoroughfare for travellers; but has little other trade except <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TANNING">tanning</a>, and a small manufacture of checks. Formerly it had a castle, but it is now in ruins. In the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-yard is a monument of great antiquity, consisting of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-pillars 11 feet 6 inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and five in circumference in the lower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, which is rounded; the upper is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and tapers to a point; in the square part is some fret-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and the relievo of a crofs; and on the interior side of one is the faint representation of some animal. Both these <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are mortised at their lower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENRYN">Penryn</a> lower part into a round one: they are about 15 feet asunder, and the space between them is inclosed on each side with two very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> but thin semicircular stones; so that there is left between pillar and pillar a walk of two feet in breadth. Two of these lesser stones are plain, the others have certain figures, at present scarce intelligible. Not far from these pillar's is another called the giant's thumb, five feet eight inches high, with an expanded head, perforated on both sides; from the middle the stone rises again into a lesser head, rounded at top; but no part has a tendency to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, being in no part mutilated. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 16'. N. Lat. 54° 35'.

PENRYN

Pages 440-440

a town of Cornwall in England, seated on a creek of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FALMOUTH">Falmouth</a>-haven. It consists of about 300 houses, and the streets are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and paved. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 35'. N. Lat. 50° 23'.

PENSACOLA

Pages 440-440

a settlement in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, situated at the mouth of a river on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>. It was established by the French, and ceded to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> in 1763; but has lately been taken by the Spaniards. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 87° 20'. N. Lat. 30° 22'.

PENSION

Pages 441-441

a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> paid annually for services <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> considerations already past. The yearly payment of each member to the houses of the inns of courts are likewise named pensions; and the yearly <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of Gray's Inn, to consult on the affairs of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, is also called a pension.

PENSIONARY

Pages 441-442
or PENSIONER, a person who has an appointment, or yearly sum, payable during life, by way of acknowledgment, charged on the estate of a prince, company, or particular person. Grand Pensionary, an appellation given to the first minister of the States of Holland. The grand pensionary is chairman in the assemblies of the states of that province; he proposes the matters to be consulted on; collects the votes; forms and pronounces the resolutions of the states; opens letters; confers with foreign ministers, &c. His business is also to inspect the finances, to maintain the authority of the states, and to see that the laws are observed; and he is perpetual deputy of the states-general of the United Provinces. His commission is, however, given him only for five years; after which it is deliberated whether or no it shall be renewed; but there is no instance of its being revoked; therefore death only puts an end to the functions of this important minister. Pensionary, is also the first minister of the regency of each city in Holland. His office is to give his advice in affairs relating to the government, either of the state in general, or of the city in particular; and in assemblies of the states of the province, he is speaker in behalf of his city. The function, however, of these pensionaries is not everywhere alike; in some cities they only give their advice, and are never found in assemblies of the magistrates, except when expressly called. Pensioner called thither: in others they attend constantly; and in others they make the propositions on the part of the burgo-masters, draw up their conclusions, &c. They are called pensionaries, because they receive an appointment or pension.

PENSIONER

Pages 442-442

in general, denotes a person who receives a pension, yearly salary, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> allowance. Hence, The Band of Gentlemen-Pensioners, the noblest sort of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s person, consists of 40 gentlemen, who receive a yearly pension of 100l. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> band was first instituted by king Henry VIII. and their office is to attend the king's person, with their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>-axes, to and from his chapel-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, and to receive him in the presence-chamber, or coming out of his privy-lodgings: they are also to attend at all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> solemnities, as coronations, St George's feast; public audiences of ambassadors, at the sovereign's going to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, &c. They are each obliged to keep three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> horses and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, and so are properly a troop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. They wait half at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> quarterly; but on <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRISTMAS_DAY">Christmas-<a </a>class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, Easter-day, Whitunday, &c. and on extraordinary occasions, they are all obliged to give their attendance. They have likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to carry up the sovereign's dinner on the coronation-day and St George's feast; at which times the king or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> usually confer the honour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> on two such gentlemen of the band as their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> presents. Their arms are gilts battle-axes; and their weapons, on horse-back, in time of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, are curassiers-arms, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> and pistols. Their standard in time of war is, argent, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GULES">gules</a>. Their captain is always a nobleman, who has under him a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>, a standard-bearer, a clerk of the check, secretary, pay-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and harbinger.

PENSTOCK

Pages 442-442

a sluice <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>-gate, serving to retain or let go at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> of a mill-pond, or the like.

PENTACROSTIC

Pages 442-442

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a set of verses so disposed, as that there are always five acrostics of the same name, in five divisions of each <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. See ACROSTIC

PENTADROSTYLA

Pages 442-442

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name of a genus of spars. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAR">SPAR</a>. The bodies of this genus are spars in form of pentagonal columns, terminated by pentangular pyramids at one end, and regularly affixed at the other to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body.

PENTAGON

Pages 442-442

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of five sides and five <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>. See GEOMETRY. In fortification, pentagon denotes a fort with five battions.

PENTAGRAPH

Pages 442-442

an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> designed for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> figures in what proportion you please, without any skill in the art. It consists of four bras <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> wooden rulers, two of them from 15 to 18 inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and the other two half that length. At the ends and middle of the long rulers, as also at the ends of the shorter, are holes, upon the exact fixing of which the perfection of the instrument chiefly depends. Those in the middle of the long rulers are to be at the same distance from those at the ends of the long ones, and those of the short ones so as to form a parallelogram. It is fitted together by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pillar a, having at one end a screw and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, whereby the long rulers are joined, and at the other a little knot for the instrument to slide on: b is Pentagraph a rivet with a screw and nut, wherewith each short ruler is fastened to the middle of each long one; c is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENTAPOLIS">Pentapolis</a>, a pillar, one end whereof being hollowed into a screw, Plate has a nut fitted to it: at the other end is a worm to CCXXXIV screw into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a> when the instrument is to be used; it joins the ends of the two short rulers: d is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> screwed into a little pillar: e is a bras point moderately blunt, screwed likewise into a little pillar. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">Use</a> of the Pentagraph. 1. To copy a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> in the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> as the original. Screw the worm c into the table; lay a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> under the pencil d now placed at f; and the design under the point e now placed at g; then conducting the point over the several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of the design, the pencil f <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> draw the same on the paper. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the design is to be reduced into a half, &c. the worm must be placed at the end of the long ruler d, and the paper and pencil in the middle. In this situation conduct the bras point as before, and the pencil will draw its copy in the proportion required, the pencil here moving through half the length that the point does. On the contrary, if the design is to be enlarged one half, the bras point, with the design, must be placed in the middle at c, the pencil and paper at the end of the long ruler, and the worm at the other. 2. To enlarge and reduce in other proportions, there are holes drilled at equal distances on each ruler; namely, all along the short ones, and half-way up the long ones, for placing of the bras point, pencil, and worm, in a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line therein; that is, if the piece carrying the point be put in the third hole, the two other pieces must be put in its third hole.
