If then the point and design be placed at any hole of the short ruler, which forms the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> therewith, the copy will be less than half the original. On the contrary, if it be placed at one of the holes of that short ruler which is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the long ruler, the copy will be greater than half the original. Few of these instruments will do anything but straight lines, and many of them not even those.

PENTAMETER

Pages 442-442

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> consisting of five feet, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> metres, whence the name. The two first feet may be either dactyls or spondees at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; the third is always a spondee; and the two last analectes: such is the following verse of Ovid. \[ \text{Carmindibus vivos tenbus in omne neatis.} \] A pentameter verse subjoined to an hexameter, constitutes what is called elegiac. See ELEGIAIC.

PENTANDRIA

Pages 442-442

(from πέντε, "five," and ἀνήρ, "a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> husband"); the name of the fifth class in Linnæus's sexual method, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which have hermaphrodite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, with five stamens or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> organs. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a>, p. 1296.

PENTAPOLIS

Pages 442-443

(<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a> x.) the five cities of the plain in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, all destroyed by fire from heaven, except Zoar. Pentapolis, (<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); a district of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYRENAICA">Cyrenaica</a>, situate on the Mediterranean; denominated from its five cities; namely, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERENICE">Berenice</a>, Arsinoe, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMAIS">Ptolemais</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APOLLONIA">Apollonia</a>. Pentapolis of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>, (Josephus); taking name Pentapolis name from five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cities, Gaza, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GATH">Gath</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASCALON">Ascalon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AZOTUS">Azotus</a>, and Ekron. Pentapolis, (<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>); five cities of Doris, a district of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; namely, Camirus, Cnidus, Cos, Jalyfus, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINDUS">Lindus</a>, (Scholiast on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a>). Pentapetalous, an appellation given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which consist of five petals <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> leaves. Pentapetes, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a genus of the decandra order, belonging to the monodelphia clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There is but one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> known in the gardens of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, viz. the phoenicia, with halbert-pointed, spear-shaped, sawed leaves. It is an annual plant, a native of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and rises to the height of two or three feet; adorned with fine scarlet flowers, consisting of one petal cut into five segments. In the centre of the flower arises a short thick <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, to which adhere 15 short stamens. It is a tender plant, and must be brought up in the hot-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, an appellation given to the first five books of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEUTERONOMY">Deuteronomy</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENTATHLON">Pentathlon</a>, in antiquity, a general name for the five exercises performed at the Grecian games, viz. wrestling, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOXING">boxing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a>, running, and playing at the discus. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENTECOST">Pentecost</a>, a solemn festival of the Jews; so called because it was celebrated on the 50th <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> after the 16th of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> Nisan, which was the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> day of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PASSOVER">passover</a>. See Passover. The feast of Pentecost was instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>'s being given on the 50th day after the Israelites came out of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. It was on the feast of Pentecost that the Holy Ghost miraculously descended on the apostles. See Whitsunday. Penthesilea, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMAZONS">Amazons</a>, succeeded Orythia, and gave proofs of her courage at the siege of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, where she was killed by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>. Pliny says that she invented the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>-ax. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENULTIMA">Penultima</a>, or Penultimate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYLLABLE">Syllable</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, denotes the last syllable but one of a word; and hence the antepenultimate syllable is the last but two, or that immediately before the penultima. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENUMBRA">Penumbra</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, a partial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> observed between the perfect shadow and the full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> in an eclipse. It arises from the magnitude of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s body; for were he only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> point, the shadow would be all perfect; but, by reason of the diameter of the sun, it happens, that a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which is not illuminated by the whole body of the sun, does yet receive rays from a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> thereof. Pepin de Heristal, or Le Gros, mayor of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> under Clovis III., Childebert, and Dagobert. The power of these mayors in France was so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that they left the sovereign only the empty <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, and in the end seized on the throne itself. Pepin le <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIEF">Brief</a>, or le Petit, grandson to Pepin le Gros, and first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of the second <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a> of French monarchs, was mayor of the palace to Childeric III., a weak <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; he contrived to confine him and his son Thierry in different monasteries; and then, with the assistance of Pope Stephen III., he usurped the sovereign power. He died in 768, aged 54. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEPPER">Pepper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIPER">Piper</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an aromatic berry of a hot dry <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, chiefly used in seasoning. We have three kinds of pepper at present used in the shops, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> pepper. Black pepper is the fruit of the piper, and is brought from the Dutch settlements in the East Indies. See Piper. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> white pepper is factitious, being prepared from the black in the following manner: they steep this in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the sun for several days, till the rind or outer bark loosens; they then take it out, and, when it is half dry, rub it till the rind falls off; then they dry the white fruit, and the remains of the rind blow away like chaff. A great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of the heat of the pepper is taken off by this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, so that the white kind is more fit for many purposes than the black. However, there is a sort of native white pepper produced on a species of the same plant; which is much better than the factitious, and indeed little inferior to the black. The long pepper is a dried fruit, of an inch or an inch and a half in length, and about the thickness of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> goose-quill: it is of a brownish grey <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, cylindrical in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and said to be produced on a plant of the same genus. Pepper is principally used by us in food, to assist digestion; but the people in the East-Indies esteem it as a stomachic, and drink a strong infusion of it in water by way of giving them an appetite: they have also a way of making a fiery spirit of fermented fresh pepper, with water which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for the same purpose. They have also a way of preserving the common and long pepper in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, and eating them afterwards at meals. Jamaica Pepper, or Pimento. See Pimento. Pepper-Mint. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MENTHA">Mentha</a>. Pepper-Water, a liquor prepared in the following manner, for microscopical observations: put common black pepper, grossly powdered, into an open vessel so as to cover the bottom of it half an inch thick, and put to it <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> or river-water, till it covers it an inch; shake or stir the whole well together at the first mixing, but never disturb it afterwards: let the vessel be exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> uncovered; and in a few days there <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be seen a pellicle or thin skin <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> on the surface of the liquor, looking of several colours. This is a congeries of multitudes of small animals; and being examined by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, will be seen all in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>: the animals, at first sight, are so small as not to be distinguishable, unless to the greatest magnifiers; but they grow daily till they arrive at their full size. Their numbers are also continually increasing, till the whole surface of the liquor is full of them, to a considerable depth. When disturbed, they will sometimes all dart <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the bottom; but they soon after come up to the surface again. The skin appears soonest in warm <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and the animals grow the quickest; but in the severest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> it will succeed, unless the water freezes. About the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIN">pin</a>'s head of this scum, taken up on the nib of a new <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, or the tip of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, is to be laid on a plate of clear glass; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> applied first to the third magnifier, then to the second, and finally to the first, will shew the different animalcules it contains, of several kinds and shapes as well as sizes. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERA">Pera</a>, one of the suburbs of Constantinople, where

PEONIA

Pages 295-295

PIONY; a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the polyandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, both of them very hardy, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> flourish in any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. They are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> herbaceous flowering perennials, with tuberous roots, sending up strong annual stalks from one to three feet in height; terminated by very large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and much larger than any rose. The common officinal, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> piony, also is remarkable for its capsules <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> backward, opening and displaying their red inside, together with the numerous seeds, in a singularly agreeable order, appearing very ornamental after the flower is past. The plants may be propagated either by parting the roots, or by seed. This plant was formerly celebrated in nervous distempers, but the present practice pays very little regard to it. PÆSTUM, called Posidonia by the Greeks, a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUCANIA">Lucania</a>, on the Sinus Positanus: an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> colony <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the first Punic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, according to Livy; but later, according to Velleius, Peñane rose were in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem, and produced twice a-year. (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Ovid).

PERAMBULATOR

Pages 443-444

in surveying, an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for measuring distances, called also <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEDOMETER">pedometer</a>, way-wiser, and surveying wheel. It consists of a wheel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">AA</a>, two feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> inches and a half in diameter; consequently half a pole, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> eight feet three inches in circumference. On one end of the axis is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, three <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an inch in diameter, and divided into eight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; which, upon moving the wheel round, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the eight teeth of another nut C, fixed on one end of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-rod Q, and thus turn the rod once round in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the wheel makes one revolution. This rod, lying along a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> in the side of the carriage of the instrument, under the dotted line, has at its other end a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> hole, into which is fitted the end b of a small <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> P. This cylinder is disposed under the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIAL">dial</a>-plate of a movement, at the end of the carriage B, in such a manner as to be moveable about its axis: its end a is cut into a perpetual screw, which falling into the 32 teeth of a wheel perpendicular thereto, upon driving the instrument forward, that wheel makes a revolution each 16th pole. On the axis of this wheel is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PINION">pinion</a> with six teeth, which, falling into the teeth of another wheel of 60 teeth, carries it round every 160th pole, or half a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a>. This last wheel, carrying a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> round with it over the divisions of a dial-plate, whose outer limb is divided into 160 parts, corresponding to the 160 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of poles passed over. Again, on the axis of this last wheel is a pinion, containing 20 teeth, which falling into the teeth of a third wheel which hath 40 teeth, drives it once round in 320 poles, or a mile. On the axis of this wheel is a pinion of 12 teeth, which, falling into the teeth of a fourth wheel having 72 teeth, drives it once round in 12 miles. This fourth wheel, carrying another index over the inner limb of the dial-plate, divided into 12 for miles, and each mile subdivided into halves, quarters, and furths, serves to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> the revolutions of the other hand, and to keep account of the half miles and miles passed over as far as 12 miles. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this instrument is obvious from its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>. Its proper office is in the surveying of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> distances, where a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of expedition, and not much accuracy, is required. It is evident, that driving it along and observing the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, has the same effect as dragging the chain and taking account of the chains and links. Its advantages are its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> and expedition; its contrivance is such, that it may be fitted to the wheel of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COACH">coach</a>, in which state it performs its office, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> without any trouble at all.

PERCA

Pages 444-445

the Perch; a genus of fishes belonging to the order of thoracici. The head is furnished with scaly and furred opercula; there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> rays in the membrane of the gills; and the fins on the back are prickly. There are 38 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, principally distinguished by peculiarities in the back-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIN">fin</a>. The most remarkable are, 1. The fluviatilis, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> perch, hath a deep body, very rough scales, and the back much arched. The colours are beautiful; the back and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the sides being of a deep green, marked with five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> bars pointing downwards; the belly is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, tinged with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>; the ventral fins of a fine scarlet; the anal fins and tail of the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, but rather paler. In a lake called Llyn Raitllyn, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERIONETHSHIRE">Merionethshire</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, is a very singular variety of this fish; the back part is quite hunched, and the lower part of the backbone next the tail strangely distorted: in colour and other respects it resembles the common perch, which are as numerous in this lake as the deformed fish. They are not peculiar to this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>; for Linnaeus takes notice of them in a lake at Falun in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. It is said that they are also met with in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> near Marlow. The perch was much esteemed as food by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, nor is it less admired at present as a firm and delicate fish; and the Dutch are particularly fond of it when made into a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISH">dish</a> called water-souchy. It is a gregarious fish, and loves deep holes and gentle streams; is exceedingly voracious, and an eager biter; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the angler meets with a shoal of them, he is sure of taking every one.—It is a common notion that the pike <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not attack this fish, on account of the spiny fins which the perch erects on its approach. This may be true of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fish; but it is well known that small perch are the most tempting bait which can be laid for the pike. The perch is very tenacious of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and has been known to survive a journey of 50 miles in dry straw. It seldom grows to a large size, though Mr Pennant mentions one that weighed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> pounds; but this, he tells us, is very uncommon. 2. The labrax, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a>, is a very voracious, strong, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> fish. Ovid calls them rapidi lupi, a name <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to them by after-writers; and they are said to grow to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of fifteen pounds. The irides are silvery; the mouth large; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> are situated in the jaws, and are very small; in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the mouth is a triangular rough space, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> at the gullet are two others of a roundish form. The scales are of a middling size, are very thick set, and adhere closely. The body is formed somewhat like that of a salmon. The colour of the back is dusky, tinged with blue. The belly white. In young fish the space above the side line is marked with small black spots.—It is esteemed a very delicate fish. 3. The perca marina, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-perch, is about a foot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; the head large and deformed; eyes <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; teeth small and numerous. On the head and covers of the gills are strong spines. The colour red, with a black spot on the covers of the gills, and some transverse dusky <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> on the sides. It is a fish held in some esteem at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. 4. The cernua, or russe, is found in several of the English streams: it is gregarious, assembling in large shoals, and keeping in the deepest part of the water. It is of a much more slender form than the perch, and seldom exceeds six inches in length. The teeth are very small, and disposed in rows. It has only one dorsal fin, extending along the greatest part of the back: the first rays, like those of the perch, are strong, sharp, and spiny; the others soft. The body is covered with rough <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> scales. The back and sides are of a dirty green, the last inclining to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, but both spotted with black. The dorsal fin is spotted with black; the tail marked with transverse bars. Perception, 5. The nilotica, or perch of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, is taken about <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> has a sweet and exquisite flavour, and is not hard, but very white. It is one of the best fishes of the Nile; and as it is of the largest size in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, it adorns a table if brought upon it entire and well fried.

PERCEPTION

Pages 445-446

in logic, the first and most simple <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the mind, whereby it perceives, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> is conscious of its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>. See LOGIC, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>, n° 36—39. 77. PERCEPTIVE <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind.—Concerning this there have been very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> controversies. Every one knows that there are sensations arising in our minds; but the question is what it is that perceives them, whether it is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> being of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> and body, or whether the living percipient is not a mind, or spirit alone, without a body, or else a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> only, resulting from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of a body without any distinct or separate spirit annexed thereto. These are difficulties probably never to be demonstrated, and we must at last be content with a probable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> only. Man is so wonderfully made, that he seems to assign a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to every one of his sensations, and yet reason and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> tell him, that in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> they cannot exist, or be, where he is apt too hastily to judge, or suppose them to be; for as nothing can act where it is not, so the perceptive power of man cannot possibly perceive any thing without or beyond himself. It is generally agreed, that the secondary qualities of body (as they are called) do not exist <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> to the man, but only the primary ones; though Dr Berkeley attempted to show that they both exist together, and that wherever the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> was, there likewise was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this could be satisfactorily made to appear, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s system would stand good for the non-existence of every thing but spirit and ideas; but it cannot, and to confine the argument to one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> alone, to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, sight; that man perceives colour we are sure of, and therefore it must be within him, or he would act where he was not. Now if he perceived extension, that must likewise be within him too, but then he could perceive no extension larger than himself:—but as neither extension nor colour have any place assigned them in the body, surely it is not the body, or any conformation thereof, that perceives. We may then suppose that it is something else, which is joined with the body that is the percipient, which let us name mind or soul; this mind should seem to be one simple uncompounded being, otherwise it could not be conscious that successive perceptions were the affections of the same thing. Colour, though hastily judged to be without the mind, Berkeley and Malbranche have sufficiently shewn not to be so; and that extension is so, seems also true; because it perceives none of its sensations extended, but only assigns or fixes a place for them, these of colour in particular, external to the man, although in fact they may not be without him; and this place is only determined by an operation of the mind, foggling or supposing distance, from an experimental obstruction to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of some members of the body by which the touch is affected as well as the sight, and so both the tangible and visible object concluded, though too precipitately, to be in one and the same place where the obstruction is likewise judged to be; Perceptive, and hence it obtained the supposition or suggestion of distance; and as we have no sensations to which we do not ascribe some distance or place, there must be place or space existing, or it could not be supposed. And therefore as nothing is perceived or suggested but what is supposed in some place, so nothing can exist but what constitutes space, or is in it, and must have some extension. But then the mind of man surely cannot be extended beyond his body, though it often supposes an extension far beyond; and if the extension imagined was in the mind, and not a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> operation thereof, by way of supposition, it could not guess so much amiss about the extension of objects, which has not been familiar to the other organs of sense, as we often find it does; for it seems to be a vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> to entertain a notion of the mind's judging of any distance or magnitudes from any pictures conjectured to be in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of the eye, or in itself: in the former <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, if there be any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> in the bottom of the eye, it would judge every object in an inverse position to the body, which is contrary to experience; neither does the mind judge of any magnitude according to any such pictures, but of the real external magnitudes; and seldom errs much, unless the objects be very remote.—If the bulk of objects were judged of by the pictures in the eye, a flea or mite must judge every object very small to what a man does, because the picture <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be diminished nearly as the eye is less: indeed these insects may see distinctly smaller things than man, because the objects may be brought nearer their small eyes, without throwing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of the rays beyond the retina, as the same distance of object would do in a larger eye, and prevent distinct vision; and it is highly probable, that these small insects cannot see objects at a great distance, unless they are much larger than what a man can see at the like distance; but then what they do see they judge to be of the same bigness that a man does; and so must every creature, let its eyes be of what <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIMENSION">dimension</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> you please. It is a vague notion opticians have, who imagine that one, like a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENS">lens</a>, will magnify the picture on the retina, whereas <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> the contrary takes place; for when the eye is used alone, without such a lens, the shorter focus of the eye forms the picture, and the longer is at the object; but when a lens is used by way of a microscope, the object is in the shorter, and the picture at the longer focus, just contrary to the method of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> vision. So, again, if the mind was conscious of a picture in the eye, it would perceive as many objects the creature had eyes; whereas it judges of no more, let the number of eyes be as they will, than it does by the help of any other of the senses. From all which we may conclude, that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, extension, and motion, are not perceptible objects; but that sensations alone are such, the former being only imagined, by an operation of the mind, to exist external to it; and that if they did not so exist, the mind could not imagine any extension, figure, and motion; for there never is found any of them perceivable by it, nor any figure or motion attending a simple <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>. Indeed it is too <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> thought, that there is a shape perceived with colour, or a coloured shape; but no object appears of one simple colour to a fixed eye, but every part of the object exhibits a different <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of colour; and these degrees separate sensations, to which the mind ascribes a place, though, in fact, the colour is not in the place so judged of; but something else that gives reliance to the actions of the mind on the body; and from hence it supposes there must be something existing there which gives rise to the colour perceived by it.—It is impossible the mind should perceive the images of things within itself, unless it was equally extended with the things themselves; and if not, how can it be thought that an ideal world can exist within the mind, as some philosophers have conjectured? Surely it cannot be; but it must be only imagination that directs as to the external existence of real things. We cannot properly be said to imagine what does not or has not really existed; for let a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> man try if he can imagine colour, or a deaf man <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, and he will find himself at a loss. Father Malbranche indeed tells us, that a man may have an idea of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> mountain that never existed; and a man may recollect the figure of a mountain which he has formerly imagined, and remember the colour of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> which he lately had a perception of, and suppose it possible they may be connected, and call this operation of his mind an idea if he pleases; but, after all his efforts, if he should happen to think of a mountain as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as Shooter's hill, he will hardly allow it to be contained in his mind.

PERCH

Pages 446-446

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>-measuring, a rod <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> pole of 16½ feet in length, of which 40 in length and 4 in breadth make an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> of ground. Crompt. Jurif. 222. But, by the customs of several counties, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a> it is 24 feet; and in the forest of Sherwood 25 feet; the foot being there 18 inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a> a perch of ditching is 21 feet, the perch of walling 16½ feet, and a pole of denshired ground is 12 feet, &c. Skene.

PERCHE

Pages 446-446

a territory of Orleanais in France, 35 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 30 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Normandy; on the south, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a> and Dunois; on the east, by Beauce; and on the west, by Maine. It takes its name from a forest, and is pretty fertile. The inhabitants carry on a pretty good trade; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is Bellesme.

PERCUSSION

Pages 446-446

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> a body makes in falling <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> striking upon another; or the shock of two bodies in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. PERDIX. See Tetrao.

PEREASLAW

Pages 446-446

a strong populous town of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of Kievia, situated on the river Tribecz; in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 32. 44. N. Lat. 49. 46.

PERENNIALS

Pages 446-446
or Perennial Flowers, in botany, a term applied to those plants whose roots will abide many years, whether they retain their leaves in winter or not. Those which retain their leaves are called evergreens; but such as cast their leaves are named deciduous, or perditious.

PERFECT

Pages 446-446

something to which nothing is wanting, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> that has all the requisites of its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and kind. PERFECT Cadence, in Music. See Cadence. PERFECT Tense, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>. See Preterite.

PERFECTION

Pages 446-446

the state <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of a thing perfect. Perfection is divided, according to Chauvinus, into physical, moral, and metaphysical. Physical or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> perfection, is that whereby a thing has all its powers and faculties, and those too in full vigour; and all its parts both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> and secondary, and those in their due proportion, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, &c. in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> is said to be perfect when he has a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> mind in a sound body. This perfection is by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> frequently termed imperium, because a thing is enabled thereby to perform all its operations. Moral perfection is an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of virtue or moral goodness, to which men arrive by repeated acts of piety, beneficence, &c. This is usually subdivided into <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> or inherent, which is actually in him to whom we <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> it; in imputative, which exists in some other, and not in him it is attributed to. Metaphysical, transcendental, or essential perfection, is the possession of all the essential attributes, or of all the parts necessary to the integrity of a substance; or it is that whereby a thing has or is provided of everything belonging to its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. This is either absolute, where all imperfection is excluded, such is the perfection of God; or secundum quid, and in its kind.

PERFUME

Pages 446-446

denotes either the volatile effluvia from any body affecting the organ of smelling, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the substance emitting those effluvia; in which last <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the word is most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used. The generality of perfumes are made up of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AMBERGRIS">ambergris</a>, civet, rose and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a> woods, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, jasmines, jonquils, tuberoses, and other odoriferous flowers. Those drugs commonly called aromatics, such as storax, frankincense, benzoin, cloves, mace, &c. enter the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of a perfume; some are also composed of aromatic herbs or leaves, as lavender, marjoram, fage, thyme, hyssop, &c. Perfumes were anciently very much in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; but, since people are become sensible of the harm they do to the head, they are generally diluted among us; however, they are still <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>.

PERGAMA

Pages 446-446

(<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>), the citadel of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>; which, because of its extraordinary height, gave name to all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> buildings, (Servius). Others say the walls of Troy were called Pergama.

PERGAMUM

Pages 446-447

(Pliny); called also Pergamea, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>); Pergamia, (Plutarch); a town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, built by Agamemnon in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his victory, (Velleius). Here was the burying-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a>, (Arictoxenus, quoted by Plutarch). It was situate near <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYDONIA">Cydonia</a>, (Servius); to what point not said; but <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SCYLAX">Scylax</a> helps him out, who places the Dacynnean temple of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, which stood near Cydonia, (Strabo), to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the territory of Pergamia.—Another Pergamum, (Pliny, Strabo); a town of Mygia, situate on the Caicus, which runs by it. It was the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUMENES">Eumenes</a>, and of the kings of the Attali, (Livy). There an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> temple of Esculapius. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERGAMUS">Pergamus</a>. Iapius stood; an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>, (Tacitus). The ornament of Pergamus was the royal library, vying with that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; the kings of Pergamus and Egypt rivaling each other in this respect, (Pliny). Strabo ascribes this rivalry to Eumenes, Plutarch reckons up 200,000 volumes in the library at Pergamus. Here the membrane pergamenta, whence the name <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, were invented for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of books, (Varro, quoted by Pliny). The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Galen, and of Oribasius <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> physician, to Julian the Apostate, (Eunapius), called by some the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Galen. Here P. Scipio died, (Cicero). Attalus son of Eumenes dying without issue, bequeathed his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> to the Roman people, who reduced it to a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, (Strabo). Pergamenus, the epithet, (Martial). Here was one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> conventus juridici, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> assemblies of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> Romana, called Pergamenus, and the ninth in order, (Pliny); which he also calls jurisdictio Pergamena.

PERGAMUS

Pages 447-450

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, formed out of the ruins of the empire of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. It commenced about the year 283. The first sovereign was one Phileterus, an eunuch, by birth a Paphlagonian, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, and in his youth a menial <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> to Antigonus one of Alexander's captains. He afterwards served Lysimachus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of Macedon and Thrace, who appointed him keeper of his treasuries lodged in Pergamus. While he held this employment, having fallen under the displeasure of Ariadne wife to Lysimachus, she found means to make a quarrel between him and his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; upon which Phileterus seized on the castle of Pergamus, together with the treasures entrusted to his care, amounting to 90,000 talents. At first he offered his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, together with his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, to Seleucus king of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>; but both Seleucus and Lysimachus dying soon after, he kept possession of the town and treasure also till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; which happened 20 years after his revolt from Lysimachus. Phileterus left the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Pergamus to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to some, to his brother's son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUMENES">Eumenes</a> I.; and he laying hold of the opportunity offered by the dissensions among the Seleucidæ, possessed himself of many strong-holds in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Asia; and having hired a body of Galatians, defeated Antiochus, as he was returning from a victory gained over his brother Seleucus Callinicus. By this victory he obtained possession of the greater <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Asia; however, he did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> enjoy his acquisitions; for he died next year of immoderate drinking, a vice to which he was greatly addicted. Eumenes was succeeded by Attalus I., nephew of Phileterus, and the first who took upon him the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of king of Pergamus. He defeated the Gauls, who were desirous of settling in his territory; and, according to Livy, was the first of the Asiatic princes who refused to pay a contribution to these barbarians. When Seleucus Ceraunus was engaged in other wars, he invaded his territories, and conquered all the provinces on this side of Mount Taurus; but was soon driven out of his new acquisitions by Seleucus and his grandfather Achæus, who entering into an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> against him, deprived him of all his newly acquired territories, and even besieged him in his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. Upon this Attalus invited to his assistance the Gauls who had settled in Thrace; and with their help not only obliged the enemy to raise the siege of Pergamus, but quickly recovered all the provinces he had lost. After this he invaded <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a> and the neighbouring provinces, where several cities voluntarily submitted to him. The Teians, Colophonians, with the inhabitants of Egæa and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEMNOS">Lemnos</a>, sent deputies declaring themselves ready to acknowledge him for their sovereign; the Carianes, on the other side the river Lyceus, opened their gates to him, having first expelled the governor set over them by Achæus. From thence he advanced to Apia, and encamping on the banks of the river Megithus, received homage from the neighbouring nations. But here the Gauls, being frightened by an eclipse of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, refused to proceed farther; which obliged Attalus to return to the Hellespont, where he allowed his allies to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a>, giving them a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and fruitful territory, and promising that he would always assist and protect them to the utmost of his power. Attalus having thus settled his affairs with equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and advantage to himself, entered into an alliance with Rome, and afterwards joined them in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> king of Macedon. Here he had the command of the Rhodian fleet; with which he not only drove the Macedonians quite out of the seas, but having landed his men, he, in conjunction with the Athenians, invaded Macedon, and obliged Philip to raise the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, which he had greatly disturbed; for which services the Athenians not only heaped on him all the favours they could, but called one of their tribes by his name; an honour they had never bestowed on any foreigner before. Attalus, not contented with all he had yet done against Philip, attempted to form a general confederacy of the Greeks against him. But while he was haranguing the Boeotians to this purpose, and exhorting them with great vehemence to enter into an alliance with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> against their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> enemy, he fell <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> speechless. However, he came to himself again, and desired to be carried by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> from Thebes to Pergamus, where he died soon after his arrival, in the 72d year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and 43d of his reign. This <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of great generosity, and such an enthusiast in learning and learned men, that he caused a grammarian, named Daphidas, to be thrown into the sea from the top of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rock, because he spoke disrespectfully of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. Attalus was succeeded by his eldest son Eumenes II. He was exceedingly attached to the Romans, insomuch that he refused the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Antiochus the Great in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, lest he should thus have been led into a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> with that people. He also gave notice to the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> of the transactions of Ariarathes king of Cappadocia, who was making great preparations both by sea and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>. Nor did Eumenes stop here; for when he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the war about to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out between Antiochus and the Romans, he sent his brother Attalus to Rome to give information of the proceedings of Antiochus. The senate heaped honours both on Eumenes and his brother; and in the war which followed, gave the command of their fleet to the king of Pergamus in conjunction with C. Livius Salinator. The victory gained on this occasion was in a great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> owing to Eumenes, who boarded some of the enemy's ships. Pergamus. Ships in person, and during the whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> behaved with uncommon bravery. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> afterwards Eumenes, entering the territories of Antiochus with a body of 5000 men, ravaged all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about Thyatira, and returned with an immense booty. But in the mean time Antiochus invading Pergamus in his turn, ravaged the whole country, and even laid siege to the capital. Attalus, the king's brother held out with a handful of men till the Achaeans, who were in alliance with Eumenes, sent 1000 foot and 100 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> to his assistance. As this small body of auxiliaries were all chosen men, and commanded by an experienced officer, they behaved with such bravery that the Syrians were obliged to raise the siege. At the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNESIA">Magnesia</a>, too, Eumenes behaved with the greatest bravery; not only sustaining the first attack of the enemy's elephants, but driving them back again on their own troops, which put the ranks in disorder, and gave the Romans an opportunity of giving them a total defeat by attacking them opportunely with their horse. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this defeat, Antiochus was obliged to conclude a peace with the Romans on such terms as they pleased to prefer; one of which was, that he should pay Eumenes 400 talents, and a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of corn, in recompense for the damage he had done him. Eumenes now thought of obtaining some reward from the Romans <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to the services he had done them. Having gone to Rome, he told the senate, that he was come to beg of them that the Greek cities which had belonged to Antiochus before the commencement of the late war, might now be added to his dominions; but his demand was warmly opposed by the ambassadors from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, as well as by deputies from all the Greek cities in Asia. The senate, however, after hearing both parties, decided the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in favour of Eumenes, adding to his dominions all the countries on this side of Mount Taurus which belonged to Antiochus; the other provinces lying between that mountain and the river Meander, excepting Lycia and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, were bestowed on the Rhodians. All the cities, which had paid tribute to Attalus, were ordered to pay the same to Eumenes; but such as had been tributary to Antiochus were declared free. Soon after this Eumenes was engaged in a war with Prusias king of Bithynia, who made war upon him by the advice of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> the celebrated Carthaginian general. But Eumenes, being assisted by the Romans, defeated Prusias in an engagement by sea, and another by land; which so disheartened him, that he was ready to accept of peace on any terms. However, before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> was concluded, Hannibal found means to draw Philip of Macedon into the confederacy, who sent Philocles, an old and experienced officer, with a considerable body of troops to join Prusias. Hereupon Eumenes sent his brother Attalus to Rome with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, worth 15,000 talents, to complain of Prusias for making war on the allies of the Roman people without any provocation. The senate accepted the present, and promised to adjust every thing to the satisfaction of their friend Eumenes, whom they looked upon to be the most steady ally they had in Asia. But in the mean time Prusias, having ventured another sea-fight, by a contrivance of Hannibal's, gained a complete victory. The Carthaginian commander advised him to fill a great many earthen vessels with various kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> and other poisonous reptiles, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the fight to throw them into the enemies' ships so as to break the pots and let the serpents loose. All the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> and seamen were commanded to attack the ship in which Eumenes was, and only to defend themselves as well as they could against the rest; and that they might be in no danger of mistaking the ship, an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALD">herald</a> was sent before the engagement with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the king. As soon as the two fleets drew near, all the ships of Prusias, singling out that of Eumenes, discharged such a quantity of serpents into it, that neither soldiers nor sailors could do their duty, but were forced to fly to the shore, lest they should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. The other ships, after a faint resistance, followed the king's example, and were all driven ashore with great slaughter; the soldiers being no less annoyed by the stings of the serpents, than by the weapons of the enemy. The greatest part of the ships of Eumenes were burnt, several taken, and the others so much shattered, that they became quite unserviceable. The same year Prusias gained two remarkable victories over Eumenes by land, both of which were entirely owing to stratagems of Hannibal. But, while matters were thus going on to the disadvantage of Eumenes, the Romans interfered, and by their deputies not only put an end to the differences between the two kings, but prevailed on Prusias to betray Hannibal; upon which he poisoned himself, as hath been related under the article HANNIBAL. Eumenes, being thus freed from such a dangerous enemy, engaged in a new war with the kings of Capadocia and Pontus, in which also he proved victorious. His friendship for the Romans he carried to such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of enthusiasm, that he went in person to Rome to inform them of the machinations of Perseus king of Macedon. He had before quarrelled with the Rhodians, who sent ambassadors to Rome to complain of him. But as the ambassadors happened to arrive while the king himself was present in the city, the Rhodian ambassadors could not obtain any hearing, and Eumenes was dismissed with new marks of favour. This journey, however, had almost proved fatal to him; for, on his return, as he was going to perform a sacrifice at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>, two assassins, sent by Perseus, rolled down two great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> upon him as he entered the straits of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. With one he was dangerously wounded on the head, and with the other on the shoulder. He fell with the blows from a steep <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and thus received many other bruises; so that he was carried on board his ship when it could not well be known whether he was dead or alive. His people, however, soon finding that he was still alive, conveyed him to Corinth, and from Corinth to Aegina, having caused their vessels to be carried over the Isthmus. Eumenes remained at Aegina till his wounds were cured, which was done with such secrecy, that a report of his death was spread all over Asia, and even believed at Rome; nay, his brother Attalus was so convinced of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this report, that he not only assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, but even married Stratonice the wife of Eumenes. But in a short time Eumenes convinced them both of his being alive, by returning to his kingdom. On the receipt of this news Attalus resigned the sovereignty in great haste, and went to meet his brother; carrying an halberd, as one of his guards. Eumenes received both him and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> with great tenderness, nor did he ever say anything which might tend to make them uneasy; only it is said he whispered in his brother's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a> when he first saw him, "Be in no haste to marry my wife again till you are sure that I am dead." The king being now more than ever exasperated against Perseus, joined the Romans in their war against Perseus; but during the course of it he suddenly cooled in his affection towards those allies whom he had hitherto served with so much zeal, and that to such a degree, that he admitted ambassadors from Perseus, and offered to stand <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEUTER">neuter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he would pay him 1000 talents, and for 1500, to influence the Romans to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> him a safe and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> peace. But these negotiations were broke off without effect, by reason of the distrust which the two kings had of one another. Eumenes could not trust Perseus unless he paid him the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> beforehand; while, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, Perseus did not care to part with the money before Eumenes had performed what he promised; neither could he be induced to pay the sum in question, though the king of Pergamus offered to give hostages for the performance of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>. What the reason of such a sudden change in the disposition of Eumenes was, is nowhere told; however, the fact is certain. The negotiations above mentioned were concealed from the Romans as long as possible; however, they soon came to be known, after which the republic began to entertain no small jealousy of their old friend, and therefore heaped favours on his brother Attalus, without taking any notice of the king himself. Eumenes had sent him to Rome to congratulate the senate on the happy issue of the war with Perseus, not thinking that his practices had been discovered. However, the senate, without taking any notice of their disaffection to Eumenes at first, entertained Attalus with the greatest magnificence; then several of the senators who visited him proceeded to acquaint him with their suspicions of the king, and desired Attalus to treat with them in his own name, assuring him, that the kingdom of Pergamus would be granted him, if he demanded it, by the senate. These speeches had at first some effect; but Attalus, being of an honest disposition, and assisted by the advice of a physician called Stratius, a man of great probity, resolved not to comply with their desire. When he was admitted to the senate, therefore, he first congratulated them on the happy issue of the Macedonian war, then modestly recounted his own services; and lastly, acquainted them with the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of his journey; intreating them to send ambassadors to the Gauls, who by their authority might secure his brother from any danger of their hostilities; and he requested them also, that the two cities of Ænus and Maronea might be bestowed on himself. The senate, imagining that Attalus designed to choose some other <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> to sue for his brother's kingdom, not only granted all his requests, but sent him richer and more magnificent presents than they had ever done before. Upon this Attalus immediately set out on his return to Pergamus; which so provoked the senators, that they declared the cities free which they had promised to Attalus; thus rendering ineffectual their promise which they were ashamed openly to revoke; and as for the Gauls, who were on all occasions ready to invade the kingdom of Pergamus, they sent ambassadors to them, with instructions to behave in such a manner as would rather tend to encourage them in their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> than dissuade them from it. Eumenes, being alarmed at those proceedings, resolved to go in person to Rome, in order to justify himself. But the senate, having already condemned him in their own minds, resolved not to hear his vindication. For this reason, as soon as they heard of his design, they made an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> that no king should be permitted to enter the gates of Rome. Eumenes, however, who knew nothing of this act, set forward on his journey, and landed at Brundusium; but, no sooner did the Roman senate get intelligence of his arrival there, than they sent a quaestor acquainting him with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the senate; and telling him at the same time, that if he had any business to transact with the senate, he was appointed to hear it and transmit it to them; but if not, that the king must leave <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> without delay. To this Eumenes replied, that he had no business of any consequence to transact, and that he did not stand in need of any of their assistance; and without saying a word more, went on board his ship, and returned to Pergamus. On his return home, the Gauls, being encouraged by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> reception which he had met with at Rome, invaded his territories, but were repulsed with great loss by the king, who afterwards invaded the dominions of Prusias, and possessed himself of several cities. This produced new complaints at Rome; and Eumenes was accused, not only by the ambassadors of Prusias, but also by those of the Gauls and many cities in Asia, of keeping a secret correspondence with Perseus king of Macedon. This last <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> was confirmed by some letters which the Romans themselves had intercepted; so that Eumenes found it impossible to keep up his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> any longer at Rome, though he sent his brothers Athenæus and Attalus thither to intercede for him. The senators, in short, had conceived the most implacable hatred against him, and seemed absolutely bent on his destruction, when he died, in the 39th year of his reign, leaving his kingdom and his wife to his brother Attalus. He left one son, but he was an infant, and incapable of governing the kingdom; for which reason Eumenes chose rather to give the present possession of the crown to his brother, reserving the succession to his son, than to endanger the whole by committing the management of affairs to his son's tutors. Attalus, in the beginning of his reign, found himself greatly distressed by Prusias king of Bithynia, who not only overthrew him in a pitched battle, but advanced to the very walls of Pergamus, ravaging the country as he marched along; and at last reduced the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> city itself. The king, however, saved himself by a timely flight, and dispatched ambassadors to Rome, complaining of the bad usage of Prusias. The latter endeavoured to defend himself, and to throw the blame on Attalus. But, after a proper inquiry was made into the matter, Prusias was found to be entirely in the wrong; in consequence of which, he was at last obliged to conclude a peace with his adversary on the following Pergamus. lowing terms. 1. That he should immediately deliver up to Attalus 20 ships with decks. 2. That he should pay 500 talents to Attalus within the space of 20 years. 3. That he should pay 100 talents to some of the other Asiatic nations by way of reparation for the damages they had sustained from him. And, 4. Both parties should be content with what they had before the beginning of the war. Some time after this, Prusias having made an unnatural attempt on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of his son Nicomedes, the latter rebelled, and, with the affluence of Attalus, drove his father from the throne, and, as is said, even murdered him in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. The Romans took no notice of these transactions, but showed the same kindness to Attalus as formerly. The last enterprise in which we find Attalus engaged, was against Andrifens the pretended son of Perseus king of Macedon, where he assisted the Romans; after which he gave himself up entirely to ease and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, committing state affairs entirely to his ministers; and thus <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to his death, which happened in the 82d year of his age, about 138 B.C. Attalus II. was succeeded by Attalus III. the son of Eumenes; for the late king, considering that he only held the crown as a trust for his nephew, passed by his own children in order to give it to him, tho' he appears to have been by no means worthy of it. He is said to have been deprived of his senses thro' the violence of his grief for his mother's death; and indeed, throughout his whole reign, he behaved more like a madman than any thing else. Many of his subjects of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> were cut off with their wives and children, upon the most groundless suspicions; and for these executions he made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of mercenaries hired out from among the most barbarous nations. Thus he proceeded till he had cut off all the best men in the kingdom; after which he fell into a deep melancholy, imagining that the ghosts of those whom he had murdered were perpetually haunting him. On this he shut himself up in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, put on a mean apparel, let his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> grow, and sequestered himself from all mankind. At last he withdrew from the palace, and retired into a garden, which he cultivated with his own hands, and filled with all sorts of poisonous herbs. These he used to mix with wholesome <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, and send packets of them to such as he suspected. At last, being weary of this amusement, and living in solitude, because nobody durst approach him, he took it in his head to follow the trade of a founder, and make a brazen monument. But, while he laboured at melting and casting the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, the heat of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> threw him into a fever, which in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days put an end to his tyranny, after he had sat on the throne five years. On the death of the king, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> was found, by which he left the Roman people heirs of all his goods; upon which they seized on the kingdom, and reduced it to a province of their empire by the name of Asia Proper. But Ariftonicus, a son of Eumenes by an Egyptian courtezan, reckoning himself the lawful heir to the crown, could by no means be satisfied with this usurpation of the Romans, and therefore assembled a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> to maintain his pretensions. The people in general, having been accustomed to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, dreaded a republican form of government; in consequence of which, they assisted Ariftonicus, and Pergamus soon put him in a condition to reduce the whole kingdom. The news, however, were soon carried to Rome, and Licinius Crassus, the pontifex maximus, was sent into the east, with orders to enforce obedience to the king's will. Historians take no notice of any forces which were sent along with this commander; whence it is supposed, that he depended on assistance from the Asiatics, who were in alliance with Rome, or from the Egyptians. But when he came thither, he found both the Syrians and Egyptians so reduced, that he could not expect any assistance from them. However, he was soon supplied with troops in plenty by the kings of Pontus, Bithynia, Cappadocia, and Paphlagonia; but managed matters so ill, that he was entirely defeated and taken prisoner. Those who took him designed to carry him to Ariftonicus; but he, not able to endure the disgrace, would have laid violent hands on himself if he had not been disarmed. However, being allowed to keep a rod for managing the horse on which he sat, he struck a Thracian soldier who stood near him so violently with it, that he <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> out one of his eyes; upon which the other drew his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and ran him through on the spot. His head was brought to Ariftonicus, who exposed it to public view; but the body was honourably buried. Ariftonicus had no great time to enjoy the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of his victory. Indeed he behaved very improperly after it; for, instead of preparing to oppose the next army, which he might have been assured the Romans would send against him, he spent his time in feasting and revelling. But he was soon routed out of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETHARGY">lethargy</a> by Perpenna the new <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, who having assembled with incredible expedition the troops of the allies, came unexpectedly upon him, obliged him to venture an engagement at a disadvantage, and entirely defeated him. Ariftonicus fled to a city called Stratonice; but was so closely pursued by the conquerors, that the garrison, having no method of supplying themselves with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, delivered up their leader, as well as a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> named Blosius, who had been the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> and counsellor of Ariftonicus. The philosopher behaved with great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> after being taken, and openly defended his siding with Ariftonicus, because he thought his cause <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a>. He exhorted the latter to prevent the disgrace and misery of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> by a voluntary death; but Ariftonicus, looking upon death as a greater misery than any captivity, suffered himself to be treated as his conquerors pleased. In the mean time, a new consul, named Manius Aquilius, being arrived from Rome, sent a most haughty message to Perpenna, requiring him immediately to deliver up Ariftonicus as a captive belonging to his triumph when the war should be ended. With this demand Perpenna refused to comply, and his refusal had almost produced a civil war. However, this was prevented by the death of Perpenna, which happened soon after the dispute commenced. The Pergamenians, notwithstanding the defeat and captivity of their leader, still held out with such obstinacy, that Aquilius was obliged to besiege, and take by force almost every city in the kingdom. In doing this, he took a very effectual, though exceeding cruel method. Most of the cities in the kingdom had no other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> than what was brought from a considerable distance in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>.

PERIAGOGUE

Pages 451-451

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, is used where many things are accumulated into one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> which might have been divided into several.

PERIANDER

Pages 450-451
tyrant of Corinth and Corcyra, was reckoned among the seven wise men of Greece; though he might rather have been reckoned among the most wicked men, since he changed the government of his country, deprived his countrymen of their liberty, usurped the sovereignty, and committed the most shocking crimes. In the beginning of his reign he behaved with mildness; but after his having sent to the tyrant of Syracuse to consult him on the safest method of government, he abandoned himself to cruelty. The latter, having heard Periander's envoys, took them into a field, and, instead of answering them, pulled up before them the ears of corn which exceeded the rest in height.
