Periander, on being told of this action, understood what was meant by it. He first secured himself by a good guard, and then put the most powerful Corinthians to death. He abandoned himself to the most enormous crimes; committed incest with his mother, kicked to death his wife Melissa, daughter of Procles king of Epidaurus, notwithstanding her being with child; and was so enraged at Lycophron, his second son, for lamenting his mother's death, that he banished him into the island of Corcyra. Yet he passed for one of the greatest politicians of his time; and Heracleides tells us, that he forbade voluptuousness; that he imposed no taxes, contenting himself with the custom arising from the sale and the import and export of commodities; that, though wicked himself, he hated the wicked, and caused all pimps to be drowned; lastly, that he established a senate, and settled the expense of its members. He died 585 B.C.

PERIANTHIUM

Pages 451-451

(from περι, "round," and ανθος, "the flower,") the flower-cup properly so called, the most <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of calyx, placed immediately under the flower, which is contained in it as in a cup. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, p. 1296.

PERICARDIUM

Pages 451-451

in anatomy, a membranous bag filled with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which contains the heart in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> and many other animals. It is formed by a duplication of the mediastinum, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> membrane which divides the thorax into two unequal parts. See Anatomy, p. 382, 305, 386.

PERICARPIUM

Pages 451-451

(from περι, "round," and καρπος, "fruit,") the seed-vessel; an ential of the plant big with seeds, which it discharges when ripe. The seed-vessel is in fact the developed seed-bud, and may very properly be compared to the fecundated ovary in animals; for it does not exist till after the fertilizing of the seeds by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a>-dust, and the consequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the flower. All <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, however, are Perichoruses not furnished with a seed-vessel; in such as are deprived of it, the receptacle <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> calyx performs its functions—Perimeter, by inclosing the seeds, as in a matrix, and accompanying them to perfect maturity.

PERICHORUS

Pages 451-451

in antiquity, a name given by the Greeks to their profane games <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> combats, that is, to such as were not consecrated to any of the gods.

PERICLES

Pages 451-451

was one of the greatest men that ever flourished in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. He was educated with all imaginable care; and beside other matters, he had for his tutors Zeno, Eleates, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANAXAGORAS">Anaxagoras</a>. He learned from the last of these to fear the gods without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, and to account for an eclipse from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> cause. Many were unjust enough to suspect him of atheism, because he had perfectly studied the doctrine of that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of undoubted courage; and of such extraordinary eloquence, supported and improved by knowledge, that he gained almost as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> an authority under a republican <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had been a monarch; but yet he could not escape the satirical strokes of the comic poets. His dissoluteness with the women was one of the vices with which he was chiefly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a>. He died the third year of the Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> sickness, which had weakened his understanding. Alpasia, Pericles' favourite, was a learned woman of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILETUS">Miletus</a>; she taught <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> and politics. As Pericles cared not much for his wife, he willingly gave her up to another, and married Alpasia, whom he passionately loved.

PERICRANIUM

Pages 451-451

in anatomy, a thick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> coat <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> membrane, covering the outside of the cranium or skull. See Anatomy, p. 4.

PERIGEE

Pages 451-451

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, that point of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>'s orbit wherein they are at the least distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands opposed to apogee.

PERIGEUX

Pages 451-451

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> episcopal town of France, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Perigord, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 33. N. Lat. 45. 18. It is remarkable for the ruins of the temple of Venus, and an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>.

PERIGORD

Pages 451-451

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, which makes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Guienne, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGOUMOIS">Angoumois</a>, and a part of Marche, and on the east by Quercy and Limousin; on the south, by Agenois and Bazadois; and on the west, by Bourledois, Angoumois, and a part of Saintonge. It is about 83 miles in length, and 60 in breadth. It abounds in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is pure and healthy. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIGUEUX">Perigueux</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

PERIGRAPHE

Pages 451-451

a word usually understood to express a careless <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> inaccurate delineation of any thing; but in Vesalius it is used to express the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> or impressions that appear on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MUSCULUS">musculus</a> rectus of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>.

PERIHELION

Pages 451-451

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of a planet <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> comet's orbit wherein it is in its least distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands in opposition to aphelion.

PERILOCA

Pages 452-452

Virginian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the pentandria class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are four <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, all of them natives of warm climates. They are perennial shrubby plants with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> branches, rising from three to 40 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, adorned with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and purple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. The seeds are inclosed in capsules filled with a soft <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. Two of the species, viz. the Graeca and Africana, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> live in the open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and are propagated by layers;

PERIMETER

Pages 451-452

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, the bounds <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> limits of any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> or body. The perimeters of surfaces or figures are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; those of bodies are surfaces. In circular cular figures, instead of perimeter, we say circumference, or periphery. PERINÆUM, or Perineum, in anatomy, the space between the anus and the parts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, divided into two equal lateral divisions by a very distinct line, which is longer in males than in females.

PERINKSKIOLD

Pages 452-452

a learned Swedish writer, born at Stregnefia in Sudermania, in 1544, studied under his father, who was professor of eloquence and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and afterwards became well skilled in the antiquities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a>. He was made professor at Upsal, secretary antiquary of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and counsellor of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> of antiquities. He died in 1720. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are: 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>. 2. A history of the kings of the North. 3. An edition of John Mefflenius on the kings of Sweden, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, and Norway, in 14 vols folio, &c. All Peringkiold's works are excellent, and highly esteemed.

PERIOD

Pages 452-452

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> taken up by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> planet in making a revolution round the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of its course till it return to the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of its orbit. The periodical times of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> round the sun are as follow: | Planet | Seconds | Min. | Hrs. | Days | |----------|---------|------|------|------| | <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> | 87 | 23 | 15 | 53 | | Venus | 224 | 16 | 49 | 24 | | The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>| 365 | 6 | 9 | 14 | | <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> | 686 | 23 | 27 | 30 | | <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> | 4332 | 12 | 20 | 25 | | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> | 10759 | 6 | 36 | 26 | There is a wonderful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> between the distances of the planets from the sun, and their periods round him; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> whereof is, that the squares of the periodical times of the primary planet, are to each other as the cubes of their distances from the sun: and likewise, the squares of the periodical times of the secondaries of any planet are to each other as the cubes of their distances from that primary. This harmony among the planets is one of the greatest confirmations of the Copernican <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>. See Astronomy, n° 132. For the periods of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, see Astronomy, n° 223. The periods of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a> are now pretty well ascertained. See Astronomy, n° 46 et seq. Period, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, denotes a revolution of a certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years, or a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of years, whereby, in different nations, and on different occasions, time is measured; such are the following. Calippic Period, a system of seventy-six years. See Calippic. Dionysian Period, or Victorian Period, a system of 532 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a>-solar and Julian years; which being elapsed, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the moon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> again upon the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> and feria, and revolve in the same order, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. This period is otherwise called the great paschal cycle, because the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> first used it to find the true time of the pascha or Easter. The sum of these years arise by multiplying together the cycles of the sun and moon. See Astronomy, n° 308. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIPPARCHUS">Hipparchus</a>'s Period, a system of 304 years, both lunar and solar; which being elapsed, Hipparchus thought that the reckoning by the lunar <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> would coincide again with the solar <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. This period comprehends 3760 lunar months, or 111,039 days; the sum of which arises from the multiplication of the Calippic period by 4, subtracting unity from the product. Julian Period. See Julian. Period, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, denotes a small compass of discourse, containing a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, and distinguished at the end by a point, or full stop, thus (.); and in members or divisions marked by commas, colons, &c. Period, in oratory, See there, n° 44. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIODIC">Periodic</a>, or Periodical, something that terminates and comprehends a period; such is a periodic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; being the space of time wherein the moon dispatches her period.

PERIOECI

Pages 452-452

περιοικοι, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, such inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> as have the same latitudes, but opposite longitudes, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> live under the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> and the same meridian, but in different semicircles of that meridian, or in opposite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the parallel. These have the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> seasons throughout the year, and the same phenomena of the heavenly bodies; but when it is noonday with the one it is midnight with the other, there being twelve hours in an east and west <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. These are found on the globe by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a>, or by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the globe half round, that is, 180 degrees either way.

PERIOSTEUM

Pages 452-452
or Periostium, in anatomy, a nervous vascular membrane, ended with a very quick sense, immediately surrounding, in every part, both the internal and external surfaces of all the bones in the body, excepting only so much of the teeth as stand above the gums, and the peculiar places on the bones, in which the muscles are inserted. It is hence divided into the external and internal periosteum; and where it externally surrounds the bones of the skull, it is generally called the pericranium. See Anatomy, n° 4. PERIPATETIC philosophy, that system taught and established by Aristotle, and maintained by his followers the Peripatetics, called also the Aristotelians. See the next article.

PERIPATUS

Pages 452-452

(anc. geog.) the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> taught; a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Lyceum, a gymnasmus at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, situate on the banks of the Ilissus. The reason of the appellation is, that Aristotle walked as he taught. (Cicero, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laertius). Peripatetici the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> followers of Aristotle.

PERIPETIA

Pages 452-452

in the drama, that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of a tragedy wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> is turned, the plot unravelled, and the whole concludes. See Catastrophe.

PERIPHERY

Pages 452-452

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, the circumference of a circle, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELLIPSIS">ellipsis</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> any other regular curvilinear <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>.

PERIPNEUMONY

Pages 453-453

an inflammation of the lungs. See MEDICINE, n° 289, 290. and FARRIERY, § 5.

PERISCII

Pages 452-453

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, the inhabitants of either frigid zone, between the polar circles and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, when in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> signs, moves only round about them, without setting; and consequently their shadows in the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> turn to all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the horizon.

PERISTALTIC

Pages 453-453

a vermicular spontaneous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the intestines, performed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the circular and longitudinal fibres of which the fleathy coats of the intestines are composed; by means whereof the chyle is driven into the orifices of the lacteal veins, and the faeces are protruded towards the anus.

PERISTYLE

Pages 453-453

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> encompassed with a row of columns on the inside. PERITONÆUM, in anatomy, is a thin, smooth, and lubricous membrane, investing the whole internal surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>, and containing most of the viscera of that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> as it were in a bag. See ANATOMY, n° 350.

PERITROCHIUM

Pages 453-453

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, denotes a wheel, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> circle, concentric with the base of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, and moveable together with it about its axis. See MECHANICS.

PERIZONIUS

Pages 453-453

a very learned and laborious writer, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DAM">Dam</a> in 1651. He became professor of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and eloquence at the university of Franeker, when, by his merit and learning, he made that university flourish. However, in 1693, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, where he was made professor of history, eloquence, and the Greek tongue; in which employment he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1715. He wrote many Dissertations, and other learned and curious works, particularly Origines Babylonica et Ægyptiaca, 2 vols 8vo, &c.

PERJURY

Pages 453-453

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is defined by Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> to be a crime committed when a lawful oath is administered, in some judicial proceeding, to a person who (wears wilfully, absolutely, and falsely, in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> material to the issue <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> point in question. The law takes no notice of any perjury but such as is committed in some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> having power to administer an oath; or before some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> or proper officer invested with a similar authority, in some proceedings relative to a civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> or a criminal prosecution; for it esteems all other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> unnecessary at least, and therefore <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not punish the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of them. For which reason it is much to be questioned, how far any magistrate is justifiable in taking a voluntary affidavit in any extrajudicial matter, as is now too frequent upon every petty occasion; since it is more than possible that, by such idle oaths, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> may frequently, infopo ro conscientie, incur the guilt, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> evade the temporal penalties of perjury. The perjury must also be corrupt, (that is, committed malo animo), wilful, positive, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>; not upon surmise, or the like; it also must be in some point material to the question in dispute; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it only be in some trifling collateral circumstance, to which no regard is paid, it is no more penal than in the voluntary extrajudicial oaths before-mentioned. Subornation of perjury is the offence of procuring another to take such a false oath, as constitutes perjury in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of perjury and subornation, at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, has been various. It was anciently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; afterwards banishment, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> out the tongue; then forfeiture of goods; and now it is fine and imprisonment, and never more to be capable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> testimony. But the statute 5 Eliz. c. 9. (if the offender be prosecuted thereon) inflicts the penalty of perpetual infamy, and a fine of 20l. or to have both ears nailed to the pillory. But the prosecution is usually carried on for the offence at common law; especially as, to the penalties before inflicted, the statute 2 Geo. II. c. 25. superadds a power for the court to order the offender to be sent to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of correction for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> not exceeding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years, or to be transported for the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>; and makes it felony, without benefit of clergy, to return or escape within the time. It has sometimes been wished, that perjury, at least upon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> accusations, whereby another's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> has been or might have been destroyed, was also rendered capital, upon a principle of retaliation; as it is universally by the laws of France. And certainly the odiousness of the crime pleads strongly in behalf of the French law. But it is to be considered, that there they admit witnesses to be heard only on the side of the prosecution, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACK">rack</a> to extort a confession from the accused. In such a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, therefore, it is necessary to throw the dread of capital punishment into the other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, in order to keep in awe the witnesses for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; on whom alone the prisoner's fate depends: so naturally does one cruel law beget another. But corporal and pecuniary punishments, exile and perpetual infamy, are more suited to the genius of the English law; where the fact is openly discussed between witnesses on both sides, and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> for the crown may be contradicted and disproved by those of the prisoner. Where indeed the death of an innocent person has actually been the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of such wilful perjury, it falls within the guilt of deliberate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, and deserves an equal punishment; which our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> law in fact inflicted. But the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> attempt to destroy life by other means not being capital, there is no reason that an attempt by perjury should; much less that this crime should, in all judicial <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, be punished with death. For to multiply capital punishments lessens their effect, when applied to crimes of the deepest dye; and, detestable as perjury is, it is not by any means to be compared with some other offences, for which only death can be inflicted; and therefore it seems already (except perhaps in the instance of deliberate murder by perjury) very properly punished by our present law; which has adopted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Cicero, derived from the law of the twelve tables, Perjurii pena divina, exuitum; humana, dedecus.

PERMEABLE

Pages 453-453

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to bodies of so loose a texture as to let something <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through them.

PERMSKI

Pages 453-454
or Permia, a town of the Russian empire, and capital of a province of the same name, seated on the river Kama between the Dwina and the Oby; E. Long. 55. 50. N. Lat. 70. 26. The province is bounded on the north by the Samoiedes, on the west by Zirania and Ulatka, and on the east by Siberia. PERNAMBUÇO, a province of Brazil in South America, bounded on the north by Tamera, on the east by the ocean; on the south by Seregiipa, and on the west by Tapuyers. It is about 200 miles in length, and 150 in breadth. The Dutch became masters of it in 1630, but the Portuguese soon retook it from them. It produces a great quantity of sugar, and the best Brazil wood.

PERMUTATION

Pages 453-453

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, the same with bartering. In the canon-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, permutation denotes

PERNIO

Pages 454-454

a kibe, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> chilbain, is a little ulcer, occasioned by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, feet, heels, nose, and lips. It <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> come on when warm parts are too suddenly exposed to cold, or when parts from being too cold are suddenly exposed to a considerable warmth; and has always a tendency to gangrene, in which it frequently terminates. It most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> attacks children of a sanguine <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> and delicate <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; and may be prevented or removed by such remedies as invigorate the system, and are capable of removing any tendency to gangrene in the constitution. See Medicine, p. 281. PERONÆUS, in anatomy, is an epithet applied to some of the muscles of the perone or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIBULA">fibula</a>. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the muscles.

PERONNE

Pages 454-454

a strong town of France, in Picardy, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Santerre. It is said never to have been taken, though often besieged. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOMME">Somme</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 1. N. Lat. 44. 50.

PERORATION

Pages 454-454

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, the epilogue <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> last <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>, wherein what the orator had insisted on through his whole discourse is urged afresh with greater vehemence and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. The peroration consists of two parts. 1. Recapitulation; wherein the substance of what was diffused throughout the whole speech is collected briefly and cursorily, and summed up with new force and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. 2. The moving the passions; which is peculiar to the peroration, that the matters of the art call this part sedes afficiens. The passions to be raised are various, according to the various kinds of oration. In a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, admiration, emulation, joy, &c. In an invective, hatred, contempt, &c. In a deliberation, hope, confidence, or fear. The qualities required in the peroration are, that it be very vehement and passionate, and that it be short; because, as Cicero observes, tears soon dry up.

PERPETUAL

Pages 454-454

something that endures always, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> lasts for ever. PERPETUAL <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">Motion</a>. See Movement.

PERPIGNAN

Pages 454-454

a considerable town of Roussillon in France, with a strong citadel, an university, and a bishop's see. It is seated on the river Tet; over which there is an handsome <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, partly in a plain, and partly on a hill, E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 43. N. Lat. 45. 18.

PERQUISITE

Pages 454-454

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is anything gotten by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s own industry, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> purchased with his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to what descends to him from his father or other ancestor.

PERRAULT

Pages 454-454

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLAUDE">Claude</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1626, with as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a genius for arts, and a greater for letters, than his brother. Colbert chose him first clerk of the buildings, of which he was superintendent, and afterward made him comptroller general of the finances under him. He was one of the first members of the academy of the belles lettres and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, and was received into the French academy in 1671. His poem, La Peinture, printed in 1668, was universally admired: that entitled La fleur de <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> le <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a>, in which he exalted the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> authors above the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, was a prelude to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> with all the learned. After he had disengaged himself from this contest, he applied himself to draw up eulogies of several great men of the 17th century, with their portraits, of which he has collected 102. There are other esteemed works of Perrault.—Besides these there were two other brothers, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and Nicholas, who made themselves known in the literary world.

PERRON

Pages 454-455

a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> distinguished by his abilities and learning, was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of Bern in 1556. He was educated by Julian Davy, his father, a very learned Calvinist, who taught him Latin and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; after which, he by himself became acquainted with the Greek and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and the poets. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Desportes, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of Tyron, made him known to Henry III. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of France, who conceived a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem for him. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, Du Perron abjured Calvinism, and afterwards embraced the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>; and having given great proofs of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and learning, he was chosen to pronounce the funeral <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Scots. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of Henry III. he retired to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Cardinal de <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a>, and took great pains pains in bringing back the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome. Among others, he gained over Henry Spondeanus, afterwards bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PAMIERS">Pamiers</a>. He also chiefly contributed to engage Henry IV. to change his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> sent him to negotiate his reconciliation to the holy see, in which he succeeded. Du Perron was consecrated bishop of Evereaux while he resided at Rome. On his return to France, he wrote, preached, and disputed against the reformed; particularly against Du Pleffis Mornay, with whom he had a public conference in the presence of the king at Fontainbleau. He was made cardinal in 1604, by pope Clement VIII., at the solicitation of Henry IV., who afterwards nominated him to the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENS">Sens</a>. The king at length sent him to Rome with Cardinal Joyeuse, in order to terminate the disputes which had arisen between Paul V. and the Venetians. It is said that this pope had such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> of the cardinal Du Perron, that he used to say, "Let us pray to God to inspire the cardinal Du Perron, for he <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> persuade us to do whatever he pleases." After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Henry IV. he retired into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, where he put the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to his works; and, setting up a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>-house, corrected every sheet himself. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1618. His works were collected after his death; and published at Paris in 3 vols folio.

PERROT

Pages 455-455

Sieur d'Ablancourt, one of the first geniuses of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born at Chalons in 1606. After studying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> about three years, he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> to follow the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>. At eighteen years of age he was admitted advocate of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and frequented the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>; but he soon conceived a distaste for it, and therefore discontinued his practice. This displeased an uncle, but whose favour he recovered by quitting the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. He could not, however, be prevailed upon to take orders in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; and some years after, he had a desire to return to the religion he had abjured. But, that he might not do anything rashly, he resolved to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> philosophy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. For that purpose he chose for his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> Mr Stuart a Scotsman and Lutheran, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning. Almost three years he spent in the most assiduous study; and then set out from Paris to Champagne, where he abjured the Roman Catholic, and once more embraced the Protestant religion. In 1627 he was admitted a member of the French academy; a little after which, he undertook a translation of Tacitus. Whilst he was engaged in that laborious task, he retired to his small estate of Ablancourt, and lived there till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in 1664. He was a man of fine understanding, of great piety and integrity, and of universal learning. Moreri has given a catalogue of his works, the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of which consist of translations, which seemed rather originals.

PERRY

Pages 455-455

a drink made from pears, in the same manner as cider is from apples. See CYDER.

PERSECUTION

Pages 455-455

is any pain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> affliction which a person designedly inflicts upon another; and, in a more restrained <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the sufferings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> on account of their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. Historians usually reckon ten general persecutions, the first of which was under the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Nero, 31 years after our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s ascension; when that emperor having set fire to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Rome, threw the odium Persepolis of that execrable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> on the Christians, who under that pretence were wrapped up in the skins of wild beasts, and worried and devoured by dogs; others were crucified, and others burnt alive. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> was under Domitian, in the year 95. In this persecution St John the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> was sent to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATMOS">Patmos</a> in order to be employed in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. The third began in the third year of Trajan, in the year 100, and was carried on with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> violence for several years. The fourth was under Antoninus the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, when the Christians were banished from their houses, forbidden to shew their heads, reproached, beaten, hurried from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place, plundered, imprisoned, and stoned. The fifth began in the year 197, under the emperor Severus. The sixth began with the reign of the emperor Maximinus in 235. The seventh, which was the most dreadful persecution that had ever been known in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, began in the year 250, in the reign of the emperor Decius, when the Christians were in all places driven from their habitations, stripped of their estates, tormented with racks, &c. The eighth began in the year 257, in the fourth year of the reign of the emperor Valerian. The ninth was under the emperor Aurelian, A.D. 274; but this was very inconsiderable; and the tenth began in the 19th year of Diocletian, A.D. 303. In this dreadful persecution, which lasted ten years, houses filled with Christians were set on fire, and whole droves were tied together with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> and thrown into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

PERSEPOLIS

Pages 455-456

formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, situated in N. Lat. 30° 30' E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 84°; now in ruins, but remarkable for the most magnificent remains of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> temple that are to be found throughout the world.—This <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> stood in one of the finest plains in Persia, being 18 or 19 leagues in length, and in some places two, in some four, and in others six leagues in breadth. It is watered by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> river Araxes, now Bendemit, and by a multitude of rivulets besides. Within the compass of this plain, there are between 1000 and 1500 villages, without reckoning those in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, all adorned with pleasant gardens, and planted with shady trees. The entrance of this plain on the west side has received as much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, as the city it covers could do from industry or art. It consists of a range of mountains steep and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, four leagues in length, and about two miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, forming two flat banks, with a rising terrace in the middle, the summit of which is perfectly plain and even, all of native rock. In this there are such openings, and the terraces are so fine and so even, that one would be tempted to think the whole the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of art, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and prodigious elevation thereof, did not convince one that it is a wonder too great for ought but nature to produce. Undoubtedly these banks were the very <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the advanced guards from Persepolis took <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a>, and from which Alexander found it so difficult to dislodge them. One cannot from hence descry the ruins of the city, because the banks are too high to be overlooked; but one can perceive on every side the ruins of walls and of edifices, which heretofore adorned the range of mountains of which we are speaking. On the west and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, this city is defended in the like like manner: so that, considering the height and evenness of these banks, one may safely say, with a late ingenious traveller, that there is not in the world a place so fortified by nature. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> palace of the kings of Persia, called by the inhabitants Chilminar, i.e. forty columns, is situated at the foot of the mountain; the walls of this stately <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> are still standing on three sides: but as a particular account of the noble remains of antiquity to be met with there would exceed our limits, we must refer the reader to Sir John Chardin's travels, or the fifth volume of the Universal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, where a full <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of them is given.

PERSEUS

Pages 456-456

the most <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> of all the Greek heroes, founded the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Mycenae, of which he became afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, and where he and his posterity reigned for 100 years. He flourished, according to most chronologists, 1348 B.C. but, according to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, only 1628. Perseus, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. See there, n° 206.

PERSEVERANCE

Pages 456-456

in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, a Christian virtue, by which we are enabled to persist in the way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> to the end. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> perseverance of the saints is a doctrine much controverted between the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMINIANS">Arminians</a> and Calvinists; the latter of whom maintain that it is impossible for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> to be lost, and consequently make perseverance to the end a necessary <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> thereof; while the others imagine, that the most confirmed <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a> are never out of a possibility of falling.

PERSICA

Pages 473-474

PERSICA, the Peach, is by Linnæus referred to the same class and genus with amygdalus; however, as they are so commonly reckoned to be different genera, we have thought proper to distinguish them. There are a great variety of peach-trees planted in the gardens, some of which are preserved only for the beauty of their flowers, but most of them for the sake of the fruit. Of those remarkable for the beauty of their flowers the principal are, 1. The vulgaris, or common peach-tree, with double flowers, which is a very great ornament in gardens, producing very large double flowers of a beautiful red or purple colour, and grows to a considerable size. 2. The humilis, or dwarf-almond. 3. The africana, or double-flowering dwarf-almond. These two reach not above the height of three or four feet, though their flowers are of equal beauty with the former. Of the peach-trees cultivated for the sake of their fruit there are a great number, to describe which particularly would exceed the proper bounds of this article. They are raised from the stones of the fruit, which should be planted in autumn on a bed of light dry earth, about three inches deep and four inches asunder. In the winter the beds should be covered with

PERSICANA

Pages 474-474

Persicana, with mulch to protect them from the frost. In this bed they should remain for a year; when they are to be taken up and planted in a nursery, where they are to remain one or two years; after which they must be removed to the places where they are to continue. **PERSICANA**, in botany. See **POLYGONUM**. **

PERSIUS

Pages 474-474

PERSIUS** (Flaccus Aulus), a Latin poet in the reign of Nero, celebrated for his satires. He was born, according to some, at Volterra in Tuscany; and according to others, at Tigilia, in the gulf Della Specia, in the year 34. He was educated till 12 years old at Valterro; and afterwards continued his studies at Rome under Palazon the grammarian, Virginius the rhetorician, and Cornutus the Stoic philosopher, who contracted a friendship for him. Persius consulted that illustrious friend in the composition of his verses. Lucian also studied with him under Cornutus; and appeared so charmed with his verses, that he was incessantly breaking out into acclamations at the beautiful passages in his satires: an example rarely seen in poets of equal rank. He was a steady friend, a good son, an affectionate brother and parent. He was chaste, meek, and modest: which shews how wrong it is to judge of a man's morals by his writings; for the satires of Persius are not only licentious, but sharp and full of bitterness. He wrote but seldom; and it was some time before he applied himself regularly to it. Persius was of a weak constitution, and troubled with a bad stomach; of which he died in the 36th year of his age. Six of his satires remain; in their judgments of which the critics have been much divided, excepting as to their obscurity, Persius being indeed the most obscure of all the Latin poets. As a poet, he is certainly inferior to Horace and Juvenal; and all the labours of Isaac Caubon, who has written a most learned and elaborate commentary upon him, cannot make him equal to either of them as a satirist, though in virtue and learning he exceeded them both. He was a professed imitator of Horace; yet had little of Horace's wit, ease, and talent at ridicule. His style is grand, figurative, poetical, and suitable to the dignity of the Stoic philosophy; and hence he shines most in recommending virtue and integrity: here it is that satire becomes him. He was too grave to court the muses with success: but he had a great soul, susceptible of noble sentiments, which give a grace but to indifferent poetry. His contemporaries thought highly of him. Quintilian allows, that Persius, although he wrote but one book of satires, acquired a great deal of true glory, *Multum et vere gloria quaevis uno libro Persius meruit*: and Persius Martial says much the same thing, *Sepius in libro memoratur Persius unus*, &c. **

PERSON**, an individual substance of a rational intelligent nature. Thus we say, an ambassador represents the person of his prince; and that, in law, the father and son are reputed the same person. **PERSON**, in grammar, a term applied to such nouns or pronouns as, being either prefixed or understood, are the nominatives in all inflections of a verb; or it is the agent or patient in all finite or

personal verbs. See **GRAMMAR**. **PERSONAL**, any thing that concerns, or is restrained to, the person; thus it is a maxim in ethics, that all faults are personal. **
