They are succeeded by round berries about the size of small cherries, inclosed in an inflated bladder, which turns <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> in autumn, when the top opens and discloses the red berry, which is soft, pulpy, and filled with flat kidney-shaped seeds. Soon after the fruit is ripe, the stalks decay to the root. The plant is easily propagated, either by seeds, or parting the roots.

PHYSETER

Pages 679-679
or Spermaceti-fish, in zoology, a genus belonging to the order of cetaceans. There are four species; the most remarkable are, 1. The microps, or black-headed cachalot, with a long fin on the back, and the upper jaw considerably longer than the under one. A fish of this kind was cast ashore on Cramond island, near Edinburgh, December 22d, 1769; its length was 54 feet; the greatest circumference, which was just beyond the eyes, 30; the upper jaw was five feet longer than the lower, whose length was ten feet. The head was of a most enormous size, very thick, and above one-third the size of the fish: the end of the upper jaw was quite blunt, and near nine feet high: the spout hole was placed near the end of it. The teeth were placed in the lower jaw, 23 on each side, all pointing outwards; in the upper jaw, opposite to them, were an equal number of cavities, in which the ends of the teeth lodged when the mouth was closed. One of the teeth measured eight inches long, the greatest circumference the same. It is hollow within side for the depth of three inches, and the mouth of the cavity very wide: it is thickest at the bottom, and grows very small at the point, bending very much; but in some the flexure is more than in others. These, as well as the teeth of all other whales we have observed, are very hard, and cut like ivory. The eyes are very small, and remote from the nose. The pectoral fins placed near the corners of the mouth, and were only three feet long: it had no other fin, only a large protuberance on the middle of the back. The tail was a little forked, and 14 feet from tip to tip. The penis seven feet and a half long. Linnaeus informs us, that this species pursues and terrifies the porpoises to such a degree as often to drive them on shore. 2. The catodon, or round-headed cachalot, with a fistula in the snout, and having no back fin. Of this species, a hundred and two of different sizes were cast ashore at one time, on one of the Orkney Isles, the largest 24 feet in length. The head is round, the opening of the mouth small: Sibbald says it has no spout-hole, but only nostrils. But Mr Pennant is of opinion, that the former being placed at the extremity of the nose has been mistaken by him for the latter. Some teeth of this species are an inch and three quarters long, and in the largest part, of the thickness of one's thumb. The top is quite flat, and marked with concentric lines; the bottom is more slender than the top, and pierced with a small orifice; instead of a back fin there was a rough space. For the method of extracting the spermaceti from the brain of these creatures, see the article SPERMACETI.

PHYSIC

Pages 679-679
or Physick, the art of healing; properly called Medicine. The word is formed from the Greek φυσικής, "nature;" in regard medicine consists principally in the observation of nature. See Physics and Medicine.

PHYSICAL

Pages 679-679

something belonging to, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> really existing, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we say a physical point, in opposition to a mathematical one, which only exists in the imagination; a physical substance or body, in opposition to spirit, or metaphysical substance, &c.

PHYSICIAN

PHYSICS

Pages 679-681
or ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural Philosophy. By the word physics, in its most extensive sense, we understand The science of the operations of nature, and of its productions. This definition is alone sufficient to inform us, what are the particular parts of physics, and what are the means it employs to attain its ends. Thus Natural s="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History, or Zoology, Botany, and Mineralogy, describe those bodies that nature produces, as far as they are discernible by our senses. So Chemistry and Experimental Philosophy discover to us, at least in part, the composition of bodies, and the various alterations of which those compositions are susceptible. So General and Speculative Physics draws from all these preliminary observations, from all these matters of fact, just consequences relative to the universal laws of nature, to the properties, forces, action, and essential qualities of bodies. The object of physics being the examination of the whole frame of nature, so far as it is visible and palpable to man, it is easily to conceive, that it must form the most extensive branch of human knowledge, seeing that the operations of nature are varied almost to infinity. To reduce this immense subject into some order, philosophers have begun by dividing all the productions of this globe into three classes, which they call kingdoms, and distinguish into the vegetable, the mineral, and animal s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom. Botany, mineralogy, and natural history properly so called, teach therefore all that is come to the knowledge of man in each of these kingdoms. Chemistry resolves all bodies, and consequently shows the manner in which they are compounded. Philosophers have likewise discovered that the universe is composed of elements, of which there are four, Earth, Water, Fire, and Air. Experimental philosophy, by numberless essays and observations, explains the manner in which these elements operate upon each other, and the effects that they produce. The knowledge of those heavenly bodies, whose various courses fill the vast expanse of the firmament, and of their properties and courses either real or apparent, is comprised in the science of Astronomy. All the ancient oriental nations, including the Hebrews and the Egyptians, were mere novices in physics; and their ignorance seems to prove the infancy of the world. The Greeks, men of a subtle and inquisitive genius, went further, and sometimes guessed right enough, though very rarely. Empedocles, for example, who is ranked by some among the Pythagoreans, professed the system of the four elements in nature; and added thereto two principles, which he called principium amicitiae, and principium contentiones. The first, according to him, is the cause of the coalition of beings; and the second, that of their reception or separation. Was not this derived from the same origin as the celebrated system of the attraction and repulsion of bodies? Whatever was the cause, the progress of physics has ever been slow; and we are astonished when we see ancient writers of the greatest genius, as Plutarch and a hundred others, make use of such wretched reasoning when they mention those subjects that relate to physics. Among the Romans, Lucretius and Cicero have indeed written on these subjects; but they have only related the opinions of the Greeks, which were not worthy of great regard. Seneca and Pliny went further; and we are obliged to the latter for the useful observations which he has made on many parts of this science, although he is frequently too credulous. Pliny, moreover, does not belong to the class of dogmatic authors on physics, as he gives only an historical account of these matters. The first ages of Christianity were the ages of darkness for all the sciences and the arts. It was not till very late, that Bacon baron of Verulam, and some of his contemporaries, produced the first sparks of those fair lights that have since blazed forth by the happy labours of their successors. Gassendus, Descartes, Rudiger, Newton, Leibnitz, Wolff, and a multitude of other celebrated philosophers, have diffused these lights over philosophy; and all these great men have at last established that method of treating it which is alone able to discover the truth. This method is perfectly simple. They begin with establishing facts by means of experiments and observations, and draw from thence consequences relative to their causes and principles. For, as soon as experience or the senses have discovered what passes in nature, the mind endeavours to discover what cannot be distinguished by the senses; that is to say, what may be the cause or the end of each phenomenon or operation in nature; and by this means it constantly combines the accuracy of observation with the sagacity and rigour of argument. It is certain, that a diligent observation of the subjects of Mineralogy and Zoology, united with the study of Botany, affords every possible information relative to natural history in general; that is, we thereby acquire the historical knowledge of all the beings of this globe, that nature produces. Experimental Philosophy, aided by Chemistry, and several parts of the Mathematics, disclose the composition of these beings, and the springs by which nature operates in their production, and in making them produce, in their turn, the mutual effects of the elements, &c. Astronomy, of which we have in like manner treated, explains the nature of the celestial bodies and their courses; and all these various sciences, united, conduct us at last, as far as the human mind is able to proceed, to the determination of the general laws of nature in the order of the universe; from whence result universal and speculative Physics, of which it remains to give a cursory idea. This science, which for some thousand years has been justly called speculative, seeing that it has been founded altogether on vain speculations, and suppositions merely ideal, is at length supported by experiments and observations that bear the stamp of manifest demonstrations. It now forms no system, admits of no hypothesis, but such whose veracity and certainty have been previously demonstrated. For which purpose it calls to its assistance all the subordinate sciences, and makes use of their operations in the investigation and establishment of its principles. As Mineralogy, Botany, Zoology, Chemistry, Anatomy, Physiology, and almost all the other parts of Physic, Geography, Experimental Philosophy, all the particular sciences which are comprised under the general denomination of Mathematics; all these have relation to general physics, and each of them concurs more or less to furnish materials for its sublime operations. When, by the assistance of the labours of these, physics has established the veracity of facts, it then applies the most subtile, abstract, and profound ratiocination, to draw from thence just consequences, and to establish general principles, founded on these facts, relative to the universal laws of nature; to the celestial bodies, and the true order of the universe; to the elements, and their reciprocal action; to meteors; to bodies that are both visible and tangible; to the reciprocal action of palpable bodies; to the generation of beings in general, and of man in particular; to every production of nature in all the three kingdoms: in a word, it endeavours to account, as far as the weak lights of the human understanding are capable of accounting, for all the phenomena of heaven and earth. See all the abovementioned sciences generally treated in the order of the alphabet.

PHYSIOGNOMONICS

Pages 681-681

among physicians, denote such signs as, being taken from the countenance, serve to indicate the state, disposition, &c. both of the body and mind: and hence the art of reducing these signs to practice is termed physiognomy.

PHYSIOGNOMY

Pages 681-681

the art of knowing the humour, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> disposition of a person, from observation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of its members or features. The word is formed from the Greek φύσις, "<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>," and γνώσκω, "I know." Baptista Porta and Robert Fludd are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> authors on physiognomy. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ones are the sophist Adamantius, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>; the physiognomy of which last we have translated into Latin by De Lacuna. There seems to be something in physiognomy, and it may perhaps bear a much purer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> than what these authors were acquainted withal. This, at least, we dare say, that of all the fanciful arts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, diffused among the moderns, there is none has so much foundation in nature as this. There is an apparent correspondence between the face and the mind. The features and lineaments of the one are directed by the motions and affections of the other, there is even a peculiar arrangement of the members of the face, a peculiar disposition of the countenance, to each particular affection, perhaps to each particular idea of the mind. In effect, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the face, physiognomy, is as copious, nay, perhaps as distinct and intelligible, as that of the tongue. The foundation of physiognomy is this: The different objects that present themselves to the senses, nay, the different <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> that arise in the mind, do each make some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the spirits; and each an impression correspondent or adequate to its cause; therefore each a different impression. Now, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> by repeated acts, or the frequent entertaining of a favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, or vice, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> temperament has hurried or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> dragged one to, the face is often put in that posture which attends such acts; the animal-spirits <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> make such patent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> through the nerves (in which the essence of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> consists), that the face is sometimes unalterably set in that posture, or at least falls insensibly and mechanically into that posture, unless some present object distorts it therefrom, or dissimulation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> it. This reasoning is confirmed by observation. Thus we see <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> drinkers with eyes generally set to the nose; the adducent muscles being often employed to put them in that posture, in order to view their loved liquor in the glass in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of drinking; whence those muscles are also denominated bibitory muscles. Thus also lascivious persons are remarkable for the oculorum mobilis petulantia, as Petronius calls it.—Physiognomy. Hence we may account for the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a> expecting face waiting the spirit, the melancholy face of most sectaries, the studious face of men of great application of mind, &c. Were our observation a little more strict and delicate, we might doubtless not only distinguish habits and tempers, but even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>.—In effect, does there need much penetration to distinguish the fierce look of the veteran soldier, the contentious look of the practised pleader, the solemn look of the minister of state, &c. Within these few years, one M. Lavater of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a> has attempted to revive the trade of physiognomy, and published a quarto volume on the certainty and utility of the art. His reasons for believing in it, besides those already given, are to the following purpose. "Every moment we are acting upon physiognomical principles, without being aware of it; and not men only, but the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a> also, even insects, both know their most convenient food, and their enemies, by the outside. What are we doing when we choose out some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> as the best, or when we prefer one <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> to another, but judging, from the outside, of the internal qualities? We then certainly <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> the physiognomer. That every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> is undoubtedly a natural physiognomer, is still more apparent from considering the effects which result from the first sight of persons unknown. We are often much inclined to tell our friends, that we do not like the man before us, although we be in no <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> acquainted with him. Whoever is an attentive observer of what passes in his own mind, knows that he no sooner sees any person, than certain attendant ideas succeed the first impression, which involve nothing less than a judgment over his dispositions of mind, so far that we pronounce him to be of a quite different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> from some others of our acquaintance. We cannot, in every <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, tell exactly why we judge thus, whether it be from his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, from his eyes, or from his nose. Nor can we always determine, whether the impression be not from different ideas complicated. This is not to be learned by rule; we judge only from a feeling acquired by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. As physiognomical practice is general, it cannot be but founded in nature; and one should think, therefore, that it possibly might be the subject of science. Does not practice always precede theoretical knowledge?" The rules for this extraordinary art are not laid <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the volume we now speak of; however, so many things are necessary on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, that no body, it would seem, without a tolerable share of self-sufficiency, could engage in the art. The reason is, that it requires virtue in the artist to perceive virtue in the face of him whom he inspects; and consequently, unless the physiognomist is possessed of all the virtues in the world, he will be perpetually <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> false conclusions; for, "No one, (says our author,) certainly is able to discern the look of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>, or the countenance of an exalted <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, but he who is magnanimous himself, who thinks nobly, and who is disposed to act generously."

PHYSIOLOGY

Pages 681-682

properly denotes a discourse of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> bodies; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, it is that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> which treats of the various phenomena Phytology mena of nature in a scientifical and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> way. See Physiology. Picardy. Among physicians, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> physiology denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, and its several constituent parts, with their relations and functions. See Anatomy.

PHYTOLOGY

Pages 682-682

a discourse concerning the kinds and virtues of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>.

PI-BAHIROTH

Pages 687-687

(Moses); understood to be a mouth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> narrow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, called Chiroth, or Eiroth, and lying not far from the bottom of the western <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>; before which mouth the children of Israel encamped, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> before their entering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>).

PIAZZA

Pages 682-682

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; popularly called piache, an Italian name for a portico, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> covered walk, supported by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>.

PICARD

Pages 682-682

a native of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, who improved upon the errors of the Adamites. He called himself the Son of God; and pretended, that, like a new <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, he was sent by his father to restore the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which, according to him, chiefly consisted in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> with respect to women, and in going quite naked. It is said, that though <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> was instituted among them, no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> was allowed to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> with a woman without first obtaining leave of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. He fortified himself in an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the river Lifnik, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues from Thabor, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> residence of the famous Zifca; but unhappily for him, 40 of his followers being gone out upon a party, basely plundered some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> houses, and killed upwards of 200 persons; upon which Zifca attacked the island, took it, and put all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PICARDS">Picards</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, except two, whose lives he spared in order to learn from their own mouths the principles of their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. This happened in the year 1420. Picard (John), an able mathematician, and one of the most learned astronomers of the 17th century, was born at Fleche, and became <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> of Rillie in Anjou. Going to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, he was in 1666 received into the Academy of Sciences, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of astronomer. In 1671, he was sent, by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, to the castle of Uraniburg, built by Tycho Brahe in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, to make astronomical observations there; and from thence he brought the original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> wrote by Tycho Brahe, which are the more valuable as they differ in many places from the printed copies, and contain a book more than has yet appeared. He made important discoveries in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>; and was the first who travelled through several parts of France, to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the meridian. His works are, 1. A treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVELLING">levelling</a>. 2. Fragments of dioptrics. 3. Experimenta circa aquas effluentias. 4. De mensuris. 5. De mensura liquidorum & aridorum. 6. A voyage to Uraniburg, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> astronomical observations made in Denmark. 7. Astronomical observations made in several parts of France, &c. These, and some other of his works, which are much esteemed, are in the fifth and seventh volumes of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Academy of Sciences.

PICARDY

Pages 682-682

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Hainault, Artois, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; on the east, by Champagne; on the south, by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of France; and on the west, by Normandy and the British channel. It is divided into the Upper, Middle, and Lower Picardy; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOMME">Somme</a>, the Oyse, the Canche, the Lis, the Scarpe, the Deule, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">Aa</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very fertile in corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and pastures; but it produces no wine. They have a considerable trade in woollen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and the inhabitants are a very industrious people. Amiens is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

PICART

Pages 682-682

a celebrated engraver, son of Stephen Picart, also a famous engraver, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1673. He learned the elements of his art from his father, and studied <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> under Sebastien le Clerc. As he embraced the reformed <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, he settled in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> to enjoy the free <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of it; where his genius produced those masterpieces which made him esteemed the most ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>: and a multitude of books are embellished with plates of his engraving. He died in 1733.

PICENTIA

Pages 682-682

(Strabo, Pliny); the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Picentini, whose territory, called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGER">Ager</a> Picentinus, a small district, lay on the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, from the Promontorium Minervae, the south boundary of Campania on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, to the river Silarue, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> boundary of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUCANIA">Lucania</a>, extending within <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> as far as the Samnites and Hirpinii, though the exact termination cannot be assigned. The Greeks <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> confound the Picentini and Picentii, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> carefully distinguish them. The former, with no more than two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> that can be named, Sibennum and Picentia; the situation of both doubtful: only Pliny says the latter stood within land, at some distance from the sea. Now thought to be Bicenza, (Holstenius), in the Principato Citra of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>.

PICENUM

Pages 682-682

(Cæsar, Pliny, Florus); Picenus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGER">Ager</a>, (Cicero, Sallust, Livy, Tacitus); Ager Picentium, (Varro): a territory of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, lying to the east of Umbria, from the Apennine to the Adriatic; on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> extending from the river Aesis on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, as far as the Pretutiani to the south. In the upper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> northern <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of their territory the Umbri excluded them from the Apennine, as far as Camerium, (Strabo); but in the lower or southern part they extended from the Adriatic to the Apennine. A very fruitful territory, and very populous. Picentii, the people, (Cicero); from the singular, Picen, (Livy): different from the Picentini, on the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, tho' called so by the Greeks; but <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> calls them Piceni, as does also Pliny. Their territory at this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> is supposed to form the greatest part of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>, (Cluverius.)

PICKERY

Pages 682-682

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, petty theft, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> stealing things of small value.

PICKETS

Pages 682-685

in fortification, stakes sharp at one end, and sometimes shod with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, used in laying out the ground, of about three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; but, when used for pinning the fascines of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>, they are from three to five feet long. Pickets, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, are about five <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> six feet long, shod with iron, to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIN">pin</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARK">park</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, in laying out the boundaries of the park. Pickets, in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, are also stakes of about six or eight inches long, to fallen the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENT">tent</a> cords, in pitching the tents; also, of about four or five feet long, dri- wen into the ground near the tents of the horsemen, to tie their horses to. Picket, an out-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> posted before an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, to give notice of an enemy approaching. Picket, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> so called, where a soldier stands with one foot upon a sharp-pointed stake; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his standing is limited according to the offence. Picquering, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, or skirmish, made by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> detached from two armies for pillage, or before a main <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> begins. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIQUET">Piquet</a>, or Picquet, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, much in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> throughout the polite world. It is played between two persons, with only 32 cards; all the duces, threes, fours, fives, and fixes, being set aside. In reckoning at this game, every card goes for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> it bears, as a ten for ten; only all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>-cards go for ten, and the ace for eleven; and the usual game is one hundred up.—In playing, the ace wins the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, the king the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, and so <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. Twelve cards are dealt round, usually by two and two; which done, the remainder are laid in the middle; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> one of the gamblers finds he has not a court-card in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, he is to declare he has carte blanche, and tell how many cards he <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> lay out, and desire the other to discard, that he may shew his game, and satisfy his antagonist that the carte-blanche is real; for which he reckons ten. Each person discards, i.e., lays aside a certain number of his cards, and takes in a like number from the stock.—The first, of the eight cards, may take three, four, or five; the dealer all the remainder, if he pleases. After discarding, the eldest hand examines what <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> he has most cards of; and reckoning how many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> he has in that suit, if the other have not so many in that or any other suit, he tells one for every ten of that suit.—He who thus reckons most is said to win the point. The point being over, each examines what sequences he has of the same suit, viz.: how many tierces, or sequences of three, quartes or fours, quintes or fives, fixes or six's, &c. For a tierce they reckon three points, for a quarte four, for a quinte five, for a fixieme six, &c. And the several sequences are distinguished in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> by the cards they begin from: thus ace, king, and queen, are called tierce <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>; king, queen, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNAVE">knave</a>, tierce to a king; knave, ten, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, tierce to a knave, &c. and the best tierce, quarte, or quinte, i.e. that which takes its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from the best card, prevails, so as to make all the others in that hand good, and destroy all those in the other hand.—In like manner, a quarte in one hand sets aside a tierce in the other. The sequences over, they proceed to examine how many aces, kings, queens, knaves, and tens, each holds; reckoning for every three of any fort, three; but here too, as in sequences, he that with the same number of threes, has one that is higher than any the other has, e.g. three aces, has all his others made good hereby, and his adversary's all set aside.—But four of any fort, which is called a quatorze, always sets aside three. All the game in hand being thus reckoned, the eldest proceeds to play, reckoning one for every card he plays above a nine, and the other follows him in the suit; and the highest card of the suit wins the trick.—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">Note</a>, unless a trick be won with a card above a nine (except the last trick), nothing is reckoned for it; though the trick serves afterwards towards winning the cards; and that he who plays last does not reckon for his cards, unless he wins the trick. The cards being played out, he that has most tricks reckons ten for winning the cards.—If they have tricks alike, neither reckons anything.—The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> being finished, and each having marked up his game, they proceed to deal again as before, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> afresh each time for the deal. If both parties be within a few points of being up, the carte blanche is the first thing that reckons, then the point, then the sequences, then the quatorzes or threes, then the tenth cards. He that can reckon 30 in hand by carte blanche, points, quintes, &c. without playing, ere the other has reckoned any thing, reckons 90 for them; and this is called a repique.—If he reckons above 30, he reckons so many above 90. If he can make up 30, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> in hand and part play, ere the other has told any thing, he reckons for them 60. And this is called a pique. Whence the name of the game.—He that wins all the tricks, instead of ten, which is his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> for winning the cards, reckons 40. And this is called a capot. Picris, Ox-tongue; a genus of the polygamia æqualis order, belonging to the syngenesia clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are four <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, of which the only remarkable one is the echoides, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ox-tongue, growing spontaneously in corn-fields in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. It has undivided leaves embracing the stem, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> blossoms, which sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> soon after noon, at other times remain open till nine at night. It is an agreeable pot-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a> while young. The juice is milky, but not too acrid. Pickle, a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRINE">brine</a> or liquor, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> composed of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, &c. sometimes with the addition of spices, wherein meat, fruit, and other things are preserved and seasoned. Picts, the name of one of those nations who anciently possessed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Britain. It is generally believed that they were so called from their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> their bodies. But as this custom prevailed among the other <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inhabitants of Britain, who used the glastra of Pliny and the vitrum of Mela for the like purpose, it may be asked, Why the name of Picti was confined by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to only one tribe, when it was equally applicable to many others? Why should they <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> them only by an epithet without ever annexing their proper name? Or why should they impose a new name on this people only, when they give their proper name to every other tribe which they have occasion to speak of? As these questions cannot be answered in any satisfactory manner, it is plain we must look for some other derivation of the name. The Highlanders of Scotland, who speak the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALEDONIA">Caledonia</a>, express the name of this once famous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> Pitich; a name familiar to the ears of the most illiterate, who could never have derived it from the Roman authors. The word Pitich means pilferers or plunderers. The appellation lation was probably imposed upon this people by their neighbours, or assumed by themselves, some time after the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARACALLA">Caracalla</a>, when the unguarded state of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, on which this people bordered, gave them frequent opportunities of making incursions thither, and committing depredations. Accordingly this name seems to have been unknown till the end of the 3rd century. Eumenius the Panegyrist is the first Roman author who mentions this people under their new name of Pictish, or, with a Latin termination, Picci. When we say that this name may have been probably assumed for the reason <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> now mentioned, we must observe, that, in those days of violence, the character of a robber was attended with no disgrace. If he had the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to form his schemes well, and to execute them successfully, he was rather praised than blamed for his conduct; providing he made no encroachments on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of his own tribe, or any of its allies. We <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> this as no peculiar stigma upon the Picts; for other nations of antiquity, in the like rude state, thought and acted as they did. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a>, lib. 3. p. 3. and Virg. Aen. 7. 745 & 749. Concerning the origin of the Picts, authors are much divided. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a> derives them from the Agathyrsi, Pomponius Laetus from the Germans, Bede from the Scythians, Cambden and father Innes from the ancient Britons, Sillingfleet from a people inhabiting the Cherestoneus Cymbricae, and Keating and O'Flaherty, on the authority of the Pictish Cashel, derive them from the Thracians. But the most probable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is, that they were the descendents of the old Caledonians. Several reasons are urged in support of this opinion by Dr Macpherson; and the words of Eumenius, "Caledonum, aliorumque Pictorum, filvas, &c." plainly imply that the Picts and Caledonians were one and the same people. As there has been much dispute about the origin of the Picts, so there has been likewise about their language. There are many reasons which make it plain that their tongue was the Gaelic or Celtic; and these reasons are a further <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of their having been of Caledonian extract. Through the east and north-east coasts of Scotland (which were possessed by the Picts) we meet with an innumerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of names of places, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, &c. which are manifestly Galic. From a very old <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the priory of St Andrews (Dalrymple's Collections, p. 122.) it appears, that in the days of Hurtus, the last Pictish king of that name, St Andrew's was called Mukros; and that the town now called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEENSFERRY">Queensferry</a> had the name of Ardchinnichan. Both these words are plain Gaelic. The first signifies "the heath or promontory of boars;" and the latter, "the height or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Kenneth." In the list of Pictish kings published by father Innes, most of the names are obviously Galic, and in many instances the same with the names in the list of Scottish or Caledonian kings published by the same author. Had Innes understood anything of this language, he would not have supposed with Cambden that the Picts spoke the British tongue. It was unlucky that the two words on which they built their conjecture (Strath and Aber) are as common in the Galic as they could have been in the British, and at this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> make a part of the names of places in countries to which the Pictish empire never extended. The names of Strathfillan and Lochaber may serve as instances. The venerable Bede, as much a stranger to the Celtic as either of the antiquaries just now mentioned, is equally unhappy in the specimen which he gives of the Pictish language in the word penuachol, "the head of the wall." Allowing the commutation of the initial p into c, as in some other <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, this word has still the same meaning in Gaelic, which Bede gives it in the Pictish. It is true, there might have been then, as well as now, a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between different dialects of the Celtic; and thus, perhaps, that pious author was led to discover five languages in Britain agreeably to the five books of Moses: A conceit from which the good <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> derived a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> deal of harmless satisfaction. The Picts of the earliest ages, as appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> testimony of all writers who examined the subject, possessed only the east and north-east <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Scotland. On one side, the ancient Drumalbin, or that ridge of mountains reaching from Lochlomond near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUMBARTON">Dumbarton</a> to the frith of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAIN">Tain</a>, which separates the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUTHERLAND">Sutherland</a> from a part of Ross, was the boundary of the Pictish dominions. Accordingly we find in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Columba, that, in travelling to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Brudius, king of the Picts, he travelled over Drumalbin, the Dorsum Britanniae of Adamnan. On the other side, the territory of the Picts was bounded by the Roman province. After Britain was relinquished by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Honorius, they and the Saxons by turns were masters of those countries which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> between the frith of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> and the river Tweed. We learn from Bede, that the Saxons were masters of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a> when he finished his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>. The Picts, however, made a conquest of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> soon after; so that, before the extinction of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, all the territories bounded on the one side by the Forth and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, and one the other by the Tweed and Solway, fell into their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. The history of the Picts, as well as of all the other ancient inhabitants of Britain, is extremely dark. The Irish historians give us a long list of Pictish kings, who reigned over Pictavia for the space of eleven or thirteen centuries before the Christian era. After them Innes, in his Critical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a>, gives us a list of above fifty, of whom no less than five held the sceptre, each for a whole century. It is probable that these writers had confounded the history of the Picts with that of their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> the old Caledonians. In any other view, their accounts of them are highly fabulous; and have been long ago confuted by Dr Macpherson of Slate, an antiquary of much learning and research. The Picts, as has been already observed, were probably not known by that name before the 2nd or 3rd century. Adamnan, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IONA">Iona</a>, is the first author that expressly mentions any Pictish king; and the oldest after him is Bede. We are informed by these two writers that St Columba converted Brudius king of the Picts to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Columba came into Britain in the year of the vulgar era 565. Before that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> we have no general record to ascertain so much as the name of any Pictish king. The history of Druis or Dreis, who is said to have reigned over the Picts in the beginning of the fifth century, when St Ninian first preached the gospel to that that nation, has all the appearance of fiction. His having reigned a hundred years, and his putting an end to a hundred wars, are stories which exceed all the bounds of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>. Brudius, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> of Columba, is the first Pictish king mentioned by any writer of authority. What <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> his ancestors made, or who were his successors on the throne of Pictavia, cannot be ascertained. Bede informs us, that, during the reign of one of them, the Picts killed Egfred king of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a> in battle, and destroyed the greatest part of his army. The same author mentions another of their kings called Naitan, for whom he had a particular regard. It was to this Naitan that Ceolfrid, abbot of Wiremouth, wrote his famous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> concerning Easter and the Tonfure; a letter in which Bede himself is supposed to have had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> hand. Roger Hoveden and Simon of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a> mention two other Pictish kings Onnust and Kinoth, the first of whom died in 761, and the latter flourished about the 774, and gave an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> to Alfred of Northumberland, who was much about that time expelled his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. The accounts given by the Scots historians of several other Pictish kings cannot be depended on; nor are the stories told by the British historians, Geoffrey of Monmouth and the author of the Eulogium Britanniae, worthy of much greater <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. In the ninth century the Pictish nation was totally subdued by the Scots in the reign of Kenneth MacAlpin. Since that time their name has been lost in that of the conquerors, with whom they were incorporated after this conquest; however, they seem to have been treated by the Scottish kings with great lenity, so that for some ages after they commanded a great deal of respect. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> of Hoghilthead, an old English historian, relates that they made a considerable figure in the army of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a> the Saint, in his disputes with Stephen, king of England. In a battle fought in the year 1136, by the English on one side, and the Scots and Picts on the other, the latter insisted on their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> right of leading the van of the Scots army, and were indulged in that request by the king. The principal seat of the Pictish kings was at Abernethy. Brudius, however, as appears from the accounts given by Adamnan, in his life of Columba, had a palace at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, which was probably near the extremity of his territory in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>; for, there is no good reason for believing, with Cambden, that this king had any property in the Western Isles, or that he had made a gift of Fona to St Columba when he visited him in that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. With respect to the manners and customs of the Picts, there is no reason to suppose they were any other than those of the old Caledonians and Scots, of which many particulars are related in the Greek and Roman writers who have occasion to speak of those nations. Picts Wall, in antiquity, a wall begun by the emperor Adrian, on the northern bounds of England, to prevent the incursions of the Picts and Scots. It was first made only of turf strengthened with palisadoes, till the emperor Severus, coming into Britain in person, built it with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. This wall, part of which still remains, begun at the entrance of the Solway Frith in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, and running north-east extended to the German Ocean. See Adrian and Picus. Severus.

PICTURE

Pages 685-685

a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a subject represented in colours, on wood, canvas, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, or the like. See Painting.

PICUS

Pages 686-686
earl of Mirandula, a prodigy of parts and learning, was the youngest child of John Francis Picus, earl of Mirandula and Concordia; and was born in the year 1463. The progress that he made in letters was so extremely rapid, that it was matter of astonishment to see even a boy one of the first poets and orators of his age. After visiting the most famous universities of France and Italy, he went to Rome; where, in 1486, before he was 24 years of age, he published 900 propositions in logic, mathematics, physics, divinity, cabalistic learning, and magic, drawn not only from Greek and Latin, but even from Jewish and Arabian writers: subjoining to his advertisement, that, "if any philosopher or divine would come to Rome to dispute with him, upon any or all of them, he would defray the expenses of his journey from the remotest corners of Italy." He enjoyed, however, the honour of this disputatious challenge quietly, without danger to his credit; for envy procured some of his propositions to be charged with heresy, and he was forbid to dispute upon them. At the age of 28, he confined himself wholly to the study of the scriptures; and undertook to combat the Jews and Mahometans, as well as to confound judicial astrology; but in this intention his credit was also saved, tho' with the loss of his life, by his dying in 1494, in his 32d year. He was called the phoenix of his age; and composed a great number of works, which have often been printed both separately and together. Picus (John Francis), prince of Mirandula, nephew of John Picus mentioned above, was born about the year 1469. He cultivated learning and the sciences after the example of his uncle; but he had a principality and dominions to superintend, which involved him in great troubles, and at last cost him his life. He was twice driven from his principality, and twice restored; and at last, in 1533, was, together with his eldest son Albert, assassinated in his own castle by his nephew Galeotti. He was a great lover of letters; and such of his works as were then composed, were inserted in the Strasbourg edition of his uncle's in 1504, and continued in future impressions, besides some others, which were never collected.

PIECE

Pages 686-686

in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, signifies sometimes the same thing with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; and sometimes, by adding the value of the pieces, it is used to express such as have no other particular name. For the piece of eight, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> piastra, see MONEY-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>. Piece, is also a kind of money of account, or rather a manner of accounting used among the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. See MONEY-Table. Piece, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, denotes an ordinary or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> pieces of the shield are the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, fess, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, saltier, chevron, and in general all those which may take up one-third of the field, when alone, and in what manner soever it be. See HERALDRY. Pieces, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, include all sorts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> guns and mortars. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTERING">Battering</a> pieces are the larger sort of guns used at sieges for making the breaches; such are the 24-pounder and culverine, the one carrying a 24 and the other an 18 <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a>. Field-pieces are 12-pounders, demi-culverines, 6-pounders, falcons, minions, and 3-pounders, which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and encamp always behind the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> line, but in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> are in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a>.—A soldier's firelock is likewise called his piece.

PIEDMONT

Pages 686-687

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a principality; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Vallois; on the east, by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> and the duchy of Montferrat; on the south, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Nice and the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>; and on the west, by Dauphiny and Savoy. It comprehends 11 small provinces, Piedmont Proper, the valleys between France and Italy, the valley of Saluza, the county of Nice, the marquisate of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUSA">Susa</a>, the duchy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AOSTA">Aosta</a>, the Canavese, the lordship of Verfail, the county of Alt, and the Langes. It was formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>; but now belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>; and lies at the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, which separate France from Italy. It is 175 miles in length, and 40 in breadth. It contains many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; among which there are rich and fruitful ful valleys, as pleasant and populous as any part of Italy. In the mountains are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of several kinds, and the forests afford a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAME">game</a>. The Piedmontese have more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> than the Savoyards, but then they are not so sincere. They are generally strongly attached to the Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and carry on so great a trade in raw <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, that the English alone have purchased to the value of 200,000 pounds in a year. Besides this, they have corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and cattle. Their sovereign is the king of Sardinia; who generally resides at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of this country. The valleys between France and Italy are inhabited by the Vaudois, who are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. Towards the end of the last century, the French king persuaded the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy to drive them out of the country, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which 20,000 of them retired to Germany, England, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; and yet they are not at all extinguished, though they are obliged to have a Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>.

PIEPOUDRE

Pages 687-687

the lowest, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the most expeditious, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> known to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> of England. It is called piepoudre, (<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CURIA">curia</a> pedis pulverizati), from the dusty feet of the suitors; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>, because justice is there done as speedily as dust can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the foot: Upon the same principle that justice among the Jews was administered in the gate of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, that the proceedings might be the more speedy, as well as public. But the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> given us by a learned <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writer is much more ingenious and satisfactory; it being derived, according to him, from pied puldeaux, "a pedlar," in old French, and therefore signifying the court of such petty chapmen as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>. It is a court of record, incident to every fair and market; of which the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of him who owns or has the toll of the market, is the judge. It was instituted to administer justice for all commercial injuries done in that very fair or market, and not in any preceding one. So that the injury must be done, complained of, heard, and determined, within the compass of one and the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, unless the fair continues longer. The court hath cognizance of all matters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> that can possibly arise within the precinct of that fair or market; and the plaintiff must make oath that the cause of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> arose there. From this court a writ of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> lies, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>, to the courts at Westminster. The reason of its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> seems to have been, to do justice expeditiously among the variety of persons that resort from distant places to a fair or market; since it is probable, that no other inferior court might be able to serve its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, or execute its judgments, on both or perhaps either of the parties; and therefore, unless this court had been erected, the complaint must necessarily have resorted even in the first instance to some superior judicature.

PIERIA

Pages 687-687

a district of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, contained between the mouths of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Ludias and Peneus; extended by Strabo beyond the Ludias, to the river Axios on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and on the south no farther than the Aliacmon, along the west side of the Sinus Thermaticus.—Another Pieria of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, the north <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the Antiochena, situate on the Sinus Ilicicus, and lying next <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a> to the north-west.

PIERIDES

Pages 687-687

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the daughters of Pierus a Macedonian <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, presuming to dispute with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSES">muses</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, were turned into magpies. The name of Pierides was also given to the mules, from mount Pieris in Thessaly, which was consecrated to them; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, from Pierus, a Thessalian poet, who was the first who sacrificed to them. See PIERIS.

PIERINO DEL VAGA

Pages 687-687

an eminent Italian painter, born of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> parents in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, about the year 1500. He was placed apprentice with a grocer in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, and got some instructions from the painters to whom he was sent with colours and pencils; but a painter named Vaga taking him to Rome, he was called Del Vaga, from living with him, his real name being Buonaccorsi. He studied anatomy with the sciences necessary for his profession; and had somewhat of everything that was good in his compositions. After Raphael's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he joined with Julio Romano and Francisco Penni to finish the works in the Vatican which were left imperfect by their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; and to confirm their friendship, married Penni's sister. He gained the highest reputation by his performances in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> Doria at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>: but the multiplicity of his business and the vivacity of his imagination, drained his spirits in the flower of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; for he died in the year 1547.

PIERIS

Pages 687-687

a mountain which is thought to have given name to Pieria of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>; taking its name from Pierus a poet, who was the first that sacrificed to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>, thence called Pierides, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> may be given to an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> scholiast on Juvenal.

PIETISTS

Pages 687-687

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> sprung up among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> of Germany, seeming to be a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a> of England, and the Quietists of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. They despise all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> polity, all school <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, and all forms and ceremonies, and give themselves up to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> and the mystic theology.

PIGMENTS

Pages 687-687

preparations used by painters, dyers, &c. to impart colours to bodies, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> to imitate particular colours. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">Colour</a>-Making, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DYEING">Dyeing</a>.

PIKE

Pages 688-688

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, an offensive weapon, consisting of a wooden shaft, 12 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> 14 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, with a flat <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> head, pointed, called the spear. This weapon was long in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the infantry; but now the bayonet, which is fixed on the muzzle of the firelock, is substituted in its stead. It is still used by some of the officers of infantry, under the name of spontoon.—The Macedonian phalanx was a battalion of pike-men.

PILCHARD

Pages 688-689

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>, a fish which has a general likeness to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERRING">herring</a>, but differs in some particulars very essential. The body of the pilchard is less compressed than that of the herring, being thicker and rounder: the nose is shorter in proportion, and turns up: the under jaw is shorter. The back is more elevated; the belly less sharp: the dorsal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIN">fin</a> of the pilchard is placed exactly in the centre of gravity, so that when taken up by it, the body preserves an equilibrium, whereas that of the herring dips at the head: The scales of the pilchard adhere very closely, whereas those of the herring very easily drop off. The pilchard is in general less than the herring; but it is fatter, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> more full of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. The pilchard appears in vast shoals off the Cornish coasts about the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, disappearing the beginning of winter, yet sometimes a few return again after Christmas. Their winter retreat is the same with that of the herring, and their motives for migrating the same. They affect, during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, a warmer latitude; for they are not found in any quantities on any of our coasts except those of Cornwall, that is to say, from Fowey harbour to the Scilly isles, between which places the shoals keep shifting for some weeks. The approach of the pilchard is known by much the same signs as those that indicate the arrival of the herring. Persons, called in Cornwall huers, are placed on the cliffs, to point to the boats stationed off the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> the course of the fish. By the 1st of James I. c. 23, fishermen are empowered to go on the grounds of others to hue, without being liable to actions of trespass, which before occasioned frequent lawsuits. The emoluments that accrue to the inhabitants of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and are best expressed in the words of Dr. W. Borlase, in his account of the Pilchard Fishery. "It employs a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, training them thereby to naval affairs; employs men, women, and children, at land, in salting, pressing, washing, and cleaning, in making boats, nets, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, casks, and all the trades depending on their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> is fed with the offals of the captures; the land with the refuse of the fish and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; the merchant finds the gains of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> and honest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; the fisherman, the gains of the fish. Ships are often freighted hither with salt, and into foreign countries with the fish, carrying off at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of our tin. The usual produce of the number of hogsheads exported each year, for ten years, from 1747 to 1756 inclusive, from the four four ports of Fowey, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FALMOUTH">Falmouth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENZANCE">Penzance</a>, and St Ives, it appears that Fowey has exported yearly 1732 hogheads; Falmouth, 14,651 hogheads and two-thirds; Penzance and Mounts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>, 12,140 hogheads and one-third; St Ives, 1282 hogheads; in all amounting to 29,795 hogheads. Every hoghead for ten years last past, together with the bounty allowed for every hoghead exported, and the oil made out of each hoghead, has amounted, one year with another at an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>, to the price of £1.13s.3½d.; so that the cash paid for pilchards exported has, at a medium, annually amounted to the sum of £49,532.10s. The numbers that are taken at one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> out of the nets, is amazingly great. Mr Pennant says, that Dr Borlase assured him, that on the 5th of October 1767, there were at one time inclosed in St Ives's Bay 7000 hogheads, each hoghead containing 35,000 fish, in all 245,000,000.

PILE-ENGINE

Pages 689-689

a very curious machine invented by Mr Vaucluse for driving the piles of Westminster <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. It is represented Plate CCXLV. A is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> upright shaft <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> axle, on which are the great wheel B, and the drum C, turned by horses joined to the bars S, S. The wheel B turns the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNDLE">trundle</a> X, on the top of whose axis is the fly O, which serves to regulate the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and also to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> against the horses, and to keep them from falling when the heavy ram Q is discharged to drive the pile P <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into the mud in the bottom of the river. The drum C is loose upon the shaft A, but is locked to the wheel B by the bolt Y. On this drum the great rope HH is wound; one end of the rope being fixed to the drum, and the other to the follower G, to which it is conveyed over the pulleys I and K. In the follower G is contained the tongs F, that takes hold of the ram Q by the staple R, for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> it up. D is a spiral or fulcrum fixed to the drum, on which is wound the small rope T that goes over the pulley U, under the pulley V, and is fastened to the top of the frame at 7. To the pulley-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> V is hung the counterpoise W, which hinders the follower T from accelerating as it goes down to take hold of the ram; for as the follower tends to acquire velocity in its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, the line T winds downwards upon the fulcrum, on a larger and larger radius, by which means the counterpoise W acts stronger and stronger against it; and so allows it to come down with only a moderate and uniform velocity. The bolt Y locks the drum to the great wheel, being pushed upward by the small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> 2, which goes through a mortise in the shaft A, turns upon a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIN">pin</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> 3, fixed to the great wheel B, and has a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> 4, which always tends to push up the bolt Y through the wheel into the drum. L is the great lever <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> on the axis m, and resting upon the forcing bar 5, 5, which goes through a hollow in the shaft A, and bears up the little lever 2. By the horses going round, the great rope H is wound about the drum C, and the ram Q is drawn up by the tongs F in the follower G, until the tongs comes between the inclined planes E; which, by shutting the tongs at the top, opens it at the foot, and discharges the ram which falls down between the guides bb upon the pile P, and drives it by a few strokes as far into the mud as it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> go; after which, the top <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> is sawed off <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the mud by an engine for that purpose.
