Immediately after the ram is discharged, the piece 6 upon the follower G takes hold of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">aa</a>, which raise the end of the lever L, and cause its end N to descend and press down the forcing bar 5 upon the little lever 2, which, by pulling down the bolt Y, unlocks the drum C from the great wheel B; and then the follower being at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, comes down by its own weight to the ram; and the lower ends of the tongs slip over the staple R, and the weight of their heads causes them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> outward, and thus upon it. Then the weight 4 pushes up the bolt Y into the drum, which locks it to the great wheel, and so the ram is drawn up as before. As the follower comes down it causes the drum to turn backward, and unwinds the rope from it, whilst the horses, great wheel, trundle and fly, go on with an uninterrupted motion; and as the drum is turning backward, the counterpoise W is drawn up, and its rope T wound upon the spiral fulcrum D. There are several holes in the under side of the drum, and the bolt Y always takes the first one that it finds when the drum stops by the falling of the follower upon the ram; until which stoppage the bolt has not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to slip into any of the holes. This engine was placed upon a barge on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and so was easily conveyed to any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> desired. The ram was a ton weight; and the guides bb, by which it was let fall, were 30 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>.

PILES

Pages 689-689

in medicine, the same with hemorrhoids. See MEDICINE, no 354, 358.

PILGRIM

Pages 689-689

one who travels through foreign countries to visit holy places, and to pay his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> to the relics of dead saints. See PILGRIMAGE. The word is formed from the Flemish pelgrim, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Italian pellegrino, which signifies the same; and those originally from the Latin peregrinus, a "stranger or traveller."

PILGRIMAGE

Pages 689-690

a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, which consists in taking a journey to some holy <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in order to adore the relics of some deceased saint. Pilgrimages began to be made about the middle ages of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but they were most in vogue after the end of the 11th century, when every one was for visiting places of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, not excepting kings and princes themselves; and even <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> made no difficulty of being absent from their churches on the same account. The places most visited were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, Rome, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOSTELLA">Compostella</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a>; but the greatest numbers now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORETTO">Loretto</a>, in order to visit the chamber of the blest virgin, in which she was born, and brought up her son <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> till he was 12 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

PILKINGTON

Pages 690-690

a famous poetical genius, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Dr Van Lewin, a physician of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, where she was born in 1712. She was married very young to the Rev. Matthew Pilkington, a poet also of no inconsiderable merit; and these two wits, as is often the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, lived very unhappily together. They were at length totally separated, on the husband accidentally discovering a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> in her bedchamber at two o'clock in the morning; a circumstance which she accounted for in a very unsatisfactory manner. The story is told at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in her <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>; where she says, "Lovers of learning, I am sure, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> me, as I solemnly declare it was the attractive charms of a new book, which the gentleman would not lend me, but consented to stay till I read it through, that was the sole <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of my detaining him." As there are not wanting some who form objections to the marrying learned wives, the chance of such literary appointments may perhaps be added to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of them. After this unlucky adventure, Mrs Pilkington came to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and having recourse to her <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a> for subsistence, through the means of Colley Cibber, she lived some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> on the contributions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. She was however thrown into the Marshalsea for debt; and being set at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, opened a pamphlet shop. She raised at length a handsome subscription for her Memoirs; which are written with great sprightliness and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, containing several entertaining anecdotes of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> Swift, with whom she was intimate, as well as many pretty little pieces of her <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. This ingenious but unhappy woman is said at last to have killed herself with drinking, at Dublin, in 1750.

PILLAR

Pages 690-690

in the manege, is the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> manege-ground, round which a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> turns, whether there be a pillar in it or not. Besides this, there are pillars on the circumference or sides of the manege-ground, placed at certain distances, by two and two, from whence they are called the two pillars, to distinguish them from that of the centre. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the pillar in the centre, is for regulating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of ground, that the manege upon the volts may be performed with method and justness, and that they may <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, by rule and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, upon the four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of the volts; and also to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> unruly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-mettled horses, without endangering the rider. The two pillars are placed at the distance of two or three paces one from the other, and the horse is put between those, to teach him to rise before, and jerk out behind, and put himself upon raised <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>, &c. either by the aids, or chastisements.

PILLORY

Pages 690-690

(collifrigium, "collum stringens;" pilloria, from the French pilleur, i.e. depeculator, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> pelori; derived from the Greek πυλή, jana, a "door," because one standing on the pillory puts his head as it were through a door; and ἀγκαλιά, videa), is an engine made of wood to punish offenders, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> them to public view, and rendering them infamous. There is a statute of the pillory, 51 Hen. III. And by statute it is appointed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a>, forestallers, and those who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> false weights, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>, forgery, &c. 3 Inst. 219. Lords of leets are to have a pillory and tumbrel, or it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the cause of forfeiture of the leet; and a will may be bound by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a> to provide a pillory, &c. 2 Hawk. P. C. 73.

PILOT

Pages 690-691

the officer who superintends the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, either upon the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> on the main ocean. It is, however, more particularly applied by our mariners to the person <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a ship's course on or near the sea-coast, and into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, bays, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, havens, &c. within his respective district. Pilots of ships, taking upon them to conduct any ship from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>, &c. to any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> up the river <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, are to be first examined and approved by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and wardens of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of Trinity <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, &c. or shall forfeit 10l. for the first offence, 20l. for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and 40l. for every other offence; one moiety to the informer, the other to the master and wardens; but any master or mate of a ship, may pilot his own vessel up the river; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any ship be lost through the negligence of any pilot, he shall be for ever after disabled to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> as a pilot. 3 Geo. I. c. 13. Also the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Warden of the Cinque Ports may make rules for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of pilots, and order a sufficient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to ply at sea to conduct ships up to the Thames: 7 Geo. I. c. 21. No person shall act as a pilot on the Thames, &c. (except in collier ships) without a licence from the master and wardens of Trinity-House at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a>, on pain of forfeiting 20l. And pilots are to be subject to the government of that corporation; and pay <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> dues, not exceeding 1s. in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, out of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> thereof. Stat. 5 Geo. II. c. 20. By the laws of France, no person shall be received as pilot, till he has made several voyages, and passed a strict <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>; and after that, on his return in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> voyages, he is to lodge a copy of his journal in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>: and if a pilot occasion the loss of a ship, he is to pay 100 livres fine, and to be for ever deprived of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of pilotage; and if he doth it designedly, be punished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Lex Mercat. 70, 71. The laws of Oleron ordain, That if any pilot designedly misguide a ship, that it may be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> away, he shall be put to a rigorous death, and hung in chains: and if the lord of a place, where a ship be thus lost, abet such villains in order to have a share of the wreck, he shall be apprehended, and all his goods forfeited for the satisfaction of the persons suffering; and his person shall be fastened to a stake in the midst of his own mansion, which, being fired on the four corners, shall be burned to the ground, and he with it. Leg. Ol. c. 25. And if the fault of a pilot be so notorious, that the ship's crew see an apparent wreck, they may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> him to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HATCHES">hatches</a>, and strike off his head; but the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> denies this hasty execution: an ignorant pilot is sentenced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> thrice under the ship's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, by the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. Lex Mercat. 70. The regulations, with regard to pilots in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, are as follow: The commanders of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s ships, in order to give all reasonable encouragement to so useful a body of men as pilots, and to remove all their objections to his Majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, are strictly charged to treat them with good usage, and an equal respect with warrant-officers. "The purser of the ship is always to have a set of bedding provided on board for the pilots; and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> is to order the boatswain to supply them with hammocks, and a convenient place to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in, near their duty, and apart from the common men; which bedding and hammocks are to be returned when the pilots leave the ship. "A pilot, when conducting one of his Majesty's ships in pilot-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, shall have the sole <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> and command of the ship, and may give orders for steering, setting, trimming, or furling the sails; tacking the ship; or whatever concerns the navigation: and the captain is to take care that all the officers and crew obey his orders. But the captain is diligently to observe the conduct of the pilot; and if he judges him to behave so ill as to bring the ship into danger, he may remove him from the command and charge of the ship, and take such methods for her preservation as shall be judged necessary; remarking upon the log-book, the exact <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the pilot was removed from his office, and the reasons assigned for it. "Captains of the king's ships, employing pilots in foreign parts of his majesty's dominions, shall, after performance of the service, give a certificate thereof to the pilot, which being produced to the proper naval officer, he shall cause the same to be immediately paid; but if there be no naval-officer there, the captain of his majesty's ship shall pay him, and send the proper vouchers, with his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, to the navy-board, in order to be paid as bills of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. "Captains of his majesty's ships, employing foreign pilots to carry the ships they command into or out of foreign ports, shall pay them the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RATES">rates</a> due by the establishment or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, before they discharge them; whose receipts being duly vouched, and sent, with a certificate of the service performed, to the navy-board, they shall cause them to be paid with the same exactness as they do bills of exchange." Regulations and Instructions of the Sea-service, &c.

PIMENTO

Pages 691-691

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, JAMAICA <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEPPER">PEPPER</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Allspice. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MYRTUS">MYRTUS</a>, of which it is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> are gathered when green, and are exposed to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> for many days on cloths, frequently shaking and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> them till they are thoroughly dry: <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care is taken that they be not wetted by the morning and evening dews; and when thus dry, they are sent over to us. Pimento abounds with a fragrant essential <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which is separated in great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, and is so heavy that it sinks in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. This spice is much used in our foods, and sometimes in medicine: it is indeed a very good aromatic, and imitates the flavour of all the rest; so that the essential oil of Jamaica pepper is frequently substituted in the room of those drawn from the more costly spices.

PIMPINELLA

Pages 691-692

BURNET SAXIFRAGE; a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the pentandria class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; the most remarkable of which are, 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> greater burnet saxifrage, growing naturally in chalky woods, and on the sides of the banks near hedges, in several parts of England. The lower leaves of this sort are winged; Pimpinella. The lobes are deeply sawed on their edges, and fit <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the midrib, of a dark green. The stalks are more than a foot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, dividing into four or five branches. The lower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the stalk is garnished with winged leaves, shaped like those at the bottom, but smaller: those upon the branches are short and trifid: the branches are terminated by small umbels of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which are composed of smaller umbels or rays. The flowers have five heart-shaped petals, which turn inward, and are succeeded by two narrow, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, channelled seeds. 2. The anisum, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> anise, is an annual plant, which grows naturally in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; but is cultivated in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, from whence the seeds are annually imported into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. The lower leaves of this plant are divided into three lobes, which are deeply cut on their edges: the stalk rises a foot and a half high, dividing into several slender branches garnished with narrow leaves, cut into three or four narrow segments, terminated by pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> loose umbels, composed of smaller umbels or rays, which stand on pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> foot-stalks. The flowers are small, and of a yellowish white; the seeds are oblong and swelling.—The former species requires no culture; the latter is too tender to be cultivated for profit in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. However, the seeds <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> come up <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> sown, in the beginning of April, upon a warm border. When they come up, they should be thinned, and kept clear of weeds; which is all the culture they require. Uses. Both these spices are used in medicine. The roots of pimpinella have a grateful, warm, very pungent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, which is entirely extracted by rectified spirit: in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> the menstruum arises, leaving all that it had taken up from the root united into a pungent aromatic resin. This root promises, from its sensible qualities, to be a medicine of considerable utility, though little regarded in common practice: the only official <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> in which it is an ingredient is the pulvis ari compositus. Stahl, Hoffman, and other German physicians, are extremely fond of it; and recommend it as an excellent stomachic, resolvent, detergent, diuretic, diaphoretic, and alexipharma. They frequently gave it, and not without success, in scorbutic and cutaneous disorders, foulness of the blood and juices, tumours and obstructions of the glands, and diseases proceeding from a deficiency of the fluid secretions in general. Boerhaave directs the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this medicine in asthmatic and hydropic <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, where the strongest resolvents are indicated: the form he prefers is a watery infusion; but the spirituous tincture possesses the virtues of the root in much greater perfection. Aniseeds have an aromatic smell, and a pleasant warm taste, accompanied with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of sweetness. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">Water</a> extracts very little of their flavour, rectified spirit the whole. These seeds are in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the four greater hot seeds: their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> use is in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> flatulent disorders, where tenacious phlegm abounds, and in the gripes to which young children are subject. Frederic Hoffman strongly recommends them in weaknesses of the stomach, diarrhoeas, and for strengthening the tone of the viscera in general; and thinks they well deserve the appellation given them by Helmont, integit. The smaller kind of aniseeds brought from Spain are preferred.

PIN

Pages 692-692

a very learned French writer, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1657. In 1685 he undertook to publish an universal bibliothèque of all the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, containing the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of their lives, &c.; which vast <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> he accordingly accomplished. The freedom our author used in his judgements on the style, character, and doctrine of the ecclesiastical writers, having displeased some persons, it was complained of to the archbishop of Paris, who published a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> ordonnance against it. To this decree was annexed Mr du Pin's retraction; notwithstanding which, his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> was suppressed by an arrêt of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. However, he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> it under another <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. His many different books shew his prodigious readiness in composing. He was at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> a divine, canonist, historian, critic, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. At last being exhausted by his labours, and by a regimen which contributed to shorten his days, he died in 1719.

PINDAR

Pages 692-693

the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of lyric poets, was born at Thebes, about 520 years B.C. He received his first musical instructions from his father, who was a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>-player by profession; after which, according to Suidas, he was placed under Myrtis, a lady of distinguished abilities in lyric <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. It was during this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> that he became acquainted with the poetess Corinna, who was likewise a student under Myrtis. Plutarch tells us, that Pindar profited from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> which Corinna, more advanced in her studies, gave him at this school. It is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to suppose, that the first poetical effusions of a genius so full of fire and imagination as that of Pindar would be wild and luxuriant; and Lucian has preserved six verses, said to have been the exordium of his first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a>; in which he crowded almost all the subjects for song which <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a> then furnished. Upon communicating this attempt to Corinna, she told him, smiling, that he should sow with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and not empty his whole sack at once. Pindar, however, soon quitted the leading-strings of these ladies, his poetical nurses, and became the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIMONIDES">Simonides</a>, now arrived at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; after which he soon surpassed all his masters, and acquired <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation over all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>: but, like a true prophet, he was less honoured in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> than elsewhere; for at Thebes he was frequently pronounced to be vanquished, in the musical and poetical contests, by candidates of inferior merit. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of having these public trials of skill in all the great cities of Greece was now so prevalent, that but little fame was to be acquired by a musician <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> poet, any other way than by entering the lists; and we find, that both Myrtis and Corinna publicly disputed the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> with him at Thebes. He obtained a victory over Myrtis, but was vanquished five different times by Corinna. The judges, upon occasions like these, have been frequently accused of partiality or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, not only by the vanquished, but by posterity: and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the merit of Pindar was pronounced inferior to that of Corinna five several times, it was, says Paufanias, because the judges were more sensible to the charms of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> than to those of music and poetry (4). Was it not strange, said the Scythian Anacharsis, that the Grecian artists were never judged by artists, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>? Pindar, before he quitted Thebes, had the vexation to see his Dithyrambics traduced, abused, and turned into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>, by the comic poets of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and Athenæus tells us, that he was severely censured by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> lyrics, for being a lipogrammatist, and composing an ode from which he had excommunicated the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> S. Whether these censures proceeded from envy, or contempt, cannot now be determined; but they were certainly useful to Pindar, and it was necessary that he should be lashed for such puerilities. Thebes seems to have been the purgatory of our young bard; when he quitted that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, as his judgment was matured, he avoided most of the errors for which he had been chastised, and suddenly became the wonder and delight of all Greece. Every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, prince, and potentate, desirous of lasting fame, courted the Muse of Pindar. He seems frequently to have been present at the four great festivals, of the Olympian, Pythian, Nemean, and Isthmian games, as may be inferred from several circumstances and expressions in the odes, which he composed for the victors in them all. Those at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OLYMPIA">Olympia</a>, who were ambitious of having their achievements celebrated by Pindar, applied to him for an ode, which was first sung in the Prytaneum, or town-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of Olympia, where there was a banqueting room, set apart for the entertainment of the conquerors. Here the ode was rehearsed by a chorus, accompanied by instruments. It was afterwards performed in the same manner at the triumphal entry of the victor into his own country, in processions, or at the sacrifices that were made with great pomp and solemnity on the occasion. Pindar, in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Isthmian ode, has apologized for the mercenary custom among poets, of receiving <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for their compositions. "The world (says he) is grown interested, and thinks in general with the Spartan <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> Aristodemus, that money only makes (A) Paufanias says, that Corinna was one of the most beautiful women of her time, as he judged by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of her, which he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> at Tanagris, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the public exercises were performed. She was represented with her head ornamented by a riband, as a memorial of the victories she had obtained over Pindar at Thebes. makes the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>: a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> which this sage himself experienced, having with his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> lost all his friends." It is supposed that Pindar here alludes to the avarice of Simonides, who first allowed his muse to sell her favours to the highest bidder. There is no great poet in antiquity, whose moral character has been less censured than that of Pindar. Plutarch has preserved a single <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> of his *Epicedium*, or *Dirge*, that was sung at his funeral; which, short and simple as it is, implies great praise: *This man was pleasing to strangers, and dear to his fellow-citizens*. His works abound with precepts of the purest morality: and it does not appear that he ever traduced even his enemies; comforting himself, for their malignity, by a maxim which he inserted in his first *Pythic*, and which afterwards became proverbial, *That it is better to be envied than pitied*. Pausanias says, that the character of poet was truly consecrated, is the person of Pindar, by the God of verse himself, who was pleased, by an express oracle, to order the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHOS">Delphos</a> to set apart, for Pindar, one half of the first-fruit offerings brought by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> to his shrine, and to allow him a conspicuous place in his temple; where, in an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, he used to sit and sing his hymns in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of that god. This chair was remaining in the time of Pausanias, several centuries after, and shown to him as a relic not unworthy of the sanctity and magnificence of that place. But though Pindar's muse was penioned at Delphos, and well paid by princes and potentates elsewhere, the feasts, however, sometimes to have sung the spontaneous strains of pure friendship. Of this kind were, probably, the verses belloved upon the musician <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MIDAS">Midas</a>, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRIGENTUM">Agrigentum</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, who had twice obtained the palm of victory by his performance on the flute at the Pythic games (b). It is in his 12th Pythic Ode, that Pindar celebrates the victory of Midas over all Greece, upon that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> herself had invented (c). Fabricius tells us, that Pindar lived to the age of 90; and, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> of Dr Blair, he died 435 years B.C. aged 86. His fellow-citizens erected a monument to him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIPPODROME">Hippodrome</a> at Thebes, which was still subsisting in the time of Pausanias; and his renown was so great after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, that his posterity derived very considerable honours and privileges from it. When Alexander the Great attacked the city of Thebes, he gave express orders to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to spare the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and family of Pindar. The Lacedemonians had done the same before this period; for when they ravaged <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a> and burned the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, the following words were written upon the door of the poet: *Forbear to burn this house, it was the dwelling of Pindar*. Respect for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of this great poet <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, that, even in Plutarch's time, the best <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the sacred victim at the Thoexonian festival was appropriated to his descendants. Vol. VIII. (b) This Midas is a very different personage from his long-eared majesty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, whose decision in favour of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAN">Pan</a> had given such offence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>; as is manifest, indeed, from his having been <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Pindar. (c) The most extraordinary part of this musician's performance, that can be gathered from the scholiast upon Pindar, was his finishing the solo, without a reed or mouth-piece, which broke accidentally while he was playing. The legendary account given by the poet in this ode, of the occasion upon which the flute was invented by Minerva, is diverting: "It was (says he) to imitate the howling of the Gorgons, and the hissing of their snakes, which the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> had heard when the head of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEDUSA">Medusa</a> (one of these three anti-graces) was cut off by Perseus."

PINDARIC ODE

Pages 693-693

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, an ode formed in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>. See Poetry, no 59.—61.

PINDUS

Pages 693-693

a Doric <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Aetolia, situate on the cognominal river, which falls into the Cephissus, (Strabo).

PINGUICULA

Pages 694-694

Butterwort; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the diandra clafs of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are four <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the most remarkable is the vulgaris, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> butterwort, growing <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> on bogs or low moist grounds, in England and Scotland. Its leaves are covered with felt, upright pellucid prickles, secreting a glutinous liquor. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, purple, or deep violet <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and hairy within. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the fresh-gathered leaves of this plant are put into the strainer through which warm <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> from the cow is poured, and the milk let by for a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> or two to become acidulent, it acquires a consistency and tenacity, and neither whey nor cream separate from it. In this state it is an extremely grateful food, and as such is used by the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. There is no further occasion to have recourse to the leaves; for half a spoonful of this prepared milk, mixed with fresh warm milk, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> convert it to its own <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and this again will change another <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fresh milk, and so on without end. The juice of the leaves kills <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a>; and the common people <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it to cure the cracks or chops in cows' udders. The plant is generally supposed injurious to sheep, by occasioning in them that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> called the rot. But from experiments made on purpose, and conducted with accuracy, it appears, that neither sheep, cows, goats, horses, or swine, will feed upon this plant.

PINION

Pages 694-694

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, an arbor, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> spindle, in the body whereof are several notches, which catch the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of a wheel that serves to turn it round, or it is a lesser wheel that plays in the teeth of a larger.

PINNA

Pages 694-694

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of vermes tectacea. The animal is a slug. The shell is bivalve, fragile, and furnished with a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>; fig. 2, gapes at one end; the valves hinge without a tooth. The largest and most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> inhabits the Mediterranean. It is <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>, as are all of the genus; but furnished with very strong calcareous valves. The scuttle-fish (Sepia), an inhabitant of the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, is a deadly foe to this animal: As soon as the pinna opens its shell, he rushes upon her like a lion; and would always devour her, but for another animal whom she protects within her shell, and from whom in return she receives very important services. It is an animal of the crab kind, (see Cancer, no 15.), naked like the hermit, and very quick-fighted. This cancer <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> crab the pinna receives into her covering; and when she opens her valves in quest of food, lets him out to look for prey. During this the scuttle-fish approaches; the crab returns with the utmost speed and anxiety to his hostess, who being thus warned of the danger shuts her doors, and keeps out the enemy. That very sagacious observer Dr Haffelquist, in his voyage towards <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, beheld this curious phenomenon, which tho' well known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> had escaped the moderns. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> (Hist. lib. 5. c. 15.) relates, that the pinna kept a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> to watch for her: That there grew to the mouth of the pinna a small animal, having claws, and serving as a caterer, which was like a crab, and was called the pinnothylax. Pliny (lib. 9. 51.) says, The smallest of all the kinds is called the pinnoterex, and therefore liable to injury; this has the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> to hide itself in the shells of oysters. Again, lib. 9. 66. he says, The pinna is of the genus of shell-fish; it is produced in muddy waters, always erect, nor ever without a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, which some call the pinnoterex, others the pinnothylax. This sometimes is a small eel, sometimes a crab, that follows the pinna for the sake of food. The pinna is blind; and when, upon opening its shell, it exposes itself as a prey to the smallest kind of fishes, these immediately assault her, and growing bolder upon finding no resistance venture in. The guard watching its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> gives notice by a bite; upon which the pinna, closing its shell, shuts in, kills, and gives <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of whatever happens to be there to its companion. The pinna and the crab together dwell, For mutual succour, in one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> shell. They both to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a livelihood combine; That takes the prey, when this has given the sign. From hence this crab, above his fellows fam'd, By <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks was pinnoterex nam'd.

PINNACE

Pages 694-695

a small vessel navigated with oars and sails, PINNACE sails, and having generally two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, which are rigged like those of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SCHOONER">schooner</a>. PINNACE is also a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> usually rowed with eight oars. See the article BOAT.

PINNACLE

Pages 695-695

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, the top <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, terminating in a point. This kind of roof among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> was appropriated to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>; their ordinary roofs were all flat, or made in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> way.

PINNATED LEAVES

Pages 695-695

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. See BOTANY, p. 1296, col. 2, n° 59.

PINT

Pages 695-695

(pinta), a vessel, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, used in estimating the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of liquids, and even sometimes of dry things.—Budaeus derives the word from the Greek πίναξ; others from the German pint, a little measure of wine; Nicod from the Greek πίνω, "to drink." The English pint is twofold; the one for wine-measure, the other for beer and ale-measure. See MEASURE.—Two pints make a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUART">quart</a>, two quarts a pottle, two pottles a gallon, &c. See GALLON, QUART, &c. The Scots pint was formerly regulated by a standard jug of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> metal, the custody of which was committed to the borough of Stirling. This jug was supposed to contain 105 cubic inches; and though after several careful trials it has been found at a medium to contain only about 103½ inches, yet, in compliance with established <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, founded on that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, the pint-stoups are still regulated to contain 105 inches.—It was enacted by James I. of Scotland, that the pint should contain 41 ounces Trone-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the clear <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> of Tay, and by James VI. that it should contain 55 Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>-ounces of the clear water of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEITH">Leith</a>. This affords another method of regulating the pint, and also affords the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> standard of the Trone-weight. As the water of Tay and Leith are alike, the Trone-weight must have been to the Scots Troy-weight as 55 to 41; and therefore the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> Trone must have contained about 21½ ounces Scots Troy. See TRONE.—The Scots pint contains two chopins, the chopin two mutchkins, and the mutchkin four pills.—Two pints make a quart, and four pints a Scots gallon.

PINTLES

Pages 695-695

certain pivots <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> hooks, fastened upon the back <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a>, with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> downwards, in order to enter into, and rest upon, the goings, fixed in the stern-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a>, to hang the rudder. See HELM.

PINTURICCO

Pages 695-695

a celebrated Italian painter, born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERUGIA">Perugia</a> in 1454. He was the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Perugino, under whom he became so good an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, that he employed him on many occasions as his assistant. He principally painted <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a>; but he also excelled in portraits, among which those of pope Pius II. and Innocent VIII. of Giulia Farnese, Cesar Borgia, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> Isabella of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, are particularly distinguished. The most memorable performance of Pinturicco is the history of Pius II. painted in ten compartments in the history of Siena; in which undertaking, Raphael, then a young <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and bred under the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, assisted him so far as to sketch out cartoons of many parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. The story of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is worth relating, especially as it illustrates his character. The last <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> he was engaged in was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">Nativity</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of St Francis at Siena: the monks accommodated him with a chamber to work in, which they cleared of all the furniture, except one old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> that appeared too rotten to move; but Pinturicco, naturally positive and peevish, insisting on its being taken away, the monks, willing to gratify him, complied. It was no sooner stirred than one of the planks bursting, out tumbled 500 pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, which had been secreted there for many years. The monks were overjoyed at finding this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, and the painter proportionably mortified at losing his chance of the discovery by his indirect obstinacy: it affected his spirits so much that he survived but a few months, and it was generally looked on as the cause of his death.

PINUS

Pages 695-697

the Pine-tree; a genus of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONADELPHIA">monadelphia</a> order, belonging to the monocota class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are 14 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the most remarkable are, 1. The pinea, pineafter, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> wild pine, grows naturally on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and the south of France. This grows to the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tree; the branches extend to a considerable distance; and while the trees are young, they are fully garnished with leaves, especially where they are not so <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> as to exclude the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> from those within; but as they advance in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, the branches appear naked, and all those which are situated below become unsightly in a few years, for which reason they are now much less in esteem than formerly. 2. The rubra, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the Scots fir or pine. It is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> throughout Scotland, whence its name; though it is also found in most of the other countries of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. M. du Hamel, of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy of Sciences, mentions his having received some seeds of it from St Domingo in the West Indies; and thence concludes, that it grows indifferently in the temperate, frigid, and torrid zones. The wood of this tree is the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>, which is the most durable of any of the kinds yet known. The leaves of this tree are much shorter and broader than those of the former sort, of a greyish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, growing two out of one sheath; the cones are small, pyramidal, and end in narrow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; they are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> colour, and the seeds are small. 3. The trobus, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Weymouth's pine, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> American <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> pine. This grows sometimes to the height of 100 feet and upwards, and is highly valued on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. The bark of the tree is very smooth and delicate, especially when young; the leaves are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and slender, five growing out of one sheath; the branches are pretty closely garnished with them, and thus make a fine appearance. The cones are long, slender, and very loose, opening with the first warmth of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are not gathered in winter, the scales open and let out the seeds. The wood of this sort is esteemed for making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> for ships. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> there was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> made for the preservation of these trees, and for the encouragement of their growth in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. Within these last 50 years they have been propagated in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> in considerable plenty. Culture. All the sorts of pines are propagated by seeds produced in hard woody cones. The way to get the seeds out of these cones is to lay them before a gentle fire, which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> cause the cells to open, and then the seeds may be easily taken out. If the cones are are kept entire, the seeds will remain good for some years; so that the surest way of preserving them is to let them remain in the cones till the time for sowing the seeds. If the cones are kept in a warm <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, they will open and emit the seeds; but if they are not exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, they will remain close for a long time. The best season for sowing the pines is about the end of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. When the seeds are sown, the place should be covered with nets to keep off the birds; otherwise, when the plants begin to appear with the husk of the seed on the top of them, the birds will peck off the tops, and thus destroy them. **Ugo.** From the first species is extracted the common turpentine, much used by farriers, and from which is drawn the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of that name. A decoction of the nuts or seeds of this species in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, or of the extremities of the branches pulled in spring, is said, with a proper regimen, to cure the most inveterate scurvy. The wood of this species is not valued; but that of the Scots pine is superior to any of the rest. It is observable of the Scots pine, that when planted in bogs, or in a moist <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, though the plants make <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress, yet the wood is white, soft, and little esteemed; but when planted in a dry soil, tho' the growth of the trees is there very slow, yet the wood is proportionably better. Few trees have been applied to more uses than this. The tallest and straightest are formed by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> for masts to our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> is resinous, durable, and applicable to numberless <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> purposes, such as flooring and wainscoting of rooms, making of beds, chests, tables, boxes, &c. From the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> and branches of this, as well as most others of the pine tribe, tar and pitch is obtained. By incision, barras, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a> pitch, and turpentine, are acquired and prepared. The resinous roots are dug out of the ground in many parts of the Highlands, and, being divided into small splinters, are used by the inhabitants to burn instead of candles. At Loch <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BROOM">Broom</a>, in Rossshire, the fishermen make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> of the inner bark; but hard <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> has taught the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, and Kamchatka, to convert the same into <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. To effect this, they, in the Spring season, make choice of the tallest and fairest trees; then stripping off carefully the outer bark, they collect the soft, white, succulent interior bark, and dry it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. When they have occasion to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it, they first toast it at the fire, then grind, and, after steeping the flour in warm <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> to take off the resinous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, they make it into thin cakes, which are baked for use. On this strange food the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> inhabitants are sometimes constrained to live for a whole year; and, we are told, through <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, become at last even fond of it. Linnæus remarks, that this same bark-bread will fatten swine; and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> obliges us to wish, that men might never be reduced to the necessity of robbing them of such a food. The interior bark, of which the above-mentioned bread is made, the Swedish boys frequently peel off the trees in the spring, and eat raw with greedy appetite. From the cones of this tree is prepared a diuretic oil, like the oil of turpentine, and a resinous extract, which has similar virtues with the balsam of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. An infusion or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEA">tea</a> of the buds is highly commended as an antilcorbutic. The farina, or yellow powder, of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, is sometimes in the spring carried away by the winds, in such quantities, where the trees abound, as to alarm the ignorant with the notion of its raining brimstone. The tree lives to a great age; Linnæus affirms, to 400 years. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PIONEERS">Pioneers</a>.** In the art of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, are such as are commanded in from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to march with an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> for mending the ways, for working on intrenchments and fortifications, and for making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> and approaches. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> are likewise employed in all these things.—Most of the foreign regiments of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> have half a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of pioneers, well instructed in that important branch of duty. Our regiments of infantry and cavalry have three or four pioneers well instructed in that important branch of duty. Our regiments of infantry and cavalry have three or four pioneers each, provided with aprons, hatchets, saws, spades, and pick-axes. Each pioneer must have an ax, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, and an apron; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> bearskin <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, on which is to be the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s crest in white, on a red ground; also an ax and a saw. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the regiment to be on the back <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the cap. **PIP,** or **PEP,** a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> among <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, consisting of a white thin skin, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILM">film</a>, that grows under the tip of the tongue, and hinders their feeding. It usually arises from want of water, or from the drinking puddle-water, or eating filthy meat. It is cured by pulling off the film with the fingers, and rubbing the tongue with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. Hawks are particularly liable to this disease, especially from feeding on stinking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. **PIPE,** in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, &c., a canal, or conduit, for the conveyance of water and other liquids. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PIPES">Pipes</a> for water, water-engines, &c., are usually of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, or wood; the latter are usually made of oak or elder. Those of iron are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in forges; their usual length is about two feet and a half; several of these are commonly fastened together by means of four screws at each end, with leather or old hat between them, to stop the water. Those of earth are made by the potters; they are fitted into one another, one end being always made wider than the other. To join them the clover, and prevent their breaking, they are covered with tow and pitch; their length is usually about that of the iron pipes. The wooden pipes are trees bored with large iron augers, of different sizes, beginning with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, and then proceeding with a larger successively; the first being pointed, the rest being formed like spoons, increasing in diameter, from one to six inches or more; they are fitted into the extremities of each other (as represented fig. 5.), and are held by the foot. Wooden pipes are bored as follows. The machine represented fig. 4. is put in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> by the wheel A, which is moved by a current of water; upon the axle of this wheel, is a cog-wheel B, which causes the lanterns C, D, to turn horizontally, whose common axis is consequently in a perpendicular <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANTERN">lantern</a> D turns at the same time two cog-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, E and F; the first, E, which is vertical, turns the auger which bores the wood; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, F, which is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a>, causes the carriage <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the piece to advance by means of the arms H, I, which takes hold of the notches in the wheel K. The first, H, H, by means of the notches, draws the wheel towards F; and the other, I, pushes the under-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a> of the wheel in an opposite direction; both which motions tend to draw the carriage towards F, and consequently cause the augre to pierce the wood. The augre being from 9 to 12 feet in length, and of a proportionable bigness, it will be necessary to have two pieces, as L, L, to support its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and cause it to enter the piece to be bored with the same uniformity. For the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of leaden pipes, see the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLUMBERY">PLUMBERY</a>. Air-Pipes. See Air-Pipes. Pipes of an Organ. See Organ. Bag-Pipe. See Bag-Pipe. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a>-Pipe, a machine used in the smoking of tobacco, consisting of a long tube, made of earth or clay, having at one end a little cale, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, called the bowl, for the reception of the tobacco, the fumes whereof are drawn by the mouth through the other end. Tobacco-pipes are made of various fashions; long, short, plain, worked, white, varnished, unvarnished, and of various colours, &c. The Turks use pipes three or four feet long, made of rushes, or of wood bored, at the end whereof they fix a kind of a pot of baked earth, which serves as a bowl, and which they take off after smoking. Pipe, also denotes a vessel or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> for wine, and things measured by wine-measure. See the article MEASURE. Pipe, in mining, is where the ore runs forwards endwise in a hole, and doth not sink downwards or in a vein. Pipe, Pipa, in law, is a roll in the exchequer, called also the great roll. See the next article. Pipe-Office, is an office wherein a person called the clerk of the pipe, makes out leaves of crown-lands, by warrant from the lord-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, or commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the exchequer. The clerk of the pipe makes out also all accounts of sheriffs, &c. and gives the accountants their quietus eft. To this office are brought all accounts which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the remembrancer's office, and remain there, that if any stated debt be due from any person, the same may be drawn <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into the great roll of the pipe: upon which the comptroller issues out a writ, called the summons of the pipe, for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> thereof; and if there be no goods or chattels, the clerk then draws down the debts to the lord treasurer's remembrancer, to write estreats against their lands. All tallies which vouch the payment of any sum contained in such accounts, are examined and allowed by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> secondary of the pipe. Besides the chief clerk in this office, there are eight attorneys, or sworn clerks, and a controller. Pipe-Fish, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>. See SYNGNATHUS.

PIPER

Pages 697-697

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIGLA">TRIGLA</a>. Piper, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEPPER">Pepper</a>; a genus of the trigynia order, belonging to the diandria class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are 20 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, of which the most remarkable is the siriboa, with oval, heart-shaped, nerved leaves, and reflexed spikes. This is the plant which produces the pepper so much used in food. It is a shrub whose root is small, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>; it rises into a stem, which requires a tree <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a prop to support it. Its wood has the same sort of knots as the vine; and when it is dry, it exactly resembles the vine-branch. The leaves, which have a strong smell and a pungent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, are of an oval shape; but they diminish towards the extremity, and terminate in a point. From the flower-buds, which are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and are sometimes placed in the middle and sometimes at the extremity of the branches, are produced small berries resembling those of the currant-tree. Each of these contains between 20 and 30 grains of pepper; they are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> gathered in October, and exposed to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight days. The fruit, which was green at first, and afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, when stripped of its covering assumes the appearance it has when we see it. The largest, heaviest, and least shrivelled, is the best. The pepper-plant flourishes in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>, and Ceylon, and more particularly on the Malabar <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. It is not sown, but planted; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> nicety is required in the choice of the shoots. It produces no fruit till the end of three years; but bears to plentifully the three succeeding years, that some plants yield between six and seven pounds of pepper. The bark then begins to shrink; and the shrub declines to fast, that in 12 years <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> it ceases <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>. The culture of pepper is not difficult: it is sufficient to plant it in a rich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and carefully to pull up the weeds that grow in great abundance round its roots, especially the three first years. As the sun is highly necessary to the growth of the pepper-plant, when it is ready to bear, the trees that support it must be lopped to prevent their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> from injuring the fruit. When the season is over, it is proper to crop the head of the plant. Without this precaution, there would be too much wood, and little fruit. The pepper exported from Malabar, which was formerly entirely in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Portuguese, and is at present divided between the Dutch, British, and French, amounts to about 10,000,000 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>.

PIRACY

Pages 697-698

the crime of robbery and depredation upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> seas. By the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, piracy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> committed by a subject, was held to be a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, being contrary to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>; and by an alien, to be felony only: but now, since the statute of treasons, 25 Edw. III. c. 2. it is held to be only felony in a subject. Formerly it was only cognizable by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> courts, which proceed by the rules of the civil Piracy, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIRATE">Pirate</a>. But, it being inconsistent with the liberties of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, that any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> should be taken away, unless by the judgment of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the common law of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, the statute 28 Hen. VIII. c. 15, established a new jurisdiction for this purpose; which proceeds according to the course of the common law. The offence of piracy, by common law, consists in committing those acts of robbery and depredation upon the high seas, which, if committed upon land, would have amounted to felony there. But, by statute, some other offences are made piracy also: as, by statute 11 & 12 W. III. c. 7, if any natural born subject commits any <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of hostility upon the high seas, against others of his majesty's subjects, under <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> from any foreign power; this, though it would only be an act of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> in an alien, shall be construed piracy in a subject. And farther, any commander, or other seafaring person, betraying his trust, and running away with any ship, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, ordnance, ammunition, or goods; or yielding them up voluntarily to a pirate; or conspiring to do these acts; or any person assaulting the commander of a vessel, to hinder him from fighting in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his ship; or confining him, or caulking or endeavouring to cause a revolt on board; shall, for each of these offences, be adjudged a pirate, felon, and robber, and shall suffer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, whether he be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, or merely <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACCESSORY">accessory</a> by setting forth such pirates, or abetting them before the fact, or receiving or concealing them or their goods after it. And the statute 4 Geo. I. c. 11, expressly excludes the principals from the benefit of clergy. By the statute 8 Geo. I. c. 24, the trading with known pirates, or furnishing them with ammunition, or fitting out any vessel for that purpose, or in any wise consulting, combining, confederating, or corresponding with them; or the forcibly boarding any merchant vessel, though without seizing or carrying her off, and destroying or throwing any of the goods overboard; shall be deemed piracy: and such accessories to piracy as are described by the statute of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> William are declared to be principal pirates, and all pirates convicted by virtue of this act are made felons without benefit of clergy. By the same statutes also, (to encourage the defence of merchant vessels against pirates), the commanders or seamen wounded, and the widows of such seamen as are slain, in any piratical engagement, shall be entitled to a bounty to be divided among them, not exceeding one fifteenth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the value of the cargo on board; and such wounded seamen shall be entitled to the pension of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>; which no other seamen are, except only such as have served in a ship of war. And if the commander shall behave cowardly, by not defending the ship, if she carries guns or arms; or shall discharge the mariners from fighting, so that the ship falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of pirates; such commander shall forfeit all his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, and suffer six months imprisonment. Lastly, by statute 18 Geo. II. c. 30, any natural born subject or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENIZEN">denizen</a>, who in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of war shall commit hostilities at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> against any of his fellow-subjects, or shall afflit an enemy on that element, is liable to be tried and convicted as a pirate.

PIRAEUS PORTUS

Pages 697-697

(anc. geog.), a celebrated port to the west of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, consisting naturally of three harbours <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> basins, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a>); which lay neglected, till Themistocles put the Athenians on making it a commodious port, (Nepos); the Phalerus a small port, and not far from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, being what they used before that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, (Pausanias, Nepos). Piraeus was originally a village of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, (Pausanias); an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, (Strabo); and though distant 40 stadia from Athens, was joined to it by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> walls, (Thucydides), and itself locked or walled round, (Nepos): A very commodious and safe harbour. The whole of its compass was 60 stadia, including the Munichia. Not far from the Piraeus, stood the sepulchre of Themistocles; whither his friends conveyed his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNESIA">Magnesia</a>, into the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, (Cicero, Plutarch, Pausanias). It is still at this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> a famous port, much frequented, and called Porto Liona.

PIRATE

Pages 698-698

(πειρατής, Gr.); a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-robbler, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> an armed ship that roams the seas without any legal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, and seizes or plunders every vessel she meets indiscriminately, whether friends or enemies.
