The colours usually displayed by pirates are said to be a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> field, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>'s head, a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>-axe, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>-glass. The last <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> is generally supposed to determine the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> allowed to the prisoners, whom they take, to consider whether they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> join the pirates in their felonious <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a>, or be put to death, which is often perpetrated in the most cruel manner. Amongst the most celebrated pirates of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> is recorded Alvilda, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> named Sypardus. She embraced this occupation to deliver herself from the violence imposed on her inclination, by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with Alf, son of Sigurds king of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. She dressed herself as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and composed her band of rowers, and the rest of her crew, of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of young women attired in the same manner. Amongst the first of her cruizes, she touched at a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of pirates bewailed the death of their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>. The strangers were captivated with the agreeable manners of Alvilda, and chose her for their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. By this reinforcement she became so formidable upon the sea, that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> Alf came to engage her. She sustained his attacks for a considerable time; but, in a vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, Alf boarded her vessel, and having killed the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of her crew, seized the captain, namely herself; whom nevertheless he knew not, because the princess had a <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-CASQUE">casque</a> which covered her visage. Being <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of her person, he removed the casque; and in spite of her <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a>, instantly recognized her, and offered her his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in wedlock.

PIRENE

Pages 698-698

(Pliny); a fountain sacred to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, springing below the top of the Acrocorinthus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and steep mountain which hangs over Corinth. Its waters were agreeable to drink, (Pausanias); extremely clear, (Strabo); very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> (Athenaeus), and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> (Persius): having relation either to the grief of Pirene, mother of Cenchrea, from whose tears this fountain arose, (Pausanias); <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> to the palens brought on by the too eager pursuits of the muses.

PISA

Pages 698-699

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated on the river Arno, 52 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>. It was a famous republic, till subdued, first by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, and then by the Florentines in the year 1406. Before it lost its freedom, it is said to have contained near 150,000 inhabitants, but now it has not above 16,000 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> 17,000. Its territory is very fruitful; abounding in corn, wine, and fruit, and fine cattle. The houses are well built, and the streets even, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and well paved; but in many places over-run with grass. The university is well endowed, and has able professors, but is not in a very flourishing condition. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> is a stately structure, but little frequented. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> duke's galleys are built, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> stationed here. This <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> is also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> residence of the order of St Stephen, and the see of an archbishop. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, a large Gothic pile, contains a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of excellent paintings and other curiosities. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECHO">echo</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAPTISTERY">Baptistery</a> is said to exceed that near Milan, though the repetitions are not quite so distinct. Hard by the cathedral is the city burying ground, called Il Campo Santo; and in that the famous leaning tower, the inclination of which is so great, that a plumb-line let <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the top touches the ground at the distance of near 15 feet from the bottom. In the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> della Spina, they pretend to have one of the thorns of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> that was placed on our Saviour's head. The city for its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> has a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOAT">moat</a>, walls, a castle, fort, and citadel; the last of which is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The Arno is of a considerable breadth here, and has three bridges over it, one of them of marble: two leagues below the town, it falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The phyle garden is very spacious, contains a great number of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and is decorated with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER_WORKS"><a class="x</a>ref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>-works: over the door leading into it are these words, Hic Argus sed non Briareus est; i.e. Employ the eye of Argus, but not the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Briareus. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is said to be unwholesome here in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, on account of the neighbouring marshes. Many buffaloes are bred in the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> commonly eaten. A canal runs from this city to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>; and between it and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a> are hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>.

PISCARY

Pages 699-699

in our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> statutes, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> in another <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s waters.

PISCES

Pages 699-699

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, the 12th sign <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> constellation of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>.

PISCIDIA

Pages 699-699

a genus of the decandra order, belonging to the diadelphia clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. 1. The erythrina, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> dog-wood tree. This grows plentifully in Jamaica, where it rises to the height of 25 feet or more; the stem is almost as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s body, covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-coloured smooth bark, and sending out several branches at the top without order; the leaves are about two inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, winged, with oval lobes. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are of the butterfly kind, and of a dirty <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; they are succeeded by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> pods, with four longitudinal wings, and jointed between the cells which contain the seeds. 2. The Carthaginensis, with oblong oval leaves, is also a native of the West Indies. It differs from the former only in the shape and consistence of the leaves, which are more oblong and flatter than the former; but in other respects they are very similar. Both species are easily propagated by seeds; but require <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> to preserve them in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.—The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> in the West Indies make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the bark of the first species to intoxicate fish. When any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of gentlemen have an inclination to divert themselves with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, or, more properly speaking, with fish-hunting, they send each of them a negro-slave to the woods, in order to fetch some of the bark of the dog-wood tree. This bark is next morning pounded very small with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, put into old sacks, carried into rocky parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, steeped till thoroughly soaked with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and then well squeezed by the negroes to express the juice. This juice immediately colours the sea with a reddish hue; and, being of a poisonous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> in an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> make the fishes, such as groopers, rock-fish, old wives, Welchmen, &c. to drunk or intoxicated, as to swim on the surface of the water, quite heedless of the danger: the gentlemen then send in their negroes, who pursue, both <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVING">diving</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> inebriated fishes, till they catch them with their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; their masters <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time standing by, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rocks, to see the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASTIME">pastime</a>. It is remarkable, that though this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a> kills millions of the small fry, it has never been known to impair any bad <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to the fish which have been caught in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the intoxication. The wood of this tree, although pretty hard, is only fit for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>; and even for this purpose the negroes very seldom, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> ever, employ it, on account of its singular quality <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned. The bark is rough, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, and thick; the tree sends forth a considerable number of branches, and is well cloathed with leaves, which resemble those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>, are thick, cottony, and of a deep green. The bark used for the above-mentioned purpose is chiefly that of the roots.

PISCINA

Pages 699-699

in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> basin in a public <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, where the Roman youth learned to swim; and which was surrounded with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> wall, to prevent filth from being thrown into it.—This word is also used for a lavatory among the Turks, placed in the middle <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of a mosque or temple, where the Mussulmen wash themselves before they offer their prayers.

PISISTRATUS

Pages 699-699

a famous general of the Athenians. He usurped the supreme power, and, in order to obtain it, was a cruel <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>; but having gained it, he became a wise <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>, and an excellent governor. He died 327 B.C.

PISSAPHALTUM

Pages 699-699
earth-pitch; a fluid, opaque, mineral body, of a thick consistence, strong smell, readily inflammable, but leaving a residuum of greyish ashes after burning. It arises out of the cracks of the rocks, in several places in the island of Sumatra, and some other places in the East Indies, where it is much esteemed in paralytic disorders. PISELÆUM INDICUM, Barbados Tar; a mineral fluid, of the nature of the thicker bitumens, and of all others the most approaching, in appearance, colour, and consistence, to the true pissaphaltum, but differing from it in other respects. It is very frequent in many parts of America, where it is found trickling down the sides of mountains in large quantities, and sometimes floating on the surface of the waters. It has been greatly recommended internally in coughs, and other disorders of the breast and lungs.

PISTACIA

Pages 699-700

turpentine-tree, Pistacia-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> and Majestic tree; a genus of the pentandra order, belonging to the dioecia clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the most remarkable are, 1. The es-rebinthus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> pistachio-tree. This grows naturally in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, whence the nuts are annually brought to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In those countries it grows to the height of 25 or 30 feet; the bark of the stem and old branches is of a dark russet <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, but that of the young branches is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. These are garnished with winged leaves, composed sometimes of two, at other times of three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of lobes, terminated by an odd one; these lobes approach towards an oval shape, and their edges are turned backward; and these, when bruised, emit a smell similar to that of the shell of the nut. Some of these trees produce <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a>, and others <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, and some have both male and female on the same tree. The male flowers come out from the sides of the branches, in loose bunches or catkins. They have no petals, but five small stamens crowned by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> four-cornered summits filled with farina; and when this is discharged, the flowers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> off. The female flowers come out in clusters from the sides of the branches; they have no petals, but a large oval germen supporting three reflexed styles, and are succeeded by oval nuts. Pistacia nuts. 2. The lentiscus, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> mastic-tree, grows naturally in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Being an evergreen, it has been preserved in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in order to adorn the green-houses. In the countries where it is a native, it rises to the height of 18 or 20 feet, covered with a grey bark on the stem; but the branches, which are very numerous, are covered with a reddish-brown bark, and are garnished with winged leaves, composed of three or four pair of small spear-shaped lobes, without an odd one at the end. 3. The orientalis, or true mastic-tree of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, from which the mastic is gathered, has been confounded by most botanical writers with the lentiscus, or common mastic-tree, above described, though there are considerable differences between them. The bark of the tree is brown; the leaves are composed of two or three pair of spear-shaped lobes, terminated by an odd one: the outer lobes are the largest; the others gradually diminish, the innermost being the least. These turn of a brownish colour towards the autumn, when the plants are exposed to the open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are under glass, they keep green. The leaves continue all the year; but are not so thick as those of the common sort, nor are the plants so hardy. Culture. The first species is propagated by its nuts; which should be planted in pots filled with light <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>-garden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and plunged into a moderate hot-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> to bring up the plants; when these appear, they should have a large share of air admitted to them, and by degrees they should be exposed to the open air, which at last they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> bear in all seasons, though not without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> danger of being destroyed in severe winters. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> sort is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> propagated by laying <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the branches, though it may also be raised from the seed in the manner already directed for the pistachia-nut tree: And in this manner also may the true mastic-tree be raised; but this, being more tender than any of the other sorts, requires to be constantly sheltered in winter, and to have a warm situation in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. Uses. Pistachia nuts abound with a sweet and well-tasted <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which they yield in great abundance on being pressed after bruising them: they are reckoned wholesome and nutritious; and are very proper to be preserved by way of reftoratives, eaten in small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, to people emaciated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> illness.

PISTIL

Pages 700-700

among botanists, the little upright <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> which is generally found in the centre of every flower. According to the Linnaean system, it is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, whose office is to receive and secrete the pollen, and produce the fruit. It consists of three parts, viz. germin, stylus, and stigma.

PISTOL

Pages 700-700

the smallest piece of fire-arms, borne at the saddle-bow, on the girdle, and in the pocket.

PISTOLE

Pages 700-700

a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, struck in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and in several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, &c.—The pistole has its augmentations and diminutions, which are quadruple pistoles, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> pistoles, and half pistoles. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">Money</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>.

PISTON

Pages 700-700

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, is a short <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> of metal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> substance, fitted exactly to the cavity of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> or body of the pump. See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HYDROSTATICS">Hydrostatics</a>, &c. v.

PISUM

Pages 700-702

PEASE; a genus of the decandria order, belonging to the diadelphia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The sativum, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> greater garden-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>, whose lower stipule are roundish, indented, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> foot-stalks and many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> on a foot-stalk. 2. The humile, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a> pea, with an erect branching stalk, and leaves having two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of round lobes. 3. The umbellatum, rose, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>-pea, with four-pointed acute stipulae, and foot-stalks <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> many flowers, which terminate the stalks. 4. The martimum, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-pea, with foot-stalks which are plain on their upper side, an angular flak, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>-pointed stipulae, and foot-stalks bearing many flowers. 5. The Americanum, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">Horn</a> pea, with an angular trailing stalk, whose lower leaves are spear-shaped, sharply indented, and those at the top arrow-pointed. 6. The ochrus, with membranaceous running foot-stalks, having two leaves and one flower upon a foot-stalk. There is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of garden peas now cultivated in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, which are distinguished by the gardeners and seedsmen, and have their different titles; but as great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of these have been seminal variations, so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are not very carefully managed, by taking away all those plants which have a tendency to alter before the seeds are formed, they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> degenerate into their original state: therefore all those persons who are curious in the choice of their seeds, look carefully over those which they <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> for seeds at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> when they begin to flower, and draw out all the plants which they dislike from the other. This is what they call roguing their peas; meaning hereby, the taking out all the bad plants from the good, that the farina of the former may not impregnate the latter; to prevent which, they always do it before the flowers open. By thus diligently <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> out the bad, referring those which come earliest to flower, they have greatly improved their peas of late years, and are constantly endeavouring to get forwarder varieties; so that it would be to little purpose in this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, to attempt giving a particular account of all the varieties now cultivated: therefore we shall only mention their titles by which they are commonly known; placing them according to their time of coming to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, or gathering for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> hotspur. Nonpareil. The Charlton. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a> dwarf. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">Reading</a> hotspur. Sickle pea. Maller's hotspur. Marrowfat. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> hotspur. Rose or crown pea. The dwarf pea. Runcival pea. The sugar pea. Gray pea. Spanish Morotto. Pig pea; with some others. The English pea-pea is found wild upon the shore in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a> and several other counties in England, and is undoubtedly a different species from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pea. The fifth species hath a biennial root, which continues two years. This was brought from Cape Horn by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Anson's cook, when he passed that Cape, where these peas were a great relief to the sailors. It is kept here as a curiosity, but the peas are not so good for eating as the worst sort now cultivated in Britain. It is a low trailing plant: the leaves have two lobes on each foot-stalk: those below are spear-shaped, and sharply indented on their edges; but the upper leaves are small, and arrow-pointed. The flowers are blue, each foot-stalk containing four or five flowers; the pods are taper, near three inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and the seeds are round, about the size of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARES">tares</a>. The sixth sort is annual. This grows naturally among the corn in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> and some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, but is here preserved in botanic gardens for the sake of variety. It hath an angular stalk rising near three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; the leaves stand upon winged foot-stalks, each sustaining two <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> lobes. The flowers are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, shaped like those of the other sort of pea, but are small, each foot-stalk sustaining one flower; these are succeeded by pods about two inches long, containing five or six roundish seeds, which are a little compressed on their sides. These are by some persons eaten green; but unless they are gathered very young, they are coarse, and at best not so good as the common pea. It may be sown and managed in the same way as the garden pea. We shall now proceed to set <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the method of cultivating the several sorts of garden peas, so as to continue them throughout the season. It is a common practice with the gardeners near <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, to raise peas upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOT_BEDS">hot-beds</a>, to have them very early in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; in order to which, they sow their peas upon warm borders, under walls or hedges, about the middle of October; and when the plants come up, they draw the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> up gently to their stems with a hoe, the better to protect them from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a>. In these places they let them remain until the latter end of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, or the beginning of February, observing to earth them up from time to time as the plants advance in height (for the reasons before given); as also to cover them in very hard frosts with pease-haulm, straw, or some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> covering, to preserve them from being destroyed; then, at the time before-mentioned, they make a hot-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> (in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of peas intended), which must be made of good hot dung, well prepared and properly mixed together, that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> may not be too great. The dung should be laid for two or three feet thick, according as the beds are made earlier or later in the season; when the dung is equally levelled, then the earth (which should be light and fresh, but not over rich), must be laid thereon about six or eight inches thick, laying it equally all over the bed. This being done, the frames (which should be two feet high on the back side, and about 14 inches in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a>), must be put on, and covered with glasses; after which, it should remain three or four days, to let the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> of the bed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> off before you put the plants therein, observing every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> to raise the glasses, to give vent for the rising steam to pass off; then, when you find the bed of a moderate temperature for heat, you should, with a trowel, or some other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, take up the plants as carefully as possible to preserve the earth to their roots, and plant them into the hot-bed in rows about two feet asunder, and the plants about an inch distant from each other in the rows, observing to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> them until they have taken root; after which you must be careful to give them <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> at all times when the season is favourable, otherwise they will draw up very weak, and be subject to grow mouldy and decay. You should also draw the earth up to the shanks of the plants as they advance in height, and keep them always clear from weeds. The water they should have must be given them sparingly; for if they are too much watered, it will cause them to grow too <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and sometimes rot off the plants at their shanks <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> above ground. When the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> is very hot, you should cover the glasses with mats in the heat of the day, to screen them from the violence of the heat of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, which is then too great for them: but when the plants begin to fruit, they should be watered oftener, and in greater plenty than before; for by that time the plants will have nearly done growing, and the often refreshing them will occasion their producing a greater plenty of fruit. The sort of pea which is generally used for this purpose, is the dwarf; for all the other sorts ramble too much to be kept in frames: the reason for sowing them in the common ground, and afterwards transplanting them on a hot-bed, is to check their growth, and cause them to bear in less compass; for if the seeds were sown upon a hot-bed, and the plants <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> thereon, they would produce such luxuriant plants as could not be contained in the frames, and would bear but little fruit. The next sort of pea, which is sown to succeed those on the hot-bed, is the hotspur, of which there are reckoned several varieties, as the golden hotspur, the Charlton hotspur, the Masters's hotspur, the Reading hotspur, and some others; which are very little differing from each other, except in their early bearing, for which the golden and Charlton hotspurs are chiefly preferred; though if either of these sorts are cultivated in the same place for three or four years, they are apt to degenerate, and be later in fruiting; for which reason, most curious persons procure their seeds annually from some distant place; and in the choice of these seeds, if they could be obtained from a colder situation and a poorer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> than that in which they are to be sown, it will be much better than on the contrary, and they will come earlier in the spring. These must also be sown on warm borders, toward the latter end of October; and when the plants are come up, you should draw the earth up to their shanks and treat them in every other respect as above directed. In the spring you must carefully clear them from weeds, and draw some fresh earth up to their stems; but do not raise it too high up to the plants, lest by burying their leaves you should rot their stems, as is sometimes the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, especially in wet seasons. You should also observe to keep them free from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a>, which, if permitted to remain amongst the plants, will increase so plentifully as to devour the greatest part of them. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the vermin which infect peas are fleas, which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> all the day in the small hollows of the earth, near the stems of the plants, and in the nighttime come out and make terrible destruction of the peas; and these chiefly abound in wet soils, or where a garden is neglected and overrun with weeds; therefore you should make the ground clear every way round the peas to destroy their harbours; and afterwards in a fine mild morning very early, when these vermin are got abroad from their holes, you should flake a quantity of lime, which should be strewed over the ground pretty thick, which will destroy the vermin wherever it happens to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon them, but will do very little injury to the peas, provided it be not scattered too thick upon them. If this crop of peas succeeds, it will immediately follow those on the hot-bed; but for fear this should miscarry, it will be proper to sow two more crops at about a fortnight or three weeks distance from each other, so that there may be the more chances to succeed. This will be sufficient till the spring of the year, when you may sow several more crops of these peas at a fortnight distance from each other. The late sowings will be sufficient to continue the early sort of peas through the season, but it will be proper to have some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sort to succeed them for the use of the family; in order to which, you should sow some of the Spanish Morotto, which is a great bearer and a hardy sort of pea, about the middle of February, upon a clear open spot of ground. These must be sown in rows about four feet asunder, and the peas should be dropped in the drills about an inch distance, covering them about two inches deep with earth, being very careful that none of them lie uncovered, which will draw the mice, pigeons, or rooks, to attack the whole spot; and it often happens, by this neglect, that a whole plantation is devoured by these creatures; whereas, when there are none of the peas left in sight, they do not easily find them out. About a fortnight after this you should sow another spot, either of this sort or any other large sort of pea, to succeed those; and then continue to repeat sowing once a fortnight, till the middle or latter end of May; only observing to allow the marrowfats, and other very large sorts of peas, at least four feet and a half between row and row; and the rose-pea should be allowed at least eight or ten inches distance plant from plant in the rows; for these grow very large, and if they have not room allowed them, they will spoil each other by drawing them up very tall, and will produce no fruit. When the plants come up, the earth should be drawn up to their shanks (as was before directed), and the ground kept entirely clear from weeds; and when the plants are grown eight or ten inches high, you should stick some brushwood into the ground <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the peas for them to ramp upon, which will support them from trailing upon the ground, which is very apt to rot the growing sorts of peas, especially in wet seasons; besides, by thus supporting them, the air can freely pass between them, which will preserve the blossoms from falling off before their time, and occasion them to bear much better than if permitted to lie upon the ground, and there will be room to pass between the rows to gather the peas when they are ripe. The dwarf sorts of peas may be sown much closer together than those before-mentioned; for these seldom rise above a foot high, and rarely spread above half a foot in width, so that these need not have more room than two feet row from row, and not above an inch asunder in the rows. These will produce a good quantity of peas, provided the season be not over-dry; but they seldom continue long in bearing, so that they are not so proper to sow for the main crop when a quantity of peas is expected for the table, their chief excellency being for hot-beds, where they will produce a greater quantity of peas (provided they are well managed) than if exposed to the open air, where the heat of the sun soon dries them up. The large growing sorts may be cultivated for the common use of the family, because these will produce in greater quantities than the other, and will endure the drought better; but the early kind are by far the sweeter-tasted peas. The best of all the large kinds is the marrowfat, which, if gathered young, is a well-tasted pea; and this will continue good through the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of August, if planted on a strong soil. The gray and other large winter-peas are seldom cultivated in gardens, because they require a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of room, but are usually sown in fields. For the proper method of managing them, see <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>, p. 124.

PITCAIRNE

Pages 702-705

a most eminent physician and ingenious poet, was descended from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family of the Pitcairnes of Pitcairne in Fife-shire, and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> on the 25th of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1652. He commenced his studies at the school of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DALKEITH">Dalkeith</a>; and from thence he was removed to the university of Edinburgh, where he improved himself in classical learning, and completed a regular course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. His friends, according to the authors of the Biographia Britannica, were delirious that he should follow the profession of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. The unpleasant gloom, however, which at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> hung over <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and its professors in Scotland, could not but very ill <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> with that native cheerfulness of temper and liberality of mind which made him, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after, a mark for the arrows of preciseness and grimace. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> seems to have been his own choice, and to this science he turned his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. With an ardour peculiar to himself, and an ambition to excel in whatever he undertook, he pursued it with so much intenseness, that his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> began to be impaired. On this account, his physicians advised him to set out for the south of France. By the time he reached <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, he was happily so far recovered, that he determined to renew his studies; but being informed that there was no able professor of law in that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and finding several gentlemen of his acquaintance engaged in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physic, he went with them to the lectures and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and employed himself in this manner for several months, till his affairs called him home. On his return, he applied himself chiefly to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. It is not usual to see the briars of this science and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> growing in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. Here, however, they were happily united; and to this union perhaps was owing that singular command of judgment, over one of the liveliest of fancies, which appears in every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his works. His intimacy with Dr <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Gregory, the celebrated mathematical professor, began about the same time; and probably conducted to cherish his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> aptitude for this study. It was then, in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, new to him; it soon became his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> delight; his progress in it was rapid, and correspondent to his progress in other pursuits. His improvements on the method of infinite <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> then adopted, which Dr Wallis of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> afterwards published, were a conspicuous and early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his abilities in this science. Had Dr Pitcairne <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to prosecute the study of the law, and could he have moulded his principles to the times, the first offices and honours of the state might have been looked for without presumption as the probable reward of such talents as he possessed. Struck, however, with the charms of mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> which had been lately introduced into the philosophy of medicine, and hoping to reduce the healing art to geometrical method, he unalterably determined on this less aspiring profession. At the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when he formed this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the medical world, already sufficiently confused, were still farther jumbled by the discovery of the circulation of the blood, which had as yet produced nothing but doubt, uncertainty, and astonishment. In Edinburgh at that time there was no school, no <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, no opportunity of improvement but the chamber and the shop. He therefore soon after returned to Paris. Genius and industry are unhappily not often united in the same character; of such an union Dr Pitcairne is a celebrated instance. During his residence in France, he cultivated the object of his pursuit with his natural enthusiasm, and with a steadfastness from which he could not be diverted by the allurements of that joy, which, in his hours of social and festive intercourse, he always felt and always gave. Among his various occupations, the study of the ancient physicians seems to have had a principal share. This appears from a treatise which he published some time after his return; and it shows, that he wisely determined to know the progress of medicine from its earliest periods, before he attempted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> and improve that science. On the 13th of August 1689, he received, from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>; which, on the 7th of August 1699, was likewise conferred on him by the university of Aberdeen; both being attended with marks of peculiar distinction. Other medical honours are said to have been conferred on him in France and elsewhere; but nothing affords a more unequivocal testimony to his abilities than that which the surgeons of Edinburgh gave, in admitting him, freely and unostentatiously, a member of their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. None had such opportunities of judging of his merit as a practitioner, and on no physician did they ever bestow the same public mark of respect. Soon after his graduation at Rheims, he returned to Edinburgh; where, on the 29th of November 1681, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> College of Physicians was instituted; and his name, among others, graced the original patent from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">Crown</a>. In his Solutio problematis de inventoribus, the treatise above alluded to, he discovers a wonderful degree of medical literature, and makes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it in a manner that does great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> both to his head and his heart. His object is to vindicate Dr Harvey's claim to the discovery of the circulation of the blood. The discovery was, at first, controverted by envy, and reprobated by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>. When at length its truth was fully established, many individually attempted to tear the laurels from the illustrious Englishman, and to plant them on the brows of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> and others. Had the attempt been directed against himself, the generous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of Pitcairne could not have exerted more zeal in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; and his arguments remain unanswered. During his residence in Scotland, his reputation became so considerable, that, in the year 1691, the university of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> solicited him to fill the medical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, at that time vacant. Such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> testimony of respect, from a foreign <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and from such a university, cannot perhaps be produced in the medical biography of Great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. The lustre of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> reflects honour on their profession, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which has the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> of giving them birth; and serves to give the individuals of that country not only a useful estimation in their own eyes, but in those also of the rest of the world. Dr Pitcairne's well-known <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> principles excluded him from public honours and promotion at home; he, therefore accepted the invitation from abroad; and, on the 26th of April 1692, delivered, at Leyden, his elegant and masterly inaugural <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>: Oratio qua defenditur medicinam <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> omni philosophorum secta effe liberam. In this he clears medicine from the rubbish of the old philosophy; separates it from the influence of the different sects; places it on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and only sure foundation of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; shows how little good inquiries into the manner how medicines operate have done to the art; and demonstrates the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of a fulsome attention to their effects, and to the various appearances of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. Nothing (says an elegant panegyrist* of our author) marks a superiority of intellect so much as the courage requisite to stem a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a> of obstinately prevailing and groundless opinions. For this the genius and talents of Pitcairne were admirably adapted; and, in burgh for his oration, he displays them to the utmost. It was received with the highest commendations; and the administrators, to testify their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of such an acquisition to their university, greatly augmented the ordinary appointment of his chair. He discharged the duties of his office at Leyden so as to answer the most sanguine expectations. He taught with a perspicuity and eloquence which met with universal applause. Independently of the encomiums of Boerhaave and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEAD">Mead</a>, who were his pupils, the numerous manuscript copies of his lectures, and the mutilated specimen of them† which found its way‡ into the world without his knowledge, show how justly it was bestowed. At the same time, he was not more celebrated as a professor than as a practical physician; and notwithstanding the multiplicity of his business in both these characters, he found leisure to publish several treatises on the circulation and some other of the most important parts of the animal economy (A). At the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the session, he set out for Scotland, with an intention of returning in time for the succeeding one. On his marrying (B) the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir Archibald Stevenson, the object of his journey, her relations would on no account consent to part with him again. He was therefore reluctantly obliged to remain; and he wrote the university a polite apology, which was received with the utmost regret. He even declined the most flattering solicitations and tempting offers to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. Indeed he soon came into that extensive practice to which his abilities entitled --- (A) Dr Boerhaave gives the following character of these and some other of Dr Pitcairne's dissertations, which were collected and published at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>, anno 1701: "Haec scripta optima sunt et perfecta, five legas Differtationem de Motu Sanguinis per Pulmones, five alia opuscula, five ultimum tractatum de Opio." Methodus studii, ab Hallero edita, p. 569. (B) He had been married before to a daughter of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> James Hay of Pitfour, by whom he had a son and daughter, who both died young. Pitcairne titled him, and was also appointed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITULAR">titular</a> professor of medicine in the university of Edinburgh. The uniformity of a professional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is seldom interrupted by incidents worthy of record. Specimens, however, of that brilliant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a> with which he delighted his friends in the hours of his leisure, continue to entertain us (c); and the effects of that eminent skill which he exerted in the cure of disease, still operate to the good of posterity. The discovery of the circulation, while in some measure it exploded the chemical and Galenical doctrines, tended to introduce mathematical and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> reasoning in their stead. Of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> (d) Dr Pitcairne was the principal support, and the first who introduced it into Britain. A mathematical turn of mind, and a wish for mathematical certainty in medicine, biased him in its favour, and he pushed it to its utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. One is at a loss whether most to admire <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> regret such a waste of talents in propounding a theory, which, though subversive of former ones, was to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> before others but a little more satisfactory than itself. Mechanical physicians expected more from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> than that science could <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>. They made it the foundation instead of an auxiliary to their inquiries, and applied it to parts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> not admitting mathematical calculations. By paying more attention afterwards to the supreme influence of the living principle, the source of all the motions and functions of the body, it was found that these could not be explained by any laws of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> or mechanism. They are still, however, involved in obscurity; and, notwithstanding the numberless improvements which have taken <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the sciences connected with medicine, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> perhaps remain inscrutable while <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> continues in his present stage of existence. In a science so slowly progressive as that of medicine, Dr Pitcairne did a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>. By labouring in vain for truth in one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, he saved many the same drudgery, and thereby shewed the necessity of another. He not only exploded many false notions of the chemists and Galenists, which prevailed in his time, but many of those too of his own feet. In particular, he shewed the absurdity of referring all diseases and their cures to an alkali or an acid (e). He refuted the idea of secretion being performed by pores differently shaped (f), Bellini's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of effervescences in the animal-spirits with the blood, and Borelli's of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> entering the blood by respiration (g). He proved the continuity of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> and veins (h); and seems to have been the first who shewed that the blood flows from a smaller capacity into a larger, that the aorta, with respect to the arterial system, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APEX">apex</a> of a cone (i). In this therefore he may be considered as the latent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the discoveries respecting the powers moving the blood. He introduced a simplicity of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, unknown in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a> before his time (k); and such was the state of medicine in this country, that scarcely have the works of any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> or preceding author been thought worthy even of perusal (l). As to the errors of his philosophy, let it be remembered, that no theory has as yet stood the test. (c) Vide Pitcairnii Poemata.—Several of his poems, however, are obscure, and some of them totally unintelligible without a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEY">key</a>. In those of them which are of a political kind, he wished not to express himself too clearly; and in others, he alludes to private occurrences which were not known beyond the circle of his companions. His poem (<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> Lindefiun), addressed to his friend <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINDSEY">Lindsey</a>, is commented on by the authors of the Biographia Britannica; and it is to be regretted that it is the only one on which they have been solicitous to throw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. "Some parts (say they) of this poem are hardly intelligible, without knowing a circumstance in the Doctor's life, which he often told, and never without some commotion. It is a well-known story of the two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> philosophers, who promised one another, that which ever died first should make a visit to his surviving <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>. This story being read together by Mr Lindsey and our author, they, being both then very young, entered into the same engagement. Soon after, Pitcairne, at his father's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Fife, dreamed one morning, that Lindsey, who was then at Paris, came to him, and told him he was not dead, as was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> reported, but still alive, and lived in a very agreeable place, to which he could not yet carry him. By the course of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a>, news came of Lindsey's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened very suddenly the morning of the dream. When this is known, the poem is easily understood, and shines with no <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> degree of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>." "Dii faciant reditus fit comes ille tui! Every one sees how much keener an edge is given to the satire upon the Revolution, by making it an additional reason for his friend's keeping his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to return him a visit after his death." (d) See the article Medicine, no. 99.—Borelli, Bellini, &c. espoused the same. (e) Pitcairnii Dissertationes, Edin., edit. 1713. De <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> quam praestant corpora acida vel alkalica in curatione morborum. (f) De circulatione sanguinis per vasa minima. (g) De diversa <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> qua sanguis fluit per pulmones. (h) De circulatione sanguinis per vasa minima. (i) De circulatione sanguinis in animalibus genitis et non genitis. (k) Elementa Medicinae, lib. i. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 21. et passim. (l) The first medical publication which distinguished this country, after Dr Pitcairne's, was that of the Edinburgh Medical Essays, in the year 1732. Vid. the article Monro. test of many years in an enlightened period. His own hung very loosely about him (m), and the present generally received practice differs from his very little in reality. He treated inflammatory and hemorrhagic diseases by bleeding, purging, and blistering, as has been done uniformly and solely on the different theories since. His method of administering <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> and the bark is observed at this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and with respect to febrile, nervous, glandular, and dropsical affections, they seem to be as often the opprobriums of the art now, as they were then. Dr Pitcairne was universally considered as the first physician of his time. No one appears ever to have had so much practice in this country, or so many consultations from abroad; and no one, from all accounts, ever practised with greater sagacity and success. The highest thought themselves honoured by his acquaintance, and the lowest were never denied his affluence and advice. The emoluments of his profession must have been great; but his charities are known to have been correspondent. The possession of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> he postponed to more liberal objects: he collected one of the finest private <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> in the world; which was purchased, after his death, by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CZAR">Czar</a> of Muscovy. Notwithstanding the fatigues he underwent in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of his profession, his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was naturally delicate. About the beginning of October 1713, he became affected with his last illness; and on the 23d he died, regretted by science as its ornament, by his country as its boast, and by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> as its friend. He left a son and four daughters; of whom only one of the latter now survives. The present noble family of Kelly are his grandchildren. Some anonymous publications are attributed to Dr Pitcairne, particularly a treatise De Legibus Historiae Naturalis, &c.; but the only ones he thought proper to legitimate are his Dissertations Medicae, and a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> De Salute.

PITCH

Pages 705-705

a tenacious oily substance, drawn chiefly from pines and firs, and used in shipping, medicine, and various arts: <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> it is more properly tar inspissated by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> it over a slow fire. See TAR.

PITCHING

Pages 705-705

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-affairs, may be defined, the vertical vibration which the length of a ship makes about her centre of gravity; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the movement by which she plunges her head and after <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> alternately into the hollow of the sea. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> may proceed from two causes: the waves, which agitate the vessel; and the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> upon the sails, which makes her stoop to every blast thereof. The first absolutely depends upon the agitation of the sea, and is not susceptible of inquiry; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is occasioned by the inclination of the mast, and may be submitted to certain established maxims. When the wind acts upon the sails, the mast yields to its effort, with an inclination, which increases in proportion to the length of the mast, to the augmentation of the wind, and to the comparative <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and distribution of the ship's lading. The repulsion of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, to the effort of gravity, opposes itself to this inclination, or at least sustains it, by as much as the repulsion exceeds the momentum, or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> effort of the mast, upon which the wind operates. At the end of each blast, when the wind suspends its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, this repulsion lifts the vessel; and these successive inclinations and repulsions produce the movement of pitching, which is very inconvenient; and, when it is considerable, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> greatly retard the course, as well as endanger the mast, and strain the vessel.

PITISCUS

Pages 705-705

a learned antiquary, born at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZUTPHEN">Zutphen</a>, was rector of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and afterwards of St Jerome at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, where he died on the 1st of February 1717, aged ninety. He wrote, 1. Lexicon Antiquitatum Romanorum, in two volumes folio; a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> which is esteemed. 2. Editions of many Latin authors, with notes; and other works.

PITS

Pages 705-706

the biographer, was born in 1560, at Aulton in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>; and educated at Wykeham's school, near <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, till he was about 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; when he was sent to New-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and admitted probationer fellow. Having <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in that university not quite two years, he left the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> as a voluntary Romish exile, and retired to Dowsay; thence he went to the English college at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>, where he remained about a year; and then proceeded to Rome, where he continued a member of the English college near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years, and was made a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. In 1589 he returned to Rheims; and there, during two years, taught <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> and the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. He now quitted Rheims, on account of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> in France; and retired to Pont à Mousson in Lorraine, where he took the degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts and bachelor in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. Hence he travelled into Germany; and resided a year and a half at Triers, where he commenced <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LICENTIATE">licentiate</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>. From Triers he visited several of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cities in Germany; and continuing three years at Ingolstadt in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, took the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> in divinity. Thence having made the tour of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, he returned once more to Lorraine; where he was patronized by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>, who preferred him to a canonry of Verdun; and about two years after, he became confessor to the duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLEVES">Cleves</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Lorraine. During the leisure he enjoyed in this employment, he wrote in Latin the lives of the kings, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, apostolical men, and writers of England. The last of these, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known and quoted by this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, De illustribus Anglicis scriptoribus, was published after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The three first remain still in manuscript, among the archives of the collegiate <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Liverdun. The duke of Cleves dying, after Pits had been about twelve years confessor to the duchess, she returned to Lorraine, attended by our author, who was promoted to the deanery of Liverdun, which, with a canonry and officialship, he enjoyed to the end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He died in 1616, and was buried in the collegiate church. Pits was undoubtedly a scholar, and not an inelegant writer; but he is justly accused of ingratitude to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALE">Bale</a>, from whom he borrowed his materials, without acknowledgment. He quotes Le- --- (m) Patel, says he, medicinam esse memoriam eorum quae cuilibet morbo utus ostendit suisse utilia. Nam notas non esse corporum intra venas fluentium aut consistentium naturas, adeoque sola observatione innotescere quid cuique morbo conveniat, postquam saepius eadem eadem morbo profuisse comperimus. De Div. Morb. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> familiarity, without ever having seen his book: his errors are innumerable, and his partiality to the Romish writers most obvious; nevertheless we are obliged to him for his account of several popish authors, who lived abroad at the beginning of the Reformation.

PITT

Pages 706-707

an eminent English poet, celebrated for his excellent translation of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s Aeneid, was born in the year 1699. Having studied four years at New-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, he was presented to the living of Pimperne in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, which he held during the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He had so poetical a turn, that while he was a school-boy he wrote two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> folios of manuscript poems, one of which contained an entire translation of Lucan. He was much esteemed while at the university; particularly by the celebrated Dr Young, who used familiarly to call him his son. Next to his fine translation of Virgil, Mr Pitt gained the greatest reputation by his excellent English translation of Vida's art of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. This amiable poet died in the year 1648, without leaving, it is said, one enemy behind him. PITT (William) <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>, a most celebrated British statesman and patriot, was born in November 1708. He was the youngest son of Robert Pitt, Esq.; of Boconock in Cornwall; and grandson of Thomas Pitt, Esq.; governor of Fort St George in the East Indies, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, who sold an extraordinary fine <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of France for £135,000l. and thus obtained the name of Diamond Pitt. His intellectual faculties and powers of elocution very soon made a distinguished appearance; but, at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 16, he felt the attacks of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> and incurable gout, by which he was tormented at times during the rest of his life. His lordship entered early into the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and served in a regiment of dragoons. Through the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, he obtained a seat in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> before he was 21 years of age. His first appearance in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was as representative of the borough of Old Sarum, in the ninth parliament of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. In the 10th he represented <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAFORD">Seaford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDBOROUGH">Aldborough</a> in the 11th, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Bath in the 12th; where he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till he was called up to the house of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> in 1766. The intention of the duchess in bringing him thus early into parliament was to oppose Sir Robert Walpole, and whom he kept in awe by the force of his eloquence. At her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> the duchess left him £10,000l. on condition, as was then reported, that he should never receive a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in administration. However, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any such condition was made, it certainly was not kept on his Lordship's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>. In 1746 he was appointed vice-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and soon after paymaster general of the forces, and sworn a privy-counsellor. He discharged the office of paymaster with such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and inflexible integrity, refusing even many of the perquisites of his office, that his bitterest enemies could lay nothing to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, and he soon became the darling of the people. In 1755 he resigned the office of paymaster, on seeing Mr Fox preferred to him. The people were alarmed at this resignation; and being disgusted with the unsuccessful beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, complained so loudly, that, on the 4th <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1756, Mr Pitt was appointed secretary of state in the room of Mr Fox afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; and other promotions were made in order to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> his plans. He then took such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> as were necessary for the honour and interest of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; but in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of February 1757, having refused to assent to the carrying on a war in Germany for the sake of his majesty's dominions on the continent, he was deprived of the seals on the 5th of April following. Upon this the complaints of the people again became so violent, that on the 29th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> he was again appointed secretary, and his friends to other important offices. The success with which the war was now conducted is universally known; yet on the 5th of October 1761, Mr Pitt, to the astonishment of almost the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, resigned the seals into his majesty's own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. The reason of this was, that Mr Pitt, having received certain intelligence that the family-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> was signed between France and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and that the latter was about to join France against us, thought it necessary to prevent her by commencing hostilities first. Having communicated this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in the privy-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, the other ministers urged that they would think twice before they declared war against this kingdom. "I <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not give them leave to think," replied Mr Pitt; "this is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, let us crush the whole house of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a>. But if the members of this board are of a different opinion, this is the last time I shall ever mix in its councils. I was called into the ministry by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of the people, and to them I hold myself answerable for my conduct. I am to thank the ministers of the late king for their support; I have served my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> with success; but I will not be responsible for the conduct of the war any longer than while I have the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of it." To this bold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>, the lord who then presided in council, made the following reply. "I find the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> is determined to leave us; nor can I say that I am sorry for it, since he would otherwise have certainly compelled us to leave him.
