This method of culture may be recommended for all kinds of soil: for as by this practice the rank luxuriant canes will be more matured, so the poor soils will be rendered more fruitful; and as the roots of the canes which expand into these spaces, will be kept moist by being covered with rotten trash, so they must bear dry weather much longer in the burning soils. In those low lands which require draining by furrows, the alternate double rows and spaces must be made across the ridges; by which means, these spaces, being hoe-ploughed from the centre to the sides, will be always preserved in a proper state of roundness. By this method of planting, the canes may be so well ripened as to yield double the quantity of sugar, of canes planted in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> manner; which saves half the labour of cartage, half the time of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, and half the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, besides yielding finer sugar. Yet, how well soever the method of planting in single or double alternate rows has succeeded in the loose and stiff soils, experience has shown that it is a wrong practice in stiff lands that are thrown into round or flat ridges: for these being most apt to crack, the sun-beams penetrate soon to the cane-roots, stop their growth, and have an ill influence upon the sugar. It is therefore adviseable to plant such lands full, but in large holes, of 4 feet, by 5 feet towards the banks: after the plant-canées are cut, to dig out one, and leave two rows standing, hoe-ploughing the spaces after turning all the trash into furrows till almost rotten: for if the trash is drawn upon the hoe-ploughed spaces, they will hardly ever moulder; at least not till the trash is quite rotten. This is an infallible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> from experience, of how little advantage trash is to the soil, unless it be in great droughts, to keep out the intense sun-beams: for, in all other respects, it prevents that joint operation of the sun and air in mouldering and fructifying the soil, as has been proved by repeated experiments. But in flat stiff soils that are properly drained by round-ridging, no culture prevents cracking so effectually as hoe-ploughing into them a quantity of loose marl, of which that of a chocolate or of a yellow colour is best; and will be still much better, by lying upon the land, in small heaps, or in cane-holes, for some time, to imbibe the vegetative powers of the air, before it is intimately mixed with the soil. As to the manner of planting canes, the general practice of allowing four feet by five to an hole, and two fresh (g) plants, is found by common experience to be right and good in alternate rows. But the following precautions are necessary to be observed. First, let all the cane-rows run east and west, that the trade-wind may pass freely through them; because air and sunshine are as conducive to the growth and maturation of sugar-canes, as any other vegetable. Secondly, let not any accession of mould be drawn into hills round the young canes, except where water stagnates (h); because the fibres which run horizontally, and near the surface, are much broken and spoiled by that practice. Thirdly, let the sugar-canes be cut at their full maturity; which, in a dry loose soil, is generally at the end of 14 or 15 months after being planted; but in cold clay-soils, not till 16 or 17 months. Fourthly, as the cane-rows run east and west in as proper a direction as possible for carriage to the sugar-work, so canes must be cut the contrary way if the planter expects any great produce from his raatons: for by beginning to cut canes at the part of his field most remote from the works, the carts cannot often pass over the same tract, and consequently the cane-stools cannot be injured, more especially if he takes due care to cut the canes very close to their roots; for, by leaving a long stub, (which must perish) the cane-stools are much injured. It may be objected to the practice of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a> cane tranversely to the rows, that the negroes labour will not be so equally divided: but let every man consider both sides of the question, and be determined by his own experience; and then he will be convinced, that it matters very little which way he cuts straight (standing canes; but in cases where the sugar-canes lean, or are lodged by preceding high winds, it is a point of great importance to place the labourers so as to cut the canes first at the roots, and then, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> them, cut off the tops: for thus by two strokes each cane will (f) In stiff lands, the single alternate rows of four feet distance, as preventive of much labour in weeding, are found best; and also yield more sugar by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>; and are less apt to be affected by drought. (g) It is an odd fancy that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STALE">stale</a> plants grew best, when both reason and experience vouch that the most succulent plants are best: one good plant in the centre of a large hole is sufficient when the land is full holed. (h) The stagnation of water in pools (usual in stiff level lands) is the most injurious circumstance attending it; for that, by long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, will convert the finest mould to stiff clay. The proprietor of such a soil must therefore grudge no labour to drain it well; and yet by such easy gradation, as to prevent the mould from being washed away by great floods, in case the under stratum is a loam. be cut; and twice the quantity cut in the same time, and by the same hands, more than by cutting in any other direction. In round-ridged land, it is proper to cut canes in the same direction of the ridges, throwing the tops and trash into the furrows to render the cartage easy, and to preserve the ridges in their proper form. It is almost needless to suggest the expediency of planning the cane-pieces of a plantation in exact squares, so that the intervals may intersect at right <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>; since such regularity is not only more beautiful, more safe in case of accidental fires, and a better disposition of the whole for dividing and planting one third or fourth part of a plantation every year, but also much easier guarded by a few watchmen: for one of these walking in a line from east to west, and the other from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, look through every avenue, where the most subtile thief cannot escape the watchful eye. And if the intervals surrounding the boundary of a regular plantation be made 24 feet wide, the proprietor will receive ample recompense for so much land, by the security of his canes from fires kindled in the neighbourhood, and by planting all that land in plantain-trees, which may at once yield food and shade to the watchmen, who by that means can have no excuse for absence from their proper stations. But as fuel grows very scarce in most of our islands, it is also expedient to plant a logwood or flower-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> in all the boundaries of every plantation, which, being cut every year, will furnish good store of faggots. Logwood makes the strongest and quickest of all fences, and agrees with every soil: the cuttings make excellent oven-fuel. So much for the general operations of plantership, according to the approved directions of Mr Martin. For the particular cultivation of the sugar-canoe, the extraction of the sugar, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> of rum, see the articles SACCHARUM, SUGAR, and RUM.

PLANTIN

Pages 735-735

a celebrated printer, was born near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a> in 1533, and bred to an art which he carried to the highest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection. He went and settled at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>; and there erected a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>-office, which was considered not only as the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ornament of the town, but as one of the most extraordinary edifices in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors were printed here; and these editions were valued not only for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, but also for the correctness of the text, with regard to which Plantin was so very nice, that he procured the most learned men to be correctors of his press. He got immense <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> by his profession; which however he did not hoard up, but spent like a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>. He died in 1598, aged 65 years; and left a most sumptuous and valuable library to his grandson Balthasar.

PLANTING

Pages 735-736

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>, is setting a tree <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> plant, taken from its proper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in a new hole or pit; throwing fresh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> over its root, and filling up the hole to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the surface of the ground. The first thing in planting is to prepare the ground before the trees or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> are taken out of the earth, that they may remain out of the ground as short a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> as possible; and the next is, to take up the trees or plants, in order to their being transplanted. In taking up the trees, carefully dig away the earth round the roots, so as to come at their several parts to cut them off; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are torn out of the ground without care, the roots <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be broken and bruised, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> injury of the trees. When you have taken them up, the next thing is to prepare them for planting by pruning the roots and heads. And first, as to the roots; all the small fibres are to be cut off, as near to the place from whence they are produced as may be, except they are to be replanted immediately after they are taken up. Then prune off all the bruised or broken roots, all such as are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> and crooked each other, and all downright roots, especially in fruit-trees: shorten the larger roots in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, the strength, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the tree; observing that the walnut, mulberry, and some other tender-rooted kinds, should not be pruned so <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> as the more hardy sorts of fruit and forest trees: in young fruit-trees, such as pears, apples, plumbs, peaches, &c. that are one year old from the time of their budding or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAFTING">grafting</a>, the roots may be left only about eight or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; but in older trees, they must be left of a much greater length: but this is only to be understood of the larger roots; for the small ones must be chiefly cut quite out, or pruned very short. The next thing is the pruning of their heads, which must be differently performed in different trees; and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the trees must also be considered. Thus, if they are designed for walls or espaliers, it is best to plant them with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of their heads, which should remain on till they begin to shoot in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, when they must be cut <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to five or six eyes, at the same time taking care not to disturb the roots. But if the trees are designed for standards, you should prune off all the small branches close to the place where they are produced, as also the irregular ones which crook each other; and after having disposed these branches, you should also cut off all such parts of branches as have by any accident been broken or wounded; but by no means cut off the main leading shoots which are necessary to attract the sap from the root, and thereby promote the growth of the tree. Having thus prepared the trees for planting, you must now proceed to place them in the earth: but first, if the trees have been long out of the ground, so that the fibres of the roots are dried, place them eight or ten hours in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, before they are planted, with their heads erect, and the roots only immersed therein; which will swell the dried vessels of the roots, and prepare them to imbibe nourishment from the earth. In planting them, great regard should be had to the nature of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>: for if that be <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and moist, the trees should be planted very shallow; and if it be a hard rock or gravel, it will be better to raise a hill of earth where each tree is to be planted, than to dig into the rock or gravel, and fill it up with earth, as is too often practised, by which means the trees are planted as it were in a tub, and have but little room to extend their roots. The next thing to be observed is, to place the trees in the hole in such a manner that the roots may be about the same depth in the ground as before they were taken up; then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the earth fine with a spade, and scatter it into the hole, so that it may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in between every root, that there may be no hollows in the earth; then having filled up the hole, gently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a> down the earth with your feet, but do not make it too hard; which is a great fault, especially if the ground be strong or wet. Having thus planted the trees, they should be fastened to stakes driven into the ground to prevent their being displaced by the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, and some mulch laid upon the surface of the ground about their roots; as to such as are planted against walls, their roots should be placed about five or six inches from the wall, to which their heads should be nailed to prevent their being blown up by the wind. The seasons for planting are various, according to the different sorts of trees, or the soil in which they are planted. For the trees whose leaves fall off in winter, the best time is the beginning of October, provided the soil be dry; but if it be a very wet soil, it is better to defer it till the latter end of February, or the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>: and for many kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">evergreens</a>, the beginning of April is by far the best season; though they may be safely removed at Midsummer, provided they are not to be carried very far; but should always make choice of a cloudy wet season. Reversed Planting, a method of planting in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> position of the plant or shoot is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>; the branches being set into the earth, and the root reared into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Dr Agricola mentions this monstrous method of planting, which he found to succeed very well in most or all sorts of fruit-trees, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>-trees, &c. Bradley affirms that he has seen a lime-tree in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> growing with its first roots in the air, which had <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> out branches in great plenty, at the same time that its first branches produced roots and fed the tree. Mr Fairchild, of Hoxton, has practised the same with us, and gives the following directions for performing it: Make choice of a young tree of one shoot, of alder, elm, willow, or any other tree that easily takes root by laying; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> the shoot gently down into the earth, and so let it remain till it has taken root. Then dig about the first root, and raise it gently out of the ground, till the stem be nearly upright, and stake it up. Then prune the roots, now erected in the air, from the bruises and wounds they received in being dug up; and anoint the pruned parts with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of two ounces of turpentine, four ounces of tallow, and four ounces of bees wax, melted together, and applied pretty warm. Afterwards prune off all the buds or shoots that are upon the stem, and dress the wounds with the same composition, to prevent any collateral shootings, that might spoil the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the stem.

PLANUDES

Pages 736-736

a Greek monk of Constantinople, towards the end of the 14th century, who published a collection of epigrams intitled Anthologia; a Greek translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Æsop, which is rather a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a> than a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; and some other works. We know nothing more of him, than that he suffered some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> on account of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. PLASHING of Quickset-hedges, an operation very necessary to promote the growth and continuance of old hedges. See the article Hedge. It is performed in this manner: The old stubs must be cut off, &c. within two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> three inches of the ground; and the best and longest of the middle-sized shoots must be left to lay <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. Some of the strongest of these must also be left to answer the purpose of stakes. These are to be cut off to the height at which the hedge is intended to be left; and they are to stand at ten feet distance one from another: when there are not proper shoots for these at the due distances, their places must be supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> stakes of dead wood. The hedge is to be first thinned, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> away all but those shoots which are intended to be used either as stakes, or the other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the plashing; the ditch is to be cleaned out with the spade; and it must be now dug as at first, with sloping sides each way; and when there is any cavity on the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a> on which the hedge grows, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> has been washed away from the roots of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, it is to be made good by facing it, as they express it, with the mould dug from the upper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ditch: all the rest of the earth dug out of the ditch is to be laid upon the top of the bank: and the owner should look carefully into it that this be done; for the workmen, to spare themselves trouble, are apt to throw as much as they can upon the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the bank; which being by this means overloaded, is soon washed off into the ditch again, and a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of the work undone; whereas what is laid on the top of the bank always remains there, and makes a good <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> of an indifferent hedge. In the plashing the quick, two extremes are to be avoided; these are, the laying it too low, and the laying it too thick. The latter makes the sap run all into the shoots, and leaves the plashes without sufficient nourishment; which, with the thickness of the hedge, finally kills them. The other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> of laying them too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, is equally to be avoided; for this carries up all the nourishment into the plashes, and so makes the shoots small and weak at the bottom, and consequently the hedge thin. This is a common <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England. The best hedges made anywhere in England, are those in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>; for they are plashed in a middle way between the two extremes, and the cattle are by that prevented both from cropping the young shoots, and from going through; and a new and vigorous hedge soon forms itself. When the shoot is bent down that is intended to be plashed, it must be cut half way through with the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a>: the cut must be given sloping, somewhat downwards, and then it is to be wound about the stakes, and after this its superfluous branches are to be cut off as they stand out at the sides of the hedge. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> for the first year or two, the field where a new hedge is made can be ploughed, it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> thrive the better for it; but if the stubs are very old, it is best to cut them quite down, and to secure them with good dead hedges on both sides, till the shoots are grown up from them strong enough to plash; and wherever void spaces are seen, new lets are to be planted to fill them up. A new hedge raised from sets in the common way, generally requires plashing in about eight or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years after.

PLASTER

Pages 736-737

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> application of a harder consistence than an ointment; to be spread, according to the different circumstances of the wound, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> patient, either upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. See Pharmacy, no 854, &c. Plaster, or Plaister, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> tion of lime, sometimes with sand, &c. to parget, or cover the nuditics of a building. See Pargetting and Stucco. Plaster of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of several <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of gypsum dug near Mont Maitre, a village in the neighbourhood of Paris; whence the name. See Gypsum; and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, no 127, 128. The best sort is hard, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, shining, and marbly; known by the name of plaster-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or parget of Mount Maitre. It <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> neither give fire with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, nor ferment with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> fortis; but very freely and readily calcines in the fire into a fine plaster, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of which in building and casting <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> is well known. The method of representing a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> truly in plaster of Paris is this: The person whose <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is designed is laid on his back, with any convenient thing to keep off the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. Into each nostril is conveyed a conical piece of stiff <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, open at both ends, to allow of respiration. These tubes being anointed with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, are supported by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of an assistant; then the face is lightly oiled over, and the eyes being kept shut, alabaster fresh calcined, and tempered to a thinish consistence with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, is by spoonfuls nimbly thrown all over the face, till it lies near the thickness of an inch. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> grows sensibly hot, and in about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> hardening into a kind of stony concretion; which being gently taken off, represents, on its concave surface, the minutest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the original face. In this a head of good clay may be moulded, and therein the eyes are to be opened, and other necessary amendments made. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> face being anointed with oil, a second mould of calcined alabaster is made, consisting of two parts joined lengthwise along the ridge of the nose; and herein may be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>, with the same matter, a face extremely like the original. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> finely powdered alabaster, or plaster of Paris, be put into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASON">bason</a> over a fire, it will, when hot, assume the appearance of a fluid, by rolling in waves, yielding to the touch, steaming, &c. all which properties it again loses on the departure of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; and being thrown upon paper, will not at all wet it, but immediately discover itself to be as motionless as before it was set over the fire; whereby it appears, that a heap of such little bodies, as are neither spherical nor otherwise regularly shaped, nor small enough to be below the discernment of the eye, may, without fusion, be made fluid, barely by a sufficiently strong and various agitation of the particles which compose it; and moreover lose its fluidity immediately upon the cessation thereof. Two or three spoonfuls of burnt alabaster, mixed up thin with water, in a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> coagulate, at the bottom of a vessel full of water, into a hard lump, notwithstanding the water that surrounded it. Artificers observe, that the coagulating <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of burnt alabaster will be very much impaired or lost, if the powder be kept too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, especially if in the open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, before it is made use of; and when it hath been once tempered with water, and suffered to grow hard, they cannot, by any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> or powdering of it again, make it serviceable for their purpose as before. This matter, when wrought into vessels, &c. is still of a loose and spongy a texture, that the air has easy passage through it. Mr Boyle gives an account, among his experiments with the air-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>, of his preparing a tube of this plaster, closed at one end and open at the other; and on applying the open end to the cement, as is usually done with the receivers, it was found utterly impossible to exhaust all the air out of it; for fresh air from without pressed in as fast as the other, or internal air, was exhausted, though the sides of the tube were of a considerable thickness. A tube of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> was then put on the engine; so that being filled with water, the tube of plaster of Paris was covered with it; and on using the pump, it was immediately seen, that the water passed through into it as easily as the air had done, when that was the ambient fluid. After this, trying it with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> turpentine instead of water, the thing succeeded very well; and the tube might be perfectly exhausted, and would remain in that state several hours. After this, on pouring some hot oil upon the turpentine, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> was much altered; for the turpentine melting with this, that became a thinner fluid, and in this state capable of passing like water into the pores of the plaster. On taking away the tube after this, it was remarkable that the turpentine, which had pervaded and filled its pores, rendered it transparent, in the manner that water gives transparency to that singular stone called oculus mundi. In this manner, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of air, under proper management, will be capable of making several sorts of glues penetrate plaster of Paris; and not only this, but baked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, wood, and all other bodies, porous enough to admit water on this occasion. PLASTERING. See Pargetting.

PLASTIC

Pages 737-738

denotes a thing endowed with a formative power, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of forming or fashioning a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> after the likeness of a living being; such a virtue, as some of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Epicureans, and perhaps the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a> too, imagined to reside in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, or at least to have anciently resided therein, by means whereof, and without any extraordinary intervention of a Creator, it put forth <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, &c. Some of them seem to have been of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that animals, and even <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> himself, were the effects of this plastic power. Plastic Art, the art of representing all sorts of figures by the means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> is derived from the Greek word πλαστικός, which signifies the "art of forming, modelling, or casting in a mould." A mould, in general, is a body that is made hollow for that purpose. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> makes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them to form figures in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, or any other metal, or fusible substance. The mould is made of clay, stucco, or other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, and is hollowed into the form of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> that is to be produced; they then apply the jet, which is a sort of funnel, through which the metal is poured that is to form the figures, and that is called running the metal into the mould. It is in this manner, but with much practice and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, that the artist forms, 1. Equestrian and pedestrian <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of every kind; 2. Groups; 3. Pedestals; 4. Bases reliefs; 5. Medallions; 6. Cautionary mortars, and other pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>; 7. Ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, as capitals, bases, &c.; 8. Various sorts of furniture, as lustres, branches, &c. in every kind of metal; and in the same manner figures are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in stucco, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, or any other fusible matter. Wax being a substance that is very easily put in fusion, plastics makes much use of it. There are impressions which are highly pleasing in coloured wax, of medallions, baso and alto relievo, and of detached figures; which however are somewhat brittle. But this matter has been carried too far: they have not only formed moulds to represent the likenesses and the bust of a living person, by applying the plaster to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> itself, and afterward casting melted wax into the mould; but they have also painted that waxen bust with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> colours of the face, and have then applied glass eyes and natural <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>; to which they have joined a stuffed body and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of wax; and have, lastly, dressed their figure in a real <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; and by these means have produced an object the most shocking and detestable that it is possible to conceive. It is not a statue, a bust, a natural resemblance that they form; but a dead body, a lifeless countenance, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> carcass. The stiff <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, the inflexible muscles, the haggard eyes of glass, all contribute to produce an object that is hideous and disgusting to every man of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. Figures like these offend by affording too exact an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. In no one of the polite arts ought imitation ever to approach so near the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> as to be taken for nature herself. Illusion must have its bounds; without which it becomes ridiculous. There is another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, far more ingenious and pleasing, which is that wherein M. Lippart, antiquary and artist at Dresden, now excels. He has found the means of resembling, by indefatigable labour, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> expense, and infinite taste, that immense <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, engraved and in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CAMEO">cameo</a>, which are to be seen in the most celebrated cabinets. He has made choice of those that are the most beautiful; and, with a paste of his own invention, he takes from these stones an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> that is surprisingly accurate, and which afterward become as hard as marble; these impressions he calls pasti. He then gives them a proper <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and isolates each with a gold rim; and, by ranging them in a judicious order, forms of them an admirable system. They are fixed on pasteboards, which form so many drawers, and are then inclosed in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, which represent folio volumes, and have titles wrote on their backs; so that these fictitious books may conveniently occupy a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in a library. Nothing can be more ingenious than this invention; and, by this method, persons of moderate fortune are enabled to make a complete collection of all antiquity has left that is excellent of this kind; and these copies are very little inferior to the originals. There is also another method of taking the impressions of cameos, medals, and coins, which is as follows: They wash or properly clean the piece whose impression is to be taken, and surround it with a border of wax. They then dissolve the glass in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and make a decoction of it, mixing with it some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a> to give it an agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> colour. They pour this paste, when hot, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or medal, to the thickness of about the tenth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of an inch; they then leave it exposed to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, in a place free from dust. After a few days this paste becomes hard, and offers to the eye the most admirable and faithful representation of the medal that it is possible to conceive: they are then carefully placed in drawers; and thousands of these impressions, which comprehend many ages, may be included in a small compass. The proficient in plastics have likewise invented the art of casting, in a mould, papier mâché or dissolved <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and forming it into figures in imitation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, of ornaments and decorations for ceilings, furniture, &c. and which they afterwards paint or gild. There are, however, some inconveniences attending this art; as, for example, the imperfections in the moulds, which render the contours of the figures inelegant, and give them a heavy air: these ornaments, moreover, are not so durable as those of bronze or wood, seeing that in a few years they are preyed on by the worm. The figures that are given to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, delph <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, &c. belong also to plastics; for they are formed by moulds, as well as by the art of the sculptor and turner; and by all these arts united, are made vases of every kind, figures, groups, and other designs, either for use or ornament. From this general article the reader is referred to Foundery, Casting, Glass, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a> Ware, Papier-Mâché, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POTTERY">Pottery</a>.

PLATA

Pages 738-739

the name of a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> river of South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, running through the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Paraguay; whence the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is sometimes called Plata; though this name is usually bestowed only upon a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of Paraguay. In the latter <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it comprehends all that country bounded on the east and south-east by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic Ocean</a>; on the south, by Terra Magellanica; on the west, by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUCUMAN">Tucuman</a>; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by the provinces of Paraguay Proper, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARANA">Parana</a>. The great river La Plata, from which the country has its name, was first discovered, in 1515, by Juan Diaz de Solis; but denominated La Plata by Sebastian Gabato, from the great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> he procured from the adjacent inhabitants, imagining it was the produce of the country, though in fact they brought it from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. The country lies between 32° and 37° of south latitude. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is pleasant and healthy. Their winter is in May, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, when the nights are indeed very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, but the days moderately warm; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a> is neither violent nor lasting, and the snows are very inconsiderable. The country consists mostly of plains of a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and exceeding rich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, producing all sorts of European and American <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, wheat, maize, cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, &c. and abounding with such excellent pastures, that the beasts brought hither from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> are multiplied to such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that they are all in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> claiming any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in them, but every man takes what he hath occasion for. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, especially, is so prodigious, that many thousands of them are killed merely for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the ships go for Spain, and their carcases left to be devoured by wild beasts and birds of prey, which are also very numerous. Sometimes, when they cannot vend their hides, they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> kill them for their tongues; and those who care not to be at the trouble to fetch them from the plains, may buy them for a trifle. There is a curious account in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Anson's voyage of the manner of hunting them on horseback; and of catching and killing them, by throwing a noose on their horns at full gallop, the horses being trained to the sport. Horses are no less numerous, and in common, like the other cattle; so that a man may have as many as he pleases for the catching; and of those that are already broke, one may buy some of the beef, and of the true Spanish breed, for a piece of eight per head. Wild-fowl also is in great plenty here; partridges, in particular, are more numerous, and as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and tame as our hens, so that one may kill them with a stick. Their wheat makes the finest and whitest of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; and, in a word, they seem to want for nothing here, especially the natives, but <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>. The former the Spaniards have brought to them from other parts; and the latter they supply themselves with, by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> vast numbers of almond, peach, and other trees, which require no other trouble than putting the kernels into the ground, and by the next year, we are told, they begin to bear fruit. The return for European commodities is so great here, that it almost exceeds <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>; an ordinary two-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> fetching a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a> of the value of 10 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> 12 shillings, 20 or 30 crowns, and so of the rest. The river Plata rises in Peru, and receives a great many others in its course, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which is the Paraguay. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> of it is said to be very clear and sweet, and to petrify wood; and contains such plenty and variety of fish, that the people catch great quantities of them without any other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> than their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. It runs mostly to the south and south-east; and is navigable the greater part of its course by the largest vessels, and full of delightful <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. All along its banks are seen the most beautiful birds of all kinds; but it sometimes overflows the adjacent country to a great extent, and is infested by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> of a prodigious size. From its junction with the Paraguay to its mouth is above 200 leagues. We may form some judgment of its largeness by the width of its mouth, which is said to be about 70 leagues. Before it falls into the Paraguay, it is called <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a>. PLATÆÆ, (anc. geogr.), a very strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACTRIA">Bactria</a>, in its situation exposed to the north <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>); burnt to the ground by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a>, (<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, Justinus); mentioned much in the course of the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>: Famous for the defeat of Mardonius, the Persian general; and for the most signal victory of the Lacedemonians and other Greeks under Pausanias the Lacedemonian, and Ariades an Athenian general, (Nepos, Diodorus, Plutarch); in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of which the Greeks erected a temple to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Eleutherius, and instituted games which they called <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELEUTHERIA">Eleutheria</a>; and there they show the tombs of those who fell in that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, (Strabo). It stood at the foot of mount Cithaeron, between that and Thebes to the north, on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, and on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a> and Megaris. Now in ruins.

PLATAEA

Pages 739-739

the Spoonbill, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of grallæ. The beak is plain, and dilates towards the point into an orbicular form; the feet have three toes, and are half palmated. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, distinguished by their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. They inhabit the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. See Plate CCXLIV. fig. 3.

PLATANUS

Pages 739-740

the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANE">Plane</a>-tree; a genus of the polyandria order, belonging to the monoeia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">Species</a>. 1. The orientalis, oriental <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> eastern plane-tree, 'rifes with a very straight smooth branching stem, to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height. It has palmated leaves, five or eight inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and as much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, divided into five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> segments, having the side ones cut into two smaller, green above, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> underneath; and long pendulous pedunculi, each sustaining several round heads of clove-sitting very small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>; succeeded by numerous downy seeds, collected into round, rough, hard balls. It is a native of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and many parts of the east, and grows in great plenty in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>. 2. The occidentalis, occidental, or western plane-tree, 'rifes with a straight smooth stem, to a great height, branching widely around; it has lobated leaves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight inches long, and from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten to twelve or fourteen broad, divided into three large lobes; and very small flowers, collected into round heads, succeeded by round, rough, balls of seed. It is a native of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; where it attains an enormous size, and is remarkable for having its stem all of an equal girt for a considerable length: we have an account of some trees being eight or nine yards in circumference, and which when felled afforded 20 loads of wood. The varieties of these two species, are the Spanish or middle plane-tree, having remarkably large leaves of three or five narrower segments; and the maple-leaved plane-tree, having smallest leaves, somewhat lobated into five segments, resembling the mapple-tree <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>. All these elegant trees are of hardy temperature, so as to prosper here in any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and exposure in our open plantations, &c. and are some of the most desirable trees of the deciduous tribe. They were in singular esteem among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> of the east, for their extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and the delightful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> they afforded by their noble foliage. The leaves <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> expand in May, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> off early in autumn; and the flowers appear in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, a little before the leaves, being succeeded by seeds, which in fine seasons frequently <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> here in September. These fine trees have singular merit for all ornamental plantations. Their straight growth, regular branching heads, and the lofty stature they attain, together with the extraordinary breadth of their luxuriant leaves, render them extremely desirable furniture to adorn avenues, lawns, parks, and woods; some disposed in ranges, some as single standards, others in clumps, some in groves, &c. They are most excellent for shade; for it is observable, that no tree is better calculated to defend us from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, by its noble spreading foliage, and to admit the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s rays more freely in winter, on account of the distance of its branches, which is always in proportion to the size of the leaves. They may also be employed in the collection of forest-trees, in woods, to grow up to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, in which they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> also prove advantageous in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. In short, these noble trees claim the esteem of every one concerned in plantations of every kind; but more particularly in extensive works, where they may be so variously disposed as to have a charming effect. The propagation of these trees is by seed, layers, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>. The seeds frequently ripen in these parts, and are also procured from other countries, and may be obtained of the nurserymen or seedmen. The best season for sowing them is autumn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they can. can be then possibly procured. Choose a somewhat shady moist soil; and having dug the ground, and raked it fine, form it into four-feet wide beds, and either scatter the seeds evenly on the surface and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a> them in, or previously with the back of a rake turn the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> off the surface near half an inch deep into the alleys; then sow the seed, and directly, with the rake turned the proper way, draw the earth evenly over the seeds, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a> the surface smooth; many of the plants will rise in spring, and probably may not till the spring following. When they are one or two years old, plant them out in nursery-rows, two or three feet asunder, and about half that distance in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; here to remain till of a proper size for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> transplantation. The method of propagation by layers is very commonly practised in the nurseries, in default of seed, and by which they most readily grow; for which purpose, some stout plants for stools must be planted, which in a year after must be headed <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> near the bottom, that they may throw out many shoots near the ground, convenient for laying; which, in the autumn after they are produced, lay by for slit-laying; and by autumn after, they will be well rooted, and form plants two or three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, so may be separated, and planted in nursery-rows, like the seedlings. —All the sorts will take tolerably by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the strong young shoots; but the platanus occidentalis more freely than the oriental kind. Autumn is the best season: as soon as the leaf falls, choose strong young shoots, and plant them in a moist soil; many of them will grow, and make tolerable plants by next autumn. It should be remarked, that in order to continue the distinction of the varieties more effectually, they should be propagated either by layers or cuttings: for when raised from seed, those of the respective species generally vary.

PLATBAND

Pages 740-740

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>, a border <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, along a wall, or the side of a parterre, frequently edged with box, &c. PLATBAND of a door or window, is used for the lintel, where that is made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, or not much marked.

PLATE

Pages 740-740

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by our sportsmen to express the reward given to the best <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> at our races. The winning a plate is not the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of a few days to the owner of the horse; but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> is to be made for it, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there is any great dependence on the success. A <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> is the least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> that can be allowed to draw the horse's body clear, and to refine his <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> to that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection that is attainable by art. It is first necessary to take an exact view of his body, whether he be low <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>; and it is also necessary to consider whether he be dull and heavy, or brisk and lively, when abroad. If he appear dull and heavy, and there is reason to suppose it is owing to too hard riding, or, as the jockeys express it, to some grease that has been dissolved in hunting, and has not been removed by scouring, then the proper remedy is half an ounce of diapente given in a pint of good sack; this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> at once remove the cause, and revive the creature's spirits. After this, for the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> of the month, he is to be fed with oats, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, and split beans; giving him sometimes the one and sometimes the other, as he likes best; and always leaving some in the locker, that he may feed at leisure when he is left alone. When the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> returns at the feeding-time, whatever is left of this must be removed, and fresh given; by this means the creature will soon become high spirited, wanton, and full of play. Every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> he must be rode out on an airing, and every other day it will be proper to give him a little more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>; but not so much as to make him sweat too much. The beans and oats in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> are to be put into a bag, and beaten till the hulls are all off, and then winnowed clean; and the bread, instead of being chipped in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way, is to have the crust clean cut off. If the horse be in good flesh and spirits when taken up for its month's preparation, the diapente must be omitted; and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> business will be to give him good food, and so much exercise as will keep him in wind, without over-sweating him or tiring his spirits. When he takes larger exercises afterwards, towards the end of the month, it will be proper to have some horses in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to run against him. This will put him upon his mettle, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> them will give him spirits. This, however, is to be cautiously observed, that he has not a bloody <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; given him for ten days or a fortnight before the plate is to be run for; and that the last heat that is given him the day before the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a>, must be in his clothes: this will make him run with greatly more vigour, when stripped for the race, and feeling the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> wind on every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> week, the horse should have the same food, and more exercise. In the last fortnight, he must have dried oats, that have been hulled by beating. After this they are to be wetted in a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of whites of eggs beaten up, and then laid out in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> to dry; and when as dry as before, the horse is to have them. This sort of food is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of digestion, and very good for the creature's wind. The beans in this time should be given more sparingly, and the bread should be made of three parts wheat and one part beans. If he should become coltive under this course, he must then have some ale and whites of eggs beaten together; this will cool him, and keep his body moist. In the last week the malt is to be omitted, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARLEY_WATER">barley-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> given him in its place, every day, till the day before the race: he should have his fill of hay; then he must have it given him more sparingly, that he may have time to digest it; and in the morning of the race day, he must have a toast or two of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> bread soaked in sack, and the same <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> before he is led out to the field. This is an excellent method, because the two extremes of fullness and fasting are at this time to be equally avoided; the one hurting his wind, and the other occasioning faintness that may make him lose. After he has had his food, the litter is to be shook up, and the stable kept quiet, that he may be disturbed by nothing till he is taken out to run.

PLATFORM

Pages 740-747

in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, an elevation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, on which cannon is placed, to fire on the enemy; such are the mounts in the middle of curtains. On the ramparts there is always a platform, where the cannon are mounted. It is made by the heaping up of earth on the rampart, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> by an arrangement of madders, rising insensibly, for the cannon to roll on, either in a casemate, or on attack in the outworks. All Platform, practitioners are agreed, that no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> can be depend- ed on, unless the piece can be placed on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> plat- form; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the platform shakes with the first im- <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> of the powder, the piece must likewise shake, which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> alter its directions and render the shot un- certain. Platform, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, is a row of beams, which support the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on the top of a wall, where the entablature ought to be raised. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> is also used for a kind of terrace, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> smooth open walk at the top of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, from whence a fair prospect may be taken of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a>- jacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Hence an edifice is said to be covered with a platform, when it is flat at top, and has no ridge. Most of the Oriental buildings are thus covered, as were all those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. Platform, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLOP">Orlop</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on the lower deck, abaft the main mast, between it and the cockpit, and round about the main <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, where provision is made for the wounded men in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of ac- tion. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLATINA">Platina</a>, a metallic substance, analogous to the perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, especially to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, as many properties are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to both. Although metals, from their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> utility, have been always diligently searched for, yet this has remained undiscovered till lately; which is a very surprising cir- cumstance, and which seems to prove, that platina is not, like the other metals, scattered in different parts of the world, and in all climates. Platina is found in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and chiefly in those of Santa Fé near <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>, and in the Bail- liwick of Choco in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. This metal was probably known to the workers of these mines <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before it was brought into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>: but as its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is not very fine, and as it is almost intractable, especially by fusion, without addition, they seem to have neglected it, considering it as some refractory mineral or marcasite: some of them, how- ever, had attempted to melt it, and to make toys of it, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>-boxes and other things of that kind; but this must certainly have been by alloying it with other metals, as we shall soon see the impossibility of their doing it otherwise. Nevertheless, this metal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be so neglec- ted, that it was entirely unknown in Europe till <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a> Antonio Ulloa, a Spanish mathematician, who accom- panied the French academicians sent by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of France to Peru to determine the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the earth by measuring a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the meridian, first mention- ed it in the relation of his voyage, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a> in the year 1748: but he says little of it, and repre- sents it as an untractable metallic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which impe- ded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> of gold from the ore when it was in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. This account was not very like- ly to excite the curiosity of chemists concerning a new perfect metal, and a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> so interesting and surpri- sing as they afterwards found it to be. But before that time, that is, in 1741, an English metallurgist, called Wood, who had brought from Ja- maica some specimens of it, which he was informed had come from Carthagena, attended more to it, and made some good chemical trials of it. Since that time, several chemists, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which are M. Scheffer, Vol. VIII. of the Swedish Academy, and Dr <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, have very particularly exami- ned this singular metal, and have published their ex- periments. Dr Lewis has in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> exhausted this matter, in four excellent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> communicated to the Royal Society. Platina was, nevertheless, little known in France till the year 1758, when Mr Morin collected, translated into French, and publish- ed, an account of all that had hitherto been done upon platina, in a work entitled, Platina, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> gold, an eighth metal. This publication excited the curiosity of French chemists, to whom it was a new and interesting ob- ject; but the difficulty of obtaining a matter so dear, prevented all of them from being able to satisfy their desire of examining it. Messrs Macquer and Beaumé were the only persons who made experiments upon it, which they have published amongst the Memoirs of the Academy for the year 1751. About the same time also, Mr Margraaf exami- ned platina, and published a dissertation concern- ing it. These are the only chemists who have examined, at least who published their researches concerning this new metal. But although their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> be small, yet their experiments are so numerous, made with such ac- curacy, and in general so consistent with each other, that, by collecting and comparing them, we may ac- quire a certain and almost as extensive knowledge of platina as of the other metals that have been known from time immemorial. The most general and certain results of the experiments made by the above-men- tioned chemists are the following. Platina, a Spanish word, is a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of plata, which in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signifies silver. It is therefore called by the Spaniards little silver. This name is im- proper; since it resembles silver only in being inde- structible, and very imperfectly in its colour. The name of white gold, given to it by some chemists, is more suitable: for we shall see that it resembles gold more than any one metal resembles any other; and hence we shall chiefly compare it to gold. We do not certainly know the origin and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of platina. We can only assert, that all that we see in masses, or worked into forms, is not pure nor in its natural state; for we are certain that it is unfusible, without addition, by the most violent fire of our furnaces, unless perhaps where the fire is blown up by depoliticated <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, or when precipitated from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> regia, as we shall afterwards see. All the platina that is found in the cabinets of curious persons con- sists of small angular grains, the corners of which are a little rounded. It is mixed with a considerable quantity of small <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> sand, as attractive by mag- nets as the best <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, but insoluble by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, unfusible, and untractable. This sand is perfectly similar to that which is found at St Quay in Bretagne. The grains of platina are also frequently intermixed with par- ticles of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAR">spar</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-QUARTZ">quartz</a>, and sometimes with spangles of gold. Messrs Macquer and Beaumé found a pretty large spangle of gold in the platina examined by them. But these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> matters are quite fo- reign to platina, and are not combined with it; for it contains nothing extraneous excepting a little gold and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, which latter substance it probably receives during the operations for extracting gold from the ores by the means of mercury. These matters may easily be separated from the platina without decomposing it, by washing and by magnets. Some chemists, who know platina only by name, and deny that it is a peculiar metal, have therefore, with great impropriety, advanced, that Mr Margraaf had decomposed it, and had obtained from it gold, iron, and arsenic. The contrary appears from Mr Margraaf's Dissertation. Mr Margraaf only separated the heterogeneous matters which were merely mixed with platina, as other chemists have done; but he is too good a chemist to pretend that he has decomposed it: on the contrary, he does not hesitate to call it a perfect metal, which name is also given to it by all who understand metals. The colour of the grains of platina is metallic, white, livid, not very brilliant, intermediate between the white of silver and the grey of iron. At first view they resemble large filings of iron. They are smooth, and are nearly as hard as iron; they are somewhat ductile; so that some of them may be flattened upon an anvil, while others are bruised into small pieces. The specific gravity of platina is very great, and nearly equal to that of gold. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> it loses only something between an eighteenth and a nineteenth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. The tenacity of the parts of this metal has not been determined, because it cannot be formed into a proper figure to make the experiment. But if this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> is proportionate to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCTILITY">ductility</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of metals, we may presume, that as platina is much harder than gold, its tenacity is also greater, if all the ductility of which it seems susceptible could be given to it by art. Platina is, like pure gold and silver, free from all smell and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. It is unalterable by the combined <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of air and water, and is no more susceptible than the other perfect metals of acquiring rust. Like them also it is indestructible by the most violent and long-continued fire: but the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> which peculiarly distinguishes this metal is its unfusibility by the most intense <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. As fusion is necessary for the application of metals to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, chemists have made their utmost efforts to melt platina. The most violent heat which could be raised in air-furnaces, or by the united action of several large bellows, has been applied repeatedly, and continued a long time, without success. In all these trials, the grains of platina remained unaltered in form and weight, and were only agglutinated to each other, nearly as sand is by exposure to violent heat, but so slightly, that by the smallest effort they were separable. Messrs Macquer and Beaumé exposed platina during five days and five nights to the greatest heat of a glass-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> did only confirm the unfusibility and unalterability of platina by ordinary fires, as it was found to be only a little agglutinated, and its weight to be a little increased; which latter phenomenon has been also observed by Mr Margraaf, and which was undoubtedly owing to the fixed air absorbed by the calcareous of the imperfect metals mixed with it. Lastly, Messrs Macquer and Beaumé, having exposed platina to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of a large <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>-glass, melted a little of it in a minute. It first smoked, then emitted sparks, and those parts of it melted well which were exposed to the centre of the focus. These chemists carefully examined the properties of this platina. According to their memoirs, the melted parts were distinguishable from the others by a brilliancy like that of silver, and by a rounded, shining, polished surface. They were easily flattened upon an anvil, and formed into very thin plates without cracking or splitting; so that these grains seemed to be much more malleable than platina in its natural state. These metals by repeated strokes of the hammer became hard and brittle, as all other metals do, particularly gold and silver; and by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNEALING">annealing</a>, their malleability was restored, as it is also to other metals by the same means. After experiments so certain and well authenticated, we cannot doubt that platina is truly a metal, and even a third metal, as perfect in its kind as gold and silver are in theirs. This proposition will be further confirmed by the other properties of platina. Platina resists as perfectly as gold the action of the vitriolic, marine, or nitrous acids; in a word, of any pure acid, in whatever manner applied. These acids, concentrated or diluted, may be boiled any length of time upon platina without dissolving an atom of it: but a mixture of nitrous and marine acids, aqua regia, the solvent of gold, is also the solvent of platina. Messrs Macquer and Beaumé have observed, that an aqua regia composed of equal parts of the two acids dissolves most of this metal. But, however the aqua regia is made, more of it is required to dissolve platina than gold. These chemists employed a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of aqua regia to dissolve an ounce of platina.
